About the same time Agetas, the general of the Aetolians, having called up the Aetolians in a general levy, plundered the territory of the Acarnanians and proceeded to ravage all of Epirus without hindrance.

Having accomplished this, he returned and dismissed the Aetolians to their cities.

The Acarnanians, making a counter-invasion into the territory of Stratus, were overcome by a panic and returned in disgrace, though without any loss, since the people of Stratus did not dare to pursue them, supposing that their withdrawal was being made to lure them into an ambush.

A case of counter-treachery also occurred at Phanoteus, in the following manner. Alexander, who had been put in charge of Phocis by Philip, organized an operation against the Aetolians through a certain Jason, who happened to have been placed by him in command of the city of Phanoteus.

This Jason sent word to Agetas, the general of the Aetolians, and agreed to hand over to them the citadel at Phanoteus, and concerning this he swore oaths and made a compact.

When the appointed day arrived, Agetas came by night to Phanoteus with his Aetolians, and after hiding the rest at a distance, he stayed back, while selecting a hundred of the fittest men he sent them to the citadel.

Jason, meanwhile, had Alexander ready with soldiers inside the city, and taking the young men in accordance with the oaths, he led them all up into the acropolis.

When Alexander and his men at once burst in upon them, the picked Aetolians were captured; and Agetas, when daylight came and he understood what had happened, led his force back again, having fallen victim to a stratagem not unlike the ones he himself had often employed.

Chapter 97 Philip Secures His Frontier

At about this same time King Philip seized Bylazora, the largest city of Paeonia and very conveniently positioned with respect to the passes leading from Dardania into Macedonia, so that by this stroke he was very nearly freed altogether from his fear of the Dardani.

For it was no longer easy for them to invade Macedonia while Philip controlled the approaches through the city just mentioned.

Having secured this place, he sent Chrysogonus off in haste to muster the upper Macedonians,

while he himself, taking up the men of Bottia and Amphaxitis, came to Edessa. There he waited until the Macedonians under Chrysogonus joined him, then set out with his whole army and arrived at Larisa on the sixth day.

Pressing straight on with a hard night march, he reached Meliteia at dawn, and, setting scaling ladders against the walls, he tried to storm the town.

By the suddenness and surprise of the attack he so terrified the Meliteians that he would easily have taken the town; but because the ladders fell far short of the height required, he was cheated of his attempt.

Chapter 98 Importance of Careful Measurement

It is in failures of this sort that one might most of all blame the commanders.

For if certain men, taking no forethought and never measuring out the walls, cliffs, or other such obstacles by which they intend to make their entry, simply turn up on the spot, unprepared, to capture a city—who would not censure them?

And again, if men who have measured their own side of the matter then hand over the construction of the ladders, and of such devices generally—things that take little labor to make but are put to the proof in a great undertaking—carelessly and to any chance persons, how can it not deserve reproach?

For in operations of this kind it is not possible either to do what is needed or else to suffer nothing serious;

rather, harm follows upon failure in many ways: at the very moment of the action, danger to the bravest of the men, and still greater danger during the withdrawal, once the troops have been treated with contempt.

There are many—indeed very many—examples of such things: one would find that, of those who fail in attempts of this kind, more have perished or been brought to the utmost peril than have come off unharmed.

As for the future, moreover, they unquestionably breed distrust and hatred against themselves, and besides they put everyone on his guard;

for not only those who have suffered, but also those who merely learn of what happened, are thereby in a sense warned to take heed and be on their watch.

For this reason men placed in positions of responsibility should never undertake such schemes lightly.

The method of measuring and of constructing such equipment is easy and reliable, provided it is taken in hand methodically.

For the present, then, I must resume the thread of my narrative; but on this kind of subject I shall, taking up a suitable time and place again in the course of my work, try to show how one might best avoid mistakes in undertakings of this sort.

Chapter 99 Capture of Thebes In Phthiotis

Philip, cheated of that attempt, encamped beside the river Enipeus and gathered up the siege equipment from Larisa and the other cities, which he had had prepared during the winter for the siege;

for the whole purpose of his campaign was to capture the city called Phthiotic Thebes.

This city lies not far from the sea, about three hundred stades distant from Larisa, and is conveniently placed in relation to both Magnesia and Thessaly—commanding in particular, in Magnesia, the territory of the Demetrians, and in Thessaly, that of the Pharsalians and the Pheraeans.

From it, at that very time, while the Aetolians held it and made continual raids, great harm was being done to the Demetrians, the Pharsalians, and the Larisaeans as well;

for they often pushed their forays as far as the plain called Amyric.

For this reason Philip, regarding it as no small matter, made great efforts to take the place by storm.

When a hundred and fifty catapults and twenty-five stone-throwing engines had been assembled, he advanced upon Thebes, and dividing his army into three parts he took up the ground around the city:

with one division he encamped near Scopium, with another near the place called Heliotropium, and the third he posted by the mountain overlooking the city;

the spaces between the camps he fortified, sectioning them off with a trench and a double palisade, and he further secured them with wooden towers, stationing these at intervals of a plethron with a sufficient guard.

Next, after these works, he brought all his equipment together and began to move the engines up against the citadel.

Chapter 100 Thebes Renamed Philippopolis

For the first three days he was unable to push forward any of the works, owing to the brave, even reckless, resistance of the men in the city.

But when, through the unceasing skirmishing and the volleys of missiles, the defenders of the city who fought in the forefront were—some killed, others disabled by wounds—and a brief slackening of the defense followed, the Macedonians then began their mining.

By sheer persistence, although the ground worked against them, they barely reached the wall on the ninth day.

After this, carrying on the work in relays so as to break off neither by day nor by night, in three days they had undermined and shored up with timber two plethra of the wall.

When the props could not bear the weight but gave way, the wall came down before the Macedonians had even set fire to them.

When they had vigorously cleared away the rubble of the collapse and made their preparations for the entry, and were now on the very point of forcing their way in, the Thebans took fright and surrendered the city.

By this success Philip secured the situation in Magnesia and Thessaly and stripped the Aetolians of rich plunder; he also proved to his own forces that he had been right to put Leontius and his associates to death for their earlier deliberate treachery in the siege of the Palaeans.

Having become master of Thebes, he sold its existing inhabitants into slavery, and, settling Macedonians in their place, renamed the city Philippopolis instead of Thebes.

When he had already completed his arrangements at Thebes, envoys came once again to discuss terms—from the Chians, the Rhodians, and the Byzantines, and from King Ptolemy.

Giving them answers much like those he had given before, and declaring that he was not averse to a settlement, he sent them off, telling them to sound out the Aetolians as well.

He himself, however, cared little for a settlement, and held firmly to pursuing the next stages of his designs.

Chapter 101 Philip Hears of Thrasymene

And so, hearing that the light galleys of Scerdilaidas were raiding the waters off Malea and treating every merchant as an enemy, and that he had even broken the treaty by seizing some of Philip's own ships that lay at anchor with them at Leucas,

Philip fitted out twelve decked warships, eight undecked vessels, and thirty light craft known as hemioliae, and sailed through the Euripus, eager to catch the Illyrians and, in general, full of high hopes for his plans regarding the war against the Aetolians—since he still knew nothing of what had taken place in Italy.

For it happened that, at the very time Philip was besieging Thebes, the Romans were being defeated by Hannibal in the battle in Etruria, though the report of these events had not yet reached the Greeks.

Philip arrived too late for the galleys, and so anchored off Cenchreae. He sent away his decked warships with orders to make the voyage around Malea toward Aegium and Patrae, while he had the remaining vessels hauled across the Isthmus and ordered them all to lie at anchor at Lechaeum.

He himself hurried with his friends to Argos to attend the Nemean festival.

He had only just begun watching the gymnastic contest when a courier arrived from Macedonia making it plain that the Romans had lost a great battle and that Hannibal was master of the open country.

For the moment he showed the dispatch to Demetrius of Pharos alone, charging him to keep silent.

Demetrius seized this opening and urged that Philip ought to throw off the war against the Aetolians as quickly as possible and instead hold fast to affairs in Illyria and to a crossing into Italy.

For all of Greece, he said, was already doing Philip's bidding and would continue to do so afterward—the Achaeans out of genuine goodwill, the Aetolians cowed by what had befallen them in the present war—

while Italy and the crossing there, he said, were the beginning of the design for universal dominion, to which no one had a better claim than Philip;

Chapter 102 Philip and the Aetolians Discuss Peace

and now, he said, was the very moment, with the Romans having stumbled. By using such arguments he quickly fired Philip's ambition—naturally enough, I think, given that Philip was a young king who had been successful in his enterprises and was reckoned bold in general, and who, on top of this, sprang from a house that has always, more than any other, somehow aspired to dominion over the whole world.

In any case, Philip, as I have said, at that time disclosed the news brought by the letter to Demetrius alone. Afterward he gathered his friends and opened a debate about coming to terms with the Aetolians.

And since Aratus and his party were not opposed to such a settlement—on the view that they would be making peace as the stronger party in the war—

the king, without even waiting any longer for the ambassadors who were jointly handling the negotiations, at once sent Cleonicus of Naupactus to the Aetolians—

for he found him still lingering, after his release from captivity, awaiting the meeting of the Achaean assembly—while he himself took the ships and the land force from Corinth and came with them to Aegium.

Advancing to Lasion and taking the tower in the Perippia, he pretended he was going to invade Elis, so as not to seem too ready to bring the war to an end.

After this, when Cleonicus had gone back and forth two or three times, and the Aetolians begged that he meet them in conference, Philip consented;

and laying aside all the operations of war, he sent couriers to the allied cities, calling on them to send delegates who would sit in council and take part in the joint discussion about the settlement.

He himself crossed over with his force and encamped near Panormus—a harbor of the Peloponnese lying directly opposite the city of Naupactus—and waited for the delegates of the allies.

During the time in which these delegates were to assemble, he sailed to Zacynthus and on his own authority settled the affairs of the island, and then returned,

Chapter 103 Philip Goes to Naupactus

sailing back again. When the delegates had now gathered, he sent Aratus, Taurion, and some of those who had come along with them to the Aetolians.

They joined the Aetolians, who were assembled in full numbers at Naupactus, and after a brief discussion, seeing how eager they were for a settlement, sailed back to Philip to report on the matter.

The Aetolians, anxious to end the war, sent envoys along with them to Philip, asking him to come to them with his force, so that, with the conference conducted at close hand, affairs might reach a fitting conclusion.

Moved by these appeals, the king sailed across with his force to the place called the Hollows of Naupactus, which is about twenty stades from the city.

There he encamped, enclosed both his ships and his camp with a palisade, and waited for the time of the meeting.

The Aetolians came in full numbers but without their arms, and keeping about two stades away from Philip's camp, sent messages and held discussions about the matters at hand.

At first the king sent out all the delegates who had come from the allies, instructing them to propose peace to the Aetolians on these terms: that both sides keep what they now held.

The Aetolians readily accepted this, and from then on there was a continuous exchange of messages between them about the particulars. Most of these I shall pass over, since they contain nothing worth recording,

but I shall make mention of the exhortation of Agelaus of Naupactus, which he delivered at the first meeting before both

Chapter 104 The Cloud in the West

the king and the allies present. He said that the best thing of all would be for the Greeks never to make war on one another, but to be deeply grateful to the gods if, all speaking with one voice and joining hands like men fording a river, they might be able to beat off the assaults of the barbarians and so preserve themselves and their cities.

But if that was altogether impossible, then at least for the present he asked them to be of one mind and on their guard, foreseeing the weight of the armaments and the magnitude of the war now massing in the west.

For it was plain, he said, to anyone who paid even moderate attention to public affairs that, whether the Carthaginians defeated the Romans or the Romans the Carthaginians in the war, it was in no way likely that the victors would rest content with dominion over the Italians and the Sicilians; rather, they would come and extend their designs and their forces farther than they ought. He therefore asked them all to be on guard against the crisis,

and above all Philip.

And the way to guard against it, he said, was for Philip to abandon the aim of crushing the Greeks and making them easy prey for those who attacked them, and instead to take thought for them as he would for his own person, and in general to look after all parts of Greece as belonging and akin to himself.

For if he handled affairs in this way, the Greeks would be well disposed toward him and steadfast allies in his enterprises, while those outside Greece would be less inclined to plot against his power, dismayed by the loyalty of the Greeks toward him.

And if he longed for action, he urged him to look to the west and to fix his attention on the wars now raging in Italy, so that, biding his time prudently as one who waits in reserve, he might at the right moment make his bid for dominion over the whole world.

And the present moment, he said, was not unsuited to such a hope.

He urged Philip to put off his quarrels and wars with the Greeks to times of peace, and to make this his chief concern: to keep the power, whenever he wished, both to make peace and to make war with them—

because, if he once allowed the clouds now appearing from the west to settle upon the regions of Greece, he greatly feared that the truces and wars and, in a word, all the games we now play against one another would be so utterly struck from the hands of us all

that we should pray to the gods to grant us this very power: to make war and to make peace with one another whenever we wished, and in general to be masters of the disputes among ourselves.

Chapter 105 The Peace is Ratified

By speaking in this way, Agelaus spurred all the allies toward a settlement, and Philip most of all, since he used arguments well suited to the inclination that had already been prepared in him by the urgings of Demetrius.

And so, having reached a mutual understanding among themselves on the particular terms and having ratified the settlement, they parted, each carrying back to his own homeland peace in place of war.

All these things happened in the third year of the 140th Olympiad — I mean the battle of the Romans in Etruria, that of Antiochus over Coele-Syria, and besides these the settlement between the Achaeans and Philip on the one side and the Aetolians on the other.

This moment in time, and this single deliberation, were the first to weave together the Greek and the Italian affairs, and the Libyan ones as well.

For from now on neither Philip nor the leading statesmen of the Greeks made their wars and their settlements with one another by reference to affairs within Greece; instead they were all already fixing their gaze on the situation in Italy.

Before long the same thing happened to the islanders and the inhabitants of Asia as well.

For those who were dissatisfied with Philip, and some of those who were at odds with Attalus, no longer leaned toward Antiochus and Ptolemy, nor toward the south and the east, but from this time on looked toward the west; and some sent embassies to the Carthaginians, others to the Romans.

In the same way the Romans too sent embassies to the Greeks, fearing Philip's audacity and taking care that he should not join in attacking them amid the crisis that then surrounded them.

Now that I have, I think, shown clearly — in keeping with my promise at the outset — when, how, and for what reasons the affairs of Greece became interwoven with those of Italy and Libya,

it remains for me to carry the narrative of Greek affairs forward continuously, down to the time when the Romans were defeated at the battle of Cannae, the point at which I brought the account of Italian affairs to its climax; and there I will close this book as well, bringing it level with the events already described.

Chapter 106 Greece At the End of the Social War

As soon as the Achaeans had laid the war aside, they chose Timoxenus as their general and withdrew to their own customs and ordinary pursuits.

Together with the Achaeans, the other cities throughout the Peloponnese likewise set about recovering their private livelihoods, tending their land, and reviving their ancestral sacrifices, festivals, and the other religious observances established among each people.

For these things had all but fallen into oblivion among most of them, owing to the unbroken succession of the wars that had gone before.

Indeed I do not know how it has always somehow come about that the Peloponnesians, who of all men are by nature the most suited to a gentle and civilized life, have in earlier times enjoyed it least of all; rather, as Euripides puts it, they were always "men sold to toil and never at rest from the spear."

This, it seems to me, they suffer with good reason: for being all of them by nature fond of leadership and of freedom, they fight one another continually, never willing to yield the first place.

The Athenians, on the other hand, had been released from their fears of Macedonia and now believed they held their freedom securely.

Taking Eurycleidas and Micion as their leading men, they took no part whatever in the rest of Greek affairs, but, following the policy and the impulses of these statesmen, poured out their flattery upon all the kings, and most of all upon Ptolemy.

They submitted to every kind of decree and proclamation, paying little heed to what was fitting, because of the poor judgment of their leaders.

Chapter 107 Revolt in Egypt

As for Ptolemy, immediately after these events he found himself drawn into a war with the Egyptians.

For the aforesaid king, by arming the Egyptians for the war against Antiochus, had taken a decision adequate for the moment but mistaken as to the future.

Emboldened by their success at Raphia, they were no longer willing to submit to orders, but began looking for a leader and a figurehead, on the grounds that they were capable of defending themselves. And this is just what they did, not long afterward.

Antiochus, after making great preparations during the winter, then crossed the Taurus when the following summer came, and, having made a compact of joint action with King Attalus, set about the war against Achaeus.

The Aetolians at first were pleased with the settlement that had been reached with the Achaeans, since the war had not gone according to their expectations — which is also why they chose as their general Agelaus of Naupactus, who was thought to have contributed most to the settlement —

but after no time at all they grew dissatisfied and reproached Agelaus, on the grounds that he had cut off all their opportunities for profit from abroad and their hopes for the future, since the peace had been made not with certain particular states but with all the Greeks.

The aforesaid man, however, bearing up under this unreasonable resentment and blame, held their impulses in check; and so they were forced to restrain themselves, against their nature.

Chapter 108 Philip's Preparations

King Philip, after the settlement, was conveyed back by sea to Macedonia, where he found that Scerdilaïdas — on the pretext of money still owed to him, the same pretext on which he had broken the treaty by seizing the vessels near Leucas — had now plundered a town of Pelagonia called Pissaeum,

had brought over cities of Dassaretis, some by fear and some by promises — Antipatria, Chrysondyon, and Gertous — and had overrun much of the part of Macedonia bordering on these places as well.

He at once set out with his army, eager to recover the cities that had revolted,

and in general resolved to make war on Scerdilaïdas, considering it absolutely essential to put the situation in Illyria in order with a view both to his other designs and, above all, to his crossing into Italy.

For Demetrius kept fanning this hope and this design in the king so constantly that Philip even dreamed of these things in his sleep and was wholly absorbed in such projects.

Demetrius did this not for Philip's sake — to him he assigned perhaps only a third share in the matter — but rather out of his own hostility toward the Romans, and most of all for his own sake and his private hopes.

For he was convinced that only in this way could he recover his dominion in Pharos.

In any case, Philip took the field and recovered the cities mentioned above, and captured besides Creonion and Gerous in Dassaretis; Enchelanae, Cerax, Sation, and Boii around Lake Lychnidus; Bantia in the territory of the Calicoeni; and, among the people called the Pisantini, Orgessus.

Having accomplished this, he dismissed his forces to their winter quarters. This was the winter during which Hannibal, having ravaged the most renowned regions of Italy, was about to make his winter quarters near Gerunium in Daunia.

The Romans at that time appointed as their generals Gaius Terentius and Lucius Aemilius.

Chapter 109 Philip Prepares to Invade Italy

During the winter, Philip reflected that his plans would require ships and a force to serve at sea—though not for fighting a naval battle.

He could never have hoped to be capable of that, of fighting the Romans at sea; what he needed instead was a fleet that could ferry soldiers, cross quickly to whatever point he intended, and appear before the enemy unexpectedly.

Concluding, therefore, that the Illyrian style of shipbuilding was best suited to these purposes, he set about constructing a hundred light galleys—being almost the first of the Macedonian kings to do so.

Once these were ready, he assembled his forces at the beginning of summer, and after giving the Macedonians a little practice at the oars he put out to sea.

It was at this same time that Antiochus crossed the Taurus, while Philip, sailing through the Euripus and around Cape Malea, came to the region of Cephallenia and Leucas. There he came to anchor and waited anxiously, busily seeking news of the Roman fleet.

Learning that it lay at anchor off Lilybaeum, he took heart and put to sea, advancing on his course toward Apollonia.

Chapter 110 Philip Withdraws to Cephallenia

As he was already drawing near the area of the river Aous, which flows past the city of the Apolloniates, a panic broke out among his crews much like those that occur in armies on land.

Some of the galleys sailing at the rear of the fleet, which had put in at the island called Sason—lying at the entrance to the Ionian channel—came to Philip by night reporting that certain ships sailing from the Strait had anchored there alongside them,

and that these men reported leaving behind at Rhegium some Roman quinqueremes bound for Apollonia and for Scerdilaidas.

Philip, supposing that the fleet was all but upon him, was seized with fear; he hastily weighed anchor and gave the order to sail back the way he had come.

Making his withdrawal and return voyage in complete disorder, he reached Cephallenia on the second day, sailing continuously day and night.

Recovering a little of his confidence, he stayed there, creating the impression that he had turned back for some operations in the Peloponnese.

As it happened, the whole alarm about him proved to be false.

For Scerdilaidas, hearing that during the winter Philip was building a considerable number of galleys, and expecting him to come by sea, had sent messages to the Romans explaining this and asking for help;

and the Romans had dispatched a squadron of ten ships from their fleet off Lilybaeum—this being the very squadron that had been sighted near Rhegium.

Had Philip not fled from it in such groundless terror, that would have been the very moment when he could best have accomplished his aims in Illyria, since the Romans were occupied with all their plans and preparations against Hannibal and the battle at Cannae; and in all likelihood he would also have captured the ships.

As it was, thrown into confusion by the report, he made his way back to Macedonia—without harm, but without honor.

Chapter 111 The Gauls In Asia

At about this same time something happened involving Prusias that deserves to be recorded.

The Gauls whom King Attalus had brought over from Europe for the war against Achaeus, because of their reputation for bravery, had parted from that king on account of the suspicions just mentioned, and were ravaging the cities along the Hellespont with great wanton violence, until at last they even set about besieging the people of Ilium.

In these circumstances a noble action was performed by the inhabitants of Alexandria in the Troad as well.

For they sent out Themistes with four thousand men, raised the siege of Ilium, and drove the Gauls out of the whole Troad by cutting off their supplies and frustrating their designs.

The Gauls then seized the place called Arisba in the territory of Abydos, and from there went on plotting against and making war on the cities founded in that region.

Against them Prusias marched out with an army, and in a pitched battle he destroyed the men in hand-to-hand fighting during the engagement itself, slaughtered nearly all their children and women in their camp, and let his soldiers who had done the fighting plunder the baggage.

By this action he freed the cities of the Hellespont from great fear and danger, and he left behind a fine example to later generations, warning the barbarians of Europe not to take crossing into Asia lightly.

Such, then, was the state of affairs in Greece and Asia. In Italy, after the battle of Cannae had been fought, most of the country went over to the Carthaginians, as I have shown in the earlier parts of this work.

At this point in time I shall break off my narrative, since I have now covered the events in Asia and Greece that fell within the 140th Olympiad.

In the book that follows, after briefly recalling the introductory matters laid out here, I shall return, in accordance with the promise made at the outset, to the account of the Roman constitution.

Book VI

Chapter 1 Preface: Political Constitutions

Having halted our narrative at this point, we will set out our account of the Roman constitution,

in which we will show, step by step, that the distinctive character of their political system contributed more than anything else not only to their winning dominion over the Italians and Sicilians, but also to their further acquisition of rule over the Iberians and the Celts,

and finally, after they had defeated the Carthaginians in war, to their conceiving the design of universal empire.

But when, in working through the Greek affairs that took place during the same Olympiad, we reach this period, then at last, taking it up as a subject in its own right, we will give our account of the Roman constitution itself,

believing that an exposition of it is not only suited to the design of our history, but also contributes greatly to the reform and construction of constitutions, for those men who are eager to learn and active in public affairs.

And one might well be puzzled as to what the reason is that the Romans, although they have now mastered the whole world and possess a superiority many times greater than before, could nevertheless neither man so many ships nor put to sea with such great fleets as they once did.

The causes of this difficulty, however, will be clearly understandable when we come to the exposition of their constitution.

Concerning this matter—which touches on certain aspects of their military affairs—we have already spoken at greater length earlier, in our discussion of the constitution.

This (the college of the Salii) is, as we have stated in our discussion of the constitution, one of the three colleges through which the most distinguished sacrifices to the gods are performed at Rome.

Chapter 2

I am well aware, then, that some will be puzzled as to why, abandoning the unbroken thread of our narrative—the joining and adding on of events—we have deferred to this point our account of the constitution mentioned above.

But that this part too was, from the very beginning, one of the necessary components of my whole design, I think I have made clear in many passages,

and most of all in the foundation and preliminary statement of my history, where I said that this was the finest, and at the same time the most useful, feature of my undertaking for readers of the work: to know and learn how, and by what kind of constitution, nearly the whole inhabited world was overcome and fell under the single rule of the Romans in not even a full fifty-three years—something that is found never to have happened before.

This being settled, I could see no time more suitable than the present for pausing to examine and test what is going to be said about the constitution.

For just as those who form private judgments about whether men are worthless or worthy, whenever they genuinely set out to test them, base their inquiry not on the untroubled ease of ordinary life, but on the reversals of misfortune and the successes of good fortune,

regarding this alone as the true touchstone of a complete man—the ability to bear the total reversals of fortune with greatness of soul and nobility—in just the same way one must examine a constitution as well.

For this reason, since I could see no sharper or greater change in our times than the one that befell the Romans, I have reserved for this moment my account of the matters mentioned above; and one may grasp the magnitude of that change from what follows.

What both engages the mind and brings benefit to lovers of learning is precisely this: the study of causes, and the choice of the better course in each case.

And in every undertaking we must regard the structure of the constitution as the greatest cause both of success and of its opposite;

for from it, as from a fountainhead, all the conceptions and undertakings of any enterprise not only spring, but also reach their completion.

For only genuine impossibility offers no excuse to those who fail; and impossibility belongs to the realm of falsehood alone.

Chapter 3 Classification of Constitutions

As for the Greek states, which have often risen to greatness and have often undergone a complete reversal into the opposite condition, it proves easy both to give an account of their past and to pronounce upon their future;

for it is easy to report what is already known, and easy to predict the future by conjecturing from what has already happened.

But concerning the Roman state it is not at all easy either to describe the present situation, owing to the complexity of its constitution, or to foretell the future, owing to our ignorance of the distinctive features of their past, both in public and in private life.

For this reason it calls for no ordinary attention and study, if one is to gain a clear and comprehensive view of its distinctive features.

Now it happens that most of those who wish to instruct us authoritatively on such matters speak of three kinds of constitutions, of which they call one kingship, another aristocracy, and the third democracy.

But it seems to me that one might quite reasonably raise a question against them: whether they propose these to us as the only constitutions, or, by Zeus, as the best.

For on both counts they seem to me to be mistaken. For it is clear that we must regard as best the constitution composed of all the features just mentioned;

and of this we have had proof not in theory only but in practice, since Lycurgus was the first to construct the Spartan constitution on this principle.

Nor again must we accept these as the only forms: for we have already seen certain monarchical and tyrannical governments which, though they differ as much as possible from kingship, nevertheless seem to bear some resemblance to it;

and it is on this ground that all monarchs falsely lay claim to, and make use of, the title of king as far as they are able.

And again, there have been many oligarchic governments that seem to bear some resemblance to aristocratic ones, from which, one might almost say, they differ as widely as possible.

And the same argument applies also to—

Chapter 4 The Rotation of Polities

—democracy. That what I say is true is evident from the following.

For surely not every monarchy is to be called a kingship outright, but only the one that is accepted by willing subjects and is governed more by reason than by fear and force;

nor, again, is every oligarchy to be considered an aristocracy, but only the one that is directed, through deliberate selection, by the most just and most prudent men.

In the same way, we should not call it a democracy where the whole multitude has the power to do

whatever it happens to wish and resolve. Rather, where it is the ancestral and customary practice to revere the gods, to care for one's parents, to respect one's elders, and to obey the laws—in such communities, when the will of the majority prevails, this is what we must call a democracy. And so we must say that there are six kinds of constitutions:

the three that everyone harps on, which have just been mentioned, and three more akin to these—I mean monarchy, oligarchy, and mob-rule.

First, then, monarchy arises spontaneously and by nature; and following upon it, and born from it through development and correction, comes kingship.

But when this changes into the evil naturally allied to it—I mean into tyranny—then in turn, from the dissolution of these, aristocracy springs up.

And again, when this has by its nature degenerated into oligarchy, and the people in their anger have avenged the injustices of their leaders, democracy is born.

And from the insolence and lawlessness of this, in turn, mob-rule is brought to fulfillment in the course of time.

One could grasp most clearly that these things are truly as I have just described by attending to the natural beginnings, origins, and changes of each.

For only the person who has understood how each of them comes into being could also understand the growth, the prime, and the transformation of each, and its end—when, how, and where it will come round again.

And I have supposed that this method of exposition will suit the Roman constitution best of all, because from the very beginning it took on both its formation and its growth in accordance with nature.

Chapter 5 The Origin of Constitutions

The natural process by which the various forms of government transform into one another is perhaps analyzed more precisely by Plato and certain other philosophers. But their account is intricate and developed at great length, so that few can follow it.

For this reason I will try to set out, in summary form, only as much of the matter as I judge relevant to a practical history and to the understanding of ordinary people.

And if my general overview should seem to leave anything out, the detailed discussion in what follows will make ample amends for whatever is left unresolved here.

What, then, are the origins I mean, and from what source do I say constitutions first arise?

Whenever floods, outbreaks of plague, crop failures, or other causes of this kind bring about a destruction of the human race—such as tradition tells us has happened before, and as reason tells us will happen again and again—

then, with all customs and skills perishing together, and when in the course of time a multitude of people grows up once more from the survivors, as though from seeds,

then, as with the other animals, these people too gather together. And it is only natural that they too, in their natural weakness, should band together with their own kind. In such circumstances it is inevitable that the one who excels in bodily strength and boldness of spirit should lead and rule the rest,

just as we observe among the other species of animals that lack reason—and this we must regard as the truest work of nature, since among them we see, by common agreement, the strongest taking the lead: I mean bulls, boars, cocks, and creatures like them.

It is likely, then, that in the beginning the lives of human beings were of this sort: gathering together like animals and following the most vigorous and powerful among them, whose authority was bounded only by strength, and whose rule one might call monarchy.

But when, with the passage of time, a sense of fellowship and familiarity grew up within these communities, this became the seed of kingship; and then, for the first time, the idea of what is noble and just—and likewise of their opposites—arose among human beings.

Chapter 6 Origin of Morality and Rule

The manner in which these notions begin and come into being is as follows.

All creatures are driven by nature toward sexual union, and the result is the begetting of children. Now whenever one of these offspring, having been raised and reached maturity, shows no gratitude and offers no protection to those who reared him, but instead sets about insulting or harming them,

it is clear that those who are present and who have witnessed the care and hardship the parents devoted to the rearing and nurturing of their children will likely be displeased and offended.

For since the human race differs from the other animals in that it alone possesses intelligence and reason, it is plain that men, unlike the other animals, will not let such a difference of conduct pass unnoticed.

Rather, they will take note of what happens and feel displeasure at it, since they look ahead to the future and reason that the same thing could befall any one of them.

So too, when someone who has received help or rescue from another in time of danger shows no gratitude to his preserver, but even attempts to harm him, it is clear that those who know of it will likely be displeased and offended with such a man—sympathizing with their fellow and imagining the same thing happening to themselves.

From all this there arises in each person some notion of the meaning and theory of duty, which is the beginning and end of justice.

Likewise, again, when someone stands out as the defender of all in times of danger and holds his ground against the assaults of the fiercest beasts, it is likely that such a man will receive marks of the people's goodwill and esteem, while the man who acts otherwise will meet with their condemnation and disapproval.

From this, in turn, it is reasonable that there should arise among the many some understanding of the base and the noble, and of the difference between them—the one to be pursued and imitated for the benefit it brings, the other to be shunned.

And when the leader, the man who holds the greatest power, consistently lends his support to these popular judgments, and so appears to his subjects to be one who allots to each man what he deserves,

then they no longer submit out of fear of force, but rather give their willing consent of mind, supporting his rule and helping to preserve it—even when he has grown quite old—rallying with one accord to his defense and fighting against any who plot against his sovereignty.

And in this way, without anyone noticing, a king emerges from a monarch, once reason has taken over leadership from raw spirit and strength.

Chapter 7 How Kingship Turns into Tyranny

This is the first conception of the noble and the just—and of their opposites—to arise naturally among human beings; this is the beginning and origin of genuine kingship.

For the people preserve the rule not only of such men themselves, but of their descendants as well, persuaded that those born from and raised by men of this kind will share their principles.

But if at some point they become displeased with the descendants, from then on they make their choice of rulers and kings no longer according to bodily and spirited strength, but according to differences of judgment and reason, having learned from actual experience the difference between the two.

In ancient times, then, those who had once been chosen and granted this office grew old in their kingships, fortifying strong positions and building walls and acquiring territory—partly for security, and partly for an abundant supply of necessities for their subjects.

And while they devoted themselves to these things, they remained free of all slander and envy, because they made no great distinctions in their dress, food, or drink, but lived much like everyone else, always sharing the same way of life as the common people.

But once they began to inherit their positions by succession and birth, and found the means of security already prepared for them, along with more than enough for their sustenance,

then, following their appetites because of this abundance, they came to think that their rulers ought to have distinctive clothing, distinctive and elaborate indulgences and provisions at the table, and unchallenged access to the sexual favors and embraces even of those they had no right to.

These things gave rise in some cases to envy and offense, in others to a blaze of hatred and bitter anger, so that the kingship turned into a tyranny. The first step toward its dissolution was taken, and a conspiracy began to form against the rulers—

a conspiracy that arose not from the worst men, but from the noblest, most high-minded, and most courageous, because such men are least

Chapter 8 Degeneration of Constitutions

able to endure the abuses of those in power. And when the people gained leaders and joined forces with them against the rulers for the reasons already described, the form of kingship and monarchy was utterly destroyed, while aristocracy in turn took its beginning and origin.

For the people, as though repaying an immediate debt of gratitude to those who had overthrown the monarchs, employed them as their leaders and entrusted their affairs to them.

At first these men gladly accepted the charge and put nothing ahead of the common good, managing every matter—both private and public—with care and watchfulness on behalf of the people.

But when their children inherited this same authority from their fathers—having no experience of hardship, no experience at all of civic equality and freedom of speech, and having been raised from the start amid their fathers' power and privileges—

some of them turned to greed and unjust love of money, others to drunkenness and the insatiable feasting that goes with it, and others to the violation of women and the abduction of boys. And so they transformed the aristocracy into an oligarchy,

and they quickly stirred up among the people feelings much like those just described. For this reason the end of their downfall turned out to be much like the misfortune that befell the tyrants.

Chapter 9 How Democracy Arises and Degenerates

Whenever someone, perceiving the envy and hatred that the citizens feel toward their rulers, then grows bold enough to say or do something against those in power, he finds the whole populace ready and eager to lend its support.

After that, having killed some of these rulers and driven others into exile, they do not dare to set up a king again, since they still dread the injustice of those who ruled before; nor do they have the confidence to entrust public affairs to a number of men, with the recent example of that folly fresh before their eyes.

So, with the only untainted hope left to them being the one that rests on themselves, they turn to this course: they transform the constitution from an oligarchy into a democracy, and take the management of public affairs and the public trust into their own hands.

As long as any survive who experienced the dominance and arbitrary power of the few, they are content with the present order and prize equality of speech and freedom of speech above all else.

But once a new generation has come along, and the democracy has been handed down to the children of children, then, through familiarity, they no longer set such great store by equality and freedom of speech, and they seek to have more than the common people. The ones who fall into this most of all are those who excel in wealth.

So when they set their hearts on holding office and cannot attain it through their own efforts and their own merit, they squander their fortunes, enticing and corrupting the masses in every possible way.

By this means, once they have made the many greedy for bribes and accustomed to feeding on them through their own foolish craving for honor, then once again democracy is dissolved, and it gives way to force and mob rule.

For the populace, grown used to feeding on the property of others and resting its hopes of livelihood on its neighbors' goods, as soon as it finds a leader of high ambition and daring—one shut out from the honors of public life by poverty—then brings about rule by the mob.

And then, banding together, it commits massacres, banishments, and redistributions of land, until, reduced to utter savagery, it once more finds a master and a monarch.

This is the cycle of constitutions,

this is the ordering set by nature, according to which forms of government change, pass from one to another, and come round again to where they began.

A man who has clearly grasped this may perhaps be mistaken about the timing when he speaks of the future of a constitution, but as for the point of growth or of decay that each has reached, or the direction in which it will change, he will rarely be wrong, provided he makes his judgment free of anger or envy.

And indeed it is in the case of the Roman constitution above all that, by this method of inquiry, we may come to understand its formation, its growth, its peak, and likewise the change into the opposite that will follow from these.

For if any constitution ever did, this one too, as I said just now, having had its formation and growth from the beginning according to nature, will also undergo its change into the contrary according to nature.

This will be possible to observe through what is to be said hereafter.

Chapter 10 Lycurgus

For now I will make a brief mention of the legislation of Lycurgus, since this discussion is not foreign to my purpose.

For that man, having taken to heart that each of the developments described above comes about necessarily and naturally, and having reasoned that every form of constitution that is simple and rests on a single kind of power is precarious—because it is quickly perverted into the vice that is its own and that follows it by nature—

just as rust is the dissolvent inborn in iron, and woodworms and grubs in timber, by which, even if they escape all external harm, they are destroyed by the very things that grow up within them—

in the same way, in each of the constitutions there is by nature bred and attendant some particular vice: in kingship, the form called monarchic (despotism); in aristocracy, that of oligarchy;

and in democracy, the bestial and mob-ruled form. Into these it is impossible that all the aforementioned constitutions should not, in the course of time, undergo their transformations, according to the argument just given.

Foreseeing this, Lycurgus did not make his constitution simple or of a single type, but gathered together all at once the virtues and distinctive features of the best forms of government,

so that no element, growing beyond what was due, should be perverted into the vices that are akin to it; but rather, with the power of each held in check by the others, none of them should incline anywhere or weigh down too far, but the constitution should remain in equilibrium and balanced for a long time, like a ship beating against the wind—

the kingship being prevented from growing arrogant by fear of the people, since the people too had been given a sufficient share in the constitution;

and the people in turn not daring to despise the kings, out of fear of the elders, who, having been chosen by selection on the grounds of merit, were always bound to attach themselves to what was just,

so that the party of those at a disadvantage, by holding fast to established custom, always became greater and weightier through the leaning and support of the elders.

And so, having framed it in this way, he preserved freedom for the Lacedaemonians for the longest time of any people we know of.

He, then, foreseeing by a process of reasoning the source and manner in which each thing naturally comes about, established the aforesaid constitution without harm.

The Romans, on the other hand, have arrived at the same end—the order of their own state—

yet not through reasoning, but through many struggles and difficulties, ever choosing the better course from the very knowledge gained amid reverses; and thus they came to the same end as Lycurgus, the finest political system of any in our time.

Chapter 11 The Roman Constitution

The Roman state, reckoning from the crossing of Xerxes into Greece and for thirty years after that period, was continually being refined in its particular features, and it reached its finest and most perfect form in the era of the war with Hannibal—the point from which I made this digression.

Therefore, now that I have given the account of how it came to be put together, I will try to make clear what its character was in those years, in which the Romans, defeated at the battle of Cannae, came to grief in their affairs as a whole.

I am well aware that to those who actually live under this constitution I shall seem to give a somewhat incomplete account of it, since I leave out some of the particular details.

For, knowing every part of it and having had experience of all of it through having been brought up from childhood in its customs and laws, they will not be impressed by what is said, but will look for what has been left out;

and they will not suppose that the writer has deliberately omitted the small distinctions, but rather that he has passed over in silence the origins and the essential workings of things out of ignorance.

The things I do say, they would not have admired as being trifling and incidental; but the things I omit, they single out as essential, wishing to appear to know more than the historians themselves.

But a good critic ought not to judge writers by what they leave out, but by what they say;

and if he catches any falsehood in this, he should recognize that those omissions too are due to ignorance, but if everything that is said is true, he should grant that those things too are passed over by deliberate judgment and not out of ignorance.

So much, then, let this be said by me against those who criticize historians more out of rivalry than out of fairness.

Every matter, when examined in its proper context, receives sound approval and sound criticism alike; but if that context shifts and the matter is judged against other circumstances, then what historians have often said in the best and truest way may appear not merely undesirable, but not even tolerable.

There were, then, three elements that controlled the constitution, all of which I have mentioned before; and everything was so fairly and fittingly ordered and administered, part by part, through these elements, that no one—not even a native—could ever say with certainty whether the constitution as a whole was aristocratic, democratic, or monarchic.

And this was a natural thing to experience. For whenever we fixed our attention on the power of the consuls, it appeared to be completely monarchic and kingly; whenever on that of the senate, aristocratic again; and indeed, if one looked at the power of the people, it seemed clearly to be democratic.

As for which of these forms held sway over each of the respective parts of the constitution—that, both then and still now (with a few exceptions), is as follows.

Chapter 11a

They give this town the name Pallantium, after their mother-city in Arcadia; but, as some relate—among them Polybius of Megalopolis—it was named after a youth named Pallas who died there. This Pallas was the son of Heracles and of Launa, the daughter of Evander; and his grandfather on his mother's side, having heaped up a tomb for him on the hill, named the place Pallantium after the youth.

For they did not think it enough, as Polybius of Megalopolis did, merely to say this much: "I am persuaded that Rome was founded in the second year of the seventh Olympiad," nor to leave the proof untested, resting on a single tablet—one and only one—kept in the custody of the high priests.

Aristodemus of Elis and his school relate that it was from the twenty-seventh Olympiad onward that the athletes—those, that is, who were victors—began to be recorded; for before that no one was recorded, since earlier generations had neglected to do so. In the twenty-eighth Olympiad Coroebus of Elis, winning the stadion race, was the first to be recorded; and that Olympiad was ranked as the first from which the Greeks count their dates. Polybius relates the same things as Aristodemus does. And among the Romans,

as Polybius says in his sixth book, women are forbidden to drink wine, but they drink what is called passum. This is made from the dried grape (raisin), and when drunk it is much like the sweet Aegosthenian wine and the Cretan; and so they use it to relieve pressing thirst. It is impossible for a woman to escape notice if she has drunk wine. For in the first place a woman has no authority over wine; and besides this, she is obliged to kiss her own kinsmen and those of her husband, down to the children of cousins, and to do this every day, whenever she first sees them. And then, since it is uncertain whom she will meet, she is on her guard; for if she has merely tasted it, there is no further need of accusation.

He also founded the city of Ostia on the Tiber.

Polybius, in his sixth book. [Stephanus of Byzantium, under "Ostia."]

Lucius, the son of Demaratus the Corinthian, set out for Rome trusting in himself and in his wealth, convinced that he would hold a position second to none in public life because of certain advantages, and having a wife who was useful both in other respects and as a naturally gifted partner in every practical undertaking. On arriving in Rome and obtaining citizenship, he at once adapted himself to winning the king's favor. And quickly, both through his wealth and through his natural cleverness, and most of all through his upbringing from childhood, he attached himself to the man in power and won great acceptance and trust with him. As time went on he came to such a degree of being received that he jointly managed and handled with Marcius the affairs of the kingdom. In this position, proving a benefit to everyone, working together with those in need and helping to secure for them whatever was useful, and at the same time using the resources of his living generously, suitably, and at the right moment on each occasion, he stored up gratitude in many quarters and worked goodwill in all, and won a reputation for nobility of character—and he attained the kingship as well.

He acted as a prudent and sensible man does, in recognizing, as Hesiod says, "how much the half is greater than the whole."

For learning to be truthful toward the gods is a foundation for truth toward one another.

For in most human enterprises, those who have acquired things are well suited to preserving them, while those who have received them ready-made are well suited to losing them.

Chapter 11b

All the works of virtue ought to be practiced from childhood by those who train themselves well, and above all courage.

Olcium, a city of Etruria: Polybius in his sixth book. [Stephanus of Byzantium, under "Olcium."]

Chapter 12 The Consuls

The consuls, before leading out the legions, while present in Rome, are masters of all public business.

For all the other magistrates, except the tribunes, are subordinate to them and obey them; and it is the consuls who introduce the embassies to the senate.

In addition to what has been said, they refer the urgent matters of deliberation to the senate, and they carry out the entire handling of its decrees.

Moreover, as for everything that must be accomplished through the people in matters bearing on public affairs, it falls to them to see to it and to convene the assemblies, to bring in the decrees, and to give effect to whatever the majority decides.

And indeed, with regard to the preparation for war and the whole management of operations in the field, they hold what is virtually absolute authority.

For it is within their power to impose on the allies whatever they think fit, to appoint the military tribunes, to enroll the soldiers, and to select those who are suitable.

Besides what has been mentioned, they are empowered to punish anyone they wish among those under their command while in the field.

They also have the authority to spend as much of the public funds as they propose, with a quaestor accompanying them who readily carries out every order.

So that one might reasonably say, whenever one looks at this portion, that the constitution is simply monarchic and kingly.

And if any of these powers, or of those that are about to be described, should undergo some change, either at the present time or after some interval, this would have no bearing on the statement we are now making.

Chapter 13 The Senate

The Senate, first of all, has control of the treasury. It manages all incoming revenue and likewise all expenditure.

For the quaestors cannot make any disbursement for the various departments of the state without a decree of the Senate, the one exception being payments to the consuls.

And of the single greatest and most comprehensive item of expenditure by far—the one the censors make every five years for the repair and construction of public works—the Senate has control, and it is through the Senate that the censors are granted these funds.

Likewise, whatever crimes committed in Italy call for a public inquiry—I mean such things as treason, conspiracy, poisoning, and assassination—are the concern of the Senate. And beyond this,

if any private individual or any community in Italy needs a dispute settled, or, by Zeus, a penalty imposed, or assistance, or protection, all of these matters are the Senate's responsibility.

So too, if it is necessary to dispatch an embassy to any people outside Italy—whether to reconcile parties, or to issue an appeal, or, by Zeus, to give commands, or to receive a surrender, or to declare war—the Senate is the body that sees to it.

In the same way, when embassies arrive in Rome, how each is to be dealt with and what answer is to be given them is all handled through the Senate. None of the matters just described involves the people at all.

For these reasons, in turn, anyone visiting Rome while no consul is present would conclude that the constitution is a complete aristocracy.

This is precisely what many of the Greeks, and likewise many of the kings, have come to believe, since nearly all the business they have is settled by the Senate.

Chapter 14 The People

Given all this, one might reasonably ask what role at all is left to the people in the constitution,

when the Senate has authority over the particular matters we have described, and—most important of all—manages the whole of revenue and expenditure; and when the consuls, again, have unchecked power over the preparations for war and unchecked authority in the field.

Nevertheless, a role is left to the people too, and a most weighty one at that.

For the people alone in the constitution have control of honor and of punishment—the very things by which, and by which alone, dynasties and constitutions, and in short the whole life of humankind, are held together.

For where this distinction either goes unrecognized or, when recognized, is badly managed, nothing within the existing order can be administered rationally. For how could it be, when the good are held in equal honor with the wicked?

The people, then, sit in judgment, often in cases involving a fine, whenever the penalty for the offense is substantial—especially against those who have held high office. And in capital cases the people are the sole judges.

In this connection there is a practice among them that deserves praise and commemoration. For those tried on a capital charge, once they are being condemned, are permitted by their custom to depart openly, even if a single one of the tribes whose votes ratify the verdict has not yet cast its vote—thereby sentencing themselves to voluntary exile.

Safety is guaranteed to such exiles in the cities of the Neapolitans and the Praenestines, and also of the Tiburtines, and in the other cities with which Rome has sworn agreements.

Furthermore, it is the people who confer offices on those who deserve them—the finest prize for merit that a constitution can offer.

The people also have authority over the approval of laws and, most important of all, they deliberate on questions of peace and war.

And in matters of alliance, the cessation of hostilities, and treaties, it is the people who confirm each of these and make them binding—or do the opposite.

So that here again one might reasonably say that the people hold the greatest share of power and that the constitution is a democracy.

Chapter 15 Division of Political Power At Rome

We have now described how the powers of the state are divided among each of its elements. We will now explain how each of these parts can, when it chooses, work against the others or cooperate with them.

The consul, once he has obtained the authority described above and set out with his army, appears to be supreme in carrying through the tasks before him,

yet he still needs the people and the Senate, and without them he is incapable of bringing his operations to completion.

For it is clear that supplies must be sent continually to the legions; but without the Senate's consent neither grain, nor clothing, nor pay can be provided to them,

so that a commander's designs come to nothing whenever the Senate chooses to be obstructive and to thwart his work.

Moreover, whether the plans and intentions of the generals are carried out or not rests with the Senate: for it has the authority, when the year has elapsed, either to send out another general to succeed the present one or to keep the current commander in place.

The Senate also has the power to magnify and play up the successes of the commanders, and, conversely, to dim and diminish them.

For the celebrations they call "triumphs"—through which the generals bring the achievements they have accomplished vividly before the eyes of the citizens—the generals cannot conduct with proper splendor, and sometimes cannot hold at all, unless the Senate gives its approval and grants the funds for them.

As for the people, the commanders are absolutely bound to keep them in view, even if they happen to be far from home; for it is the people, as I said above, who make agreements and treaties valid or void.

But most important of all, when commanders lay down their office they must render before the people an accounting of what they have done.

And so it is in no way safe for the generals to disregard the goodwill of either the Senate or the people.

Chapter 16 The Senate Controlled by the People

The Senate, again, for all the great power it possesses, is in the first place obliged in public affairs to defer to the multitude and to keep the people in view.

And it cannot carry out the most far-reaching and serious inquiries into, and corrections of, crimes against the state—those for which the penalty is death—unless the people also ratify what has been resolved.

The same holds for matters that touch the Senate itself: if anyone introduces a law that strips away some part of the authority the Senate holds by custom, or abolishes its privileges of precedence and its honors, or, by Zeus, makes inroads on the senators' personal property, in all such cases it is the people who have the power to enact it or not.

And the decisive point: if a single one of the tribunes interposes his veto, the Senate not only cannot bring any of its deliberations to a conclusion, but cannot even convene or assemble at all—

and the tribunes are always bound to do what the people decide and above all to keep the people's wishes in view. For all these reasons, then, the Senate fears the multitude and pays heed to the people.

Chapter 17 Powers of the Senate

In the same way, the people in their turn are dependent on the Senate and must take its wishes into account, both as a community and as individuals.

For a great many contracts—too many to enumerate easily—are let out by the censors throughout the whole of Italy for the upkeep and construction of public works; and besides these there is the collection of revenue from numerous rivers, harbors, gardens, mines, and tracts of land—in short, from everything that has come under Roman control.

All these matters are handled by the general public, so that, broadly speaking, virtually everyone is bound up in these purchases and in the business that arises from them.

For some buy the contracts directly from the censors; others go into partnership with them; others stand surety for the buyers; and still others pledge their own property to the treasury on their behalf.

Over all of these affairs the Senate holds final authority: it can grant an extension of time, and in the event of an accident it can lighten the burden, and if some genuine impossibility arises it can release a man from his contract entirely.

And there are many ways in which the Senate can do great harm, or again great good, to those who manage public business, since the referral of all such matters comes before it.

But most important of all is that the judges in most trials—both public and private—involving charges of any magnitude are drawn from its members.

For this reason all citizens, being bound to its goodwill and fearful of the uncertainty of when they may need its help, are wary of obstructing or actively opposing the Senate's wishes.

In the same way they are reluctant to work against the undertakings of the consuls, because, individually and collectively, all of them fall under the consuls' authority when on campaign in the field.

Chapter 18 Interdependency Brings Strength

Since each of the parts has this power both to injure and to assist the others, their combination is suited to meet every circumstance, so that it is impossible to find a better constitutional structure than this.

For whenever some common danger from outside presses upon them and forces them to think and act together, the power of the state becomes so great and so remarkable

that nothing whatever that is needful is left undone—since everyone, all at once, competes in devising plans for whatever has arisen—and no decision once made falls behind the right moment, as each man works, both publicly and privately, toward completing the task at hand.

As a result, the distinctive character of this constitution makes it irresistible and able to achieve anything it has resolved upon.

And again, whenever they are freed from external fears and settle into the prosperity and abundance that come from their successes, enjoying their good fortune and growing corrupted by flattery and idleness, and turn toward violence and arrogance—as commonly happens—

it is then above all that the constitution can be seen supplying the remedy out of its own resources.

For whenever one of the parts swells up, becomes contentious, and gains more power than it should, it is clear that—since, as just explained, none of them is self-sufficient, and the purpose of each can be counteracted and hindered by the others—none of the parts swells up or grows overbearing.

For all of them remain within their proper bounds: some are checked in their impulse, while others are restrained from the outset by fear of interference from those beside them.

The dictator differs from the consuls in this respect: whereas each of the two consuls is attended by twelve axes, the dictator has twenty-four; and whereas the consuls in many things need the Senate's cooperation to carry out their plans, the dictator is a commander with absolute power, and the moment he is appointed, all the magistracies in Rome are immediately dissolved, except for the tribunes of the people. But we shall give a more precise account of these matters elsewhere.

Chapter 19 On the Roman Army

VI. On the Roman Military

After they have elected the consuls, they next appoint military tribunes—fourteen from those who have already completed five years of service, and another ten in addition from those who have completed ten.

As for the rest, a man must by law complete ten campaigns in the cavalry, or sixteen in the infantry, within the forty-six years counted from his coming of age—except for those whose property is assessed below four hundred drachmas.

All of these latter are assigned to naval service. But if the pressure of circumstances ever demands it, the infantry are obliged to serve twenty annual campaigns.

No one is permitted to hold any civil office until he has completed ten annual campaigns.

When the holders of the consular office are about to carry out the enrollment of soldiers, they announce in advance before the people the day on which all Romans of military age must present themselves. They do this every year.

When the day has come and the men eligible for service have arrived in Rome, and then assembled on the Capitol, the junior military tribunes divide themselves up—

in whatever order they have been appointed by the people or by the commanders—into four groups, because the basic, primary division of their forces is made into four legions.

They assigned the first four appointed to the legion called the first, the next three to the second, the four following these to the third, and the last three to the fourth.

Of the senior tribunes, they place the first two in the first legion, the next three in the second, the two following them in the third, and the last three in the fourth.

Chapter 20 Allocation of Men to the Legions

Once the division and assignment of the tribunes has been made in such a way that all the legions have an equal number of officers,

they then take their seats apart from one another, legion by legion, and draw lots for the tribes one at a time, summoning each tribe as its lot comes up.

From this tribe they pick out four of the young men who are reasonably well matched in age and physical condition.

When these have been brought forward, the officers of the first legion take the first pick, those of the second legion second, those of the third third, and those of the fourth last.

When another four are brought forward, the officers of the second legion take the first choice, and so on in order, with those of the first legion choosing last.

After this, when yet another four are brought forward, the officers of the third legion choose first, and those of the second last.

With the selection proceeding by rotation in this regular way throughout, it turns out that the men taken into each of the legions are closely comparable.

When they have selected the prescribed number—which is sometimes four thousand two hundred infantry for each legion, and at other times five thousand, whenever some greater danger looms before them—

after this they pass the cavalry. In the old days they used to review the cavalry afterward, following the four thousand two hundred infantry, but now they do it beforehand, since the selection of the cavalry is now made by the censor on the basis of wealth; and they enroll three hundred for each legion.

Chapter 21 Fourfold Division of the Legionaries

Once the enrollment has been completed in the manner described above, the tribunes responsible in each legion assemble the men who have been selected, and from the whole body they pick out the single most suitable man.

They then make him swear that he will obey his commanders and carry out their orders to the best of his ability.

All the rest then come forward one by one and take the oath, simply declaring that they will do everything just as the first man did.

At the same time, the holders of the consular office send instructions to the magistrates of the allied cities of Italy from which they wish allied troops to serve alongside them, specifying the number required, the day, and the place at which the selected men must present themselves.

The cities then carry out a selection and administer an oath very much like the one described, appoint a commander and a paymaster, and send the men out.

Meanwhile the tribunes at Rome, after administering the oath, assign each legion a day and a place at which the men must present themselves without their arms, and for the time being they dismiss them.

When the men arrive on the appointed day, the tribunes sort them out: the youngest and poorest they assign to the skirmishers (velites), those next in age to the so-called hastati, those in the prime of life to the principes, and the oldest to the triarii.

For these are the divisions among the Romans, and this is their number, distinguished by name, by age, and also by their equipment, in each legion.

They divide them in such a way that the oldest, called triarii, number six hundred, the principes twelve hundred, the hastati an equal number to these, and the remainder, the youngest, form the skirmishers.

If the legion numbers more than four thousand, they make the division proportionally, except for the triarii, whose number always stays the same.

Chapter 22 Arms of the Youngest Roman Soldiers

The youngest soldiers are ordered to carry a sword, javelins, and a round shield (parma).

The parma is sturdily constructed and large enough to give protection: being circular in shape, it has a diameter of three feet.

The soldier is also equipped with a plain helmet, and at times he puts a wolf's skin or something of the kind over it, both for protection and as a mark of recognition, so that the officers of each unit can see whether he is fighting bravely in the front of danger or not.

The shaft of the javelin is about two cubits in length and roughly a finger thick, while its head is a span long and beaten out so fine and sharpened to such a degree that it inevitably bends on the first impact, so that the enemy cannot throw it back; otherwise the weapon would be of use to both sides alike.

Chapter 23 Arms of the Other Soldiers

To the second group by age, those called the hastati, they gave orders to carry the full panoply.

The Roman panoply consists, first, of a long shield (scutum)—its curved surface two and a half feet wide, four feet long, and the thickness at the rim a palm's breadth.

It is made of two layers of board fastened together with bull's-hide glue, then covered on the outer surface first with canvas and after that with calf's skin.

Around the rim, both on the upper and the lower parts, it has an iron edging, by which it is protected against the downward strokes of swords and against wear from being rested on the ground.

An iron boss is also fitted to it, which wards off the heavier blows of stones, pikes, and violent missiles generally.

Along with the shield they carry a sword, which is worn on the right thigh and is called the Spanish sword (gladius hispaniensis).

It has an excellent point and can deliver a powerful cut with either edge, because its blade is strong and rigid.

In addition to these they carry two heavy javelins (pila), a bronze helmet, and a greave. Of the pila, some are thick and some thin.

Of the heavier ones, the round-shafted have a diameter of a palm's breadth, and the square-shafted measure a palm on each side. The thin ones resemble moderate-sized hunting spears, and they are carried together with the ones already mentioned.

The wooden shaft of all of them is about three cubits long, and to each is fitted a barbed iron head equal in length to the wood.

They make the attachment and fitting of the head so secure that they sink it into the wood as far as the middle and fasten it down with a row of clasps, so that in use the iron breaks sooner than the binding works loose, even though at the base, where it joins the wood, its thickness is three half-fingers; so great is the care they take over the fastening.

On top of all this they adorn themselves with a circlet of feathers and three upright purple or black plumes,

about a cubit high; with these set on the crown of the head along with the rest of the arms, the man appears twice his own height, and his look is handsome and terrifying to the enemy.

Most of the soldiers, after adding a bronze plate a span square—which they place in front of the chest and call a heart-guard (pectorale)—have their full equipment complete.

But those rated above ten thousand drachmas (asses) wear, instead of the heart-guard and along with the rest, a coat of chain mail (lorica).
