The principes and triarii are armed in the same manner, except that instead of the heavy javelins the triarii carry thrusting spears (hastae).

Chapter 24 Officers of Infantry and Cavalry

From each of the groups mentioned above, except the youngest, they elect ten company commanders (centurions) by merit. After these they make a second selection of ten more.

All of these they have titled company commanders, and the first one chosen is also a member of the council of war. These officers in turn select an equal number of rear-rank men (optiones).

Next, together with the company commanders, they divide each age-group into ten parts, except for the skirmishers, and they assign to each part of the selected men two leaders and two rear-rank officers.

The skirmishers they distribute in equal proportion across all the parts according to their total number.

Each part they called a unit (ordo), a company (manipulus), and a vexillum, and the leaders they called centurions and ordinum ductores.

These officers in turn select for each company, from the men left over, two of the most vigorous and noble men to serve as standard-bearers.

They reasonably appoint two leaders for each unit: since it is uncertain both what a leader may do and what may happen to him, and since the demands of war allow no excuse for delay, they never want a company to be left without a leader and commander.

When both are present, the first one chosen commands the right part of the company, and the second leads the men on the left of the unit; when one is absent, the one who remains commands them all.

They want their company commanders to be not so much bold and fond of danger as men fit to command—steady, and rather of a deep spirit—men who will not rush into attack or open the battle on their own initiative, but who, when overpowered and hard pressed, will hold their ground and die in defense of their post.

Chapter 25 Officers and Armour of the Cavalry

In much the same way they divide the cavalry into ten squadrons, and from each they choose three squadron-commanders; these three then each appoint a rear-rank officer of their own.

The first commander chosen leads the squadron, while the other two hold the rank of decade-leaders, though all alike are called decurions. If the first commander is not present, the second again takes over command of the squadron.

The equipment of the cavalry is now very similar to that of the Greeks, but in early times it was not so. First, they wore no breastplates,

but went into action in loincloths only. The result was that they were ready and efficient at dismounting and quickly springing back up onto their horses, but at close fighting they were in a precarious position, since they faced danger unprotected.

Their spears, too, were useless to them in two respects. First, because they made them thin and pliant, they could neither take aim at a chosen target, nor, before they could plant the spearhead into anything, keep the spears from being shaken by the very motion of the horses, so that most of them snapped.

Besides this, since they made the spears without butt-spikes, they had the use of only the first stroke delivered with the spearhead; after that, once the shafts had broken, the weapons were of no further use and worthless to them. As for the shield, they carried one made of ox-hide,

resembling the round, knobbed sacrificial cakes that are set out for offerings. These shields were of no use for charging, since they had no firmness, and once the rains had stripped off their leather and rotted them, they were awkward to handle even before, and now became completely so. Therefore, since this equipment proved unsatisfactory,

they quickly adopted the Greek pattern of arms.

With these weapons, the first stroke of the spearhead is at once both well-aimed and effective, since by its construction the spear is steady and stable; and likewise the reversed use of the butt-spike is firm and forceful.

The same holds for the shields: both for warding off blows and for thrusting, they have a use that is solid and dependable.

Once the Romans recognized these advantages, they quickly imitated them; for the Romans, if any people ever were, are good at taking over the customs of others and emulating what is better.

Chapter 26 The Roman Camp

Having made this division of the men, and having given these orders concerning their arms, the military tribunes then dismissed the men to their homes. When the day arrived

on which they had all sworn to assemble likewise at the place appointed by the consuls —

for each consul as a rule assigns a separate place for his own legions, since to each is given a portion of the allies and two of the Roman legions —

all those enrolled present themselves without fail, since no other excuse is allowed to those who have taken the oath, except an adverse omen from the birds or sheer impossibility.

When the allies too have assembled together with the Romans, the organization and management of them is carried out by the officers appointed by the consuls, who are called praefects and are twelve in number.

These officers first select for the consuls, out of all the allies who have come, those cavalry and infantry best suited for genuine service; they are called the extraordinarii, which, translated, means "the picked men."

The total number of the allies is, in infantry, generally about equal to the Roman legions, and in cavalry three times as many.

From these they take for the picked corps roughly a third of the cavalry and a fifth of the infantry. The rest they divide into two parts,

and call the one the right wing and the other the left wing.

When these arrangements had been made, the military tribunes took over both the Romans and the allies and made camp. They have a single, simple principle governing their camps, which they apply at every occasion and in every place.

For this reason it seems to me fitting on the present occasion to try, as far as words can do so, to bring my hearers to an understanding of how the Romans handle their forces on the march, in the camp, and in the line of battle.

For who is so indifferent to fine and serious achievements that he would not be willing to take a little extra care over such matters, about which, once he has heard them, he will be knowledgeable in one of the things genuinely worth describing and knowing?

Chapter 27 How the Camp is Constructed

The manner of their encampment is as follows. Of whatever site has been chosen for the camp, the general's tent takes the spot best suited at once for a commanding view and for issuing orders. Once the standard has been set up

where they intend to pitch it, a square area is measured off around the standard, such that all its sides lie a hundred feet from the standard, and the enclosed area amounts to four plethra.

Along one face and side of this figure — whichever appears most convenient for watering and foraging — the Roman legions are laid out in the following way.

Since there are six military tribunes in each legion, as stated just now, and since there are always two Roman legions with each of the consuls, it is clear that twelve tribunes must serve with each consul.

They place the tents of these tribunes all on one straight line, which is parallel to the chosen side of the square and stands fifty feet away from it, so that there may be room for the horses, along with the pack animals and the rest of the tribunes' baggage.

The tents are pitched turned the opposite way, facing toward the outer side — which is henceforth to be understood and called by us, once and for all, the front of the whole layout.

The tribunes' tents stand at equal distances from one another, spread over enough ground that they extend along the entire width of the Roman legions.

Chapter 28 Division by Roads and Squares

When a further hundred feet have been measured off toward the front, along the whole line of tents, then, starting from the straight line that bounds this width — which runs parallel to the tribunes' tents — they begin from this line to lay out the quarters of the legions, proceeding in the following manner.

Bisecting the aforementioned line, they quarter the cavalry of each legion at this point at right angles to the line, facing one another, fifty feet apart, making the dividing line the middle of the interval.

The arrangement of the tents for the cavalry and for the infantry is much the same, for the whole figure, both of the maniple and of the troops, comes out square.

This square faces onto the passageways, and has a fixed length along the passageway — namely a hundred feet — and for the most part they try to make the depth equal too, except in the case of the allies.

But when they employ larger legions, they add proportionally to both the length and the depth.

Chapter 29 Placement of Triarii, Principes, and Hastati

The cavalry encampment lies opposite the middle of the tribunes' tents, set crosswise—like a transverse street—to the line just described and to the area in front of the tribunes.

In fact, the layout of all the passages comes out very much like a system of streets, since on either side the units are quartered lengthwise—companies on one side, squadrons on the other.

Behind the cavalry just mentioned, they place the triarii of both legions, one company opposite each squadron, in a corresponding arrangement: the two blocks touch each other, but face in opposite directions, away from the cavalry.

They make the depth of each company only half its length, because the triarii are generally only half as numerous as the other divisions.

For this reason, although the numbers of men are often unequal, all the divisions still come out equal in length, thanks to the difference in depth.

Next, leaving a space of fifty feet on each side of these, they station the principes facing the triarii.

Since the principes also face toward the spaces just mentioned, two more streets are formed here as well. These begin from the same line and have their entrances, like those of the cavalry, from the hundred-foot space in front of the tribunes, and they run down to the side of the rampart opposite the tribunes—the side we agreed from the outset to treat as the front of the whole layout.

Behind the principes, again facing the opposite way and with their blocks touching, they station the hastati.

Since all these divisions have ten companies each, according to the original division, all the streets turn out equal in length, and their ends along the front side of the rampart line up evenly. Toward that side they also turn the last companies as they pitch their camp.

Chapter 30 Placement of the Allies

Again leaving a space of fifty feet beyond the hastati, they station the allied cavalry facing them, beginning from the same line and ending at the same one.

The number of the allies, as I said above, is in infantry roughly equal to that of the Roman legions—less by the picked troops set apart—while in cavalry it is double, after a third of these too has been drawn off for the picked troops.

Therefore, increasing the depth of the allied cavalry's quarters proportionally in the camp layout, they try to make them equal in length to the Roman legions.

Once all five passages have been completed, they next set out the companies of the allied infantry facing the opposite way—just as with the cavalry—increasing their depth proportionally, and facing toward the rampart and toward each of the two side faces.

In each company, the officers take the first tents at either end. While arranging them in the manner described, they also set the sixth squadron in each division fifty feet apart from the fifth, and likewise the infantry companies,

so that here too another passage is formed across the middle of the camp, crosswise to the streets and parallel to the tribunes' tents. They call this the fifth passage, because it runs alongside the fifth units.

Chapter 31 The Camp Market-Place

The space that lies behind, beneath the tribunes' tents, and that borders the headquarters enclosure on either side, serves on one side as the market-place, and on the other for the quartermaster's office and the supplies that go with it.

Starting from the last of the tribunes' tents on each side and running back—arranged in a kind of L-shape relative to those tents—the choicest of the picked cavalry, together with some of those serving as volunteers out of personal regard for the consuls, all encamp along the side faces of the rampart, some facing the quartermaster's stores, the others, on the opposite side, facing the market-place.

As a rule, it falls to these men not only to camp close to the consuls, but also, on the march and in other duties, to attend upon and constantly remain about the consul and the quartermaster.

Facing them, looking toward the rampart, are the infantry who perform a service like that of the cavalry just described.

Next to these a passage is left, a hundred feet wide, parallel to the tribunes' tents, extending along the far side of the market-place, headquarters, and quartermaster's office, past all the parts of the rampart already mentioned.

Along the upper side of this passage the picked cavalry of the allies encamp, facing the market-place, the headquarters, and the quartermaster's office at once.

Down the middle of these cavalry quarters, in line with the headquarters enclosure itself, a passage fifty feet wide is left, leading to the rear side of the camp and lying at right angles to the broad avenue just mentioned.

Facing these cavalry, again, are placed the picked infantry of the allies, looking toward the rampart and the rear face of the whole camp.

The space left empty on either side of these, along the side faces, is given over to foreign troops and to such allies as join at the moment.

With everything arranged in this way, the overall shape of the camp comes out as a square with equal sides, while in its detailed layout—both the street plan and the rest of the organization—it has an arrangement much like a city.

They keep the rampart two hundred feet away from the tents along every face. This empty space affords them many valuable advantages.

It is well and conveniently suited for the marching in and out of the units: each body makes its exit into this space along its own street, so that they do not all converge onto one road, overturning and trampling one another.

They also bring into it the livestock driven in and the plunder taken from the enemy, and keep them safely through the nights.

Most important of all, in night attacks neither fire nor missile reaches them, except for a very few; and even these do almost no harm, because of the great distance and the screen of the tents.

Chapter 32 Arrangements When There Are More Men

Once the number of both infantry and cavalry is fixed for each plan—whether they make each legion four thousand or five thousand strong—and likewise the depth, length, and number of the companies are fixed, along with the dimensions of the passages and avenues, and everything else as well,

it becomes possible for anyone willing to attend closely to work out both the size of the site and the entire perimeter of the camp. But if at any time the number of allies grows larger,

whether of those who set out with the army from the start or of those who join at the moment,

for those who join at the moment they fill, besides the places already described, the spaces beside the headquarters as well, contracting the market-place and quartermaster's office into whatever space the need urgently demands.

For those who march out with the army from the start, if their number is fairly large, they add one extra street on each side of the Roman legions, alongside the side faces, in addition to those already there.

When all four legions and both consuls are gathered into a single camp, one need only imagine two armies, encamped according to the scheme just described, joined together facing opposite ways and meeting at the quarters of each legion's picked troops—the men we placed facing the rear face of the whole camp.

In that case the shape becomes oblong, the site twice as large, and the perimeter half as much again.

So whenever both consuls happen to encamp together, they always lay out the camp in this way; but when they camp separately, everything else is the same, except that they place the market-place, quartermaster's office, and headquarters between the two camps.

Chapter 33 Guard Duty and Other Assignments

Once the camp has been laid out, the tribunes gather everyone in it, free and slave alike, and administer an oath to each man individually.

Each swears that he will steal nothing from the camp, and that if he finds anything he will bring it to the tribunes.

From the maniples of principes and hastati in each legion they next assign two maniples to the open square in front of the tribunes' tents.

Since the Romans spend most of the daytime in that area, they are careful to have it constantly watered and kept clean.

Of the remaining eighteen maniples, each tribune receives three by lot, since each legion under this arrangement has three such maniples assigned to each of the six tribunes.

Each of those three maniples in turn performs the following services for its tribune: when the army encamps they pitch his tent and level the ground around it; if any part of his baggage has to be fenced off for protection, they do that as well.

They also provide him with two pickets, each of four men, some stationed in front of the tent and others behind it by the horses.

Since each tribune has three maniples, and each maniple contains more than a hundred men—not counting the triarii and velites, who are exempt from this duty—

and since the duty falls to each maniple only once every four days, the burden is light, while the arrangement gives the tribunes both the service they need and an impressive dignity.

The maniples of triarii are excused from attendance on the tribunes, but each maniple supplies a daily guard to the cavalry squadron quartered just behind it.

These men keep watch in general, but especially over the horses, so that they do not get entangled in their tethers, injure themselves, or break loose and plunge into the rest, throwing the camp into confusion.

Finally, one maniple out of the whole force takes turns each day in mounting guard around the consul, both to protect him from plots and to add splendor to his rank.

Chapter 34 Daily Orders and Watchwords

For digging the ditch and building the rampart, two sides of the camp are assigned to the allies, the sides by which their two wings are quartered, and two to the Romans, one for each legion.

Each side is divided maniple by maniple, and the centurions supervise the work section by section, while two tribunes oversee the entire side.

These same tribunes also direct the rest of the camp's business. They divide themselves into pairs, and each pair takes charge in turn for two months out of the six.

Whichever pair is on duty at the time supervises the operations in the field. The prefects of the allies divide their responsibilities in the same way.

At dawn the cavalry officers and centurions report to the tribunes, and the tribunes in turn go to the consul.

He gives them whatever instructions are needed, the tribunes pass these on to the officers, and the officers then convey them to the troops whenever the occasion requires.

The night watchword is distributed in the following manner.

From each class of troops, cavalry and infantry alike, one man is chosen from the tenth and last maniple, the unit quartered at the end of the street.

This man is excused from guard duty and presents himself each evening at sunset at the tribune's tent, where he receives the watchword written on a tablet; then he withdraws.

Returning to his own maniple, he hands over both tablet and watchword before witnesses to the commander of the next maniple, and that man does the same to the commander beyond him. So it passes from hand to hand until it reaches the first maniples, those nearest the tribunes, and these must return the tablet to the tribunes before dark.

If all the issued tablets are returned, the tribune knows that the watchword has passed through the whole line.

If one is missing, he can tell from the inscription where the failure occurred and immediately investigates, so that the man responsible receives the punishment he deserves.

Chapter 35 Night Watches

Their system for the night watches is as follows. The consul and his tent are guarded by the maniple assigned to that duty.

The tribunes' quarters and the cavalry squadrons are guarded by the men detailed from each maniple in the manner already described.

Each separate unit also posts its own guard from among its own men, while the remaining watches are assigned by the consul.

Usually there are three sentries at the quaestor's tent, and two at the tent of each legate and each member of the council.

The outer perimeter is guarded by the velites, who keep watch along the whole rampart by day, and who also place sentries at the gates, ten at each entrance.

As for the men appointed to the actual watches, the rear-rank officer of each company brings the one assigned to the first watch to the tribune in the evening, one man from each picket.

The tribune gives each of them a small wooden token marked for that watch, and with these they go off to their assigned posts.

The duty of making the rounds belongs to the cavalry. The first squadron commander in each legion must early in the morning order one of his rear-rank men to notify four young troopers of that squadron that they are to patrol.

In the evening that same man informs the commander of the next squadron that the duty passes to him on the following day.

That commander makes the same arrangements for the day after, and so the responsibility continues in rotation.

The four men selected from the first squadron draw lots for the different watches, then go to the tribune and receive written notice of how many watches they must inspect and which they are.

After this, the four take up their position beside the first maniple of the triarii, for the centurion of that maniple is responsible for sounding the bugle for each watch.

Chapter 36

When the time comes, the man on whom the first watch has fallen by lot goes the rounds for that watch, taking some companions with him as witnesses.

He inspects the appointed guards—not only those on the rampart and at the gates, but also those stationed with the individual maniples and cavalry squadrons.

If he finds the men of the watch awake, he takes back their token; if he finds anyone asleep or absent from his post, he calls his companions to witness it and then moves on.

Those assigned to the later watches do the same.

The sounding of the bugle for each watch, so that the patrols and the sentries keep the same reckoning, belongs to the centurions of the first maniple of the triarii, one in each of the two camps, in daily rotation.

At daybreak each patrol brings the collected tokens back to the tribune. If all are returned, the guards are dismissed without accusation.

But if any patrol brings back fewer than the proper number, the missing picket is identified from the mark on the token.

Once the responsible watch is identified, the tribune summons the centurion, who brings forward the men assigned to that guard, and they are confronted with the patrolman.

If the fault clearly lies with the guards, the patrolman is immediately acquitted, since he is required to produce witnesses and did so. But if he failed to do that, the blame falls upon the patrolman himself.

Chapter 37 The Tribunes' Court

When an accusation is brought, the tribunes at once convene a court, and if the accused is convicted he is punished by cudgeling.

The punishment works like this: the tribune takes a cudgel and merely touches the condemned man with it.

At that signal all the men in the camp attack him with clubs and stones, and most of them are killed on the spot inside the camp itself.

Even those who manage to escape are not really saved. How could they be? They cannot return to their own country, and no relative would dare receive such a man into his house. So anyone who falls into this misfortune is completely ruined.

The same penalty applies to the rear-rank officer and to the commander of the cavalry squadron if they fail to give the proper order at the proper time, the former to the patrols and the latter to the commander of the next squadron.

Because this punishment is so severe and unavoidable, the Roman night watches are kept with unfailing strictness.

The soldiers are answerable to the tribunes, and the tribunes to the consuls.

A tribune has authority to fine a man, seize his property as security, or have him flogged; among the allies the prefects have the same powers.

This cudgeling punishment is also inflicted on anyone who steals from the camp, bears false witness, is found guilty in his prime of shameful sexual misconduct, or has been punished three times for the same offense.

These are treated as crimes. But the following are classed as cowardice and military disgrace: falsely reporting brave deeds to the tribunes in order to win honors;

or, if men have been posted in reserve, abandoning the assigned position out of fear; likewise, if in the moment of danger a man throws away any of his weapons through fear.

That is why some men openly choose death at their post, unwilling to leave their station because they dread the punishment awaiting them.

Others, if they have dropped shield, sword, or some other piece of armor in battle, throw themselves recklessly at the enemy, hoping either to recover what they lost or to escape by death the certain shame and the insults of their family.

Chapter 38 Military Punishments and Rewards

If the same offense is committed by a larger body of men—for instance, if whole standards give way and abandon their ground under pressure—then they do not think it right to cudgel or execute them all.

Instead they have found a remedy that is both effective and terrifying. The tribune assembles the legion, brings the offenders into the middle, denounces them bitterly, and then selects by lot five, or eight, or sometimes twenty, always aiming at roughly a tenth of the men who were guilty of cowardice.

Those on whom the lot falls are put to death by cudgeling without mercy; the rest are given barley instead of wheat and are ordered to camp outside the rampart and outside the protection of the camp.

Since all face the same danger from the lottery, and since all alike are made an example of by the disgrace of barley rations, this is the strongest possible way both to inspire terror and to correct the failure that has occurred.

Chapter 39 Military Decorations

The Romans are also excellent at stirring young men to face danger bravely.

Whenever a battle has taken place and some men have distinguished themselves, the consul summons an assembly of the army, brings forward those whom he thinks have done anything notable, and first praises each man for his courage, mentioning any other honorable achievements of his life as well.

After that he grants rewards: to the man who has wounded an enemy, a spear; to the man who has struck him down and stripped him, a cup if he is an infantryman, horse-trappings if he is a cavalryman. In earlier times the spear alone was given.

These rewards are not given for deeds done in a pitched battle or in the capture of a city, but rather in skirmishes and similar situations where there was no strict necessity for a man to expose himself, and he took the risk deliberately and on his own initiative.

To those who are first over the wall in the storming of a city he gives a golden crown.

In the same way, the consul marks with gifts those who have shielded and saved any citizen or ally, and the tribunes require the men who were saved to crown their rescuer, whether willingly or, if necessary, by formal decision.

The man whose life was saved honors his rescuer for the rest of his life as if he were a father, and owes him every duty that a son owes a parent.

Such encouragement stirs not only those who witness it and stand present in the ranks, but also those who remain at home, to rivalry and zeal in the face of danger.

For those who win such rewards enjoy not only glory in the camp and immediate fame at home, but after returning to their own city they also take part in processions with special distinction, since only men honored by their generals for valor may wear these decorations.

They also display the spoils in the most prominent places in their houses, as signs and proofs of their own courage.

With such care given in the camp to rewards and punishments alike, it is no wonder that Roman warfare ends in brilliant and successful results.

An infantryman receives two obols a day in pay, a centurion double that, and a cavalryman a drachma.

The infantry ration is about two-thirds of an Attic medimnus of wheat per month. The cavalry receive seven medimni of barley and two of wheat.

Among the allies, the infantry receive the same amount, while the cavalry receive one and a third medimni of wheat and five of barley.

For the allies this ration is a free grant, but from the Romans the quaestor deducts at a fixed rate the cost of grain, clothing, and any additional weapons they may need, taking it out of their pay.

Chapter 40 The Army On the March

Their method of striking camp and marching is as follows.

At the first trumpet call everyone takes down the tents and packs the baggage; but no one may either strike or raise a tent before the tents of the tribunes and the consul have been dealt with.

At the second signal they load the baggage animals; at the third the first troops must advance and set the whole camp in motion.

In the vanguard they usually place the picked troops; next comes the right wing of the allies, and behind them their baggage animals.

After these follows the first Roman legion, with its own baggage behind it.

Then comes the second legion, followed by its own baggage and by the baggage of the allied wing assigned to the rear, for the left wing of the allies takes the last position in the march.

The cavalry sometimes ride behind their own divisions, and sometimes move alongside the baggage animals, keeping them together and providing them security.

If an attack is expected from the rear, the rest of the order remains much the same, except that the picked allied troops take over the rear instead of the vanguard.

On alternate days the legions and allied wings exchange the leading place, so that all alike share the advantage of reaching water and forage first.

In especially dangerous circumstances they use another order of march, when they are moving over open ground.

They then advance in three parallel columns of hastati, principes, and triarii, placing the baggage of the leading standards in front of all, the baggage of the second line behind the first, and the baggage of the third behind the second, so that baggage and fighting units alternate in succession.

With the column arranged in this way, if danger appears they wheel either to shield-side or spear-side, bring the standards clear of the baggage, and face the enemy.

Thus in a short time and by a single movement the heavy infantry take up a battle line, except when the hastati also need to wheel farther into position.

The baggage train and all those accompanying it then remain drawn up behind the line, in the proper place for safety in the coming danger.

Chapter 41 Making Camp

Whenever, on the march, they are nearing the place where they will camp, a tribune and those centurions previously selected for the task ride ahead.

After surveying the whole site, they first determine where the consul's tent must stand, in accordance with the system already described, and on which side of the praetorium the legions are to be quartered.

Once these points are settled, they measure out the enclosure of the praetorium, then the straight line on which the tribunes' tents are to stand, and next the parallel line from which the legions' quarters begin.

In the same way they mark out the lines on the other sides of the consul's tent, following the arrangement that I explained in detail earlier.

This is done quickly, because the measurements are easy and all the intervals are fixed beforehand and familiar.

Then they set up standards: first one where the consul's tent is to stand, second one on the chosen side of the enclosure, a third in the middle of the line where the tribunes camp, and a fourth beside the line from which the legions' quarters begin. These are scarlet standards,

except for the consul's, which is white. On the other sides they sometimes plant plain spears and sometimes standards of other colors.

After this they measure out the streets and set up spears along each street.

So when the troops approach and the site of the camp comes clearly into view, everyone can immediately recognize the entire layout by taking the consul's standard as the point of reference.

Since each man already knows exactly on which street and in what place on that street he is to pitch his tent, because every unit always occupies the same position in camp, the whole thing resembles an army entering its own city.

There too, once people have passed the gates and turned off, each goes straight to his own lodging without hesitation, because he knows generally and in detail where his quarters lie within the city.

Exactly the same thing happens in Roman camps.

Chapter 42 Roman Camps Designed for Facility and Familiarity

In this matter the Romans seem to me to follow a course directly opposite to that of the Greeks, because their main aim in encampment is ease and regularity.

The Greeks think the chief consideration in choosing a camp is to take advantage of the natural strength of the site, partly because they wish to avoid the labor of digging ditches, and partly because they believe artificial defenses are not equal to the protections supplied by nature.

As a result, they are forced to alter the whole shape of the camp to fit the ground, and also to rearrange its parts in irregular and shifting ways.

That means neither the individual soldier nor the individual unit has any fixed and familiar place in camp.

The Romans, by contrast, choose to endure the labor of digging and the other hardships that go with fortification for the sake of convenience and familiarity, so that they may always have one and the same camp arrangement.

These, then, are the principal features of the Roman system of camps, and especially of the way they lay them out.

Chapter 43 The Roman Republic Compared with Others

Nearly all historians have handed down to us a reputation for excellence in the constitutions of Sparta, Crete, Mantinea, and Carthage; some have also mentioned those of Athens and Thebes.

I will set the latter aside, since I am convinced that the constitutions of Athens and Thebes do not deserve much discussion: they neither grew in an orderly way, nor remained long at their height, nor passed through their changes with moderation.

Rather, like some sudden stroke of fortune, they flashed into brilliance for a moment and then, just when they still seemed to be flourishing and likely to prosper, they encountered the opposite turn.

The Thebans won their reputation among the Greeks by taking advantage of Spartan blindness and the hatred of Sparta's allies, through the excellence of one man, or at most two, who understood the situation.

That it was not the structure of the Theban constitution but the quality of its leaders that caused those successes was soon made evident by events themselves.

For the rise, the high point, and the fall of Theban power all plainly coincided with the lives of Epaminondas and Pelopidas.

So we must conclude that it was not the constitution but those men that caused the good fortune Thebes enjoyed at that time.

Chapter 44 The Athenian Constitution

A similar judgment must be made about the Athenian constitution.

It may have enjoyed more frequent intervals of excellence, but its most brilliant flowering came with the ability of Themistocles, and it quickly experienced the opposite turn because of its unstable nature.

For the Athenian people are always like a ship without a master.

When fear at sea or the pressure of a storm makes the passengers unite and heed the helmsman, they perform admirably.

But once confidence returns and they begin to despise their officers and quarrel among themselves because they no longer all want the same thing,

with some insisting on sailing on, others pressing the helmsman to put in to harbor, some letting out the sheets while others pull them in and shout to furl the sails, then the spectacle is disgraceful to outside observers because of their conflict and disorder, and dangerous to all who share in the voyage.

So it often happens that after escaping the open sea and the fiercest storms, they wreck themselves in harbor and close to land.

The same thing has repeatedly happened to the Athenian constitution. More than once it has survived the gravest and most frightening dangers through the courage of the people and their leaders, only to stumble recklessly in times of security and ease.

So there is no need to say more about either Athens or Thebes, since in both states the whole system is managed by a mob acting on its own impulse—the one distinguished by sharpness and volatility, the other trained in violence and fury.

Chapter 45 The Cretan Constitution Compared to the Spartan

Turning now to the Cretan constitution, two questions deserve attention: first, how the most learned ancient writers—Ephorus, Xenophon, Callisthenes, and Plato—could say that it was the same as the Spartan constitution; and second, how they could also praise it.

In my judgment neither claim is true.

This can be seen from the following points, and I will first explain how unlike the Spartan system it is. The first distinctive feature of the Spartan constitution, they say, concerns landed property: no citizen may possess more than another, but all must have an equal share in the civic land.

The second concerns wealth in money. Because money-making is held in disrepute there, the rivalry that grows out of having more or less is removed altogether from the state.

A third point is that among the Spartans the kings hold office for life by hereditary right, while the men called elders likewise hold office for life, and through them and with them the whole state is governed.

Chapter 46 Greed Among the Cretans

Among the Cretans the exact opposite of all this is true. Their laws allow them, as the saying goes, to acquire land without limit according to their power.

Money is held in such honor among them that possessing it seems not only necessary but positively admirable.

Indeed greed for base profit and grasping selfishness are so deeply rooted there that among the Cretans alone of all mankind no gain of any kind is considered shameful.

Their magistracies too are annual, and their system has a democratic character.

So I often wonder how anyone could describe constitutions that are so opposite in nature as if they were kindred and closely related.

And besides overlooking differences of such importance, these writers go on at length in praise of Lycurgus, saying that he alone among lawgivers grasped the essential point.

For since there are two things by which every constitution is preserved—courage against enemies and concord among citizens—they say that by abolishing greed he abolished at the same time all civil strife and faction.

That is why the Spartans, being free from such evils, became the best-governed and most united people in Greece in their relations with one another.

Yet though these same writers can see, by direct comparison, that the Cretans because of their inborn greed are constantly entangled in private and public seditions, murders, and civil wars, they still think this does not affect their argument and boldly say the two constitutions are alike.

Ephorus even uses almost the same language for both systems, so that if someone paid no attention to the proper names, he could hardly tell which constitution was being described.

So much, then, for the ways in which the two differ. I must now explain why the Cretan constitution is neither admirable nor worthy of imitation.

Chapter 47 What Makes a Constitution Good

I think there are two fundamental principles in every constitution, and by these its powers and structure become either desirable or objectionable: customs and laws.

Good customs and laws make men's private lives reverent and self-controlled, and make the public character of the city gentle and just; bad ones do the opposite.

So whenever we see excellent customs and laws among a people, we confidently conclude that the men themselves and their constitution will also be good.

And when we see private lives marked by greed and public conduct marked by injustice, it is plainly reasonable to say that their laws, customs, and whole political order are bad.

Now apart from a very few exceptions, one could hardly find private conduct more treacherous than that of the Cretans, or public measures more unjust.

Therefore, since their constitution is neither like the Spartan nor in any way worthy of choice or imitation, I reject it from this comparison.

Nor is it right to introduce Plato's republic either, even though some philosophers speak of it with admiration.

For just as we do not admit to athletic contests those performers or athletes who have neither won recognition nor undergone proper training, so we should not admit Plato's constitution to this contest for first place unless it can first demonstrate some real achievement in practice.

As things stand, to compare it with the constitutions of Sparta, Rome, and Carthage would be like setting up a statue beside living, breathing men and inviting comparison.

Even if the statue were flawless as a work of art, comparing the lifeless with the living would still strike the spectators as inadequate and entirely out of place.

Chapter 48 Institutions of Lycurgus

Leaving those aside, I return to the Spartan constitution.

It seems to me that Lycurgus legislated and planned so well for securing harmony among the citizens, preserving Laconia safely, and maintaining Sparta's freedom that one might think his insight something more than human.

Equality in property, simplicity and commonality in daily life were likely to make private conduct disciplined and the public order free from faction, while training men to endure labor and danger would make them brave and high-minded.

When courage and self-control come together in one soul or one city, vice can hardly grow from them, nor can such men easily be overcome by their neighbors.

By constructing his constitution on these principles, Lycurgus secured lasting safety for all Laconia and left the Spartans themselves a freedom that endured for a very long time.

But as for conquering neighboring peoples, gaining supremacy, and in general competing for wider power, he seems to me to have made no provision at all, either in particular measures or in the system as a whole.

What still remained was to create in the citizens some necessity or settled purpose that would make the common spirit of the city, as well as private life, self-sufficient and moderate.

In fact, although he made them utterly disinterested and sober-minded in their own personal lives and in the institutions of their own city, he left them toward the rest of Greece excessively ambitious, hungry for rule, and greedy for advantage.

Chapter 49 The Defect in the Spartan Constitution

Who does not know that the Spartans were among the first Greeks to cast covetous eyes on their neighbors' land, and for sheer greed undertook a war to enslave the Messenians?

And who has not read that, out of stubborn rivalry, they swore not to raise the siege until they had taken Messene by force?

It is equally well known to everyone that, out of their passion for supremacy in Greece, they later submitted to take orders from the very people whom they had once defeated in battle.

For when the Persians invaded, they fought and won in defense of Greek freedom.

But after the invaders had gone back and fled, the Spartans handed over the Greek cities to them in the Peace of Antalcidas, in order to get money for their domination over Greece.

It was then that the defect in their legislation became visible.

As long as they aimed only at ruling their immediate neighbors, and later the Peloponnesians themselves, the resources and supplies of Laconia were enough for them. They had provisions ready at hand and could make rapid returns home and easy transport of supplies.

But once they undertook to send fleets overseas and to campaign with armies outside the Peloponnese, it became obvious that neither their iron currency nor the exchange of yearly produce, in accordance with Lycurgus' laws, could supply what they lacked.

Such enterprises required a currency accepted everywhere and provisions from abroad.

So they were compelled to stand at Persian doors, impose tribute on the islanders, and levy silver from all the Greeks, having learned that under Lycurgus' legislation it was impossible not only to claim the leadership of Greece but, in fact, to compete for great affairs at all.

Chapter 50 Sparta Compared with Rome

Why, then, have I gone into this digression? So that the facts themselves may make clear that Lycurgus' legislation is sufficient for the secure preservation of a people's own territory and for maintaining its freedom.

And for those who regard that as the proper end of a constitution, it must be granted that no arrangement has ever existed, or does now exist, more choiceworthy than the Spartan order and system.

But if someone aims at greater things, and thinks it finer and nobler to lead many peoples, to prevail over them and rule them, and to have all men look toward him and depend on him,

then he must admit that the Spartan constitution is deficient in this respect, while the Roman constitution is superior and possesses a stronger organization for power.

This too has been made plain by events themselves. When the Spartans set out to win the leadership of Greece, they quickly put even their own freedom at risk.

The Romans, by contrast, once they had secured dominion over Italy, in a short time brought the whole inhabited world under their power, and a great part of their success came from the abundance and ready availability of their supplies.

Chapter 51 Carthage Compared with Rome

The Carthaginian constitution, in its original form, seems to me to have been well framed in its main divisions.

They had kings, their council of elders possessed aristocratic authority, and the people held power in the matters that belonged to them. In general, the fitting together of the whole closely resembled that of Rome and Sparta.

But at the time when Carthage entered the war with Hannibal, the Carthaginian constitution was already worse, while the Roman was better.

For every body, constitution, and undertaking has a natural growth, then a peak, and after that decline; and everything is strongest at its peak. That is exactly why these constitutions differed at that moment.

Carthage had become strong and prosperous earlier than Rome; and by just so much, at that time Carthage was already past its prime, while Rome, so far as its constitution was concerned, was then at its very height.

Accordingly, in Carthage the people had already gained the greater share of power in deliberations, while at Rome the senate was still in its prime.

So where policy was being debated by the many in the one state, and by the best men in the other, Roman deliberation proved stronger in public affairs.

That is why, even after suffering grave disasters, they finally overcame the Carthaginians in the war through the soundness of their counsels.

Chapter 52 The Causes of Roman Superiority

If we look at particular matters, such as the provisions for war, the Carthaginians are naturally better practiced and better prepared for naval service, since from ancient times that skill has been hereditary among them and they are more devoted to the sea than any other people.

But in land warfare the Romans train themselves far more effectively than the Carthaginians.

The Romans devote their whole effort to this; the Carthaginians neglect their infantry altogether and take only slight thought even for their cavalry.

The reason is that the Carthaginians use foreign and mercenary forces, whereas the Romans use native troops and citizens.

In this respect the Roman constitution deserves the preference over the Carthaginian. The one rests its hopes of freedom on the courage of mercenaries; the Roman state rests them on the valor of its own citizens and the support of its allies.

That is why, even if they suffer an initial defeat, the Romans recover and continue the war, whereas the Carthaginians do the opposite.

For the Romans fight for their homeland and their children, and they can never let their anger slacken, but persist with all their spirit until they overcome their enemies.

So although the Romans, as I said before, are far inferior in naval experience, they nevertheless prevail overall because of the courage of their men.

For even though seamanship contributes a great deal in fighting at sea, the bravery of the marines weighs most heavily in deciding victory.

Indeed, all the peoples of Italy are by nature superior to Phoenicians and Libyans alike in bodily strength and in daring; and beyond that, their training powerfully encourages the young toward such conduct.

One example will be enough to show how seriously the Roman constitution is concerned with producing men willing to endure anything in order to win the reputation for courage in their own country.

Chapter 53 Roman Funeral Rites

Whenever one of their distinguished men dies, during the funeral procession the body, together with all its honors, is carried into the forum to the place called the Rostra, sometimes set upright in full view, though more rarely laid out reclining.

With the whole people standing around, his son—if he has left one of full age and he happens to be present—or otherwise some other relative, mounts the Rostra and speaks about the dead man's virtues and the achievements he accomplished in life.

By this means the deeds are brought back before the eyes of the crowd, and not only those who shared in them but even those who had no part in them are moved to sympathy, so that the loss seems not a private sorrow for the mourners but a public one for the whole people.

After the burial and the customary rites, they place the likeness of the dead man in the most conspicuous part of the house, enclosed in a small wooden shrine.

This likeness is a mask made in an extraordinarily faithful resemblance, both in features and in coloring.

They display these images at public sacrifices with great care, and whenever another eminent member of the family dies, they carry them in the funeral procession, placing them on men who seem to match the originals as closely as possible in height and general build.

These men put on the garments appropriate to the offices the dead once held: if the man was a consul or praetor, garments with purple border; if a censor, purple robes; if he had celebrated a triumph or done some equivalent deed, robes embroidered with gold.

They ride in chariots, and before them are carried the rods, axes, and all the other insignia proper to the magistracies, in proportion to the rank each had reached in the service of the state during his lifetime.

When they reach the Rostra, they all sit in order on ivory chairs. A young man who loves glory and noble deeds could hardly behold a finer sight.

For who would not be stirred by seeing all at once the images of men famous for their virtue, as if they were living and breathing? What spectacle could be more splendid?

Chapter 54 The Glorious Memory of Brave Men Kept Alive

And the speaker, after finishing his account of the man who is about to be buried, goes on to the others whose representatives are present, beginning with the most ancient and recounting the successes and deeds of each.

Thus the renown of good men is continually made new, the glory of those who achieved some noble deed is made immortal, and the fame of those who benefited their country becomes known to the multitude and handed down to later generations.

Most of all, the young are inspired to endure every hardship for the common good in hopes of winning the glory that attends brave men.

And what I say is confirmed by the facts. Many Romans have voluntarily fought single combats on which the issue of the whole battle depended, and not a few have chosen certain death, some in war for the safety of others, some in peace for the security of the commonwealth.

There have even been magistrates who put their own sons to death, against every custom and every law, valuing the interest of their country above the natural bond with their nearest kin.

Many such stories are told of many Roman men, but one example named specifically will be enough for the present, both as proof and as illustration.

Chapter 55 Patriotism and Purity At Rome

They tell the story of Horatius, surnamed Cocles. While he was fighting against two of the enemy at the far end of the bridge over the Tiber, the bridge that stands before the city, he saw a large body coming up to support them and feared that they would force their way across into the city.

So he turned and shouted to the men behind him to retreat as quickly as possible and break down the bridge. They obeyed, and while they were cutting it apart he held his ground, receiving many wounds and checking the enemy's advance—not so much because they were daunted by his strength as because they were astonished by his steadfastness and daring.

Once the bridge had been broken, the enemy's attack was stopped; and Cocles, throwing himself into the river in full armor, deliberately gave up his life, valuing the safety of his country and the glory he would win thereafter more than his present life and all the years still left to him.

Such, it seems, is the zeal and ambition for noble deeds that Roman customs implant in the young.

Chapter 56 Religion Keeps the Roman Commonwealth Together

In matters of money as well, Roman customs and principles are better than those of the Carthaginians.

Among the Carthaginians nothing connected with profit is considered shameful; among the Romans nothing is more disgraceful than taking bribes and making gain from what one ought not.

For the more one kind of people honors profit from the most successful source, the more the other treats unlawful gain as a reproach.

The proof is this: among the Carthaginians men openly give gifts to obtain office, whereas among the Romans the penalty for such conduct is death.

Since the prizes offered for virtue are thus opposite among the two peoples, it is natural that their ways of pursuing them should also be different.

But the greatest superiority of the Roman constitution, in my opinion, lies in their attitude toward the gods.

Indeed, what among other peoples is criticized as superstition is, I think, the very thing that holds the Roman state together.

This element has been carried so far among them and introduced so thoroughly into both private life and public business that nothing could surpass it, and many might find that astonishing.

For my part, I think they have done this for the sake of the multitude.

If it were possible to found a state composed of wise men, perhaps such a device would not be necessary.

But since every crowd is fickle, full of lawless desires, irrational anger, and violent passion, the only thing left is to keep the masses in check by unseen fears and such theatrical impressions.

So it seems to me that the ancients were not introducing notions about the gods and beliefs about punishments in the underworld among the people at random or without purpose; rather, those of our own day act rashly and senselessly in trying to cast them out.

This is why, among other things, Greek officials entrusted with only a single talent, though they have ten clerks, as many seals, and twice as many witnesses, still cannot be trusted to keep faith.

At Rome, by contrast, men serving in offices or embassies handle very large sums of money, yet through the force of their oath alone they remain faithful to their duty.

And whereas among other peoples it is rare to find a man who keeps his hands off public money and stays clean in such matters, among the Romans it is rare to catch anyone in the act of such wrongdoing.

Chapter 57 Conclusion: Dangers Ahead for Rome

That everything which exists is subject to decay and change hardly needs further argument, for the necessity imposed by nature is enough to establish that truth.

And since every kind of constitution naturally decays in two ways, one from external causes and one from causes that grow within itself, the external mode is impossible to define with certainty, but the internal follows a set order.

I have already explained what form of constitution naturally comes first, what comes second, and how they pass into one another,

so that those able to connect the beginning with the end of the present discussion can already predict the future for themselves. In my judgment the result is plain.

For when a state has survived many great dangers and afterwards reached undisputed supremacy and power, it is obvious that as prosperity settles into it over time, private lives become more luxurious and men grow more ambitious than they should in the pursuit of office and other objects.

As these tendencies advance, the beginning of decline will come from love of office, from resentment at loss of status, and, along with these, from arrogance and luxury in private life.

The people will be the agents through whom the change gains its name, once they come to think that some men wrong them out of greed while others puff them up with flattery because they are hunting office.

For then, in anger and making every decision under the sway of passion, the people will no longer be willing to obey or even to share power equally with their leaders, but will want the whole or the greater part for themselves.

And when that happens, the constitution will take on the finest of names—freedom and democracy—but in reality it will become the worst of things, mob-rule.

Since I have now discussed the composition, growth, zenith, present condition, and differences—both for better and for worse—of the Roman constitution as compared with others, I here bring this account of the constitution to its conclusion.

Chapter 58 Even Hannibal Acknowledges the Spirit of the Romans

Now, returning to the connected course of the history at the point from which I digressed, I will briefly recall one action, so that I may make the excellence and power of the Roman constitution at that time clear not by argument alone but by deeds, as if a master craftsman were displaying one specimen of his work.

After Hannibal won the battle at Cannae and captured the eight thousand Romans who were guarding the camp, he took them all alive and allowed them to send envoys home to negotiate their ransom and salvation.

They selected ten of their most distinguished men, and after making them swear that they would return to him, Hannibal sent them off.

But one of those chosen, after already leaving the camp, said that he had forgotten something and turned back; after retrieving what he had left behind he set out again, thinking that by his return he had kept faith and released himself from the oath.

When the envoys reached Rome, they begged and urged the senate not to begrudge the captured men their safety, but to let each of them save himself by paying three minae and returning to his family, for Hannibal, they said, was willing to grant that.

They also argued that the prisoners deserved rescue, since they had neither shown cowardice in the battle nor done anything unworthy of Rome, but had merely been left to guard the camp and, after all the others had perished in battle, had been overtaken by circumstances and surrendered to the enemy.

Yet the Romans, though they had suffered terrible losses in battle, had been deprived of almost all their allies, and could expect before long to face danger for their very fatherland,

still, after hearing these pleas, neither yielded in the face of disaster in any way unworthy of themselves nor overlooked anything that sound judgment required.

They saw Hannibal's purpose: by this act he meant both to get money and to strip the opposing troops of their eagerness for battle by showing that even the defeated still had hope of safety.

So far were they from doing what was requested that they counted neither pity for the men's relatives nor the future use they might have of greater importance.

Instead, by refusing to ransom the prisoners, they proved Hannibal's calculation and his hopes empty, and they laid down for their own people the rule that in battle they must either conquer or die, since for the defeated no other hope of safety remained.

Accordingly they dismissed the nine envoys, who returned voluntarily in accordance with their oath, but the one who had tried by a trick to escape his oath they bound and sent back to the enemy.

Thus Hannibal was not so much delighted by his victory over the Romans in battle as shaken and astonished by the steadiness and greatness of spirit the Romans showed in their deliberations.

Chapter 59

There is also a place near Stratus in Aetolia called Rhynchos, as Polybius says in his Histories.

Book VII

Chapter 1 Capua and Petelia

Polybius says in the seventh book that the people of Capua in Campania, made wealthy by the excellence of their land, drifted into luxury and extravagance, surpassing even the famous reputation of Croton and Sybaris.

So, he says, being unable to bear their present prosperity, they called in Hannibal. For that reason they later suffered irreparable disasters at Roman hands.

The people of Petelia, on the other hand, kept faith with Rome and showed such endurance under Hannibal's siege that, after eating all the leather in the city and consuming the bark and tender shoots of every tree in it, and after holding out for eleven months with no help arriving—though the Romans approved of their conduct—they finally surrendered.

Capua, after going over to the Carthaginians, used its influence to draw the other cities over as well.

Chapter 2 Hieronymus of Syracuse

After the plot against Hieronymus, king of the Syracusans, and after Thraso's withdrawal, the party of Zoippus and Andranodorus persuaded Hieronymus to send envoys to Hannibal at once.

So he selected Polycleitus of Cyrene and Philodemus of Argos and sent them to Italy with instructions to discuss joint action with the Carthaginians; at the same time he sent his brothers to Alexandria.

Hannibal received Polycleitus and Philodemus graciously, held out great hopes to the young king, and quickly sent the envoys back, along with Hannibal the Carthaginian, who was then admiral of a trireme, and the Syracusans Hippocrates and his younger brother Epicydes.

These men had already been serving with Hannibal for some time and had entered Carthaginian service because their grandfather had fled Syracuse after being thought to have laid hands on Agatharchus, one of Agathocles' sons.

When they reached Syracuse, Polycleitus and his colleague delivered the report of their embassy, and the Carthaginian envoy spoke according to the instructions Hannibal had given him. Hieronymus was at once ready to join the Carthaginians in their affairs.

He declared that the Hannibal who had come to him ought to go off to Carthage at once, and he promised to send men of his own with him to conduct negotiations with the Carthaginians.

Chapter 3 Hieronymus of Syracuse

At this same time the Roman commander stationed at Lilybaeum learned what was happening and sent envoys to Hieronymus to renew the treaty that had been made with his ancestors.

But Hieronymus, already leaning strongly toward the Carthaginians, said that he pitied the Romans because wicked men had perished miserably in the battles in Italy at Carthaginian hands.

The envoys were shocked by such insolence, but they still asked who had told him such things. He pointed to the Carthaginian envoys who were present and told the Romans to expose them if they happened to be lying.

They replied that it was not their custom to trust enemies, and they urged him to do nothing contrary to the treaty, since that would be both just and greatly to his advantage. He said he would deliberate and later make his answer clear to them.

But he asked them how it had happened that, before his grandfather's death, they had sailed with fifty ships as far as Pachynus and then turned back again.

What had happened was that the Romans had shortly before heard that Hiero was dead, and had feared that some disturbance might arise in Syracuse because people would despise the age of the boy left behind.

So they admitted that they had made the voyage in order to support his youth and help preserve his rule, but that when they learned his grandfather was still alive, they had sailed back.

At this the young king answered again, "Then allow me as well, Romans, to preserve my rule now by turning back toward Carthaginian hopes."

The Romans understood the direction of his policy. For the moment they said nothing and returned, reported what had been said to the man who had sent them, and from then on kept watch on Hieronymus as an enemy.

Chapter 4 The Treaty with Carthage

Hieronymus then chose Agatharchus, Onesigenes, and Hipposthenes and sent them with Hannibal to the Carthaginians, instructing them to conclude a treaty on the following terms.

The Carthaginians were to assist him with both land and sea forces, and after driving the Romans from Sicily they were to divide the island so that the river Himera, which nearly splits Sicily in two, should be the boundary between the two spheres of rule.

When these envoys reached the Carthaginians, they negotiated on this basis and accomplished their mission, since the Carthaginians readily agreed to everything.

Meanwhile Hippocrates and his circle took the young king in hand and at first captivated him by describing Hannibal's marches, battle lines, and battles in Italy.

After that they told him that no one had a better claim than he to rule over all the Siceliots, first because he was the grandson through his mother Nereis of Pyrrhus, whom all the Siceliots alone had willingly and deliberately approved as their leader and king, and second because of the sovereign position held by his grandfather Hiero.

In the end they so completely turned the boy's head that he paid no attention to anyone else, partly because he was unstable by nature and still more because they had now filled him with lofty ambition.

At the very moment when Agatharchus and his colleagues were completing the first arrangement at Carthage, he sent another embassy, now claiming that the whole rule of Sicily belonged to him, demanding that the Carthaginians help him recover Sicily, while he in turn promised to support them in their operations in Italy.

The Carthaginians saw perfectly well the complete instability and madness of the boy, but they also believed for many reasons that it was to their advantage not to lose their hold on Sicilian affairs.

So they assented to all his demands, and, having already prepared ships and soldiers beforehand, they proceeded with plans to transport their forces to Sicily.

Chapter 5 Hieronymus Decides For War

When the Romans learned of this, they again sent envoys to him, protesting that he must not violate the treaties made with his forefathers.

Hieronymus therefore called the council together and put before it the question of what should be done.

The native members kept quiet, fearing the poor judgment of the ruler; but Aristomachus of Corinth, Damippus the Spartan, and Autonous the Thessalian urged him to stand by the treaties with Rome.

Andranodorus alone said that they must not let the opportunity slip, and that the present moment was the only one in which it was possible to win dominion over Sicily.

After he had said this, Hieronymus asked the party around Hippocrates what opinion they held. When they said they agreed with Andranodorus, the deliberation was brought to an end. In this way war against Rome was decided upon.

But because he wanted to seem clever rather than clumsy in answering the ambassadors, he fell into such a blunder that he was plainly about not only to displease the Romans, but to offend them outright.

For he said that he would keep the treaty if, first, they restored all the gold they had received from his grandfather Hiero; second, if they repaid for the whole past period the grain and the other gifts they had received from him; and third, if they acknowledged that the land and cities on this side of the river Himera belonged to the Syracusans.

On these terms the envoys and the council separated. From that time onward Hieronymus and his circle actively pushed the war forward, gathering forces, arming them, and preparing the rest of the necessary supplies.

Chapter 6 Description of Leontini

The city of Leontini as a whole faces north,

and through the middle of it there runs a level valley, in which stand the public offices, the courts, and, in general, the market-place.

On each side of this valley stretches a ridge with steep escarpments all along it; and the level tops of these hills, above the brows, are full of houses and temples.

The city has two gates. One stands at the southern end of the valley I mentioned and leads toward Syracuse; the other is at the northern end and leads to the so-called Leontine plains and the farming country.

Below one of the escarpments, the western one, there runs a river called the Lissus.

Parallel to it, immediately under the cliff, stand many continuous rows of houses; and between these houses and the river lies the road mentioned above.

Chapter 7 Fall of Heronymus

Some of the writers who have written about the downfall of Hieronymus have made a very long story of it and arranged it with a great deal of sensationalism, recounting the omens said to have come before his accession and the misfortunes of the Syracusans,

and then writing in tragic style about the savagery of his character, the impiety of his actions, and, on top of everything, the shocking and terrible circumstances of his fall, so that one would think neither Phalaris nor Apollodorus nor any other tyrant had ever been harsher than he.

And yet he was only a boy when he came to power, and after that lived no more than thirteen months.

During that time it is possible that one man or another was put to the torture and that some of his friends and some other Syracusans were killed; but it is not likely that there was any extreme excess of lawlessness or some unparalleled kind of impiety.

One should indeed say that in character he was exceptionally reckless and unlawful, but he ought not to be compared with any of the tyrants mentioned above.

It seems to me that writers of histories about particular episodes, once they have taken up subjects that are narrow and easy to cover, are forced by poverty of material to make small things great and to spend many words on matters not even worth remembering. Some too fall into much the same error through sheer lack of judgment.

How much more reasonably could someone have spent the space used to pad out books and spin the narrative out at length on Hiero and Gelo, leaving Hieronymus aside.

For such a subject is more pleasing to those who enjoy hearing history,

Chapter 8 Character of Hiero II

and altogether more useful to those who wish to learn. For Hiero, first of all, won for himself the rule over Syracuse and its allies by his own efforts, inheriting neither wealth nor reputation nor any other ready-made advantage from fortune.

Indeed, without killing, banishing, or harming a single one of the citizens, he became king of the Syracusans by his own merits,

which is the most astonishing thing of all; and still more astonishing is the fact that he not only acquired his power in this way, but preserved it in the same way.

For though he reigned for fifty-four years, he kept peace for his fatherland, preserved his own rule free from plots, and escaped the envy that usually accompanies great power.

In fact, when he more than once tried to lay down his sovereignty, he was prevented by the citizens acting together.

By proving exceptionally beneficent and eager for honor in his dealings with the Greeks, he left behind himself a great reputation and won for Syracuse no small measure of goodwill from all.

And though he lived amid immense abundance, luxury, and wealth, he survived to more than ninety years of age, kept all his senses, and preserved every part of his body unimpaired.

This seems to me no small sign, but a very great one, of a temperate life.

Gelo too, after living more than fifty years, set before himself as the noblest aim in life obedience to the father who begot him, and he counted neither wealth nor royal greatness nor anything else whatever as more important than affection and loyalty toward his parents.

Chapter 9 Treaty Between Hannibal and King Philip V. of Macedon

This is the oath that Hannibal the general, Mago, Myrcan, Barmocar, and all the Carthaginian senators who were with him, together with all the Carthaginians serving in the campaign with him, swore to Xenophanes son of Cleomachus, the Athenian envoy whom King Philip son of Demetrius sent to us on behalf of himself, the Macedonians, and their allies.

It was sworn in the presence of Zeus, Hera, and Apollo; in the presence of the god of the Carthaginians, and of Heracles and Iolaus; in the presence of Ares, Triton, and Poseidon; in the presence of the gods who go with the army, and of the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth; in the presence of rivers, harbors, and waters;

in the presence of all the gods who hold Carthage, all the gods who hold Macedonia and the rest of Greece, and all the gods of war who stand witness to this oath.

Hannibal the general, all the Carthaginian senators with him, and all the Carthaginians serving with him said that, since it seemed good both to you and to us to establish this oath concerning friendship and honorable goodwill, we should be friends, kinsmen, and brothers on the following terms.

The Carthaginians, Hannibal the general and those with him, the Carthaginian magistrates who live under the same laws, the people of Utica, all cities and nations subject to Carthage, and their soldiers and allies,

and all the cities and nations in Italy, Celtica, and Liguria with whom we are in friendship, and any others in that region with whom we may later make friendship and alliance, shall be kept safe by King Philip, the Macedonians, and the rest of the Greeks who are their allies.

Likewise King Philip, the Macedonians, and the allies among the other Greeks shall be kept safe and protected by the Carthaginians serving in this campaign, by the people of Utica, by all the cities and nations subject to Carthage, by the allies and soldiers, and by all the nations and cities in Italy, Celtica, and Liguria, and by any others who may become allies in those parts of Italy.

We shall not plot against one another or use ambush against one another, but with all zeal and goodwill, without deceit or treachery, we shall be enemies to those who make war on the Carthaginians, excepting those kings, cities, and harbors with whom we have sworn agreements and friendships.

And we in turn shall be enemies to those who make war on King Philip, excepting those kings, cities, and nations with whom we have sworn agreements and friendships.

You shall also be our allies in the war we are waging against the Romans, until the gods grant prosperity to both you and us.

And you shall help us whenever there is need and in whatever way we agree.

And if the gods grant us success in the war against the Romans and their allies, and if the Romans wish to make terms of friendship, we shall make terms on condition that the same friendship extends to you as well,

and that it shall never be lawful for them to make war against you, nor shall the Romans be masters of Corcyra, Apollonia, Epidamnus, Pharos, Dimale, Parthini, or Atintania.

They shall also restore to Demetrius of Pharos all his own people who are in the Roman commonwealth.

But if the Romans make war on you or on us, we shall help one another in the war, as each party may need.

The same shall hold if any others do so, apart from those kings, cities, and nations with whom we have sworn agreements and friendships.

And if it seems good to us to remove anything from this oath or to add anything to it, we shall remove or add it as seems good to both of us.

Chapter 10 Messene and Philip V. in B. C. 215

While democracy was in force among the Messenians, the notable men had been driven into exile, and those who had received allotments of their property held power in the state; so the members of the old citizen body who remained found it hard to endure these men's equality of speech.

Gorgus of Messene was second to no Messenian in wealth or birth, and in the prime of life he had become the most distinguished of all those who sought crowns in athletic contests.

For in outward appearance, in the dignity of the rest of his life, and in the number of his victories, he fell short of no one of his contemporaries.

And when he gave up athletics and turned to public life and the service of his country, in that sphere too he won a reputation no less than the one he already had,

being thought far removed from the vulgarity that clings to athletes, and regarded as exceptionally effective and prudent in public affairs.

Chapter 11 Philip Dissuaded from Taking Messene

For the present, after bringing my narrative to a pause, I want to speak briefly about Philip, because this was the beginning of his reversal and of his movement and change for the worse.

It seems to me that for practical men who wish, even little by little, to improve themselves from the lessons of history, this offers a very vivid example.

For both because the beginning of his career was so conspicuous and because his natural gifts were so brilliant, the impulses of this king in either direction became especially clear and widely known to all the Greeks, and the consequences that followed each set of impulses likewise stood out plainly by comparison.

That after he succeeded to the kingship Thessaly, Macedonia, and in general all the regions under his own rule were more loyal and better disposed toward him than they had been toward any former king, though he took over the Macedonian power while still a young man, can easily be learned from the following facts.

For though he was constantly drawn away from Macedonia by the war against the Aetolians and Lacedaemonians, not only did none of the peoples just mentioned break into civil disorder, but none of the neighboring barbarians even dared to touch Macedonia.
