And it would not be possible to speak adequately of the affection and eagerness shown toward him by Alexander, Chrysogonus, and his other friends.

The same may be said of the Peloponnesians and Boeotians, and likewise of the Epirotes, Acarnanians, and all the others to whom in a short time he became the cause of many benefits.

Indeed, if one may put it somewhat boldly, I think this description suited Philip very well: by the beneficence of his policy he became something like the common darling of the Greeks.

A most conspicuous and important proof of what a noble purpose and good faith can accomplish is that all the Cretans, after coming to agreement and entering the same alliance, chose Philip alone as protector of the island, and this was accomplished without arms and without danger, something one would not easily find to have happened before.

From the events at Messene onward, however, everything in his case took on the opposite character; and this happened naturally.

For once he turned to a policy opposite to his former one, and kept adding to it what was consistent with that choice, he was bound to reverse other men's opinions about him and to meet with results opposite to those he had previously enjoyed.

And that indeed is what happened. This will become clear to attentive readers from the events I am about to recount.

Chapter 12 Philip's Loss of Popularity

When Philip king of Macedon wanted to seize the acropolis of the Messenians, and told the leading men of the city that he wished to see the citadel and sacrifice to Zeus, he went up with his attendants and performed the sacrifice. Then, when according to custom the entrails of the victims that had been offered were brought to him, he took them in his hands, turned a little aside, and stretching them out toward Aratus and his party asked, "What do the omens seem to signify: that I should withdraw from the citadel, or hold it?"

Demetrius at once broke in from where he stood and said, "If you have the mind of a seer, withdraw as fast as you can; but if you have the mind of an active king, keep hold of it, so that after letting it go now you may not later be looking for a better opportunity.

For in this way, by holding both horns, you alone would keep the ox under your control," by which he meant Ithome and Acrocorinth, and by the ox the Peloponnese.

Philip turned to Aratus and said, "And do you advise the same?" When Aratus hesitated, Philip pressed him to say what he really thought.

After some uncertainty Aratus said, "If you can hold this place without breaking faith with the Messenians, I advise you to hold it.

But if by occupying this place with a garrison you mean to destroy every acropolis and the very guard

—meaning good faith—by which the allies you received from Antigonus were protected, consider whether it is not better now to lead your men out and leave their trust behind, and by that trust to guard the Messenians, and likewise the rest of your allies."

Philip by his own inclination was ready to break faith, as later events made clear.

But because he had shortly before been sharply rebuked by the younger Aratus for the destruction of those men, and because on this occasion the elder Aratus spoke with frankness and authority and begged him not to ignore what was said, Philip felt ashamed.

Taking him by the right hand, he said, "Then let us go back by the same road."

Chapter 13 Philip Begins to Become a Tyrant

Aratus, seeing that Philip had openly taken up the war against Rome and had been completely altered in his policy toward his allies, only with difficulty turned Philip aside, after raising many objections and pretexts.

We, however, now wish to remind those who are following this work that what in the fifth book we mentioned only by promise and assertion has now received confirmation from the facts themselves, so that we may leave none of our conclusions unsupported or open to dispute.

For when, in narrating the Aetolian War, we paused at the point where we said that Philip had with too much passion destroyed the porticoes at Thermus and the rest of the votive offerings, and that the cause of these actions should be referred not so much to the king, because of his youth, as to the friends around him,

we then said that Aratus' life itself was a sufficient defense of the claim that he would have done nothing base, whereas Demetrius of Pharos had exactly such a cast of mind.

And we promised to make this clear from what would be recounted later, postponing until this point the proof of that earlier judgment,

the moment when, with Demetrius present, as we have just shown in the affair at Messene, and Aratus delayed by only a single day, Philip began to lay hands on the gravest acts of impiety.

And as if, after tasting human blood and the murder and betrayal of allies, he had been changed—not from a man into a wolf, as in the Arcadian myth cited by Plato, but from a king into a savage tyrant.

An even clearer proof of the character of the two men is the advice given about the citadel, helping us not to remain uncertain even about the events concerning the...

Chapter 14 Aratus a Moderating Influence on Philip

...Aetolians. Once these points are admitted, it is already easy to reckon up the difference in the policy of the two men.

For just as now, when Philip listened to Aratus, he kept faith with the Messenians in the matter of the citadel, and, as the saying goes, applied a small remedy to the great wound created by the earlier slaughter,

so in the Aetolian affair, when he followed Demetrius, he sinned against the gods by destroying consecrated offerings, wronged men by transgressing the laws of war, and missed the mark of his proper policy, making himself an implacable and bitter enemy to those who differed with him.

The same reasoning applies also to the affairs in Crete. For there too, when he used Aratus as his guide in the larger policy, he not only committed no injustice, but did not even offend any of the islanders; he kept all the Cretans under his hand and drew all the Greeks into goodwill toward himself by the dignity of his conduct.

But then again, once he followed Demetrius and became responsible for the misfortunes of the Messenians just described, he lost at once both the goodwill of his allies and the trust of the rest of the Greeks.

So great is the weight for young kings, both toward the ruin and toward the restoration of their rule, that lies in the choice and judgment of the friends who attend them—a matter about which most men, I do not know how, are careless and give not even the slightest forethought.

Chapter 15 The War of Antiochus with Achaeus

Around Sardis there were unceasing and continuous skirmishes and dangers by night and by day, as the soldiers on both sides devised every kind of ambush, counter-ambush, and surprise attack against one another; to write out the details would be not only useless but altogether too long.

In the end, when the siege had already entered its second year, Lagoras the Cretan, a man with considerable experience in warfare, observed that the strongest cities generally fall most easily into the hands of enemies because of the carelessness of those who live in them, whenever, trusting in their natural or man-made strength, they neglect guard duty and grow wholly slack.

He had also recognized that captures tend to be made precisely at the strongest points, the very places the enemy thinks beyond hope.

So at that time, seeing that the prevailing opinion about the strength of Sardis had led everyone to despair of taking it by such an operation, and that they had only one hope left, namely to master the city through famine,

he paid all the more attention and explored every possible course, eager to seize on some opening of that kind.

When he noticed that the wall near the place called the Saw—this is the point joining the citadel and the city—was left unguarded, he conceived this hope and plan.

He discovered the negligence of the guards from the following sign.

The place was extremely precipitous, and below it lay a ravine into which the dead from the city and the carcasses of horses and pack animals were thrown; and so there was always a gathering there of vultures and other birds.

Observing this, the man I mentioned noticed that when the birds had eaten their fill they regularly settled and rested on the cliffs and on the wall, and from this he concluded that the wall was necessarily unguarded and remained deserted for most of the time.

After that he approached by night with care and examined the possible routes of access and the positions for ladders.

And finding that at one place, along one of the cliffs, an ascent was possible, he laid the matter before the...

Chapter 16 Antiochus Takes Sardis

...king. When the king took up the hope and urged Lagoras to carry out the attempt, the latter promised to do what he could,

but asked the king to assign to him Theodotus the Aetolian and Dionysius, the commander of the bodyguard, so that they might join him, lend their aid, and share in the enterprise, since each of them seemed to possess enough strength and daring for the plan in hand.

The king immediately did as he asked, and the men mentioned, after coming to an understanding and sharing all the details among themselves, waited for a moonless night in the hours before dawn.

Once they had obtained such a night, on the very day on which they intended to act, late in the afternoon they selected from the whole camp fifteen of the strongest men in body and spirit, who were to carry the ladders, climb up with them, and share the danger.

After these they chose another thirty men to wait in reserve at some distance, so that when the first party had crossed over and reached the gate nearby, these men should rush up from outside and try to break through the hinges and the gate-fastening, while the others from within dealt with the bar and the bolt-pins.

They also appointed two thousand men to follow after these, who, once they had burst in, were to seize the area around the theatre, which was favorably situated against both those coming from the citadel and those coming from the city.

And so that the selection of the men might not arouse any suspicion of the truth, the king spread the story that the Aetolians were about to force an entry into the city through a certain ravine, and that energetic precautions had to be taken in view of that report.

Chapter 17 The Sack of Sardis

When everything was ready for them, as soon as the moon had gone down, Lagoras and his party came secretly to the cliffs with their ladders and hid themselves under an overhanging ledge.

When day came, and the guards had left that place, and the king, according to custom, had sent some men to their reserve posts while bringing the main body out into the hippodrome and drawing them up, at first what was happening aroused no suspicion in anyone.

But once the two ladders had been set in place, and Dionysius went up first by one while Lagoras went up by the other, excitement and movement spread through the camp.

For those climbing the overhanging brow toward the cliff were out of sight for the people in the city and for Achaeus and his men in the citadel, but from the camp the daring of those who were climbing and pressing on was plainly visible.

Therefore the soldiers there stood speechless, amazed by the strangeness of the thing and at the same time, as they foresaw and feared what would happen, filled alike with dread and delight.

The king, seeing the stir throughout the whole camp and wishing to draw off both his own people and those in the city from what was actually under way, led his force forward and attacked the gates on the opposite side, called the Persian Gates.

Achaeus, seeing from the citadel that the movement among the opposing forces was different from what was usual, was greatly perplexed, distressed, and utterly unable to understand what was happening.

Still, he sent men to meet the attack at the gate; but because they had to make their descent by a narrow and precipitous route, the relief was slow in arriving.

Aribazus, who had been posted in the city, rushed in all innocence to the gates where he saw Antiochus attacking; he sent some men up onto the wall, while others he let out through the gate, urging them to keep the attackers off and engage the enemy hand to hand.

Chapter 18 Sardis Destroyed

At this very moment the party with Lagoras, Theodotus, and Dionysius crossed the cliffs and came to the gate below them.

Some of them fought with the men coming to meet them, while others cut through the bars. At the same time the men stationed outside for this purpose rushed up and did nearly the same thing.

The gates were quickly opened, the two thousand entered, and they took possession of the area around the theatre.

Once this happened, all those who had left the walls and the gate called the Persian Gate—the point to which Aribazus and his men had earlier hurried with reinforcements—rushed off in haste to bring support against those who had burst in.

And while this was happening, because the gate was standing open during the withdrawal, some of the king's men burst in as well, following close behind the men who were retreating.

When these men gained control of the gate, others were now entering in an unbroken stream, while others cut through the neighboring gates.

After only a brief struggle against those who had entered, Aribazus and all the people in the city turned and fled toward the citadel.

When that happened, the men with Theodotus and Lagoras remained at the positions by the theatre, acting with intelligence and practical skill as a reserve for the whole operation, while the rest of the force poured in from every side and took the city.

And from then on, some killed everyone they met, some set the houses on fire, and others rushed to plunder and profit, so that the destruction and sack of the city became complete.

Thus Antiochus became master of Sardis.

Book VIII

Chapter 1 The Necessity of Caution in Dealing with an Enemy

It does not seem to me out of place, in view of the whole plan of this work and the purpose I set out at the beginning, to call my readers' attention to the greatness of the events and to the ambitious resolve shown by each of the two states—I mean Rome and Carthage.

For who would not be struck by the fact that, while they were engaged in so great a war over Italy, and in another no less serious over Iberia, and while both alike still faced uncertain hopes for the future and dangers equally pressing in the present,

they were nevertheless not content with the enterprises already before them, but were disputing over Sardinia and Sicily as well, and were trying to grasp everything, not only in their hopes, but also with money and military preparation?

This becomes even more astonishing when one looks at the details. The Romans had two complete armies in Italy with the consuls, and two in Iberia, of which Gnaeus held the land command and Publius the naval command.

The same thing, naturally enough, was true among the Carthaginians.

And besides this, a fleet was stationed off the coasts of Greece to watch Philip's movements, first under Marcus Valerius and afterward under Publius Sulpicius.

At the same time Appius, with a hundred quinqueremes, and Marcus Claudius, with land forces, lay ready for operations in Sicily.

Hamilcar on the Carthaginian side was doing the same.

Chapter 2 Immense Exertions of Rome

These facts, I think, now prove by the events themselves the truth of what I said more than once at the beginning of this history.

What I said was that it is impossible, from writers who treat history in separate parts, to gain a view of the management of the whole.

For how can anyone who reads only a narrative of Sicilian affairs or Iberian affairs, taken by themselves, come to understand either the scale of what happened or the continuous connection of events, or by what method and under what form of government Fortune accomplished the most astonishing achievement of our age?

That achievement was to bring all the known parts of the inhabited world under one rule and power—something for which no earlier precedent can be found.

It is possible, to some extent, to learn from separate accounts how the Romans took Syracuse, or how they got possession of Iberia.

But how they reached dominion over all, and what in these separate regions opposed their larger plans, and what in turn helped them, and at what moments—this is hard to grasp without a general history of events as a whole.

For the same reasons, it is not easy to understand either the greatness of their achievements or the strength of their constitution.

Taken by itself, the statement that the Romans laid claim to Iberia or to Sicily, and campaigned there by land and sea, would not seem particularly marvelous.

But when all this is happening at once, together with many other undertakings carried out at the same time by the same state and constitution, and when one considers along with them the crises and wars within their own country that were pressing upon the men directing all these affairs,

only then do the events become fully clear and truly astonishing, and only then do they receive the attention they deserve.

Let this stand as my answer to those who suppose that acquaintance with partial narratives gives them knowledge of universal and common history.

Chapter 3 Rome and Carthage Continue to Covet Sardinia and Sicily

When Epicydes and Hippocrates gained control of Syracuse and alienated both themselves and the other citizens from friendship with Rome, the Romans, who had by then also received news of the fall of Hieronymus, tyrant of Syracuse, appointed Appius Claudius to command the land force, while Marcus Claudius was given charge of the fleet.

These commanders pitched their camp not far from the city, and decided to attack by land in the region of the Hexapylae, and by sea against Achradina at the place called the Scythian Stoa, where the wall runs directly along the edge of the sea.

Having prepared screens, missiles, and the other equipment needed for a siege, they expected, thanks to the large number of men employed, to overwhelm the defenders with their preparations within five days. They did not reckon with the power of Archimedes, nor did they foresee that, at certain moments, a single mind can achieve more than the labor of multitudes. But in this case they learned the truth from experience.

For the city was strong because the wall ran all around along high ground and overhanging ridges, to which even without opposition one could not easily approach except at certain fixed points.

The man just mentioned had prepared such defenses within the city, and likewise against those attacking from the sea, that the defenders would never need to waste time in improvising, but could meet every move of the enemy immediately and with resources already in hand.

Appius therefore advanced with screens and ladders toward the section of wall adjoining the Hexapylae on the eastern side.

Chapter 3a

Most people can least endure the lightest burden of all—I mean silence.

Chapter 4 History of Universal Supremacy Must Be a Universal History

Marcus, meanwhile, sailed against Achradina with sixty quinqueremes, each one filled with men carrying bows, slings, and javelins, by which they meant to drive back those fighting from the battlements.

At the same time, with eight quinqueremes whose oars had been removed on one side—on the right side of some and the left of others—and which had then been lashed together in pairs along the cleared sides, they brought up against the wall, by means of the outside banks of oars, the machines called sambucae.

The construction of these engines was as follows.

They prepared a ladder four feet wide and of a height equal to that of the wall from the point where it would be landed; they fenced both sides of it and roofed it over with protective coverings, and then laid it slantwise across the touching sides of the coupled ships so that it projected far beyond their prows.

Pulleys with ropes were attached high up on the masts.

Then, when they came near the point of action, they fastened the ropes to the top of the ladder, and men standing on the sterns drew on them through the pulleys, while others standing on the prows braced the machine and secured its lifting with props.

Then, using the oars on the outer sides of the paired ships, they brought the vessels close inshore and tried to set the engine against the wall.

At the top of the ladder there was a platform protected on three sides by wicker shields, on which four men stood and fought against those on the battlements who tried to prevent the sambuca from being set in place.

Once they had planted it and stood above the level of the wall, these men unfastened the side shields on either hand and stepped out onto the battlements or towers.

The rest followed them up the sambuca, since the ladder was firmly secured by ropes to both ships.

The device naturally got this name, because when it is raised the combined shape of ship and ladder looks very much like the musical instrument called a sambuca.

Chapter 5 Syracuse's Defenses

Yet while the Romans were preparing to bring their machines up against the towers in this way,

Archimedes, having readied engines for every possible range, struck at the ships while they were still far off with his stronger stone-throwers and larger missiles, and threw them into confusion and helplessness.

And when these shots began to pass over them, he switched to smaller engines proportioned to the distance at hand, and by constantly adapting his fire to the range so completely checked their advance and attack

that Marcus, driven to despair, was forced to try bringing up his ships secretly by night.

But when they came within bowshot close to land, Archimedes had prepared yet another device against the men fighting from the decks.

He had pierced the wall on the outer face, at the height of a man, with numerous loopholes about the size of a palm; and inside the wall he stationed archers and small scorpions, shooting through these openings and making the marines useless.

Thus he not only rendered the enemy ineffective both at a distance and close at hand, but destroyed a great number of them besides.

And whenever they tried to raise the sambucae, he had prepared engines all along the wall, invisible at ordinary times, but at the needed moment rising from within above the wall and projecting far out over the battlements with their beams.

Some of these carried stones weighing no less than ten talents, and others great lumps of lead.

Then, when the sambucae came near, the beams were swung into position by their pivoting apparatus and, through a release mechanism, let fall the stone upon the machine.

The result was that not only was the engine itself smashed to pieces, but the ship and those aboard it were put in extreme danger.

Chapter 6 Siege of Syracuse

He also used other machines against those who advanced and sheltered themselves behind projecting screens, believing that in this way they would suffer nothing from missiles shot through the wall. Against these men he hurled stones heavy enough to drive the fighters from the prow,

and he also let down an iron hand hanging from a chain. The man handling the beam seized whatever part of the prow he could grasp and then drew the butt of the engine down inside the wall.

When he had thus lifted the prow and made the ship stand upright on its stern, he fixed the machine fast and then, by means of a release, suddenly let go the hand and chain.

As a result some ships fell over sideways, some even capsized, and most, with their prows dropped from on high, shipped great quantities of seawater and were thrown into complete confusion.

Marcus, hard pressed by the contrivances of Archimedes and watching from within the city his own assaults beaten off with loss to himself and laughter from the defenders,

bore the situation badly, though he mocked his own failure by saying that Archimedes was ladling the sea out of his ships, and that the sambucae had been soundly whipped and disgracefully turned away from the feast.

Such was the end of the siege by sea.

Chapter 7 Archimedes

The men under Appius met with similar difficulties and gave up the attack.

For while they were still at a distance they were battered and destroyed by the stone-throwers and catapults, the missiles being extraordinary both in number and in force, since Hiero had supplied the resources and Archimedes had devised and engineered the machines.

And when they approached the city, some were kept from advancing by the archers shooting through the wall, as I said before, while others who pressed on under screens were crushed by the blows of stones and beams falling from above.

They also suffered no little harm from the grappling hands of the machines, as I said earlier; for the men were lifted up with their armor and hurled down.

In the end Appius and his officers withdrew to camp and, after consulting with the military tribunes, unanimously resolved to try every possible means of taking Syracuse except storming it—and that is what they did.

For though they sat before the city for eight months and did not shrink from any other stratagem or bold effort, they never again dared to attempt a direct assault.

So true it is that one man and one mind properly adapted to a particular situation can prove to be a thing of immense and astonishing power.

Those men at least, though they possessed such large forces by land and sea, believed that if one old Syracusan were removed they would at once become masters of the city,

but so long as he was there they did not even dare to attack it in any way against which Archimedes was able to defend it.

Instead, they thought that the people inside would most likely be brought under their power by want of necessities, because of the great number crowded within; and so they pinned their hopes on this, cutting off aid by sea with their fleet and by land with their army.

Yet, not wishing to let the time spent sitting before Syracuse be useless,

the generals divided themselves and the army, so that Appius with two parts remained before the city, while Marcus, taking the third, went out against those in Sicily who had sided with the Carthaginians.

Chapter 8 Other Inventions of Archimedes

Philip, when he arrived in Messenia, ravaged the country in a hostile spirit, acting more from anger than from reason.

For, so it seems to me, he imagined that by continually injuring men he would somehow never provoke indignation or hatred among those he was wronging.

I was led, both here and in the previous book, to speak more plainly about these matters, not only for the reasons already given before, but also because some historians have altogether passed over Philip's treatment of the Messenians,

while others, through favor toward kings or through fear, have represented Philip's impiety and lawlessness toward the Messenians not merely as no fault at all, but as something praiseworthy and successful.

Nor is it only in the case of the Messenians that writers on Philip's deeds can be seen doing this, but in other matters as well.

Hence their compositions turn out not to have the character of history at all, but rather of panegyric.

For my own part, I say that one ought neither falsely to abuse monarchs nor falsely to praise them, as many have done; one should always fit one's account to what has already been set down and to the actual character and purpose of each person.

Perhaps that is easy to say but very difficult to do, because human situations and pressures are many and varied, and men yielding to them in life often cannot say or write what truly appears to them.

For that reason some deserve pardon—but not all.

Chapter 8a

Demetrius, after rashly and recklessly attempting, with Philip's approval, to seize the city of the Messenians, was killed in the very crisis of the action. We shall explain the details of this matter when we come to the proper point in the narrative.

Chapter 9 The Assault By Land Repulsed

In this respect one might especially find fault with Theopompus. At the beginning of his history of Philip he says that what chiefly moved him to undertake the work was that Europe had never produced such a man as Philip son of Amyntas.

Yet immediately afterward, both in the preface and throughout the whole history, he represents him as utterly uncontrolled in his dealings with women, so much so that he says Philip ruined his own household by his passion and favor in this regard,

as profoundly unjust and treacherous in his treatment of friends and allies, as having enslaved many cities and seized them by fraud and violence,

and as so given over to drunkenness that he was repeatedly seen drunk in broad daylight by his friends.

And if anyone cares to read the beginning of his forty-ninth book, he will be utterly astonished at the extravagance of the historian, who among other things has ventured to say the following. I quote his very words:

“If there was among Greeks or barbarians any man who was debauched or shameless in character, all such men flocked to Macedonia and were called the king's companions of Philip.

For Philip in general disapproved of those whose conduct was orderly and who took care of their private lives, but honored and promoted those who lived extravagantly in drunkenness and dice.

Therefore he not only encouraged them in such practices, but made them athletes in every kind of injustice and foulness. For what shameful or dreadful thing did they not possess?

Or what honorable and noble quality did they not lack? Some of them, though men, went about shaved and smoothed; others, though bearded, dared to abuse one another.

They dragged about with them two or three catamites, and themselves in turn rendered the same services to others.

So one would rightly think of them not as companions but as courtesans, and call them not soldiers but common prostitutes.

For though man-slayers by nature, they were male prostitutes in their habits.

In short, to stop my long-windedness, especially when so many matters press upon me, I think that the so-called friends and companions of Philip were such beasts in nature and conduct that not even the Centaurs on Pelion nor the Laestrygonians in the Leontine plain were anything like them.”

Chapter 10 Philip Devastates Messene

Who would not reject such bitterness and such reckless abuse on the part of a historian?

For he deserves censure not only because he says things inconsistent with his own purpose, but also because he has slandered both the king and his friends, and most of all because he has framed the slander in language at once disgraceful and indecent.

If he had been speaking about Sardanapalus or his circle, he would scarcely have dared to use language so foul—and the kind of life and wantonness that man pursued we infer from the inscription on his tomb.

For the inscription says:

These are the things I possess: what I ate, what insolence I indulged in, and the pleasures I enjoyed in love.

But when speaking of Philip and his friends, one should be on guard not against accusing them of softness and cowardice, or even shamelessness, but rather lest, in trying to praise them, one should fail to speak worthily of their courage, hardiness, and, in a word, their excellence.

For it was plainly by their own hard work and daring that they turned the Macedonian kingdom from a very small one into the most renowned and greatest power of its day.

And quite apart from Philip's own achievements, what they accomplished after his death under Alexander has handed down to all men a reputation for excellence that is universally acknowledged.

A large share of the credit must perhaps be assigned to Alexander, who stood at the head of everything, though he was still very young;

yet no less belongs to his helpers and friends, who won many astonishing battles over their enemies, endured many severe labors, dangers, and hardships, and though they came into possession of immense wealth and every opportunity for indulgence, never by that means weakened their bodily strength or gave themselves to any unjust or licentious course.

In a word, all who lived with Philip and then with Alexander proved truly royal in greatness of soul, self-restraint, and daring. There is no need to list them by name.

And after Alexander's death, when they contended over the greater part of the inhabited world, they left their fame recorded in many histories.

Thus the bitterness with which Timaeus attacks Agathocles, ruler of Sicily, though it seems excessive, is still intelligible—for he is accusing an enemy, a wicked man, and a tyrant—but the invective of Theopompus does not even admit of rational defense.

Chapter 11 Criticism Of Theopompus

For after proposing to write about a king exceptionally endowed by nature for virtue, he omits none of the shameful or dreadful charges he can find.

The result is that the historian must necessarily appear either a liar and flatterer in his opening and statement of purpose, or else childish and foolish in his treatment of particulars, if he thought that by irrational and borrowed abuse he would make himself seem more credible and his praises of Philip more acceptable.

Nor indeed would anyone approve even the broad design of this writer, since he set out to write Greek history from the point at which Thucydides ended, and when he had drawn near to the age of Leuctra and to the most brilliant achievements of Greece, he threw Greece and its deeds aside and instead proposed to write the acts of Philip.

Yet it would have been far nobler and fairer to include Philip's actions within a history of Greece than to include the affairs of Greece within a history of Philip.

For no one, once preoccupied with the grandeur of Greek history and having advanced some distance in it, would voluntarily exchange that subject for the role and life of a monarch; whereas someone already occupied with a royal court, if chance and opportunity offered, might perhaps shift to the greater and more illustrious name of Greece.

So what was it that forced Theopompus to overlook contradictions of this scale? Surely only this: that the aim of the first subject was what was honorable, but the aim of the subject centered on Philip was what was advantageous.

About the error itself—his change of subject—he might perhaps have had something to say if one questioned him.

But about the shameful abuse directed against Philip's friends, I do not think he could have given any account at all, except to admit that he had strayed very far from what was fitting.

Chapter 12 Philip, Alexander, And the Diadochi

Philip, though he regarded the Messenians as enemies and set himself to ravage their land, was unable to inflict any damage worth mentioning on them; but against his most intimate friends he displayed the grossest misconduct.

For when the elder Aratus showed displeasure at what Philip had done at Messene, the king not long afterward, through Taurion who managed his affairs in the Peloponnese, had him taken off by poison.

At the time the deed was not recognized by outsiders; for the drug was not one of those that kill on the spot, but one that worked over time and produced a wasting condition.

Aratus himself, however, was not ignorant of the evil done to him. This became clear from what follows.

Concealing it from everyone else, he nevertheless could not keep silence with one of his attendants, Cephalon, because of their familiarity. When this man was carefully attending him in his illness and once noticed some spittle by the wall that was bloody, Aratus said, “So, Cephalon, this is the reward we have received for our friendship with Philip.”

Such a great and noble thing is moderation, that the sufferer was more ashamed of what had happened than the man who committed the crime—ashamed that after sharing in so many and such great deeds for Philip's advantage he had received this return for his goodwill.

And since Aratus had often held the chief office among the Achaeans, and because of the number and greatness of the benefits he had conferred upon the nation, when he died he received fitting honor both from his own city and from the Achaean League as a whole.

For they voted him sacrifices and heroic honors, and in general everything that contributes to eternal remembrance; so that, if there is any awareness among the dead, it is reasonable to suppose that he looks with approval both on the gratitude of the Achaeans and on the hardships and dangers he endured during his life.

Chapter 13 Flawed Structure of Theopompus's History

Philip had long had his mind fixed on Lissus and Acrolissus and was eager to gain possession of those places, so he set out with his army.

After marching for two days and passing through the narrow defiles, he encamped by the river Ardaxanus, not far from the city.

But when he surveyed the circuit of Lissus and saw how strongly it was secured both toward the sea and inland, by nature as well as by construction, and when he also saw nearby Acrolissus, which because of its height and general strength looked like a place no one could even hope to carry by force, he entirely gave up hope of taking the citadel, though he did not wholly despair of the city itself.

Observing that the space between Lissus and the foot of Acrolissus was suitable for an assault on the town, he decided to create a skirmish there and use a stratagem adapted to the situation.

After giving the Macedonians a day of rest and addressing to them during it the words appropriate to the moment, he hid the greater and more useful part of his light troops by night in some wooded ravines on the inland side above the space just mentioned,

while on the following day he himself, taking the peltasts and the rest of the light-armed troops, marched around to the other side of the city by the sea.

When he had gone round the city and reached the appointed place, he made it plain that he meant to begin the ascent and attack there.

Philip's presence had not gone unnoticed, and accordingly a sufficient crowd from all the surrounding parts of Illyria had gathered into Lissus.

For because they trusted in the strength of Acrolissus, they had assigned only a moderate guard to it.

Chapter 14 Aratus Poisoned

So when the Macedonians drew near, the defenders immediately poured out of the city, confident in their numbers and in the strength of the ground.

The king stationed his peltasts on the level ground, and ordered the light troops to advance toward the hills and engage the enemy vigorously. When this order was carried out,

the struggle remained equal for a time; but afterward Philip's men, giving way both to the rough terrain and to the enemy's greater numbers, were driven back.

When these men fled for refuge to the peltasts, those who had come out from the city pushed forward contemptuously, descended to the level ground, and joined battle with the peltasts.

But the men guarding Acrolissus, seeing Philip gradually drawing back his companies in succession and thinking that he was retreating altogether, were lured from their post by their confidence in the natural strength of the place.

Little by little they abandoned Acrolissus and came streaming down by the slopes into the level ground, expecting already some gain and a complete rout of the enemy.

At that very moment the troops hidden in ambush on the inland side rose unseen and charged in earnest; and at the same time the peltasts turned and attacked the enemy afresh.

The men from Lissus were thrown into confusion and, retreating in disorder, made their way back to the city; but those who had left Acrolissus were cut off by the men who sprang from the ambush.

Thus the unexpected happened: Acrolissus was taken at once and without danger, and Lissus on the following day, after severe fighting, when the Macedonians pressed the attack with energy and terror.

Philip, having thus in a wholly unexpected way made himself master of these positions, brought all the neighboring peoples into subjection by this exploit, so that most of the Illyrians voluntarily surrendered their cities to him.

For after such fortresses had been taken by force, no stronghold or security any longer seemed sufficient against Philip's power.

The Dassaretae are a people of Illyria.
