Chapter 15 Philip Takes Lissus in Illyria, B.C. 213

Bolis was a Cretan by birth who had spent a long time at the royal court in a position of command, and he was thought to possess intelligence, reckless courage, and practical experience in warfare inferior to no one.

Sosibius won this man's confidence by many arguments, made him loyal and eager for his cause, and then entrusted the enterprise to him, saying that at the present juncture he could render the king no greater service than by devising some means and method to save Achaeus.

Bolis listened for the moment and said he would consider what had been proposed, then withdrew.

But after reflecting on the matter, he came back to Sosibius two or three days later and undertook the business, saying that he had spent considerable time at Sardis and knew the ground, and that Cambylus, commander of the Cretans serving under Antiochus, was not only a fellow citizen of his but also a kinsman and friend.

It also happened that Cambylus and the Cretans under him had charge of one of the guard-posts on the rear side of the citadel, a place not open to siege-works but held secure by the continuous presence of Cambylus' men.

When Sosibius heard this plan, he concluded that either Achaeus could not possibly be saved from the situation around him, or, if there was any possible way, none would be better than Bolis. Since Bolis too showed such eagerness for the business, the matter at once began to move forward quickly.

Sosibius provided money in advance so that nothing would be lacking for the attempt, and promised much more if all went well.

By enlarging on the gratitude that would come both from the king himself and from Achaeus if he were saved, he raised Bolis to high hopes.

And Bolis, being ready for the task, waited no time but sailed off at once, taking tokens and pledges addressed to Nicomachus at Rhodes, who was believed to feel toward Achaeus with a father's loyalty and goodwill, and likewise to Melancomas at Ephesus.

For these were the men through whom Achaeus had previously managed both his dealings with Ptolemy and all his other outside negotiations.

Chapter 16 Philip V. In Illyria

When Bolis arrived at Rhodes and then afterward at Ephesus, and had shared the matter with the men just mentioned and found them ready for what he asked, he next sent a man named Arianus, one of those under his command, to Cambylus.

The message was that he had been sent out from Alexandria to recruit mercenaries, but wished to meet Cambylus about certain urgent matters; he therefore thought it necessary that they appoint a time and place where they could confer without anyone else knowing.

Arianus quickly met Cambylus and delivered the message. Cambylus readily agreed, appointed a day and a place known to both of them where he would be present by night, and sent Arianus away.

Bolis, being a Cretan and naturally full of cunning, weighed every possibility and examined every idea.

At last, meeting Cambylus according to Arianus' arrangement, he handed over the letter, and when it was laid before them they considered the matter in true Cretan fashion.

For they did not deliberate about the safety of the man in danger, nor about the trust reposed in them by those who had given them the task, but only about their own security and profit.

Thus, being both Cretans, they quickly came to the same decision: first, to divide between themselves the ten talents advanced by Sosibius,

and second, after informing Antiochus of the whole plan and making him their partner, to promise that they would hand Achaeus over to him, provided they received money and future rewards worthy of so great an enterprise.

After this agreement had been settled, Cambylus undertook the dealings with Antiochus, while Bolis arranged that after some days Arianus should be sent to Achaeus carrying ciphered letters from Nicomachus and Melancomas.

Cambylus was to consider how Arianus could safely get into the citadel and back out again.

If Achaeus accepted the plan and sent an answering message to Nicomachus and Melancomas, Bolis said that he himself would then place his services at their disposal and meet Cambylus again.

Once these arrangements had been made, they parted and each carried out what had been assigned.

Chapter 17 Bolis the Cretan Agrees to Rescue Achaeus

At the first opportunity Cambylus brought the proposal before the king.

Antiochus found the offer both agreeable and astonishing. Delighted at first, he promised everything; but then, in some distrust, he examined in detail the several plans and preparations.

Afterward, when he had become convinced and thought that the undertaking seemed to be advancing with divine favor, he urgently begged Cambylus again and again to carry it through.

Bolis acted in a similar way toward Nicomachus and Melancomas. Believing that the attempt rested on the strongest assurances, they at once prepared letters to Achaeus written in cipher, as was their custom,

in such a way that anyone who got hold of the letter would be unable to understand any of what was written in it; and they sent them, urging him to trust Bolis and Cambylus.

Arianus, by means of Cambylus, entered the citadel and delivered what had been written to Achaeus and his circle. Since he had been present from the start, he gave an exact account of every particular, even under repeated and varied questioning about Sosibius and Bolis, about Nicomachus and Melancomas, and most of all about Cambylus.

Yet he endured the examination with natural confidence and resolution, chiefly because he did not know the essential point of the scheme that Bolis and Cambylus had actually agreed upon.

Achaeus, convinced both by Arianus' answers and especially by the ciphers sent from Nicomachus and Melancomas, replied and immediately sent Arianus back again.

After this had happened several times between the two sides, Achaeus and his friends at last entrusted themselves to Nicomachus' group, since absolutely no other hope of safety remained, and told them to send Bolis along with Arianus on a moonless night, as they were prepared to place themselves in their hands.

For Achaeus had formed a plan somewhat like this: first to escape the danger immediately around him, and afterward to make his move, by a circuitous route, toward Syria.

He had great hopes that if he appeared suddenly and unexpectedly among the people of Syria while Antiochus was still occupied around Sardis, he would stir up a great movement and receive a warm welcome from the people of Antioch, Coele-Syria, and Phoenicia.

Chapter 18 Bolis Turns Traitor

So Achaeus, with expectations and calculations of this kind, awaited the arrival of Bolis.

Meanwhile Melancomas and the others, after receiving Arianus and reading the letters, sent Bolis off, encouraging him at length and setting before him great hopes if he should bring the attempt to completion.

Bolis first sent Arianus ahead to notify Cambylus of his arrival, and then himself came by night to the appointed place.

After the two had spent a day together and arranged the details of how each part should be handled, they entered the camp by night.

Their plan had been formed in this way: if Achaeus should come out of the citadel alone, or only with Bolis and Arianus or one other man, he would be easy to despise and still easier for the men in ambush to seize.

But if he came with several companions, the task would be difficult for those in whom he trusted—especially since they were eager to capture him alive, because the greatest part of the favor they expected from Antiochus depended on that.

Therefore Arianus, when leading Achaeus out, was to go in front because he knew the path, having often gone in and out that way.

Bolis was to follow behind the others, so that when they reached the place where, through Cambylus, the ambush was supposed to be ready, he might lay hold of Achaeus and make sure that in the confusion of the night and among wooded ground he neither escaped nor, in desperation, threw himself down a cliff, but instead fell alive into the enemy's hands according to their design.

After these arrangements had been agreed upon, Cambylus, on the very night Bolis arrived, led him by the same route by which he had come, and brought him alone before Antiochus.

The king received him graciously, gave pledges for the promised rewards, and urged both men at length to delay no further over the matter before them. Then they returned to their own camp,

and toward dawn Bolis went up with Arianus and entered the citadel while it was still night.

Chapter 19 Antiochus Approves the Plan

Achaeus received Bolis with marked warmth and friendliness and questioned him at length on every detail.

Judging from both his appearance and his conversation that the man had the steadiness needed for such an undertaking, he was at one moment full of joy because of the hope of safety, and at another terrified and full of anxiety because of the greatness of what hung in the balance.

Yet though he was second to no one in intelligence and quite experienced in practical affairs, he still decided that he ought not to suspend all trust entirely upon Bolis.

So he told him that for the moment it was impossible for him to come out himself, but that he would send three or four of his friends with him, and once these had met Melancomas and his people, he would make himself ready for departure.

Thus Achaeus did what he could; but he did not realize that, as the saying goes, he was trying to out-Cretan a Cretan. For Bolis had left no possible contrivance in this matter unexplored.

When the night came on which Achaeus had said he would send his friends with them, he first sent Arianus and Bolis to wait at the exit of the citadel until those who were to go out with them should arrive.

They obeyed. Achaeus then, at the very moment, communicated the plan to his wife, and Laodice, because of the suddenness of it, was beside herself. So for some time he stayed with her, pleading with her, calming her, and strengthening her with the hopes he expected from the venture.

After this he himself set out as the fifth in the party, having given ordinary clothes to the others while he himself took a plain chance garment and made his appearance as humble as possible.

He instructed one of his friends always to answer whatever Arianus and his companions said, and to keep asking them what was urgent; as for the rest, he was to say they were barbarians.

Chapter 20 The Final Arrangements are Made

When they joined Arianus and his party, Arianus led the way because of his knowledge of the path, while Bolis followed behind in accordance with the original plan, uneasy and perplexed by what was happening.

For though he was a Cretan and ready to suspect anything against his neighbor, the darkness was such that he could not make out Achaeus—not who he was, or even whether he was present at all.

The descent for the most part was steep and difficult, and in some places the path was especially dangerous and treacherous. Whenever they came to one of these places, some took hold of Achaeus while others received him below,

and because they could not entirely suppress the habitual marks of respect they were accustomed to show him, Bolis quickly understood who and which of them Achaeus was.

When they reached the place assigned to Cambylus, Bolis gave the agreed signal by a whistle. Then the men rose from the ambush and seized the others,

while Bolis himself grabbed Achaeus along with his cloak, his hands being inside it, because he feared that once Achaeus understood what was happening he might try to kill himself; for he had provided himself with a dagger.

Quickly surrounded on all sides, he fell under the power of his enemies, and at once he and his friends were led up to Antiochus.

The king, who had long been on edge in expectation of what would happen, had dismissed those who had been with him and remained awake alone in his tent with two or three bodyguards.

When Cambylus and his party entered and set Achaeus on the ground before him in bonds, Antiochus was so overcome by the unexpectedness of it that he remained speechless for a long time, and at last felt pity and burst into tears.

This happened to him, I think, because he saw how hard to guard against and how irrational are the things that come from Fortune.

For Achaeus was the son of Andromachus, brother of Laodice the wife of Seleucus, and he had married Laodice, daughter of King Mithridates, and had become master of all the country on this side of Taurus.

And yet, while he was believed, both because of his own power and because of his enemies' circumstances, to be dwelling in one of the strongest positions in the inhabited world, he was sitting bound on the ground, in the power of his enemies, before absolutely anyone knew what had happened except the men who had done it.

Chapter 21 Achaeus Takes Precautions

At daybreak, when the king's friends gathered at the tent as usual and the matter came before their eyes, the same thing happened to them as to the king: astonished at what they saw, they could hardly believe it.

When the council sat, many proposals were made as to what punishments should be inflicted on Achaeus.

It was resolved first to mutilate the wretched man, then to cut off his head, sew it into an ass's skin, and impale the body.

When this had been done and the army learned what had happened, such excitement and tumult seized the whole camp that Laodice in the citadel—who alone knew of her husband's departure—guessed what had happened from the disturbance and movement among the troops.

Soon a herald came to Laodice, explained what had happened to Achaeus, and ordered her to lay down authority and surrender the citadel.

At first inarticulate cries and dreadful lamentations possessed the people in the acropolis—not so much from affection for Achaeus as because what had happened seemed to every one utterly extraordinary and wholly beyond expectation.

After this came great uncertainty and confusion among those inside.

Antiochus, having disposed of Achaeus, kept constant pressure on the citadel, persuaded that some opening would be handed to him by the men inside, and especially by the soldiers.

And that is what happened in the end. They quarreled among themselves and split into factions, some joining Ariobazus and others Laodice. Once this had happened and the two sides distrusted one another, both quickly surrendered themselves and the citadels.

So Achaeus, after doing everything that reason could suggest, was nevertheless overcome by the faithlessness of those whom he trusted and ended his life, becoming a useful example to posterity in two ways:

first, not to trust anyone lightly; and second, not to grow boastful in prosperity, but, being human, to expect everything.

Chapter 22 Capture of Achaeus

Cauarus, king of the Galatians in Thrace, was by nature a truly royal and high-minded man, and he provided great security for the merchants who sailed into the Black Sea,

and rendered important services to the Byzantines in their wars against the Thracians and the Bithynians.

Yet this Cauarus the Galatian, though otherwise an excellent man, was corrupted by a flatterer named Sostratus, a native of Chalcedon.

Chapter 23 Antiochus In Armenia

When Xerxes was ruling from the city of Armosata, which lies on the so-called Fair Plain between the Euphrates and the Tigris, King Antiochus encamped before the city and set about besieging it.

Xerxes, seeing the king's preparations, first removed himself from danger; but after some time, fearing that if the royal residence were taken by the enemy the rest of his dominion would also be thrown into confusion, he changed his mind and sent to Antiochus saying that he wished to come to terms.

The loyal among Antiochus' friends said that once they had the young man in their hands they ought not to let him go, but advised the king, after taking the city, to hand the principality over to Mithridates, who was his sister's son by birth.

But the king paid no attention to any of this. Instead he summoned the young man, ended the hostility, and remitted most of the money that the father's unpaid tribute still owed him.

Receiving at once from Xerxes three hundred talents, a thousand horses, and a thousand mules with their equipment, he restored everything in the kingdom, gave him in marriage his sister Antiochis, and by acting in so magnanimous and kingly a fashion won over and attracted all the people of that region.

Chapter 24 The Gallic King, Cauarus

The Tarentines, in the arrogance bred by prosperity, invited Pyrrhus the Epirote. For every freedom that has enjoyed unchecked license for a long time naturally grows weary of what lies before it and then looks for a master; yet when it gets one, it quickly hates him again, because the change for the worse appears so great. And this is exactly what happened to the Tarentines then.

Whatever is still in the future always seems better than what is present.

When these troubles fell upon Tarentum and Thurii, the mass of the people grew indignant.

At first the conspirators set out from the city under the pretext of a raid, and when they came near Hannibal's camp by night, the others sat down and waited in a wooded place by the road, while Philemenus and Nicon went on to the camp.

The guards seized them and brought them before Hannibal. They said nothing about who they were or where they came from, only that they wished to meet the general.

Brought quickly to Hannibal, they said they wanted to speak with him privately.

He readily granted the interview, and they explained both their own situation and the state of their country, bringing many and varied charges against the Romans, so as not to seem to be entering into the proposed undertaking without cause.

Hannibal for the moment praised them, received their zeal kindly, and sent them away with instructions to come back and meet him again as soon as possible.

For the present, he ordered that when the first cattle driven out to pasture in the morning had gone a sufficient distance from the camp, they should boldly surround them and make off with both the animals and the herdsmen; he himself would see to their safety.

He did this because he wanted time to investigate the young men's story for himself, and at the same time to provide them with credibility among their fellow citizens, as though their expeditions outside the city really were for plundering.

When Nicon and his companions did as they had been instructed, Hannibal was delighted because he had at last obtained an opening for the enterprise he had in mind,

and Philemenus' party were even more stirred to action because the interview had taken place safely, Hannibal had been found eager, and the richness of the spoil had given them strong credibility among their own people.

For by selling some of the booty and feasting on some of it, they not only won the confidence of the Tarentines but also gained many imitators.

Chapter 25 Antiochus the Great at Armosata

After this they made a second expedition, handled matters in much the same way, and exchanged mutual pledges of good faith with Hannibal.

The agreement was that the Carthaginians would set the Tarentines free and would neither exact tribute from them in any form nor impose any other burden upon them; but once they had taken the city, the houses and lodgings occupied by Romans were to be open to the Carthaginians for plunder.

They also arranged upon a signal so that, whenever they came, the guards would promptly admit them into the camp.

Once this had been done, they were able to meet Hannibal repeatedly, sometimes going out of the city as though on a raid, at other times as though for hunting.

After putting these matters in order for the future, most of the conspirators watched for the proper opportunities, while they assigned Philemenus to manage the hunting expeditions.

For because of his excessive eagerness for the sport, he had the reputation of considering nothing in life more important than hunting.

So they entrusted it to him to win over first Gaius Livius, the officer set over the city, and then the men guarding the tower by the gate called the Temenid Gates, by means of the animals he brought in.

Having undertaken this task, partly by his own hunting and partly with game supplied to him through Hannibal, he continually brought animals in, giving some to Gaius and some to the men at the gate, so that they would open the wicket to him readily.

For he usually made his entrances and exits by night, pretending to fear the enemy, though in fact he was fitting his conduct to the design they had in hand.

When this habit of Philemenus with the gate guards had become so established that they no longer hesitated, but whenever he came near the wall and whistled by night the wicket was immediately opened for him,

they then watched for a day on which the Roman commander in the city was expected to spend the whole day with a large company in the place called the Museum near the marketplace, and fixed that day with Hannibal.

Chapter 26 The Hannibalian War — Tarentum

Hannibal had long since provided himself with the excuse of being ill, so that the Romans would not be surprised to hear that he remained for a considerable time in the same place.

At this moment he pretended illness even more strongly. His camp was three days' march from Tarentum.

When the proper time came, he selected from both cavalry and infantry those most distinguished for mobility and daring, about ten thousand in number, and ordered them to carry provisions for four days.

Then, making his camp break up just before dawn, he marched on at speed. He also chose about eighty Numidian horsemen and ordered them to ride thirty stades ahead of the army and scour the country on both sides of the road,

so that no one would catch sight of the main force, but anyone they encountered would either fall into their hands, or, if he escaped, would report in the city only that there was a raid by Numidians.

After the Numidians had advanced about one hundred and twenty stades, Hannibal took supper by a river that was hard to overlook and ran through ravines.

He assembled his officers and did not fully disclose the enterprise, but in general terms encouraged them, first, to show themselves brave men, since never before had greater prizes been set before them;

second, that each officer should keep the men under him together on the march and sternly rebuke any who left their own ranks;

and finally, that they should pay attention to the orders given and do nothing on their own initiative beyond what was commanded.

After speaking thus and dismissing the officers, he set the advance in motion just as darkness fell, eager to reach the wall around midnight, with Philemenus as guide, and having made ready for him a wild boar for the part he had to play.

Chapter 27 A Bargain Made with Hannibal

Gaius Livius, acting on the expectation fostered by the young men, spent the day with his usual companions in the Museum, and when the drinking was already at its height, toward sunset a report was brought that the Numidians were ravaging the countryside.

He concerned himself only with that, and after summoning some of his officers ordered half the cavalry to ride out before dawn and stop the enemy from plundering the land. This made him even less suspicious of the whole affair.

Nicon, Tragiscus, and the rest gathered together in the city at nightfall and waited for the return of Livius and his party.

Since they rose quickly from the banquet because it had begun early, the main body of the conspirators withdrew to a certain place and stayed there; but some of the young men met Gaius and his companions, in a loose disorderly group, joking among themselves as though they too were returning from a drinking party.

As Livius and his people were made even more unsteady by wine, laughter and playfulness sprang up on both sides the moment they met.

When they had escorted him home, Gaius went to his rest in a drunken state, as is natural for men who begin drinking in daylight, with no uneasy suspicion in his mind but full of cheerfulness and slack ease.

Nicon and Tragiscus then rejoined the young men they had left behind and, dividing themselves into three groups, watched the most favorable approaches to the marketplace, so that nothing happening either outside the walls or in the city itself would escape them.

They also took up position near the house of Gaius, knowing perfectly well that if any suspicion arose of what was coming, the first warning would be carried to Livius and that all countermeasures would begin from him.

When the return from the dinners and, in general, that sort of noise had now passed away, and the mass of the townspeople had fallen asleep, and the night was advancing while their hopes remained unshaken, they gathered together and moved forward to execute the plan.

Chapter 28 Tarentum Betrayed To Hannibal

The agreement between the young men and the Carthaginians was as follows.

Hannibal, approaching the city from the inland side on its eastern face near the so-called Temenid Gates, was to light a fire on the tomb which some called the tomb of Hyacinthus and others the tomb of Apollo Hyacinthus.

Then Tragiscus and his companions, when they saw this, were to answer with a fire from inside.

Once that signal had been completed, Hannibal's men were to extinguish their fire and advance slowly toward the gate.

With this arrangement settled, the young men passed through the inhabited quarter of the city and came to the tombs.

For the eastern side of Tarentum is full of tombs, because the Tarentines even now bury all their dead within the walls in obedience to an ancient oracle.

The god, they say, declared to them that it would be better and more profitable for them to dwell with the greater number.

Thinking that they would best obey the oracle if even their dead remained within the walls, they therefore still bury the departed inside the gates.

So the men already mentioned, after coming to the tomb of Pythionicus, waited to see what would happen.

When Hannibal and his party drew near and did what had been arranged, Nicon and Tragiscus took heart, displayed their own answering beacon, and when they saw the Carthaginians' fire again being put out, rushed at speed toward the gate,

wishing to get there first and kill the men stationed in the gate-tower, since it had been agreed that the Carthaginians should make their advance slowly and at a walk.

Everything went smoothly: the guards were caught before they were ready, some of the young men killed them, and others cut the bars.

The gates were quickly opened, and Hannibal's party arrived at exactly the right moment, having timed their march so well that they never once had to halt on the road to the city.

Chapter 29 Gaius Livius Has a Party

Once the entrance had been safely made as planned and without any disturbance at all, the Carthaginians, thinking that the greater part of the enterprise was already accomplished, now advanced boldly toward the marketplace by the broad street that rises from the district called the Deep Road.

The cavalry, however, numbering not fewer than two thousand, they left outside the walls, wishing to keep this force in reserve against any appearance from outside or against the unexpected turns that commonly arise in such undertakings.

When they came near the marketplace, they halted the force in marching order, while they themselves waited for Philemenus, anxious to see how this part too of their enterprise would succeed.

For when they had lit the fire and were about to move toward the gate, they had also sent off Philemenus, carrying the boar on a litter and accompanied by about a thousand Libyans, toward the neighboring gate, not wishing, as from the beginning, to hang the whole enterprise upon a single hope, but upon several.

Philemenus, when he came to the wall and gave his accustomed whistle, was immediately met by the guard coming down to the wicket.

When he called from outside to open quickly because they were carrying a heavy load, namely a wild boar, the guard gladly and hurriedly opened, hoping that some share of this successful hunt would also come to him, since he had always received a portion of what Philemenus brought in.

Philemenus himself, carrying the front end of the litter, entered first; with him came another man dressed as a Numidian, as though he were one of the country people, and after him came two more carrying the beast from behind.

When all four were inside the wicket, they struck down and killed the man who had opened it, as he harmlessly looked over and felt the boar, and then quietly let in through the little gate the Libyans following close behind them, about thirty in number.

Once this had been done, some were engaged in cutting the bars, others in killing the men on the tower, and others in summoning the Libyans outside by means of agreed signals.

When these too had entered safely, they advanced toward the marketplace according to the arrangement.

And when this force as well joined him, Hannibal, delighted that the business was proceeding exactly as he wished, pressed on with the plan he had set before himself.

Chapter 30 Hannibal Enters Tarentum

He selected about two thousand Celts, divided them into three bodies, and assigned to each body two of the young men who had managed the plot.

He also sent some of his own officers with them, ordering them to occupy the most favorable points along the roads leading into the marketplace.

When they had done this, he ordered the local young men to single out and spare any Tarentine citizens they encountered, crying from a distance that Tarentines should stay where they were, since they were safe.

But to the Carthaginian and Celtic officers he gave orders to kill any Romans they met. With that, they split up and carried out what had been commanded.

As the enemy's entry now became plain to the Tarentines, the city filled with shouting and confusion of every kind.

Gaius, when the enemy's entrance suddenly came upon him, realized that in his drunken state he was incapable of action. He at once rushed out of the house with his servants, came to the gate leading to the harbor, and after the guard had opened the wicket for him, slipped through and, seizing one of the little boats at anchor, was conveyed with his servants to the citadel.

At this same moment Philemenus and his people, having prepared Roman trumpets and some men able to sound them from familiarity with their use, stood in the theater and gave the signal.

The Romans, responding in arms by force of habit to the trumpet-call and hurrying toward the citadel, made the affair turn out exactly as the Carthaginians intended.

For as they came through the streets scattered and without formation, some ran into the Carthaginians and others into the Celts, and by being cut down in this manner in separate groups, a very great number perished.

At daybreak the Tarentines stayed quietly in their houses, still unable to make sense of what was happening.

For because of the trumpet and because no outrage or plundering was taking place in the city, they thought the disturbance had arisen from the Romans themselves.

But the sight of many Romans lying dead in the streets, together with some Gauls visibly stripping the bodies, brought to mind the presence of the Carthaginians.

Chapter 31 Philemenus and his Retinue Get In Too

By now Hannibal had drawn up his forces in the marketplace, and the Romans had withdrawn into the citadel, since they had long since secured it with a garrison. As the daylight became clear, Hannibal proclaimed that all Tarentines were to assemble in the marketplace without arms,

while the young conspirators went around the city crying out for freedom and urging the people to take courage, since the Carthaginians had come on their behalf.

Those Tarentines who had remained attached to the Romans understood the situation and withdrew into the citadel; but the rest obeyed the proclamation and gathered without arms, and to these Hannibal spoke graciously.

Since the Tarentines, in the joy of their unexpected hope, signaled approval of all he said with one voice, Hannibal dismissed the crowd for the moment, ordering every man to return at once to his own house and write on the door, “A Tarentine's.”

Whoever wrote the same words on a Roman dwelling, he declared, would suffer death.

He then selected the most suitable men for action and sent them to plunder the Roman houses, giving as their watchword that every unmarked house should be treated as hostile. The rest he held in reserve in formation behind them.

Chapter 32 Massacre of Romans In Tarentum

After a great and varied mass of goods had been collected from the plundering, and the Carthaginians had gained a booty worthy of their expectations,

they bivouacked under arms for the night. On the following day Hannibal consulted with the Tarentines and decided to wall off the city from the citadel, so that the Tarentines might no longer live in fear of the Romans occupying the acropolis.

First, then, he undertook to set up a palisade parallel to the wall of the citadel and to the trench that already lay before it.

But knowing clearly that the enemy would not allow this quietly and would show their strength at that point, he prepared his best troops, thinking that for the future nothing was more necessary than to strike terror into the Romans and make the Tarentines confident.

Accordingly, when the first palisade was being set up and the Romans made a bold and daring attack on the enemy, Hannibal engaged only briefly and drew out the onset of the Romans, and when most of them had come beyond the trench, he gave the signal to his own men and attacked.

A fierce struggle followed, as was natural in a narrow and enclosed space.

In the end the Romans were forced back and put to flight. Many fell by enemy hands in the fighting itself, but the greater number, pushed and hurled together into the trench, perished there.

Chapter 33 The Tarentines Themselves Spared

For the present, once Hannibal had safely completed the palisade, he remained quiet, since the enterprise had turned out exactly as he wished.

He had shut the enemy in and compelled them to stay inside their wall, afraid not only for themselves but also for the citadel,

while among the civic leaders he inspired such confidence that they believed they would be strong enough against the Romans even without the Carthaginians.

After this, at a short distance from the palisade on the side toward the city, he dug a trench parallel to both the palisade and the wall of the citadel.

Then, by piling up the earth dug from it on the edge of the embankment nearer the city and placing a palisade on top, he made from this structure a security hardly inferior to a wall.

Inside this again, leaving a suitable interval toward the city, he undertook to construct an actual wall, beginning from the place called Soteira and carrying it as far as the district called the Deep Road,

so that, even without men stationed upon them, the fortifications themselves would be enough to provide the Tarentines with safety.

Leaving behind a sufficient force and a body of cavalry suitable for guarding the city and patrolling along the wall, he encamped about forty stades from the city beside the river called by some the Galaesus but by most the Eurotas, which has that name from the Eurotas flowing by Lacedaemon.

The Tarentines have many such names in both country and city because their colony and kinship with the Lacedaemonians are openly acknowledged.

And when the wall was quickly nearing completion, thanks to the zeal and eagerness of the Tarentines and the cooperation of the Carthaginians, Hannibal next conceived the idea of taking the citadel as well.

Chapter 34 Hannibal Secures Tarentum

But just when his preparations for the siege were already complete, relief arrived by sea from Metapontum into the citadel, and the Romans, their spirits somewhat revived,

attacked the works by night and destroyed all the constructions and machines that had been prepared. After this Hannibal gave up hope of besieging the citadel; but since the wall had now already been finished, he gathered the Tarentines and showed them why it was most important in the present circumstances to gain control of the sea.

For since the citadel, as I said before, commanded the points at the entrance to the harbor, the Tarentines could not use their ships at all or sail out from the harbor, while the Romans could safely receive by sea whatever they needed.

So long as that continued, it was impossible for the city ever to be securely free.

Seeing this clearly, Hannibal explained to the Tarentines that if the men holding the citadel were cut off from hope by sea, they themselves would immediately give way, abandon the place, and surrender it.

The Tarentines agreed with what he said, but as to how this could be done under present conditions they could not at all imagine it, unless a Carthaginian fleet should appear—and that was impossible at the time.

Therefore they could not understand toward what end Hannibal was making these remarks.

But when he said that it was obvious they could themselves, without any Carthaginians, gain command of the sea at once, they were even more astonished, unable to see his idea.

Hannibal had noticed that there was a broad and well-laid street within the cross-wall, running beside it from the harbor to the outer sea, and he planned to haul the ships from the harbor across to the southern seaboard.

The moment he revealed this design to the Tarentines, they not only agreed but admired the man exceedingly, deciding that nothing could surpass his quickness of mind and daring.

Wheeled transport was quickly made ready, and the plan passed into execution almost as soon as it was spoken, such was the eagerness and abundance of labor assisting the scheme.

In this way the Tarentines dragged their ships over into the outer sea and safely blockaded the Romans in the citadel, having cut off all outside relief.

Hannibal, after leaving a guard for the city, broke camp with the army, and on the third day returned to his original palisaded camp, where he remained for the rest of the winter.

Chapter 35 Additional Fortifications

The Roman general Tiberius was caught in an ambush and, after meeting the danger bravely together with those about him, lost his life. In cases of this sort, whether one ought to blame the sufferers or excuse them, it is not safe to pronounce absolutely, because many men who have done everything that reason required have nevertheless fallen into the power of those who readily violate the laws of justice recognized among mankind.

Yet one should not on that account lazily refrain from judgment altogether; rather, by looking to the occasion and the circumstances, one should decide which generals deserve blame and which deserve pardon. What I mean will become clear from the following examples.

Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, suspected the ambition of Cleomenes and fled from Sparta; but not long afterward he was persuaded to return and entrusted himself to that same man.

He was therefore deprived at once of both power and life, and left himself no defense before posterity.

For when the situation remained the same, and the ambition and power of Cleomenes had actually increased, how could a man who handed himself over to those very persons from whom he had earlier escaped only with difficulty reasonably expect anything but such an end?

In the same way Pelopidas of Thebes, though he knew Alexander the tyrant's lawlessness and clearly understood that every tyrant regards the champions of liberty as his bitterest enemies, not only persuaded Epaminondas to stand forth as leader of freedom for Thebes and indeed for Greece,

but even when he himself had gone to Thessaly as an enemy bent on overthrowing Alexander's monarchy, he nevertheless consented to serve as ambassador to him a second time.

As a result, after falling into the enemy's hands, he inflicted great harm on the Thebans and ruined the reputation he had formerly won, by rashly and uncritically trusting the very man in whom he least ought to have trusted.

Something similar happened to Gnaeus the Roman commander during the Sicilian war, when he irrationally put himself into the enemy's power; and there are many others as well.

Chapter 36 The Tarantines Blockade the Romans

Therefore men who hand themselves over to the enemy without due caution deserve blame, but those who take every precaution that the case allows do not deserve censure.

For to trust no one at all would in the end make action impossible, whereas to act reasonably after obtaining all the guarantees one can is beyond reproach.

The guarantees available are oaths, children, wives, and, greatest of all, a previous life and character.

Thus, if someone is deceived and trapped through such guarantees as these, the reproach lies not with the sufferer but with the men who committed the act.

One ought therefore above all to seek guarantees of such a kind that the man trusted cannot violate them.

Since that is hard to find, the second-best course is to take every reasonable precaution, so that even if we fail, we do not lose the pardon of outside observers. And this has happened in the case of many before now.

The clearest example, and the one nearest to the times with which the present discussion is concerned, is what happened to Achaeus.

He omitted none of the precautions possible for prudence and safety, but after providing for everything so far as human intelligence could, he nevertheless fell into the enemy's hands.

Yet what happened won pity and pardon from outsiders for the sufferer, and brought only slander and hatred upon those who did the deed.

Chapter 37 Fall of Syracuse, B. C. 212

He counted the courses of stone; for the tower was built of regular blocks, so that it was quite easy to calculate from the ground the height of the battlements.

Some days later a deserter reported that the people in the city had now for three days been holding a public sacrifice to Artemis, and that, though they were using scanty food because of scarcity, they had wine in abundance, a large supply having been provided both by Epicydes and by the Syracusans. Marcus then selected a section of wall where it was lower, and, thinking it likely that the men would be drunk because of the festivity and the lack of solid food, decided to test the hope he had formed.

Two ladders were quickly made, fitted to the height of the wall, and he then proceeded with the remaining arrangements, speaking openly to the men best suited for the climb and for facing the first and most conspicuous danger, and filling them with great hopes for the future.

He also chose the men who were to assist them and carry the ladders, explaining nothing except that they should be ready for what was ordered. When they had obeyed exactly as instructed, he roused the foremost men at the proper hour of night.

Sending ahead the men with the ladders, along with a standard, a military tribune, and the others assigned to the attempt, and reminding them again of the rewards awaiting brave conduct, he then roused the entire army and sent out the leading contingents, one by one, under their standards and at intervals.

When about a thousand had gone, he himself followed after a short delay with the rest of the force.

The men carrying the ladders managed to set them safely against the wall without being noticed, and those appointed to the ascent at once mounted without hesitation.

When these too had escaped notice and had gained a firm position upon the wall, all the rest, no longer preserving the original order but each as he could, came running up by the ladders.

At first, as they advanced along the wall, they found the guard-posts deserted. For the men gathered in the towers because of the sacrifice were either still drinking or had long since fallen asleep in drunkenness.

Therefore the Romans came suddenly upon the first and then the next groups and quietly killed most of them before they knew what was happening.

Then, when they came near the Hexapylae and descended, they broke open the first postern gate built into the wall, through which they admitted the general and the rest of the army. In this way the Romans took Syracuse.

None of the citizens realized what was happening, because of the distance, since the city was large.

And the Romans took courage because they held the high ground around Epipolae.
