So such people are deceived in the honorable position they expected, though they generally do not miss the immediate advantage they sought.

But when a king is attempting the greatest enterprises, embracing the whole inhabited world in his ambitions, and still has all his hopes intact, how can it seem anything but irrational and mad to proclaim his own faithlessness and instability at the very first and smallest opportunities that present themselves?

Chapter 24a Egypt

III. Affairs of Egypt

Since in each year we recount the events that happened in the various parts of the inhabited world in their proper sequence, it is plain that in some cases the end must be presented before the beginning, whenever that section first falls into place in the division of the whole work and, in the progress of the narrative, the event containing the conclusion naturally comes before the one containing the beginning and first design.

Chapter 25 Ptolemy Epiphanes Succeeds To the Crown

Sosibius, the false guardian of Ptolemy, had the reputation of being a shrewd and long-enduring instrument of evil at court.

He had first arranged the murder of Lysimachus, son of Arsinoe daughter of Lysimachus and Ptolemy; next that of Magas, son of Ptolemy and Berenice daughter of Magas; third, that of Berenice, mother of Ptolemy Philopator; fourth, that of Cleomenes the Spartan; and fifth, that of Arsinoe daughter of Berenice.

Three or four days later, after building a platform in the largest colonnaded court of the palace, Agathocles and Sosibius summoned the bodyguards and household attendants, together with the officers of infantry and cavalry.

When they had assembled, Agathocles and Sosibius mounted the platform, announced the deaths of the king and queen, and proclaimed the customary mourning to the crowd.

After this they placed the diadem on the child’s head and proclaimed him king, and then read out a forged will in which the dead king had supposedly left Agathocles and Sosibius as guardians of the boy.

They urged the officers to support the child and preserve his rule. Then they brought in two silver urns, pretending that one contained the king’s bones and the other those of Arsinoe.

In reality one did contain the king’s remains, but the other was filled with spices. After these arrangements they at once proceeded with the funeral. At that moment the truth about Arsinoe became plain to everyone.

For once her death was established, people began to inquire into the manner of it. Since no other explanation was available, and the true rumor had already spread though still disputed, what had really happened now fixed itself in every mind. So a great disturbance arose among the crowd.

No one paid any attention to the king, but with regard to Arsinoe some recalled her orphaned condition, others the outrage and humiliation she had suffered throughout her life, and when to these was added the misfortune of her death, the city was filled with groaning, tears, and unceasing lamentation.

Yet to those who judged rightly, these things were less signs of affection for Arsinoe than of hatred toward Agathocles and his circle.

When Agathocles had placed the urns in the royal burial chambers and ordered mourning clothes laid aside, his first move was to issue the troops two months’ pay, convinced that the hatred of the masses could be dulled by appealing to their advantage. He next administered the customary oath taken at the proclamation of kings.

He also sent away Philammon, who had overseen the murder of Arsinoe, making him governor of the Libyan districts around Cyrene, and he placed the child in the hands of Oenanthe and Agathocleia.

After this he sent Pelops son of Pelops to Asia, to Antiochus the king, to urge him to preserve the friendship and not violate the treaty made with the child’s father; and he sent Ptolemy son of Sosibius to Philip both to settle the matter of an intermarriage alliance and to ask for help if Antiochus should attempt any more open breach of faith.

He also appointed Ptolemy son of Agesarchus as envoy to the Romans, not because he meant him to press the embassy in earnest, but so that, once he reached Greece and met friends and relatives there, he would stay away.

For his aim was to remove all prominent men from his path.

He also sent Scopas the Aetolian to Greece to recruit mercenaries, providing a large sum of gold for the advance payments.

He had two purposes in this. One was to use the men thus recruited in the war against Antiochus. The other was to send the existing mercenaries out to country forts and settlements, and by means of the newcomers refill and remake the household regiments, the palace guards, and likewise the rest of the city watch.

He thought that troops recruited and paid by himself would feel no sympathy with what had happened before, because they knew nothing of it, and that, having all their hopes both of safety and advancement resting in him, they would be ready assistants and collaborators in whatever he ordered.

All this happened before the negotiations with Philip, as I have said; but since those matters had to be taken first in the order of the narrative, it was necessary to handle these events in this way, by first describing the audiences, the diplomatic dealings, and the dispatch of the ambassadors.

Agathocles, then, once he had removed the most distinguished men and to a great extent checked the anger of the crowd by distributing pay, promptly returned to his former habits. He filled the places of his friends

by drawing from the attendants and other servants the most worthless and shameless men.

He himself spent most of day and night in drunkenness and the excesses that follow it, sparing neither mature women nor brides nor unmarried girls, and he did all this with the most offensive display.

So there was widespread and manifold resentment; yet no relief or help appeared, and instead outrage, arrogance, and carelessness were continually added to the burden.

Thus the old hatred among the people flared up again, and everyone renewed in memory the misfortunes that had already befallen the kingdom through these very people.

But since they had no respectable figure to stand in front and on whom they might lean while pressing their anger against Agathocles and Agathocleia, they stayed quiet, watching for one remaining hope in Tlepolemus and fixing their attention on him.

As long as the king lived, Tlepolemus attended to his own affairs. But when the king died, he quickly won over the troops and once more became commander in the region of Pelusium.

At first he reported what was being done in the interest of the king, believing that there would be some governing council to hold the guardianship of the child and oversight of the whole state.

But when he saw that the men fit to serve as guardians had been removed and that Agathocles was boldly seizing control of everything, he quickly changed his purpose. Fearing the danger that threatened him because of the enmity between them, he gathered troops around himself and sought money, so that he might not lie easy to the hand of any enemy.

At the same time he did not despair of gaining the guardianship of the child and the chief direction of affairs for himself, thinking that by his own judgment he was far more worthy than Agathocles in every respect, and hearing besides that both the troops under his command and those in Alexandria placed their hopes in him as the man who would put down Agathocles’ insolence.

With dispositions such as these on his side, the quarrel soon grew, since both factions helped to inflame it.

For Tlepolemus, eager to win over the generals, the taxiarchs, and the officers under them, carefully arranged drinking parties; and at these gatherings, partly from the flattery of his companions and partly from his own impulse — since he was young and the conversation was carried on over wine — he cast jibes at the family of Agathocles, at first riddling and obscure, then ambiguous, and at last open and filled with the bitterest abuse.

He mocked the writer of lampoons, the sambuca-girl, the lady’s maid, and that little page who had done and suffered everything at drinking parties when as a boy he poured wine for the king.

And because those present were always laughing and adding something to the mockery, the matter quickly reached Agathocles and his circle.

Once the hostility had become open, Agathocles at once began circulating slanders against Tlepolemus, claiming that he was alienating himself from the king and inviting Antiochus to seize control of affairs.

He found many plausible arguments for this, twisting some from actual events and inventing and dressing up others from the beginning.

He did this because he wished to provoke the crowd against Tlepolemus. But the result was the opposite. For since the people had long fixed their hopes on Tlepolemus, they were delighted to see the quarrel growing hot.

The beginning of the popular movement, however, arose from certain such causes as these. Nicon, a kinsman of Agathocles, had while the king was still alive been placed in command of the fleet...

Chapter 26 Another Murder Committed by Agathocles

Agathocles first assembled the Macedonians, and before them he entered with the king and Agathocleia.

At first he acted the part of a man unable to say what he wished because of the flood of tears that overcame him.

But after repeatedly wiping his face with his cloak and mastering the display, he lifted up the child and said, “Take this boy, whom his father, when dying, placed in this woman’s arms” — pointing to his sister — “and entrusted, Macedonians, to your keeping.

Her goodwill contributes only a slight advantage toward his safety; but his whole situation now lies with you and in your hands.

For Tlepolemus has long been clearly seen, by those who observe matters rightly, to aim at greater things than suit his station, and now he has fixed the very day and moment on which he means to take up the diadem.

Do not trust me about this,” he said, “but men who know the truth and are now present from the facts themselves.”

With that he brought in Critolaus, who declared that he had personally seen altars being prepared and sacrificial victims made ready among the populace for the proclamation of the diadem.

But when the Macedonians heard this, far from pitying him, they simply paid no attention to what he said. Muttering and whispering among themselves, they made such a confused uproar that Agathocles himself did not even understand how the assembly came to an end.

The same thing happened in his addresses to the other groups as well.

Meanwhile many people were sailing down from the upper camps, and some urged their kinsmen, others their friends, to help in the present crisis and not stand by while they were openly outraged by men so unworthy.

What especially stirred the masses to punish those in power was the knowledge that the coming struggle lay in their own hands, because they controlled all the supplies being brought into Alexandria.

Chapter 26a

Agathocles also killed Deinon son of Deinon, and this deed, as the proverb says, was the most just of all his injustices.

For when the letters concerning the murder of Arsinoe came into his hands, he had the chance to reveal the plot and save the kingdom, but instead he cooperated with Philammon and so became responsible for all the evils that followed. Later, after the murder had been carried out, he kept recalling it, pitying the victims and regretting that he had let such a moment pass; and when this became known to Agathocles, he at once met the punishment that suited him and lost his life.

Chapter 27 Growing Hatred of Agathocles

Something done by Agathocles and his own circle also helped to intensify the anger both of the people and of Tlepolemus.

They seized Danae, the mother-in-law of Tlepolemus, from the temple of Demeter, dragged her unveiled through the middle of the city, and threw her into prison, wishing to make their quarrel with Tlepolemus unmistakably public.

The populace, outraged by this, no longer kept their talk private or confined to secret circles. Some by night wrote on the walls in every quarter, while others by day gathered in groups and openly expressed their hatred toward those in power.

Agathocles and his circle, seeing what was happening and holding sinister expectations about their own future, sometimes planned flight; but because nothing had been prepared for that course, thanks to their own incompetence, they abandoned the idea.

At other times they drew up lists of conspirators and partners for a daring stroke, intending at once to cut down some enemies, arrest others, and after that seize tyrannical power.

While they were considering these plans, a report reached them against a certain Moeragenes, one of the bodyguards, that he was revealing everything to Tlepolemus and cooperating with him because of his connection with Adaeus, then commander at Bubastus.

Agathocles immediately ordered Nicostratus, the secretary in charge of correspondence, to arrest Moeragenes and examine him thoroughly, putting every form of torture before him.

So Moeragenes was at once arrested by Nicostratus and taken to a secluded part of the palace, where he was first questioned directly about the charges.

When he admitted nothing, he was stripped, and some were making ready the instruments of torture while others, with whips in hand, were taking off their cloaks.

At just that moment one of the attendants ran up to Nicostratus, whispered something in his ear, and hurried away again. Nicostratus followed close behind him,

saying nothing but repeatedly slapping his thigh as he went.

Chapter 28 Moeragenes Escapes

What happened to Moeragenes then was astonishing and beyond belief.

The floggers were standing there all but ready to bring down their whips, while others at his feet were preparing the instruments of compulsion.

But once Nicostratus had gone away, they all stood gaping and staring at one another, constantly expecting the man to come back.

As time passed, those standing by gradually slipped away one by one, until Moeragenes was left alone. Then, passing through the palace, he unexpectedly escaped half naked into a tent of the Macedonians near the court.

Finding them by chance at breakfast and gathered together, he told them what had happened to him and the strange way he had been saved.

At first they doubted him, but when they saw him naked they were forced to believe.

Taking advantage of this reversal, Moeragenes begged the Macedonians with tears to secure not only his own safety, but also that of the king and, above all, their own.

For, he said, destruction was plain to all unless they seized the moment when the hatred of the crowd was at its height and everyone stood ready to punish Agathocles.

And that moment, he said, was now in full strength.

Chapter 29 A Revolt Decided Upon By the Army

Moeragenes said that what was chiefly needed was only someone to take the lead. When the Macedonians heard this, they were stirred to anger, and in the end they were persuaded by him. They immediately went first to the Macedonian tents and then to those of the other soldiers.

All these camps lay together, facing one side of the city.

Since the impulse had long been ready in the minds of the crowd and needed only someone to call it forth and dare the first move, the affair, once begun, blazed up like fire.

For before four hours had passed, every class, military and civilian alike, had agreed on the attack.

And at this crisis chance too contributed greatly toward the outcome.

For Agathocles received both a letter and the report of spies: the letter, written by Tlepolemus to the troops, declared that he would arrive soon, and the spies reported that he was already there.

This drove Agathocles so completely out of his senses that he gave up both action and even deliberation about the danger confronting him, but at his usual hour went off to drinking and there carried through the gathering in his customary fashion.

His mother Oenanthe, in deep distress, went to the Thesmophorium, the sanctuary being open because of an annual sacrifice.

At first she knelt and made magical appeals to the goddesses; then she sat down by the altar and kept still.

Most of the women, enjoying the sight of her distress and misery, kept silent. But some female relatives of Polycrates and certain other noblewomen, still unaware of the full crisis, approached and tried to comfort her.

She cried out in a loud voice, “Do not come near me, you beasts! I know you well: your hearts are against us, and you pray to the goddesses for the worst things against us.

But I still trust that, if the gods will it, you shall taste your own children yet.”

After saying this she ordered the women carrying rods to drive them off and beat any who refused to obey.

Taking this as their excuse, all the women withdrew, lifting up their hands to the gods and praying that she herself might experience those very things she was threatening to inflict on others.

Chapter 30 A Mob Assembles

By now the men had decided on revolution, and when in every household the anger of the women was added to the general resentment, the hatred flared up doubly.

As soon as night came on, the whole city was full of noise, lights, and people running about.

Some were gathering in the stadium with shouting, some were calling one another to join them, and some were darting about and hiding in unsuspected houses and places.

Already the open spaces around the palace, the stadium, the broad street, and the area by the Dionysian theater were full of every sort of crowd.

When Agathocles learned what was happening, he roused himself out of drunkenness — he had only just dismissed his drinking party — and taking with him all his relatives except Philo, he went to the king.

After briefly lamenting his own misfortune to the boy and taking him by the hand, he went up into the covered passage that lay between the Maeander and the wrestling-school and led to the entrance of the theater.

After securing the first two doors, he retreated to the third with two or three bodyguards, the king, and his own family.

These doors were made of lattice-work so that one could see through them, though they were fastened with double bars.

By this time the crowd had assembled from the whole city, so that not only the open ground but even the steps and rooftops were packed with people, and there arose a mixed uproar of shouting and cries, since women and children were mingled with the men.

For in disturbances of this kind, both in Carthage and in Alexandria, the children play no smaller a part than the men.

Chapter 31 The King Surrendered To the Soldiers

As day was already beginning to show, the shouting was still confused, but one demand stood out clearly from it: they were calling for the king.

The Macedonians were the first to act. Rising up, they seized the gatehouse used for public business in the royal palace.

A little later, when they discovered where in the court the king was, they went round to the passage, forced open the first doors, and when they came to the second demanded the child with loud cries.

Agathocles and his party, seeing now how matters stood for them, begged the bodyguards to go as envoys on their behalf to the Macedonians and declare that they resigned the guardianship, all other authority and honors, and even all their revenues.

They asked only that life itself be granted them, together with the bare necessities of food, so that by returning to their original station they might be incapable of harming anyone in future, even if they wished to.

None of the bodyguards obeyed except Aristomenes, the very man who after some time came to hold chief power in the state.

This man was an Acarnanian, and when later in life he gained control of affairs, he seemed to have governed both king and kingdom in the noblest and most honorable way; but to the same degree he had earlier flattered Agathocles in the days of his prosperity.

For he was the first, when Agathocles dined at his house, to present him alone among the guests with a golden crown, an honor custom allowed only to kings themselves.

He was also the first who dared to wear Agathocles’ likeness on his ring; and when a daughter was born to him, he named her Agathocleia.

But enough of that. After receiving these instructions, Aristomenes went out through a small wicket and came to the Macedonians.

He spoke briefly and explained Agathocles’ intention. At first the Macedonians wanted to stab him on the spot, but some held up their hands over him and begged the crowd to spare him, and so he returned with the order that either he must come back bringing the king with him or else not come out again himself.

Having sent Aristomenes back with these words, the Macedonians came up to the second doors and forced them open as well.

When Agathocles and his party saw from the Macedonians’ actions as much as from their answer how violent they were, they first stretched out their hands through the door, while Agathocleia thrust out the breasts which, she said, had nursed the king, and with every sort of pleading begged the Macedonians to grant them bare life.

Chapter 32 The King Conducted to the Stadium

But when, for all their many lamentations over their own fate, they accomplished nothing, at last they sent out the child with the bodyguards.

The Macedonians took the king, quickly set him on horseback, and led him to the stadium.

As soon as he appeared, there arose a great shout and clapping. They stopped the horse, lifted the boy down, led him forward, and seated him in the royal place.

Among the crowd there was at once both joy and grief: they were delighted that the child had been brought, but displeased that the guilty parties had not been arrested and made to suffer the punishment they deserved.

So they kept shouting continuously, demanding that the authors of all the evils be brought out and made an example.

As the day wore on and the crowd found no one on whom it could vent its rage, Sosibius — the son of Sosibius, and at that time one of the bodyguards, a man especially attentive to the king and the state —

seeing both that the people’s fury was unchangeable and that the child was suffering from the unfamiliar faces around him and from the uproar of the crowd, asked the king whether he would hand over to the people those who had wronged him or his mother.

When the boy nodded, Sosibius told some of the bodyguards to announce the king’s decision, while he himself lifted the child up and took him to his own nearby house to be cared for.

As the king’s command was announced, the whole place burst with clapping and shouting.

At that moment Agathocles and Agathocleia separated and withdrew to their respective lodgings.

Then some of the soldiers — some volunteering, others pushed on by the crowd — rushed off to search for them.

Chapter 33 The Massacre of Agathocles and Family

The beginning of bloodshed and slaughter came about by the following chance occurrence.

One of Agathocles’ attendants and flatterers, a man named Philo, came staggering out into the stadium still drunk.

Seeing the rush of the crowd, he said to those standing by that, just as before, they would regret it again if Agathocles appeared.

Some of those who heard him abused him, others shoved him about, and when he tried to defend himself, some tore off his cloak while others thrust their spears into him and stabbed him.

As soon as he was dragged insultingly into the middle, still writhing, and the crowd had tasted blood, they all began eagerly waiting for the arrival of the others.

Not long after, Agathocles himself came first, led in bound. The moment he entered, some rushed at him and stabbed him on the spot — an act done more by friends than by enemies, since they spared him the punishment he truly deserved. After him came Nicon,

then Agathocleia naked with her sisters, and after them all the rest of the family.

Last of all they dragged Oenanthe from the Thesmophorium into the stadium, bringing her in naked on horseback.

When they were all handed over to the crowd together, some bit them, some stabbed them, some gouged out their eyes, and whenever one fell, they tore the limbs apart, until they had mangled every one of them.

For there is something terrible in the savagery of the people of Egypt when their passions are stirred.

At that same time certain girls who had grown up with Arsinoe learned that Philammon, the man who had supervised the queen’s murder, had arrived three days earlier from Cyrene, and so they rushed to his house.

Forcing their way in, they beat Philammon to death with stones and clubs, strangled his little son, and then dragged Philammon’s wife naked into the street and killed her too.

Such was the end of Agathocles, Agathocleia, and their relatives.

Chapter 34 Why Agathocles Died As He Did

I am not unaware of the marvels and embellishments with which some writers have treated these events in order to astonish their hearers, giving more attention to ornamental comment than to the facts themselves and what truly matters in them.

Some refer everything to Fortune and place before the eyes the uncertainty and slipperiness of her workings; others dwell on the unexpectedness of what happened and try to supply the events with causes and probabilities.

But I did not intend to handle the matter in that way, because Agathocles was neither distinguished for military daring and power,

nor successful and admirable in administration, nor finally remarkable for courtly cleverness and villainous intrigue — the sort of ability by which Sosibius and many others managed to survive under one king after another. In Agathocles’ case the opposite of all this was true.

For he had indeed gained an astonishing advancement because of Philopator’s incapacity to rule.

But after gaining that position, and after receiving the most favorable opportunity to preserve his power following the king’s death, he lost both his authority and his life through his own cowardice and indolence, being condemned in a very short time.

Chapter 35 Agathocles Not a Good Example of Mutability of Fortune

Therefore one ought not to attach an elaborate moralizing discourse to men of this kind, as I said, in the way one might with Agathocles and Dionysius of Sicily and certain other men whose public careers won a real name.

For one of those men began from a common and humble station, and Agathocles — as Timaeus says mockingly — was a potter who left wheel, clay, and smoke behind and came as a young man to Syracuse.

At first, in their own generations, both became tyrants of Syracuse, a city that at that time had attained the highest distinction and greatest wealth.

Afterward they were thought sovereigns of all Sicily and masters of certain parts of Italy as well.

Agathocles even made an expedition against Libya and at last died still in possession of those high fortunes.

That is why they say that Publius Scipio, the first conqueror of the Carthaginians, when asked whom he considered the most practical men of affairs and the boldest with sound judgment, answered: the Sicilians Agathocles and Dionysius.

With men like those, it is fitting to draw readers to attention, perhaps also to speak of Fortune and of human affairs, and to add an instructive reflection. But with the men we have been discussing, that is wholly out of place.

Chapter 36 Agathocles Was Not An Important Person

For these reasons we have rejected any expanded treatment of Agathocles.

And not least because all startling reversals have a single force at first encounter that is worth notice, but afterward the hearing and sight of them become not only useless but positively wearisome.

For those who present anything to ear or eye ought to aim at two ends, benefit and pleasure; and in history, where this obligation especially applies, excessive dwelling on shocking disasters misses both.

For who would wish to imitate extraordinary catastrophes? And again, no one enjoys continually seeing and hearing things that are unnatural and beyond common human expectation.

We are indeed eager once, and at first, to see or hear such things, in order to learn that what seemed impossible is actually possible.

But once we believe it, no one enjoys lingering over the unnatural, and no one would wish to encounter the same thing again and again.

So what is told ought to be either admirable or pleasant; but an excessive account of disasters beyond these belongs more properly to tragedy than to history.

Still, perhaps one should pardon those who do not attend either to nature or to the general course of events throughout the inhabited world.

For they suppose that the greatest and most astonishing events in history are precisely those they themselves happen to meet with or hear about from others, and so they fix all their attention on these.

Accordingly they do not notice that they are spending too much speech on things that are neither novel, since others have already recounted them, nor able to give either profit or pleasure. But let this be enough on that point.

Chapter 37 Antiochus

IV. Affairs of Asia

King Antiochus at the beginning of his reign seemed a man of vast designs, boldness, and energetic execution.

But as he advanced in age he proved far inferior both to his earlier self and to the expectation others had formed of him.

Book XVI

Chapter 1 Philip V. Wages War with Attalus, King of Pergamum, and the Rhodians.

I. Affairs in Macedonia

When King Philip reached Pergamum and thought he had, as good as with his own hands, finished off Attalus, he gave free rein to every kind of outrage.

In indulging a temper almost like madness, he directed most of his anger not against men but against the gods.

For the defenders of Pergamum easily beat back his assaults because the place was so strong, and Attalus had taken such careful precautions that Philip could get no profit from ravaging the countryside.

So he turned his rage against the seats and sanctuaries of the gods, insulting, as it seems to me, not Attalus so much as himself.

He did not merely burn and pull down temples and altars. He even smashed the stones so that nothing he had destroyed could ever be rebuilt.

After he had laid waste the Nicephorium, cutting down its grove, throwing down its enclosing wall, and digging up from the foundations many large and costly shrines,

he first moved against Thyatira, and from there marched into the plain of Thebe, thinking that this district would provide him with especially rich plunder.

But when this hope also failed, he came to the place called the Holy Village and kept sending to Zeuxis, asking him to provide grain and the other support required by their treaty.

Zeuxis pretended that he was carrying out the treaty, but in reality he had no wish to give Philip any real and substantial help.

Chapter 2 Great Sea-fight Off Chios Between Philip and the Allied Fleets of Attalus and Rhodes, B. C. 201

Since the siege was going badly for him, and the enemy were pressing him hard with a growing number of decked ships, Philip was at a loss and deeply uneasy about what was to come.

As the situation allowed no real choice, he put to sea unexpectedly, contrary to the enemy's expectation.

For Attalus and his side still thought he would remain where he was and continue the mining works.

Philip was especially eager to make his departure sudden, convinced that if he could throw them into confusion he would then sail the rest of the way safely along the coast to Samos.

But he was badly mistaken in his calculations. As soon as Attalus and Theophiliscus saw him putting out, they at once took action.

Their own departure was somewhat disordered, because, as I said, they had been convinced that Philip was staying where he was.

Even so, by rowing with great energy they attacked, Attalus striking the enemy's right wing and van, while Theophiliscus attacked the left.

Philip, caught in these dangerous circumstances, gave the signal to the ships on his right, ordered them to turn their prows toward the enemy and fight hard at close quarters, while he himself withdrew under the little islands that lay in the channel, taking some light craft with him and watching how the battle would turn out.

The ships engaged on Philip's side were fifty-three decked vessels, besides undecked ships, and a hundred and fifty light boats and cutters, since he had not been able to equip all the ships at Samos.

The enemy had sixty-five decked ships, including those from Byzantium, together with nine triemioliai and three triremes.

Chapter 3 Incidents of the Sea-Fight

The fighting began from the ship on which Attalus sailed, and at once all the nearby ships engaged each other without waiting for orders.

Attalus ran into an enemy eight-banked ship and struck it a well-placed blow below the waterline. After a long struggle among the men on deck, he finally sank it.

Philip's ten-banked flagship, however, fell into the enemy's hands in a most unexpected way.

A triemiolia slipped in beneath it and crashed violently into its hull amidships, below the upper bank of oars, where it became jammed fast. The helmsman could no longer recover control of the larger ship.

Because that smaller craft hung attached to it, the flagship became unwieldy and slow in every movement. At that moment two quinqueremes came up,

struck it on both sides, and destroyed both the vessel and the marines on board, among them Democrates, Philip's admiral.

At the same time Dionysodorus and Deinocrates, brothers who served as admirals under Attalus, charged enemy ships, the one a seven-banker and the other an eight-banker, and fought with remarkable daring.

Deinocrates, colliding with an eight-banked ship, received a blow above the waterline because the enemy vessel had a high-built prow, but he struck the enemy below the waterline. At first he could not break free, though he repeatedly tried to back away.

So, while the Macedonians fought bravely from the enemy ship, he was brought into extreme danger.

But Attalus came to his aid and, by driving into the enemy vessel, broke the two ships apart. Deinocrates was unexpectedly freed,

while all the marines on the enemy ship, after a gallant resistance, were killed, and their now-empty vessel fell into Attalus' hands.

Dionysodorus, on the other hand, made his attack with great force but missed the ramming blow. As he passed close by the enemy, he lost the whole right-side bank of oars, and the timbers that carried his towers were smashed together.

Once this happened, the enemy surrounded him on every side.

In the uproar and confusion that followed, all the rest of his marines were lost with the ship, but Dionysodorus himself, with only two others, managed to swim off to the triemiolia that was coming to help him.

Chapter 4 The Sea-Battle Undecided

The fight among the rest of the ships was evenly matched.

Philip had the advantage in the number of his light craft, but Attalus had the advantage in the number of decked ships.

So on Philip's right wing matters stood in such a way that the final outcome was still uncertain, though Attalus had the better hopes.

As for the Rhodians, at first, just as I said before, they became separated from the enemy during the putting out to sea; but because they were far superior in speed, they caught up with the Macedonian ships in the rear.

At first they bore down on the withdrawing vessels from astern and crippled their oars.

But when Philip's ships began turning back to support those in danger, and the Rhodian ships that had started later joined Theophiliscus,

then both sides formed line abreast, prow to prow, and charged gallantly, encouraging one another with trumpets and shouts.

If the Macedonians had not stationed their light boats among the decked ships, the sea-fight would quickly and easily have been decided. As it was, these became obstacles to the Rhodians in many ways.

For once the original order had been broken by the first collision, all the ships became mixed together.

As a result the Rhodians could neither break through the enemy line easily nor turn their ships freely nor use their own advantages at all, because the small craft kept running into their oars, hampering the rowing, or else striking their prows and sometimes their sterns, and so interfering alike with helmsmen and rowers.

Yet in direct prow-to-prow encounters they used a skilled maneuver.

By lowering their own prows they took the enemy's blows above the waterline, while they themselves struck the enemy below the waterline and made their damage hard to repair.

Still, they did this only rarely, because in general they avoided close entanglements, since the Macedonians fought bravely from the decks whenever the struggle came hand to hand.

Most often the Rhodians would row through the enemy formation and shear off their oars; then, wheeling around again, they would strike some from behind and others broadside while they were still turning, either holing them or disabling some essential part of their equipment.

By this method of fighting they destroyed a great number of the enemy ships.

Chapter 5 Attalus Barely Escapes Capture

The most brilliant and dangerous fighting was done by three Rhodian quinqueremes: the flagship on which Theophiliscus sailed, the ship commanded by Philostratus, and a third steered by Autolycus with Nicostratus aboard.

This last ship rammed an enemy vessel and left its own ram fixed in the hull. The enemy ship sank with all hands, but because sea water was pouring into Autolycus' ship through the prow, he and his men were surrounded by the enemy.

At first they fought bravely, but in the end Autolycus, wounded, fell overboard in his armor, and the rest of the marines died fighting stoutly.

At that moment Theophiliscus came to help with three quinqueremes. He could not save the ship, because it was already full of water, but after smashing two enemy vessels he drove their marines overboard.

Soon, however, he himself was swarmed by a larger number of light boats and decked ships, and he lost most of his marines after they had fought with conspicuous bravery.

He himself received three wounds and, after exposing himself to the utmost danger, only just saved his own ship, with Philostratus coming to his aid and nobly sharing the peril.

Once he had rejoined his own squadron, he attacked the enemy again from a fresh angle. Though his bodily strength was failing from his wounds, the courage in his spirit made him more brilliant and more formidable than before.

So there were really two sea-battles taking place far apart. Philip's right wing, in keeping with the original plan, kept edging toward land and was not far from Asia,

while the left wing, having turned back to support the ships in the rear, was fighting the Rhodians not far from Chios.

Chapter 6 Attalus Abandons his Ship but Escapes

Even so, Attalus' side was decisively overpowering Philip's right wing and was already drawing near the little islands under which Philip had anchored to watch the battle.

Attalus then noticed one of his own quinqueremes disabled and sinking under attack from an enemy ship, and he rushed to help it with two quadriremes.

When the enemy ship turned and tried to escape toward land, Attalus pursued too eagerly, eager to capture it.

Philip saw that Attalus had become separated by a wide distance from his own fleet. He took four quinqueremes, three hemioliai, and the nearest light boats, dashed forward, cut Attalus off from his own ships, and forced him in great panic to run his vessels aground.

Once that happened, the king himself escaped with his crews to Erythrae, but Philip captured the ships and the royal equipment on board.

Yet Attalus' people showed ingenuity even in this crisis. They spread the finest pieces of the royal equipment out on the deck.

So when the first Macedonians came up in their light craft and saw quantities of cups, purple robes, and the like, they gave up the pursuit and turned aside to plunder these things.

That is how Attalus managed to make his retreat safely to Erythrae.

Philip, though badly worsted in the battle as a whole, was elated by what had happened to Attalus. He put to sea again, busily gathering his ships and encouraging his men, saying that they had won the battle.

People found this plausible because Philip's men were towing away the royal ship, and so many assumed that King Attalus himself had perished.

But Dionysodorus guessed what had happened to his king, raised the signal, gathered his own ships around him, and then sailed off safely to the harbors on the Asiatic coast.

At the same time the Macedonians who had been fighting the Rhodians, after suffering badly for a long time, gradually slipped out of danger by withdrawing in small groups under the pretense of hurrying to help their own ships.

The Rhodians towed off some captured ships, destroyed others with their rams, and then sailed away to Chios.

Chapter 7 Losses in the Battle

Philip lost, in the battle against Attalus, a ten-banked ship, a nine-banked ship, a seven-banked ship, a six-banked ship, ten other decked ships, three triemioliai, and twenty-five light boats, together with their crews.

In the battle against the Rhodians he lost ten decked ships and about forty light boats, while two quadriremes and seven light boats with their crews were captured.

On Attalus' side one triemiolia and two quinqueremes were sunk, while two quadriremes and the king's own ship were captured.

Of the Rhodian fleet, two quinqueremes and one trireme were destroyed, but none were taken.

Of the men, the Rhodians lost about sixty, Attalus about seventy, while Philip lost about three thousand Macedonians and six thousand sailors and marines.

About two thousand of Philip's Macedonians and allies were taken alive, while of their opponents about seven hundred were captured.

Chapter 8 Philip Vainly Claims the Victory At Chios

Such was the outcome of the naval battle off Chios.

Philip claimed the victory on two grounds: first, because he had forced Attalus ashore and had taken his ship; second, because after anchoring at the place called Argennum he seemed to have made his anchorage among the wrecks.

In keeping with this claim, on the next day he gathered up the wreckage and recovered for burial such of the dead as could still be recognized, all to strengthen that appearance.

But that he did not really believe he had won was soon proved by both the Rhodians and Dionysodorus.

For on the following day, while Philip was still occupied with these matters, they communicated with one another, sailed out against him, drew up their ships in line before him, and then, when no one put out to meet them, sailed back again to Chios.

Philip had never before lost so many men at one moment, either by land or by sea, and he took the event very hard. Much of his spirit for the enterprise was broken.

Still, toward the outside world he tried by every means to hide his discouragement, though the facts themselves would not allow it.

Quite apart from everything else, even what followed after the battle struck horror into all who saw it.

So many men had been destroyed that on the very day of the battle the whole strait was full of corpses, blood, weapons, and wreckage, and on the following days the beaches could be seen heaped together in confused masses with all these things mingled.

Because of this, not only Philip himself but all the Macedonians were thrown into no small shame and consternation.

Chapter 9 Death of Theophiliscus

Theophiliscus survived for one day. After writing home to his city about the sea-fight and appointing Cleonaeus to command the forces in his place, he died of his wounds.

He was a brave man in battle and, in the purpose that guided him, worthy of remembrance.

If he had not dared to be the first to lay hands on Philip, everyone else would have let the opportunity slip, intimidated by Philip's boldness.

But by beginning the war himself he forced his own country to rise with the occasion, and he compelled Attalus not to delay and merely make preparations, but to fight in earnest and face the danger.

So the Rhodians were right to honor him after his death with distinctions that encouraged not only those then alive but also future generations to meet the critical needs of their country.

Chapter 10 The Indecisive Battle of Chios Was Followed by Another Off Lade, in Which Philip Was Partly Successful1 1 “Jam cum Rhodiis et Attalo navalibus certaminibus, neutro feliciter, vires expertus.” Livy, 31, 14.

After the battle off Lade had been fought, with the Rhodians out of his way and Attalus not yet involved, it is plain that Philip could have completed his voyage to Alexandria. Nothing makes Philip's madness in this matter clearer than that.

What then checked the rush of his purpose?

Nothing but the natural course of events.

For people often pursue impossible aims when they view them from far off, because the greatness of their hopes overpowers their reason;

but when they come close to the actual business, they abandon their plans just as irrationally, since their calculations are thrown into confusion by the difficulty and awkwardness of the obstacles they meet.

Chapter 11 Philip's Operations in Caria, B.C. 201

After this Philip made some attacks that came to nothing because the town was so strong, and then withdrew again, plundering the forts and settlements in the countryside.

From there he marched against Prinassus. He quickly prepared wicker screens and the rest of the siege equipment and began trying to take the city by mines.

When this attempt also proved useless, because the ground was rocky, he devised the following trick.

By day he had noises made underground, as if the miners were at work, and by night he had earth brought from outside and piled beside the mouths of the tunnels, so that the people in the city, judging from the amount of earth heaped up, might be frightened.

At first the people of Prinassus held out bravely. But then Philip sent and told them that he had already propped up a stretch of their wall two plethra long, and asked whether they preferred to withdraw safely or all perish together with their city

when the props were set on fire. Believing what he said, they then surrendered the city.

Chapter 12 Description of Iassus

The city of Iassus lies in Asia, on the gulf between the Poseidium of the Milesians and the city of Myndus, a gulf some call by one name and most call the Bargylian Gulf, after the cities built around its inner recess.

The Iassians claim that they were originally colonists from Argos, and later from Miletus, because after they had suffered losses in the Carian war their ancestors brought in a son of Neleus, founder of Miletus. The city is ten stades in circuit.

At Bargylia there is a famous and widely believed story that the image of Artemis Cindyas, though it stands in the open air, is never touched by snow or rain,

and among the people of Iassus there is a similar story about Artemis Astias. Some historians have repeated such tales.

But I, for my part, never know how to stop opposing and resenting such declarations by historians throughout my whole work.

It seems to me that stories of this kind belong wholly to childish foolishness, since they go beyond not only what is probable but even what is possible.

To say that certain bodies cast no shadow when placed in the light shows a mind that has lost all sense. Yet Theopompus does this when he says that those who enter the forbidden sanctuary of Zeus in Arcadia become shadowless.

That is very much like the story told here.

When such tales help preserve the reverence of the common people toward the gods, one may grant some indulgence to historians who indulge in marvels and story-making about them.

But excess must not be permitted. It may be difficult to mark the exact measure in every case,

but it is not impossible. So if such ignorance and false opinion stay within narrow bounds, let them be excused; but anything excessive should, in my judgment, be rejected.

Chapter 13 Affairs in Greece

II. Affairs in Greece

I have already explained what policy Nabis, tyrant of the Lacedaemonians, adopted from the beginning, and how, after driving out the citizens, he freed the slaves and married them to their masters' wives and daughters.

I have also shown how he built up his power by making Sparta a kind of inviolable refuge for those who fled their own countries because of impiety or wickedness, and so gathered there a crowd of lawless men.

I will now explain how, at this same time, although he was the ally of the Aetolians, Eleans, and Messenians, and was bound by oath and treaty to help them if anyone attacked them, he disregarded all these pledges and attempted a treacherous attack on the city of the Messenians.

Chapter 14 Digression on the Merits of the Historians Zeno and Antisthenes of Rhodes

Polybius says that since some historians of particular episodes have written about this same period, in which the events at Messene and the sea-battles already mentioned took place, he wishes to discuss them briefly.

He will not speak of them all, but only of those whom he thinks worthy of remembrance and distinction, namely Zeno and Antisthenes of Rhodes.

I judge them worthy of notice for several reasons. They were contemporaries of the events, they had practical political experience, and in general they composed their histories not for profit but for reputation and from a sense of duty proper to public men.

Since they write about the same events that I do, I must not pass them over in silence, lest, because of the name of their country and the idea that naval matters especially belong to the Rhodians, readers eager to learn should follow them rather than me wherever I disagree with them.

Now to begin with, both of them describe the battle off Lade as no less serious than the battle off Chios, indeed as more active and more daring both in detail and in the overall conduct of the engagement, and they declare that the victory belonged to the Rhodians.

For my part, I could allow historians some inclination to favor their own countries, but not to make statements that are contrary to the facts.

Writers already commit enough errors from ignorance, errors that it is hard for any human being completely to avoid.

But if we deliberately write falsehoods, whether for the sake of country or friends or favor, how are we any different from those who make their living by such conduct?

Just as they ruin the credit of their compositions by measuring everything by gain, so political writers, drawn by hatred or affection, often fall into the same fault.

Therefore readers ought to watch carefully in this matter, and writers ought to be on their guard themselves.

Chapter 15 The Battle of Lade According to Zeno and Antisthenes

What I mean becomes clear from the facts themselves. These writers admit in their detailed account of the battle off Lade that two Rhodian quinqueremes were captured by the enemy with all their crews.

They also admit that when one ship in the battle hoisted a sail because it had been damaged and was taking on water, many of the nearby ships did the same and withdrew toward the open sea.

In the end, they say, the admiral was left with only a few vessels and was forced to do the same.

For the moment they were driven by conditions to anchor off the territory of Myndus, and on the next day they put out again and crossed over to Cos.

The enemy meanwhile secured the quinqueremes and, anchoring off Lade, took up quarters in the Rhodian camp.

They add that the Milesians, astonished by what had happened, crowned not only Philip but also Heracleides because of the expedition.

So after relating facts that are obviously the marks of defeat, they still declare, both in their detailed account and in their general conclusion, that the Rhodians were victorious.

And this although the actual dispatch sent at that time by the admiral to the council and prytaneis still remains in their own prytaneum, and it agrees not with the judgments of Antisthenes and Zeno but with mine.

Chapter 16 Zeno's Account of the Attack on Messene

Next after this they write about the treacherous breach of treaty against the Messenians.

In this section Zeno says that Nabis set out from Sparta, crossed the Eurotas near the river called Hoplites, and marched by the narrow road past Poliasium until he reached the region around Sellasia.

From there, he says, he made for Thalamae and by way of Pharae came to the river Pamisus.

I hardly know what one ought to say about this. The whole statement is as absurd as if someone were to say that a man set out from Corinth, crossed the Isthmus, and by the Scironian road immediately came to the Contoporia and then traveled past Mycenae to Argos.

For these places are not just slightly out of line with one another; they lie in opposite directions. The Isthmus and the Scironian road are east of Corinth, while the Contoporia and Mycenae lie toward the southwest.

So it is wholly impossible to get to the latter by way of the former.

The same thing is true in the case of Laconia.

The Eurotas and the region of Sellasia lie to the northeast of Sparta, while Thalamae, Pharae, and the Pamisus lie to the southwest.

So a man intending to go into Messenia by way of Thalamae ought not to go toward Sellasia, indeed ought not even to cross the Eurotas at all.

Chapter 17 Some of Zeno's Mistakes Due to Ignorance

Besides this, he says that Nabis began his return from Messene by the gate leading to Tegea.

But that is senseless. Megalopolis lies between Tegea and Messene, so it is impossible that any gate at Messene should be called the gate to Tegea.

There is, however, among the Messenians a gate called the Tegean Gate, and it was by this that Nabis made his return. Zeno was misled by the name and supposed that Tegea lay close to Messenia.

But it does not. Between Messenia and the territory of Tegea lie both Laconia and the land of Megalopolis.

Finally, he says that the Alpheus disappears underground right from its source, travels a long way beneath the earth, and emerges near Lycoa in Arcadia.

In fact, the river disappears not far from its source and, after being hidden for ten stades, comes up again.

After that it flows through the territory of Megalopolis, at first gently, then growing larger, and after running clearly through that whole region for about two hundred stades it reaches Lycoa, having by then also taken in the stream of the Lusius and become altogether deep and unfordable.

Still, all these faults seem to me to be mistakes that admit excuse. Some arose from ignorance, and what he wrote about the naval battle came from affection for his own country.

What then could one rightly blame in Zeno? That he has spent more effort not on investigating the facts or mastering the subject, but on the polish of his language, and often shows pride in that, just as many other distinguished writers do.

I say that one should indeed take care and work hard to report events properly; that obviously contributes no little, indeed a great deal, to history.

But sensible men should not treat this as the chief and primary matter. Other parts of history are far finer, and on those a statesman ought rather to pride himself.

Chapter 18 Zeno's Account of the Battle of Panium

What I mean may be made especially clear in the following way.

When this same writer describes the siege of Gaza and the battle line drawn up by Antiochus against Scopas in Coele-Syria near Panium, he shows such concern for verbal embellishment that he leaves no room for rhetorical showmen who compose display pieces meant to astonish the crowd.

But for the facts he shows such contempt that his ease and inexperience as a historian are once more beyond all measure.

For when he sets out first to explain Scopas' line of battle, he says that the phalanx, together with a few cavalry, rested with its right wing on the slope of the hills, while its left wing, along with all the cavalry stationed there, stood on the level ground.

He then says that before dawn Antiochus sent his elder son Antiochus with part of the army to seize the higher ground above the enemy,

and that at daybreak he himself led the rest of his forces across the river between the two camps and drew them up on the plain, placing the phalangites in a single straight line opposite the middle of the enemy formation, and the cavalry on the left and right of the phalanx, including the armored horse under the command of the younger Antiochus, one of the king's sons.

After this, he says, Antiochus stationed the elephants in front of the phalanx at intervals, along with the Tarentines under Antipater, filled the spaces between the elephants with archers and slingers, and himself took position behind the elephants with the household cavalry and the hypaspists.

Yet after laying out the battle in this way, he says that this younger Antiochus, whom he had placed on the level ground on the enemy's left with the armored cavalry, charged down from the hills, routed the cavalry under Ptolemy son of Aeropus, and pursued them. This Ptolemy had command of the Aetolians stationed on the plain on the left wing.

Meanwhile, he says, the phalanxes, once they joined battle, fought stubbornly.

But he does not even see that they could not possibly have joined battle at all with elephants, cavalry, and light troops drawn up in front of them.

Chapter 19 Zeno's Description Implausible

After this he says that the phalanx, being outmatched in agility and pressed by the Aetolians, fell back step by step, while the elephants received those who gave way and, crashing into the enemy, rendered great service.

But how this happened behind the phalanx is not easy to understand, or how, once there, they rendered such great service.

For once the phalanxes had actually joined, it would no longer have been possible for the elephants to distinguish friend from foe among those who came before them.

Besides this, he says that the Aetolian cavalry were hampered in the battle by being unused to the appearance of elephants.

But, according to his own account, the cavalry originally stationed on the right remained unharmed, while the entire mass of cavalry assigned to the left had already fled after being defeated by Antiochus and his force.

What part of the cavalry, then, was there in the middle of the phalanx to be frightened by the elephants?

And where was the king, or what service did he render in the battle, when he had with him the finest body of infantry and cavalry around his own person? Nothing at all is said about these matters.

And where was the elder son Antiochus, who with part of the army had seized the high ground on the right?

For this man does not even return to camp in Zeno's account after the battle. Naturally enough, because Zeno assumed that the king had two sons named Antiochus, when in fact there was only one serving on that campaign.

Again, how is it that Scopas both withdrew first from the battle and also last? Zeno says that when Scopas saw the younger Antiochus appearing from the pursuit in the rear of the phalanx, he gave up hope of victory and began to retreat.

But afterwards he says that the greatest danger came when the phalanx was surrounded by elephants and cavalry, and that Scopas was the last to withdraw from the fighting.

Chapter 20 Zeno Acknowledges His Error

Such things, and in general blunders of this kind, seem to me to bring great shame on historians.

Therefore one ought above all to try to master every part of history, for that is the finest course. But if this is not possible, then one should take the greatest care with the most necessary and important parts.

I have been led to say this because I now observe, just as in other arts and pursuits, that what is true and useful in each field gets neglected,

while what is designed for display and appearance is praised and imitated as something great and marvelous, because it is easier to produce and wins approval more cheaply, just as in other forms of writing.

As for Zeno's ignorance of places in Laconia, since the error was a serious one, I did not hesitate to write to him personally.

I judged it honorable not to treat other people's mistakes as personal advantages, as some are accustomed to do, but to take thought, so far as I could, for correcting not only my own writings but those of others as well, for the common good.

When he received the letter and saw that it was impossible to revise the passage because his books had already been published, he was deeply distressed, though he could do nothing; still, he accepted my action graciously.

And in the same spirit I would ask my readers now and in time to come: if ever I am found knowingly falsifying matters in this work and overlooking the truth, let them censure me without pardon,

but if I err through ignorance, let them grant me indulgence, especially because of the size of my history and the vast compass of the events it covers.

Chapter 21 Egypt — Character of Tlepolemus

III. Affairs in Egypt

Tlepolemus, who had charge of the royal government in Egypt, was young in years and had spent his life continuously in military service, with a certain distinction.

By nature he was high-strung and ambitious, and in general he brought many qualities useful for action, but many harmful ones as well.

He was capable of commanding in the field and handling military operations, naturally courageous, and well suited for dealings with soldiers.

But for the management of complicated affairs, which requires steady attention and sobriety, and for guarding money and organizing finances with an eye to advantage, he was the least capable of all men.

Because of this he soon not only ruined himself but damaged the kingdom as well.

For once he had the control of the treasury, he spent most of the day playing ball and competing with young men in exercises with arms.

Then from these pursuits he went straight to drinking parties, and the greater part of his life was passed in these amusements and among these companions.

And whatever part of the day he set aside for audiences, he spent distributing—or rather, if one must tell the truth, scattering—the royal money among envoys who had come from Greece, among the artists of Dionysus, and above all among officers and soldiers of the court.

In fact, he simply did not know how to refuse. If anyone addressed him in a flattering way, he at once handed over whatever was ready to his hand.

So the evil kept growing, increasing by its own momentum.

For everyone who unexpectedly received a favor from him poured out extravagant thanks, both for what had already been gained and for what might still be gained in the future.

And when he heard the universal praise lavished on him, the toasts drunk to him at banquets, the inscriptions in his honor, and the songs and jests sung about him through the whole city, he became at last soft and foolish, more and more puffed up and more and more reckless in dispensing favors to foreigners and soldiers.

Chapter 22 Intrigues At Alexandria

These foreign and military favors irritated the people at court, and they watched everything closely, resented his arrogance, and increasingly contrasted him with Sosibius.

For Sosibius was thought to be more prudent in his management of the king than his years would suggest, and to conduct dealings with outsiders in a manner worthy of the trust committed to him, namely the royal seal and the king's person.

At this time Ptolemy son of Sosibius returned from Philip.

Before sailing from Alexandria he had already been full of vanity, partly from his own nature and partly from the favorable position his father had gained.

But once he landed in Macedonia and mixed with the young men at court, he came to think that Macedonian manliness consisted in their style of footwear and dress. So he came back imitating all these things, convinced that foreign travel and association with Macedonians had made a man of him, while those at Alexandria remained mere slaves and weaklings.

As a result he immediately grew jealous of Tlepolemus and set himself against him.

Since all the courtiers agreed with him, because Tlepolemus was handling the kingdom and its funds not like a guardian but like an heir, the quarrel quickly grew.

At first Tlepolemus, as hostile talk reached him through the spying and meddling of the courtiers, ignored it and treated their words with contempt.

But when they actually dared to sit together and openly criticize him in the middle of the court, though he was absent, for mismanaging the kingdom,

he was angered. He summoned the council and came forward saying that they made their slanders against him secretly and in private, whereas he thought it right to make his accusation against them openly and face to face.

After this public speech he also took the seal away from Sosibius, and once he had that in his possession, he managed everything henceforth according to his own will.

Chapter 22a

IV. Affairs in Syria

When King Antiochus sacked the city of the Gazans, Polybius says:

"It seems to me both just and fitting to give the people of Gaza the testimony they deserve.

For though they are no different from the other people of Coele-Syria in courage for war, they surpass them greatly in loyalty to a common cause and in keeping faith, and taken altogether they possess a courage that cannot be shaken.

For when the Persians invaded, while all the others were terrified by the greatness of that empire and surrendered themselves and their cities to the Medes, the Gazans alone all stood firm and endured the danger by accepting a siege.

And when Alexander came, while not only the others had surrendered, but even the Tyrians had been violently enslaved, and there was hardly any hope of safety left for those who opposed Alexander's onset and force, they alone among the peoples of Syria held out and proved stronger than every expectation.

They acted in much the same way in the present crisis as well, leaving nothing undone in their eagerness to preserve their loyalty to Ptolemy.

Therefore, just as we single out good men for honorable mention in our histories, so too we ought in the same way to preserve a public memory of those cities that, by inherited character and deliberate choice, are accustomed to act nobly."

Chapter 23 Scipio's Triumph

V. Affairs in Italy

Publius Scipio returned from Libya not long after the events just described.

Since the expectation of the multitude matched the greatness of his achievements, the splendor surrounding the man and the goodwill of the people toward him were correspondingly great.

And this happened reasonably and as it should.

For men who had never expected to drive Hannibal out of Italy or rid themselves and their families of the danger hanging over them now thought themselves securely beyond all fear and all peril, and not merely safe but masters of their enemies. So their joy knew no bounds. And when Scipio entered in triumph,

then, as the spectacle of the procession vividly reminded them of the dangers they had passed through, they became even more deeply moved both in their thankfulness to the gods and in their affection for the man responsible for such a great reversal.

For Syphax, king of the Masaesylii, was led through the city at that time in the triumph among the prisoners, and some time later he died in custody.

After all this was over, the people in Rome kept celebrating splendid games and festivals for many days, with Scipio's own generosity providing the means.

Chapter 24 War Between Rome and Philip V

VI. Affairs in Macedonia and Greece

At the beginning of winter, in the year when Publius Sulpicius became consul at Rome, King Philip was staying at Bargylia. Seeing that the Rhodians and Attalus were not disbanding their fleet, but actually filling up their crews and watching the coast with even greater energy, he was in a very troubled state and had many and varied thoughts about the future.

He was anxious at once about getting out from Bargylia and foresaw danger by sea, and at the same time he distrusted the situation in Macedonia and by no means wanted to winter in Asia, being afraid of both the Aetolians and the Romans.

For he was well aware of the embassies being sent to Rome against him,

now that affairs in Libya had come to an end. So he was in extreme distress, yet for the moment he was forced to stay where he was and, as the saying goes, live the life of a wolf.

For because his army was starving, he fed it now by plundering and stealing from some, now by using force against others, and at times even by fawning in a way unnatural to him; sometimes they got meat, sometimes figs, and sometimes only a very scanty amount of grain.

Some of these supplies were provided by Zeuxis, others by the people of Mylae, Alabanda, and Magnesia. When any of them gave him something he flattered them, but when they did not, he barked at them and plotted against them.

In the end he tried, through Philocles, to bring about operations against the city of Mylae, but the attempt failed through the stupidity of the scheme.

As for the territory of the Alabandians, he ravaged it like enemy land, saying that he had to secure provisions for his army.

Polybius of Megalopolis also says in the sixteenth book of his Histories: "Philip, the father of Perseus, when he was overrunning Asia and was in want of provisions for his soldiers, received figs from the Magnesians because they had no grain. For that reason, when he got possession of Myus, he granted the place to the Magnesians in return for the figs."

Chapter 25 King Attalus At Athens

The people of Athens sent envoys to King Attalus both to thank him for what had already happened and to urge him to come to Athens so that they could consult together about the present crisis.

A few days later the king learned that Roman ambassadors had arrived at the Piraeus, and since he thought it necessary to meet them, he sailed there in haste.

When the Athenian people heard that he was coming, they passed lavish decrees about meeting him and about the whole manner of receiving the king.

After Attalus landed at the Piraeus, he spent the first day in business with the Roman envoys, and he was delighted to see that they remembered their former common cause and were ready for war against Philip.

On the next day he went up to the city with the Romans and the Athenian magistrates amid great ceremony. Not only those in office and the cavalry came out to meet them, but all the citizens as well, with their children and wives.

When they met, the goodwill shown by the crowd to the Romans, and still more to Attalus, left nothing beyond it.

When he entered by the Dipylon gate, priestesses and priests stood in lines on both sides. Then all the temples were opened, victims were placed beside every altar, and they invited him to offer sacrifice.

Finally they voted him such honors as they had scarcely ever granted so quickly to any of their earlier benefactors.

Among other things they created a tribe named after Attalus and enrolled him among their eponymous founders.

Chapter 26 Athens Votes for War Against Philip

After this they summoned an assembly and invited the king to address it.

But he declined, saying that it would be vulgar to come forward in person and recount his own benefactions to those who had received them.

So they gave up asking him to appear, but requested him to write down what he thought best for the present circumstances and to hand it over.

He agreed and wrote it, and the presiding magistrates then introduced the letter.

Its main points were a reminder of the earlier benefactions he had shown the people, an account of what he had done against Philip in the present crisis,

and finally an appeal to join the war against Philip, together with a solemn warning that if they did not now choose to share nobly in the hostility together with the Rhodians, the Romans, and himself, but later, after letting the occasion pass, wanted to share in the peace once others had won it, they would miss what was truly best for their country.

When this letter was read, the people were ready to vote for war, both because of what was said and because of their goodwill toward Attalus.

Then the Rhodians also came forward and spoke at length to the same effect, and the Athenians resolved to declare war on Philip.

They also received the Rhodians magnificently, crowned their state with a crown for valor, and granted all Rhodians equal civic rights, because, among other services, they had restored to them the ships that had been captured, together with the men on board.

After accomplishing this, the Rhodian envoys sailed away with the fleet to Ceos and the islands.

Chapter 27 The Romans Warn Philip Not to Attack Greece

At the time when the Roman ambassadors were staying in Athens, Nicanor, acting for Philip, was raiding Attica as far as the Academy.

The Romans sent a herald ahead to him, met with him, and told him to report to Philip that the Romans called on the king to make war on none of the Greeks, and to submit the wrongs done to Attalus to judgment before an impartial tribunal.

They added that if he did this, he could remain at peace with Rome, but if he refused to obey, the opposite would follow. Nicanor heard this and withdrew.

The Romans delivered the same message about Philip to the Epirotes as they sailed past Phoenice, and to Amynander when they went up into Athamania; similarly they addressed the Aetolians at Naupactus and the Achaeans at Aegium.

Having thus made these terms known to Philip through Nicanor, they themselves sailed on to Antiochus and Ptolemy to arrange a settlement.

Chapter 28 Activity and Energy of Philip

It seems to me that many men have managed to make a good beginning and to keep their enthusiasm strong enough for the growth of their enterprises,

but to carry their purpose through to the end, and even when fortune stands against them to make reason supply what impulse lacks, belongs to only a few.

So in this case one might rightly blame Attalus and the Rhodians for lack of effort, while admiring in Philip what was kingly and high-spirited and his persistence in his purpose—not praising his whole character, but noting the force of his energy at that moment.

I make this distinction so that no one may think I am contradicting myself, since just now I was praising Attalus and the Rhodians and blaming Philip, and now I seem to do the reverse.

For this is exactly why I said at the beginning of my work that it is necessary sometimes to praise and sometimes to blame the same men.

Circumstances often change men's purposes for the worse, and often for the better,

and sometimes, by their own natural character, men are at one time moved toward what is right and at another toward the opposite. One of these things, I think, happened in Philip's case here.

For stung by his losses, and acting largely out of anger and passion, he adapted himself to the needs of the moment with a kind of fierce, almost inspired energy. In this way he rose up against the Rhodians and King Attalus and carried through the next series of actions.

I was led to say this because some men, like bad runners in a race, give up their purpose near the finish, while others win over their rivals most of all at that very point.

Chapter 29 The Hellespont Compared with Gibraltar

Philip wanted to deprive the Romans of their bases and landing points in that region.

That way, if he later chose to cross again into Asia, he would have Abydos as his landing place.

As for the position of Abydos and Sestos and the advantages of these cities, it seems to me pointless to describe everything at length, because all who gain even a little benefit from such knowledge already know these places on account of their special character.

Still, to remind my readers of the main points is not useless for the present discussion.

One can best understand the situation of these cities not simply by looking at the places themselves, but by setting beside them and comparing the places that I am about to mention.

Just as no one can sail from what some call Ocean and others the Atlantic Sea into our sea without passing through the mouth by the Pillars of Heracles,

so no one can sail from our sea into the Propontis and the Pontus without making the passage through the channel between Sestos and Abydos.

And as if Fortune had deliberately shaped the two straits in answer to one another, the passage by the Pillars of Heracles turns out to be many times wider than the Hellespont.

The one is sixty stades across, while that at Abydos is two, as though one might infer this from the fact that the outer sea is so much greater than ours.

Yet the crossing at Abydos is more serviceable than that at the Pillars of Heracles.

For the former, inhabited on both sides, has the character of a gate because of the intercourse between the two shores: at times people even bridge it for those who wish to cross on foot between the continents, and at all times it is traversed by shipping.

But the channel at the Pillars of Heracles is rarely used and by few, because the peoples living at the far ends of Libya and Europe have little intercourse with one another and because the outer sea remains largely unknown.

The city of Abydos itself is enclosed on both sides by promontories from Europe, and it has a harbor able to shelter ships lying there from every wind.

Apart from entering that harbor, there is nowhere at all near the city where one can anchor, because of the sharpness and violence of the current running through the strait.

Chapter 30 The Siege of Abydos

Philip, after surrounding the Abydenians partly with palisades and partly with entrenchments, besieged them both by land and by sea.

This siege was not remarkable for the scale of the preparations or for the variety of inventions in the engineering, by which besiegers and besieged usually try to outdo one another in skill.

But in respect to the courage of the defenders and the extraordinary greatness of their spirit, it was, if any siege ever was, worthy of memory and record.

At first the inhabitants of Abydos, trusting in themselves, stoutly withstood Philip's preparations. Of the machines brought against them by sea, they shook some apart by striking them with stone-throwers and destroyed others with fire, so that the enemy could scarcely drag their ships back out of danger.

Against the works on land they also held out bravely for a time, not despairing of mastering the enemy.

But when the outer wall fell because of the mines, and then the Macedonians by further tunneling reached the inner wall that had been built behind the breach,

they then sent ambassadors, Iphiades and Pantagnotus, instructing Philip to take over the city on condition that he let the soldiers from Rhodes and Attalus depart under truce, and that he allow all free persons to save themselves, each wherever he chose, with the clothing on his body.

But Philip ordered them to leave everything to his decision or else fight bravely.

Chapter 31 The People of Abydos Resolve to Conquer or Die
