Moreover, it is in the Greeks' own interest that the power of Macedon be greatly humbled, but by no means that it be removed altogether,"

—for they might soon enough come to learn the lawless violence of the Thracians and Gauls; this, he said, had already happened more than once.

In sum, he declared that he and the Romans present judged that, if Philip undertook to do everything the allies had previously demanded, they would grant him peace, subject also to the approval of the Senate; but the Aetolians were free to decide for themselves about their own affairs.

After this Phaeneas wanted to argue that everything done before would be in vain, since Philip, if he slipped through the present crisis, would soon make this the starting point for fresh troubles all over again;

but Titus, on the spot from his seat and heatedly, said: "Stop your nonsense, Phaeneas. For I will manage the settlement in such a way that Philip, even should he wish it, will be unable to wrong the Greeks."

Chapter 38 Philip Comes to the Conference

And so on these terms they parted for the day. On the next day the king arrived, and on the third, when everyone had gathered for the conference, Philip came in and skillfully and shrewdly cut short the hostility of all of them.

For he said that he conceded and would carry out everything that the Romans and the allies had previously demanded, and that on the remaining points he would refer the decision to the Senate.

When he had said this, all the rest fell silent, but Phaeneas of the Aetolians said: "Why then, Philip, do you not restore to us Larisa Cremaste, Pharsalus, Phthiotic Thebes, and Echinus?"

Philip told them to go ahead and take them over, but Titus said they should take none of the others—only Phthiotic Thebes;

for when he had approached the Thebans with his army and called on them to entrust themselves to Rome's protection, they had refused. Therefore now, he said, since they had been subdued in war, he had the authority to deal with them as he saw fit.

Phaeneas and his party were indignant and argued that the cities ought to be theirs: first, because they had now fought alongside the Romans, they should recover the cities that had formerly belonged to their league;

and second, in accordance with their original treaty of alliance, by which, of whatever was captured in war, the movable goods were to be the Romans' and the cities the Aetolians'. To this Titus replied that they were mistaken on both counts.

For the alliance had been dissolved at the time when they made their settlement with Philip and abandoned the Romans; and even if the alliance were still in force,

they were entitled to recover and take over not any cities that had voluntarily put themselves under Rome's protection—as all the cities in Thessaly had now done—but only those that had been taken by storm.

Chapter 39 Peace Terms Agreed On

The rest of the congress was pleased with what Titus said, but the Aetolians heard it with resentment, and there was being born what proved to be the beginning of great evils.

For out of this dispute and this spark there blazed up, not long afterward, both the war against the Aetolians and the war against Antiochus.

The decisive factor in Titus's eagerness to come to terms was that he had learned that Antiochus had set out from Syria with an army, directing his advance toward Europe.

For this reason he was anxious that Philip, fastening on this hope, might decide to hold his cities and drag out the war, and that then, when another consul arrived, the credit for the whole achievement might be deflected onto that man.

So it was conceded to the king, as he requested, that upon obtaining a four-month armistice he should at once give Titus the two hundred talents and his son Demetrius as a hostage, along with some others of his friends, and that concerning the whole settlement he should send envoys to Rome and refer the decision to the Senate.

For the time being they then parted, having given each other pledges about the whole matter, on the condition that, if the terms of the settlement were not ratified, Titus would return to Philip the two hundred talents and the hostages.

After this everyone sent envoys to Rome, some to support and others to oppose the settlement.—

Chapter 40 Foolish Credulity

Why on earth is it that, though we are all deceived by the same means and by the same people, we cannot give up our folly?

For this kind of trickery has already been practiced often by many.

And that it should succeed among others is perhaps not surprising; but it is astonishing that it should succeed against those who are themselves the very source of such knavery.

The cause, however, is that men do not keep ready at hand the saying so well put by Epicharmus:

"Stay sober and remember to distrust: these are the joints of the mind."—

Medion, a city near Aetolia.

Polybius, Book Eighteen.

Chapter 41 Asia: King Attalus I

Polybius says in his eighteenth book: Attalus came to the end of his life. Concerning him it is right—just as we are accustomed to do in the case of others—now to add a fitting word as well.

For from the start he possessed no other external advantage toward kingship than wealth alone—

which, when managed with intelligence and daring, truly provides great usefulness toward every undertaking, but, without the qualities just mentioned, by its nature becomes for most people a cause of evils and, in a word, of ruin.

For it breeds both envy and conspiracies, and it carries the greatest tendencies toward the corruption of body and soul. Very few indeed are the souls that are able by the power of wealth to thrust such things away.

Therefore the greatness of spirit of the man we are speaking of is worthy of admiration, because he set out to use his resources for nothing else but the winning of a kingdom, than which nothing greater or nobler can even be named—

a man who laid the foundation of the design just mentioned not only through generosity and goodwill toward his friends, but also through his achievements in war.

For after defeating the Gauls in battle—the most formidable and most warlike nation in Asia at that time—he made this his beginning and then for the first time showed himself a king.

Having obtained this honor and lived seventy-two years, of which he reigned forty-four, he lived a most temperate and dignified life toward his wife and children;

he kept faith with all his allies and friends, and he died in the very midst of the noblest of deeds, while struggling for the freedom of the Greeks.

And greatest of all, having left four sons in the prime of life, he so well ordered the affairs of his realm that the kingdom was handed down to his children's children without a single dispute.

Chapter 41a

II. Affairs of Asia

They tried to prevent Antiochus from sailing along the coast, not out of hostility toward him, but because they feared that, if he strengthened Philip, he would become an obstacle to the freedom of the Greeks.

King Antiochus was especially eager to gain Ephesus because of its strategic position: it seemed to give him, by land and by sea alike, a commanding post against Ionia and the cities on the Hellespont, and for the kings of Asia it offered an exceptionally useful defensive base against Europe.

Chapter 42 Italy: Treaty with Philip Confirmed

III. Affairs of Italy

When Claudius Marcellus had taken up the consulship, there came to Rome the envoys from Philip and those from Titus and the allies, to deal with the treaty with Philip.

After much discussion in the Senate, the Senate resolved to confirm the agreement;

but when the proposal was brought before the people, Marcus—himself eager to cross over into Greece—spoke against it and made great efforts to break off the treaty.

Nevertheless, the people, in accordance with the policy of Titus, ratified the settlement.

Once this had been carried out, the Senate immediately appointed ten men of distinction and sent them out, together with Titus, to manage the affairs of Greece and to confirm to the Greeks their freedom.

The envoys from the Achaeans, Damoxenus of Aegium and his colleagues, also made representations in the Senate concerning an alliance;

but since objection was raised for the moment—because the Eleians were disputing with the Achaeans over Triphylia, the Messenians (who were then allies of the Romans) over Asine and Pylus, and the Aetolians over the city of the Heraeans—the deliberation was deferred to the ten commissioners.

Such, then, was the state of affairs in the Senate.

Chapter 43 Greece: Murder of Brachylles

IV. Affairs of Greece

In Greece, after the battle, while Titus was wintering at Elateia, the Boeotians, being eager to bring back the men of theirs who had served in Philip's army, sent an embassy to Titus concerning their safe return.

Wishing to draw the Boeotians toward goodwill for himself—because he was already looking ahead to Antiochus—he readily consented.

When all had quickly been brought back from Macedonia, among them Brachylles, the Boeotians at once made him a boeotarch, and in like manner they honored and advanced the others who were thought to be friends of the house of Macedon no less than before.

They also sent an embassy to Philip to thank him for the return of the young men, thereby spoiling the favor done by Titus.

Observing this, Zeuxippus and Peisistratus and all who were regarded as friends of the Romans were distressed, foreseeing what was to come and fearing for themselves and their families;

for they knew clearly that, if the Romans withdrew from Greece while Philip remained at their flank, constantly lending strength to those who opposed them politically, their position in Boeotian public life would be in no way safe.

Therefore, having come to an understanding among themselves, they sent an embassy to Titus at Elateia.

Meeting with him, they put forward many and varied arguments on this matter, pointing out the popular feeling that was now already directed against them and the ingratitude of the masses.

And at last they ventured to say that, unless they did away with Brachylles and overawed the multitude, there would be no safety for the friends of the Romans once the armies had departed.

When Titus had heard all this, he said that he himself would not take part in this deed, but that he would not prevent those who wished to act;

and in general he told them to speak about these matters with Alexamenus, the general of the Aetolians.

When Zeuxippus and his colleagues complied and held discussions with him, the said Alexamenus was quickly persuaded and, agreeing to what was proposed, assigned three Aetolian and three Italian young men to lay hands on Brachylles.

For there is no witness so fearsome, nor any accuser so formidable, as the conscience that dwells in each man's soul.

Chapter 44 Decree of the Senate on the Peace with Philip

At about this time the ten commissioners arrived from Rome, through whom the affairs of the Greeks were to be managed, bringing the decree of the Senate concerning the peace with Philip.

The main provisions of the decree were these: that all the other Greeks, both those in Asia and those in Europe, should be free and use their own laws;

that those subject to Philip, and the garrisoned cities, Philip should hand over to the Romans before the festival of the Isthmian games;

that he should set free Euromus, Pedasa, Bargylia, and the city of the Iaseans, and likewise Abydos, Thasos, Myrina, and Perinthus, removing his garrisons from them;

that concerning the liberation of the Cians, Titus should write to Prusias in accordance with the decree of the Senate;

that Philip should restore to the Romans, within the same period, all the captives and all the deserters, and likewise the decked warships, except for five vessels and the sixteen-banked ship; and that he should also pay a thousand talents,

half of these at once, and half in installments over ten years.

Chapter 45 The Freedom of Greece

When this decree had been made known throughout Greece, everyone else was confident and overjoyed; only the Aetolians, vexed at not obtaining what they had hoped for, ran the decree down, claiming that it had substance only on paper and not in fact.

And from the very wording of the document they drew certain plausible arguments to unsettle those who would listen to them, such as the following.

They said that there were two distinct provisions in the decree concerning the cities garrisoned by Philip: one ordering Philip to withdraw his garrisons and hand the cities over to the Romans, and the other ordering him to withdraw his garrisons and set the cities free.

Now the cities to be set free, they argued, were specified by name, and these were the ones in Asia; while the cities to be handed over to the Romans were obviously those in Europe—namely Oreus,

Eretria, Chalcis, Demetrias, and Corinth.

From this it should be plain to everyone that the Romans were taking over the "fetters of Greece" from Philip, and that what was happening was a change of masters, not a liberation of the Greeks.

This, then, was harped on incessantly by the Aetolians.

Titus, meanwhile, set out from Elatea with the ten commissioners, put in at Anticyra, and at once crossed over to Corinth; arriving there, he sat in council with them and deliberated about the whole settlement.

But since the Aetolians' slander was spreading and was believed by some, Titus was compelled to make many varied arguments in the council,

showing that, if they really wished to win for themselves the entire credit of the Greeks' goodwill and to be universally trusted as having made their original crossing not for their own advantage but for the freedom of Greece, they would have to evacuate every position and set free all the cities now garrisoned by Philip.

This was the source of the deadlock in the council: with regard to all the other cities the matter had been settled beforehand at Rome and the ten commissioners had explicit instructions from the Senate, but in the case of Chalcis, Corinth, and Demetrias they had been given discretion on account of Antiochus, so that they might keep an eye on circumstances and decide about the cities just mentioned according to their own judgment;

for it was clear that the aforementioned king had long been fixing his attention on affairs in Europe.

Nevertheless, Titus persuaded the council to free Corinth at once and put it into the hands of the Achaeans, in keeping with the original agreements, but he held on to the Acrocorinth, Demetrias, and Chalcis.

Chapter 46 Proclamation At the Isthmian Games

These decisions having been reached, the festival of the Isthmian games came round, and since the most distinguished men from nearly all the world had gathered in anticipation of how things would turn out, much varied talk circulated throughout the whole assembly.

Some claimed it was impossible for the Romans to give up certain places and cities; others determined that they would give up the places that seemed most prominent, but would keep those of lesser appearance that could nonetheless render the same service.

And in their cleverness in arguing against one another, these speakers immediately gave themselves away.

While people were in this state of uncertainty, and the crowd had gathered in the stadium for the contest, the herald came forward and, having called for silence by means of the trumpeter, proclaimed the following announcement:

"The Senate of Rome and Titus Quinctius, proconsul and commander, having defeated King Philip and the Macedonians in war, hereby set free, without garrison, without tribute, and governed by their ancestral laws, the following: the Corinthians, Phocians, Locrians, Euboeans, Phthiotic Achaeans, Magnesians, Thessalians, and Perrhaebians."

At the very first words a tremendous burst of applause arose, so that some did not even hear the proclamation, while others wanted to hear it again.

The greater part of the people, disbelieving and seeming to hear what was said as if in a dream, so unexpected was the event,

every one of them on a fresh impulse shouted for the herald and trumpeter to come out into the middle of the stadium and repeat the announcement—because, as it seems to me, the people wanted not only to hear but also to see the speaker, in their disbelief at what was being proclaimed.

But when the herald came forward into the center and, by means of the trumpeter, hushed the uproar, then announced exactly the same words as before, such an outburst of applause broke out that those hearing of it now could scarcely grasp what it was like.

When at last the applause subsided, no one paid the slightest attention to the athletes any longer; everyone was talking, some to one another and some to themselves, as though they were out of their minds.

Indeed, after the contest, in the excess of their joy, they nearly killed Titus with their thanks:

some wanting to look him in the face and hail him as their savior, some eager to grasp his right hand, and most of them throwing wreaths and ribbons upon him, until they very nearly tore the man to pieces.

And although this show of gratitude seems to have been excessive, one could say with confidence that it actually fell far short of the magnitude of the deed.

For it was a wonderful thing that the Romans, and their leader Titus, adopted this policy, undertaking every expense and every danger for the sake of the freedom of Greece; and it was a great thing too that they brought to bear a force equal to their resolve;

but the greatest thing of all was that nothing in Fortune struck against their undertaking—rather, absolutely everything ran together to one favorable moment, so that by a single proclamation all the Greeks who inhabit Asia and those who inhabit Europe became free, without garrison and without tribute, living under their own laws.

Chapter 47 The Commissioners Make Detailed Arrangements

When the festival was over, the commissioners first dealt with the ambassadors from Antiochus, charging him to keep his hands off those cities in Asia that were autonomous and to make war on none of them, and to withdraw from all those formerly subject to Ptolemy and Philip that he had now taken over.

Along with this they warned him not to cross over into Europe with an army; for no Greek was henceforth to be made war upon by anyone or to be enslaved to anyone.

And in general, they said that some of their own number would come to visit Antiochus.

So Hegesianax and Lysias, having received these replies, returned;

and after them the commissioners summoned all who had come from the nations and cities, and made plain to them the decisions of the council.

As for the Macedonians, they declared the people called the Orestae autonomous, because they had come over to the Roman side during the war, and they freed the Perrhaebians, the Dolopes, and the Magnesians.

To the Thessalians, along with their freedom, they also assigned the Phthiotic Achaeans, with the exception of Phthiotic Thebes and Pharsalus;

for the Aetolians made a great point of their claim to Pharsalus, asserting that it ought to belong to them under the original treaties, and likewise to Leucas.

But the members of the council deferred the decision about these cities back to the Senate, to be settled with the Aetolians, while allowing them to keep the Phocians and Locrians within their league, just as they had held them before.

Corinth, Triphylia, and the city of the Heraeans they gave back to the Achaeans. Oreus, and also the city of the Eretrians, most of them thought should be given to Eumenes;

but when Titus referred the matter to the council, the resolution was not ratified, and so after some time these cities, together with Carystus, were freed by the Senate.

They also gave to Pleuratus Lychnis and Parthus, which were Illyrian towns subject to Philip.

And they granted to Amynander the right to hold whatever strongholds of Philip's he had seized during the war.

Chapter 48 The Commissioners Carry Word Throughout Greece

Having settled these matters, the commissioners divided themselves up.

Publius Lentulus sailed to Bargylia and freed its people; Lucius Stertinius went to Hephaestia and Thasos and the cities along Thrace and did the same;

Publius Villius and Lucius Terentius set off to visit Antiochus, while Gnaeus Cornelius and his colleagues went to King Philip.

Meeting him near Tempe, they discussed with him the other matters about which they had instructions, and advised him to send envoys to Rome to seek an alliance, so that he might not appear to be lying in wait for an opportunity and watching for the arrival of Antiochus.

When the king agreed to what they suggested, they parted from him at once and went to the assembly of the Thermica;

and coming before the people, they urged the Aetolians at some length to remain faithful to their original policy and to preserve their goodwill toward the Romans.

Many came forward, some finding fault with the Romans in mild and measured terms for not having shared the fruits of success in a spirit of partnership, nor kept the original agreements,

while others abused them, declaring that the Romans would never have set foot in Greece, nor defeated Philip, had it not been for the Aetolians themselves.

Gnaeus and his colleagues declined to make a defense against each of these charges, but urged them to send an embassy to Rome, on the grounds that they would obtain full justice from the Senate—which, being persuaded, they did.

And such was the outcome of the war against Philip.

Chapter 49 Asia: Roman Envoys To Antiochus

V. Affairs of Asia

If, as the saying goes, they are driven to the very last extremity, they will take refuge with the Romans and put themselves and their city into Roman hands. —

While Antiochus' undertaking was advancing just as he wished, and Antiochus himself was present in Thrace, Lucius Cornelius and his colleagues put in by sea at Selymbria.

These men were envoys dispatched by the Senate to arrange the settlement between Antiochus and [Ptolemy]—

Chapter 50 Conference Between Roman Legates and Antiochus

[Ptolemy]. At about the same time there also arrived two of the ten commissioners: Publius Lentulus from Bargylia, and Lucius Terentius and Publius Villius from Thasos.

When the king was quickly informed of their arrival, within a few days they all gathered together at Lysimacheia.

It also happened that Hegesianax and Lysias, who had been sent on the mission to Titus Flamininus, turned up at this same moment.

Now the private meetings between the king and the Romans were entirely cordial and friendly; but afterwards, when a general council was held to discuss the whole situation, affairs took on a very different character.

For Lucius Cornelius demanded that Antiochus withdraw from all the cities subject to Ptolemy that he had now seized in Asia, and he insisted earnestly that he likewise give up those subject to Philip;

for it was absurd, he said, that Antiochus should step in and take over the prizes of the war which the Romans had fought against Philip.

He further urged him to keep his hands off the autonomous cities.

And in general he said he was astonished on what grounds Antiochus had made his crossing into Europe with such great land forces and such great naval forces;

for, apart from the supposition that he intended to attack the Romans, no other explanation remained to anyone who reasoned correctly. With these words the Romans

Chapter 51 The King's Reply

finished speaking. The king began his reply by saying that, first of all, he was at a loss to understand on what grounds they were disputing with him over the cities of Asia; for it befitted anyone in the world rather than the Romans to do so.

Secondly, he asked that they not meddle at all in the affairs of Asia, since he, for his part, did not in the slightest interfere with the affairs of Italy.

He had crossed into Europe with his forces, he said, in order to recover the Chersonese and the cities of Thrace; for the rule over these regions belonged to him more rightfully than to anyone else.

For this dominion had originally been that of Lysimachus, but when Seleucus made war on him and prevailed in that war, the whole kingdom of Lysimachus passed to Seleucus as spear-won territory.

Then, during the periods when his own ancestors were distracted by other concerns, first Ptolemy and then Philip had torn these regions away and appropriated them for themselves.

He himself, however, was now not acquiring them by exploiting Philip's difficulties, but recovering them by exercising his own just claims.

As for the people of Lysimacheia, who had been unexpectedly driven from their homes by the Thracians, he was doing the Romans no wrong in bringing them back and resettling them;

for in doing this, he said, his aim was not to lay hands on the Romans, but to prepare a dwelling-place for his son Seleucus.

As for the autonomous cities of Asia, they ought to obtain their freedom not by a command from the Romans, but by his own favor.

And with regard to Ptolemy, he said that he himself would settle matters to that king's satisfaction; for he had resolved to establish with him not merely friendship, but, along with friendship, a tie of kinship as well.

Chapter 52 Antiochus Demands a Rhodian Court

When Lucius and his colleagues took the view that the representatives of the Lampsacenes and the Smyrnaeans ought to be called in and given a hearing, this was done.

Present on behalf of the Lampsacenes were Parmenio and Pythodorus, and on behalf of the Smyrnaeans, Coeranus. As these men spoke their minds freely,

the king grew annoyed at the appearance of having to defend himself before the Romans against those who were contesting matters with him, and, cutting Parmenio short, he said:

"Have done with all this talk; for it is not before the Romans, but before the Rhodians, that I am willing to have our disputed points decided."

And so, on these terms, they broke up the meeting, by no means satisfied with one another.

Chapter 53 Egypt: Fall of Scopas

Many people long for bold and glorious exploits, but few dare actually to lay a hand on them.

And yet Scopas had far finer resources than Cleomenes for taking such a risk and showing such daring.

For Cleomenes was caught in advance and shut up to rely solely on the hopes he could place in his own household servants and friends; yet even so he did not abandon those hopes, but tested them to the utmost of his power, valuing an honorable death above a life lived in disgrace.

Scopas, on the other hand, although he had both a strong arm to help him and the right opportunity—since the king was still a child—was caught while he was still hesitating and deliberating.

For when Aristomenes and his men learned that he was gathering his friends at his own house and holding council with them, they sent some of the royal guards to summon him to the council.

But he was so out of his wits that he neither dared to carry out any of his next steps nor, when summoned by the king, was able to bring himself to obey—which is the most extreme failing of all—

until Aristomenes and his men, recognizing his irrationality, stationed the soldiers and the elephants around the house,

and sent Ptolemy son of Eumenes with a band of young men, ordering him to bring Scopas in—peacefully if he was willing to obey, and if not, by force.

When Ptolemy made his way into the house and announced that the king was summoning Scopas, at first Scopas paid no attention to what was said, but kept staring fixedly at Ptolemy for some time, as if menacing him and marveling at his audacity.

But when Ptolemy stepped up and boldly seized hold of his cloak, then Scopas called on those present to come to his aid.

Since, however, the young men who had come in were many, and someone made clear to him the force surrounding the house outside, he gave way to the circumstances and went along with his friends.

Chapter 54 Scopas and Dicaearchus Punished

As soon as Scopas entered the council chamber, the king first stated the charge against him briefly; after the king came Polycrates, who had just arrived from Cyprus, and last of all Aristomenes.

In all other respects the accusation made by them all was much the same as what has just been described, but to the previous charges there was now added the council he had held with his friends and his refusal to obey when summoned by the king.

On these grounds not only did all the members of the council condemn him, but so did the foreign envoys who were present.

When Aristomenes was about to make his accusation, he brought in many other distinguished men from Greece, as well as the ambassadors sent by the Aetolians to negotiate a settlement, among whom was Dorimachus son of Nicostratus.

When these speeches had been delivered, Scopas in turn tried to offer some pleas in his defense; but since no one paid him any attention, because of the senselessness of his conduct, he was immediately led off to prison along with his friends.

Then, when night came, Aristomenes had Scopas and all his relatives and friends put to death by poison;

but Dicaearchus he subjected to the rack and the scourge, and so made an end of him, exacting from him a penalty that was fitting and shared on behalf of all the Greeks.

For this was the Dicaearchus whom Philip, when he set out to violate his treaties against the Cyclades and the cities on the Hellespont, appointed commander of the whole fleet and director of the entire operation.

Sent out to commit such open impiety, he not only thought he was doing nothing strange, but in the extravagance of his madness supposed that he would strike terror even into the gods as well as into men.

For wherever he anchored his ships he set up two altars, one to Impiety and one to Lawlessness, and on these he sacrificed and to these he bowed down as though they were divine powers.

For this reason it seems to me that he met with the punishment he deserved from both gods and men: having set the course of his own life against nature, fittingly he met an end against nature too at the hands of destiny.

As for the rest of the Aetolians, the king let all those who wished to return to their own country depart with their possessions.

Chapter 55 Anacleteria of Ptolemy Epiphanes

Scopas's love of money had been conspicuous even while he was alive—for in his greed he far surpassed all other men—but after his death it became even more apparent through the quantity of gold and the goods that were found in his possession.

For taking as his accomplice the savagery and the drunkenness of Charimortus, he had utterly plundered the kingdom to its very foundations.

Now once the courtiers had settled the affair of the Aetolians satisfactorily, they at once set about performing the Anacleteria of the king. His age did not yet make this pressing, but they thought that affairs would gain a certain stability and a fresh start toward better progress if the king were regarded as having now come into full power.

So, making their preparations on a magnificent scale, they carried out the proceedings in a manner worthy of the dignity of the kingdom, with Polycrates thought to have contributed the most toward this undertaking.

For the man just mentioned, even in the reign of the king's father, while he was still young, was reckoned second to none at court either in trustworthiness or in achievement, and likewise so under the present king.

For having been entrusted with Cyprus and its revenues at times that were dangerous and unsettled, he not only preserved the island for the boy-king, but also amassed a considerable sum of money, which he had now come bringing to the king, after handing over the governorship of Cyprus to Ptolemy of Megalopolis.

Having for these reasons won great approval and wealth in the years that followed, he afterward, as he advanced in age, drifted completely into licentiousness and a debauched life.

A reputation rather similar to his was inherited in old age by Ptolemy son of Agesarchus as well.

Concerning these men, when we come to the proper occasions, we shall not hesitate to set out plainly the disgraceful things that attended their exercise of power.

Book XIX

Chapter 1 Summary Based on Livy

I. Affairs of Italy

Polybius says that he ordered the walls of all the cities on this side of the Baetis to be pulled down in a single day; there were a great many such cities, and they were full of fighting men.

Chapter 2

II. Affairs of Greece

There was a vast number of prisoners taken in the Punic War. When their own people did not ransom them, Hannibal sold them. The scale of the matter is shown by what Polybius writes: it cost the Achaeans one hundred talents, since they fixed the payment to be returned to the owners at five hundred denarii for each man.

Book XX

Chapter 1 Greece: Antiochus and the Aetolians Meet

Olympiad 147, year 1. Greek Affairs.

And again from Polybius: they appointed thirty of the Apocleti to sit in council together with the king. And again: he convened the Apocleti and laid before them a deliberation concerning the present situation.

Chapter 2 The Boeotians Answer Antiochus

When Philip sent an embassy to the Boeotians, the Boeotians replied to the envoys that, once the king came to them in person, they would then deliberate about the proposals being urged upon them.

Chapter 3 Epirus and Elis Ask Antiochus for Help

While Antiochus was staying at Chalcis and winter was beginning, envoys came to him: from the Epirote nation, the embassy headed by Charops, and from the city of the Eleans, the embassy headed by Callistratus.

The Epirotes urged him not to drag them prematurely into the war against the Romans, since he could see that they lay directly in the path facing Italy ahead of all the rest of Greece.

If, however, he could himself take up a forward position to defend Epirus and secure their safety, they said they would receive him into both their cities and their harbors;

but if he judged it best not to do this for the present, they asked him to pardon them for being afraid of a war with the Romans.

The Eleans, for their part, urged him to send help to their city, since, now that the Achaeans had voted for war, they were wary of an attack from them.

The king answered the Epirotes that he would send envoys to discuss with them what was in their common interest,

while to the Eleans he dispatched a thousand foot soldiers, putting Euphanes the Cretan in command.

Chapter 4 The Decline of Boeotia

The Boeotians had for a long time now been in a poor condition, one that stood in stark contrast to the former vigor and renown of their state.

For these people, having won great glory and great power in the days of the battle of Leuctra, somehow—I cannot say how—steadily kept losing both of the qualities just mentioned in the years that followed, under the leadership of Abaeocritus.

And from that time on they not only kept losing them, but, turning altogether to the opposite course, they obscured their earlier reputation as far as they were able.

For when the Achaeans had stirred them up to war against the Aetolians, they adopted the same policy as the Achaeans and formed an alliance with them, and thereafter waged continual war against the Aetolians.

But when the Aetolians invaded Boeotia with an army, the Boeotians marched out in full force, and—although the Achaeans had assembled and were about to come to their aid—they did not wait for their arrival but engaged the Aetolians.

Being defeated in the battle, they were so crushed in spirit that, from that campaign on, they no longer dared to lay claim to any honorable distinction at all, nor did they share with the other Greeks in any common undertaking or contest decided by joint resolution.

Instead, having given themselves over to feasting and drunkenness, they grew slack not only in their bodies but in their souls as well.

Chapter 5 Continued Decline of Boeotia

The main stages of the Boeotians' gradual decline into folly came about among them in the following way.

Immediately after the defeat mentioned above, they abandoned the Achaeans and attached their nation to the Aetolians.

But when, some time later, the Aetolians in turn went to war with Demetrius, the father of Philip, the Boeotians abandoned them as well; and when Demetrius came into Boeotia with an army, they made no trial of the dangers of resistance but submitted themselves wholly to the Macedonians.

Yet, since a faint flicker of their ancestral glory still lingered, there were some who were displeased with the present state of affairs and with the policy of obeying the Macedonians in everything.

For this reason there came to be strong political opposition between these men and the party of Ascondas and Neon, the ancestors of Brachylles; for these were the men who at that time leaned most strongly toward Macedonia.

In the end, however, the party of Ascondas gained the upper hand, owing to a turn of events of the following kind.

After the death of Demetrius, Antigonus, who was acting as Philip's guardian, was sailing on some business toward the outermost parts of Boeotia, in the direction of Larymna, when an unexpected ebb of the tide left his ships stranded on dry land.

Just at this moment a report had reached the Boeotians that Antigonus intended to overrun their territory. Neon, who was then commander of the cavalry and was leading all the Boeotian horse about with him to guard the country, came upon Antigonus and his men while they were at a loss and helpless because of what had happened.

And though he had it in his power to inflict serious harm on the Macedonians, he decided, contrary to their expectation, to spare them.

This action of his pleased the rest of the Boeotians, but it did not please the Thebans at all.

Antigonus, however, when the tide flowed back a little later and his ships were lifted free, felt deep gratitude toward Neon for not having joined in attacking them during their misfortune; and he himself completed the voyage to Asia on which he had set out.

And so afterward, when he had defeated the Spartan Cleomenes and become master of Lacedaemon, he left Brachylles as governor of the city, repaying him in this way for the good service done by his father Neon. From these favors the house of Brachylles came to be restored to no small degree.

Nor was this the only consideration Antigonus showed them; rather, continuously—now he himself, now Philip—supplying them with funds and constantly lending them strength, they quickly overcame the rival political party in Thebes and forced everyone, except a very few, to side with Macedonia.

Such, then, was the beginning that the affairs of the house of Neon took, and of its alliance with the Macedonians—

Chapter 6 Disorganised State of Boeotia

—and of the increase of its fortune. Meanwhile the public affairs of the Boeotians had fallen into such a wretched condition that for nearly twenty-five years justice had not been administered among them, neither in private contracts nor in public charges.

Instead, some of the magistrates would order the dispatch of garrisons and others would proclaim national levies, and in this way they continually obstructed the course of justice; and some of the generals even made payments out of the public funds to the poor among the people.

From this the masses were taught to attach themselves to such men and to secure offices for them—men through whom they could expect to pay no penalty for their crimes and debts, and from time to time to gain some share of public property through the favor of those in office. The man who contributed most to this state of things was

Opheltas, who was forever devising some new scheme that seemed for the moment to benefit the many, but was bound in the end, by general admission, to ruin them all.

Along with these things followed another unfortunate fashion. Those who died childless no longer left their property to their relatives, as had earlier been the custom among them, but assigned it to feasting and drinking and made it common property for their friends.

And many even of those who had children would distribute the greater part of their estate to their dining clubs, so that there were many Boeotians who had more dinners in the month than there were days allotted to the month.

For this reason the Megarians, hating such a state of affairs and remembering their former membership in the federation alongside the Achaeans, once more turned away toward the Achaeans and their party.

For the Megarians had originally been part of the Achaean political community from the time of Antigonus Gonatas; but when Cleomenes took up a position on the Isthmus, being cut off they attached themselves to the Boeotians with the consent of the Achaeans.

A little before the times now under discussion, becoming dissatisfied with the Boeotian government, they once again turned back toward the Achaeans.

The Boeotians, enraged at what they regarded as contempt, marched out against the Megarians in full force under arms.

And when the Megarians took no notice at all of their arrival, the Boeotians, thus provoked, set about besieging the city and launching assaults on it.

But when a panic fell upon them, together with a rumor that Philopoemen had arrived with the Achaeans, they left their scaling-ladders against the wall and fled headlong back to their own land.

Chapter 7 Fortune and Degeneracy of the Boeotians

With their politics in such a condition, the Boeotians somehow slipped through, by good luck, even the crises of the times of Philip and of Antiochus.

In the period that followed, however, they did not escape; rather, as if Fortune were deliberately exacting requital, she seemed to come down heavily upon them—matters of which we shall make mention in what follows. —

The majority put forward, as the pretext for their estrangement from the Romans, the killing of Brachylles and the campaign that Titus made against Coronea on account of the murders of Romans that were taking place on the roads;

but in truth they were diseased in their souls because of the causes already described.

For when the king drew near, the leading men of the Boeotians went out to meet him; and after joining him and conversing in a friendly manner, they conducted him into Thebes. —

Chapter 8 Submission of the Aetolian Officers

Antiochus, the one called the Great, whom the Romans brought down—as Polybius records in his twentieth book—came to Chalcis in Euboea and celebrated his marriage there. He was fifty years old and had taken upon himself the two greatest of undertakings: the liberation of the Greeks, as he himself proclaimed it, and the war against the Romans.

Having fallen in love with a young Chalcidian girl in the very midst of the war, he set his heart on marrying her, being a heavy drinker and one who delighted in drunken revels.

She was the daughter of Cleoptolemus, one of the men of distinction, and she surpassed all other women in beauty.

And while celebrating his marriage there in Chalcis, he spent the whole winter on the spot, taking not the slightest thought for the business at hand; and he gave the girl the name Euboea.

So when he was defeated in the war, he fled to Ephesus with his new bride.

And out of his whole army, except for the five hundred or so who were around the king, scarcely anyone escaped; and even of the ten thousand soldiers whom—on Polybius' authority—we have recorded that the king brought across with him into Greece, only a tiny number survived.

Chapter 9 The Aetolians Seek a Truce

After Heracleia had fallen into Roman hands, Phaeneas, the general of the Aetolians, and those around him saw the crisis now closing in on Aetolia, and, keeping before their eyes what was bound to happen to the other cities, they resolved to send envoys to Manius to ask for a truce and a settlement.

Having decided on this, they sent out Archedamus, Pantaleon, and Chalepus.

When these men met with the Roman general, they intended to make a rather long speech, but they were cut off in the middle of the interview and prevented from continuing.

For Manius said that at the present moment he had no time to spare, being preoccupied with managing the spoils taken from Heracleia.

He told them, however, that he would grant a ten-day truce and would send Lucius along with them, and he instructed them to lay before Lucius whatever requests they had.

Once the truce had been made and Lucius had come to Hypata, a considerable discussion took place about the present situation.

The Aetolians built up their case by going back over the past, citing the acts of goodwill they had earlier shown toward the Romans.

But Lucius cut their enthusiasm short, saying that this kind of pleading did not fit the present circumstances; for since their original friendly relations had been dissolved by the Aetolians themselves, and the present hostility had come about because of the Aetolians, the goodwill of those earlier times contributed nothing to the present situation.

He therefore advised them to give up arguing the rights of their case and to turn instead to the language of entreaty, begging the general to grant them pardon for their offenses.

After discussing their predicament at still greater length, the Aetolians decided to entrust the whole matter to Manius, committing themselves to the good faith of the Romans—

not knowing what force this carried, but misled by the word "faith," as though through it a more complete mercy would be extended to them.

But among the Romans, to put oneself into another's "faith" carries exactly the same force as to hand over to the victor full discretion over oneself.

Chapter 10 The Aetolians Do Not Confirm the Terms

Having decided on this, they sent Phaeneas and his colleagues off in haste together with Lucius to make the resolution clear to Manius.

When these men met with the general and once again pleaded their case in the same way on their own behalf, they concluded by declaring that the Aetolians had decided to commit themselves to the good faith of the Romans.

Manius took up their words and said: "So this is how matters stand,

men of Aetolia?" When they nodded assent, he went on: "Then, first of all, none of you must cross over into Asia, neither on your own account nor by any public decree;

second, you must hand over Dicaearchus and Menestratus the Epirote"—who happened at that time to have come to the aid of Naupactus—"and along with them King Amynander and those of the Athamanians who withdrew to your side together with him."

At this Phaeneas broke in and said: "But what you demand, general, is neither just nor in keeping with Greek ways."

Manius, not so much out of anger as from a wish to bring them to a sense of their situation and to thoroughly alarm them, replied: "Do you still play the Greek with me and talk about what is fitting and proper, after you have put yourselves into our good faith? I could bind every one of you in chains and march you off, if I saw fit."

As he said this, he ordered a chain to be brought and an iron collar to be fastened around each man's neck.

Phaeneas and his companions were struck dumb with shock and stood there speechless, as if paralyzed in body and soul at the unexpected turn of events.

But Lucius and some of the other military tribunes present begged Manius to take no harsh measures against the men before him, since they were in fact envoys. When he agreed, Phaeneas began to speak:

he said that he and the Apocleti would carry out the orders, but that the assent of the people too was needed if the demands were to be ratified.

Manius said he was right, and Phaeneas then asked that another ten-day truce be granted to them. When this too was conceded, they parted on these terms for the time being.

On reaching Hypata, they reported to the Apocleti what had happened and the words that had been spoken. On hearing this, the Aetolians then for the first time grasped how mistaken they had been and what compulsion was now bearing down on them.

It was therefore decided to write to the cities and call the Aetolians together to deliberate about the orders imposed on them.

But when the report of what had befallen Phaeneas and his party was spread abroad, the people became so enraged that no one was even willing to attend the meeting for deliberation.

Since this impossibility prevented any deliberation about the demands, and since at this very moment Nicander had sailed back from Asia into Phalara on the Malian gulf—the very place from which he had set out—and was reporting the king's eagerness toward him and his promises for the future, they grew even more dismissive, so that no conclusion at all was reached about peace.

And so, as soon as the days of the truce had passed, the war was once again firmly upon the Aetolians.

Chapter 11 The Fate of Nicander

The reversal of fortune that befell Nicander is not something to be passed over in silence.

He arrived back at Phalara from Ephesus on the twelfth day after the day he had set out.

He found the Romans still occupied around Heracleia, and the Macedonians, having withdrawn from Lamia, encamped not far from the city.

He got his money safely through into Lamia, against all expectation, and then attempted that night to slip across the ground between the two camps and into Hypata.

But he fell among the Macedonian pickets and was brought up to Philip while the king's banquet was still in full swing, expecting that he would suffer something terrible, falling under Philip's anger, or else be handed over to the Romans.

When the matter was reported to the king, however, Philip quickly ordered the officers in charge to look after Nicander and to treat him with every kindness.

After a while the king himself rose from the table and met with Nicander, and after roundly reproaching the general folly of the Aetolians—first for having brought the Romans against the Greeks, and after that Antiochus as well—he nevertheless urged them even now to forget the past, to hold fast to their goodwill toward him, and not to wish to press their advantage against one another in each other's hours of crisis.

He instructed Nicander to report this to the leaders of the Aetolians; and after urging Nicander himself to remember the kindness that had been shown him, he sent him off with a sufficient escort, ordering those assigned to the task to bring him safely back to Hypata.

Nicander, to whom this reception had appeared utterly unhoped-for and astonishing, was at that time brought back safely to his own people, and in the time that followed he remained, from this connection onward, well disposed to the house of Macedon.

And so, later, in the time of the war with Perseus, bound by the gratitude just described and finding it hard to work against the designs of Perseus, he fell under suspicion and slander, and was at last summoned to Rome, where he ended his life.

Corax: a mountain between Callipolis and Naupactus. Polybius, Book 20.

Aperanteia: a city of Thessaly. Polybius, Book 20.

Chapter 12 Philopoemen's Disinterestedness

...one of their own number to speak to him about these matters; but whereas, in the case of most men who undertake public work for profit, there are many ready to offer such favors and to make this the beginning of friendship and alliance, in the case of Philopoemen no one at all could be found willing to convey this favor to him,

until at last, being wholly at a loss, they chose by vote Timolaus. He, being both a hereditary guest-friend and long on familiar terms with Philopoemen, traveled twice to Megalopolis for this very purpose, yet did not dare to utter a word about the matter—until, spurring himself on and coming a third time, he found the courage to mention the gift.

Philopoemen, against all expectation, received him on this point graciously and kindly, and Timolaus was overjoyed,

supposing that he had achieved his aim. But Philopoemen said that he would come to Sparta himself within a few days, since he wished to thank all the magistrates for this honor.

He came afterward, and being invited into the council, he said that he had long known the goodwill of the Lacedaemonians toward him, but knew it best of all from the crown now being offered to him and from such an honor.

He said, then, that he accepted their intention, but was uneasy at the manner of it. For such honors and crowns, he said, ought not to be given to one's friends—since the man who puts on such a crown can never wash off its poison—but much rather to one's enemies,

so that friends, keeping their freedom of speech, may be trusted among the Achaeans whenever they propose to come to the city's aid, while enemies, having swallowed the bait, may be forced either to plead the Spartans' cause or, by keeping silent, be unable to do them any harm.

## II. Fragment of Uncertain Place

To form a judgment about events from hearsay is not the same as having been an eyewitness; the two differ greatly, and the conviction that comes from seeing a thing vividly for oneself naturally contributes much in every case.

Book XXI

Chapter 1 Embassy from Sparta

Olympiad 147, year 2. Affairs in Italy.

At this same time the embassy that the Spartans had sent to Rome returned with its hopes disappointed.

Their mission concerned the hostages and the villages.

The senate said that it would give instructions about the villages to the envoys it would send itself, but that it still wished to deliberate further about the hostages.

As for the old exiles, it said it was amazed that they had not yet been brought home, now that Sparta had been freed.

Chapter 2 Embassy from Philip

When news of the Roman victory in the naval battle had just reached Rome, they first proclaimed a nine-day public thanksgiving.

That is, the whole people were to suspend ordinary business and offer thank-offerings to the gods for their success.

After this they brought before the senate the envoys from the Aetolians and those sent by Manius.

When both sides had spoken at length, the senate resolved to offer the Aetolians two alternatives: either they were to leave all matters concerning themselves to Roman decision, or they were to pay a thousand talents at once and treat the same people as friends and enemies that Rome did.

But when the Aetolians asked the senate to state explicitly what issues they must submit for Roman decision, the senate refused to define them. That is why the war with the Aetolians continued for them alone.

Chapter 3 The Scipios In Greece

At about the same time the senate also dealt with the envoys sent by Philip.

They had come to explain the goodwill and zeal the king had shown toward the Romans in the war against Antiochus.

After hearing them, the senate immediately released his son Demetrius from hostage status, and also promised to remit the tribute, provided that Philip continued faithful in the present circumstances.

In the same way they also released the Spartan hostages, except Armenas the son of Nabis; he later died of illness.

Chapter 3b

Affairs in Greece.

An embassy came into Achaea from King Eumenes asking for alliance.

The Achaeans assembled in public meeting, ratified the alliance, and sent out young troops—one thousand infantry and one hundred cavalry—under the command of Diophanes of Megalopolis.

Chapter 4 The Athenians Intercede for the Aetolians

While Manius, the Roman general, was besieging the Amphissians, the Athenian people learned both of the distress of Amphissa and of Publius's presence, and at this moment sent envoys headed by Echedemus.

Their instructions were, first, to greet Lucius and Publius, and at the same time to test whether a settlement with the Aetolians might be arranged.

When they arrived, Publius gladly welcomed them and treated them with great courtesy, seeing that they could be useful for the plans before him.

For he wanted to put Aetolian affairs in good order if possible; but if the Aetolians would not cooperate, he had fully resolved to leave that matter aside and cross into Asia.

He clearly understood that the true end of the war and of the whole enterprise was not the reduction of the Aetolian nation, but the defeat of Antiochus and mastery of Asia after victory.

Therefore, the moment the Athenians mentioned a settlement, he readily accepted what they said and told them to approach the Aetolians in the same spirit.

Echedemus and his colleagues first sent men ahead and then went themselves to Hypata, where they discussed peace with the Aetolian magistrates.

The Aetolians also agreed readily, and representatives were appointed to meet the Romans.

When these men came to Publius and found him encamped sixty stades from Amphissa, they spoke at length, reminding him of the kindnesses the Aetolians had shown to Rome in the past.

Publius spoke in an even gentler and more humane way. He cited what he had done in Spain and in Libya, explained how he had treated those in those regions who put their trust in him, and concluded by saying that they ought to place themselves in his hands and trust him.

At first all who were present became hopeful that the settlement would immediately be brought to completion.

But when the Aetolians asked on what terms they were to make peace, Lucius explained that two choices lay before them.

They must either submit everything concerning themselves to Roman decision, or pay a thousand talents at once and accept the same friends and enemies as Rome.

At this the Aetolians present were deeply troubled, because the decision was so unlike the previous tone of the conversation; still, they said they would report back to the Aetolians on the demands laid upon them.

Chapter 5 Truce With the Aetolians

So these men went back to deliberate on what had been proposed.

Echedemus and his colleagues met with the Apocleti and joined in their discussions.

One of the Roman demands was impossible because of the sheer amount of money involved; the other was frightening because they had already once been deceived in connection with surrender, when they had very nearly fallen into chains.

Therefore, perplexed and distressed, they again sent the same envoys to ask either that some part of the money be remitted, so that they could pay it, or that political leaders and women be excluded from the terms of submission.

When the envoys met Publius and his circle, they explained these decisions.

Lucius said that the authority granted him by the senate extended only to the terms he had just stated. So the envoys returned once more.

Echedemus and his colleagues then followed them to Hypata and advised the Aetolians that, since peace was for the moment blocked, they should ask for a truce and thus win a postponement of their present miseries, and then send an embassy to the senate.

If they obtained what they requested, well and good; if not, they must wait on circumstances.

For their position could hardly become worse than it already was, while for many reasons it might yet become better.

Since Echedemus's advice seemed sound, the Aetolians decided to send an embassy to ask for a truce.

When they reached Lucius, they begged that for the present a six-month truce be granted, so that they might send envoys to the senate.

Publius, who had long been eager for the operations in Asia, quickly persuaded his brother to grant what they asked.

The agreements were drawn up in writing. Manius then raised the siege, handed over the whole army and the supplies to Lucius, and at once departed for Rome with his military tribunes.

Chapter 6 Asia: Factions at Phocaea

Affairs in Asia.

At Phocaea there was civil strife, partly because the Romans left on board the ships were quartered there, and partly because the people resented the orders laid upon them.

At the same time the magistrates of Phocaea, fearing both the impulse of the crowd because of the grain shortage and the agitation of the supporters of Antiochus, sent envoys to Seleucus, who was near their frontier.

They asked him not to approach the city, because they intended to remain quiet, wait for the issue of the whole conflict, and afterward obey whatever settlement was made.

Among the envoys, Aristarchus, Cassander, and Rhodon were personally attached to Seleucus and favored that policy, while Hegias and Gelias opposed it and leaned toward Rome.

When they met him, Seleucus at once gave his attention to Aristarchus and his party, while he ignored Hegias and his associates.

But when he learned how the crowd felt and how scarce grain was, he dropped further discussion and audience with the envoys and advanced on the city.

Then two Galli came out carrying their sacred emblems and breast-images and begged him not to take any irreparable step against the city.

Chapter 7 The Rhodian Firing Apparatus

The fire-throwing device used by Pausistratus, the Rhodian admiral, was a brazier.

On each side of the prow two hooked fittings were placed along the inner faces of the ship's sides, and into these were set poles projecting outward over the sea.

From the end of these the brazier, full of fire, was suspended by an iron chain.

In this way, when the ship charged or came alongside an enemy vessel, the fire could be flung onto the hostile ship, while remaining far from their own because of the outward slant of the poles.

It was also thought that Pamphilidas, the Rhodian admiral, was better suited than Pausistratus for every sort of crisis, since he was by nature deeper and steadier rather than simply bolder.

Most people, after all, do not form their judgments from reasoned principle, but from whatever result has happened.

So although they had only just chosen Pausistratus for command precisely because he had drive and daring, they immediately swung to the opposite opinion when fortune turned against him.

Chapter 8 The Aetolian Truce Announced

At this time letters reached Samos for Lucius and for Eumenes, both from Lucius the consul and from Publius Scipio,

announcing the arrangements made with the Aetolians about the truce and the march of the land army toward the Hellespont.

The same facts were likewise made known to Antiochus and Seleucus by the Aetolians.

Chapter 9 Antiochus At Pergamum

Diophanes of Megalopolis had great practical experience in warfare, because during the long war against Nabis the Megalopolitans, being a neighboring people, had spent all that time serving under Philopoemen and had thus gained real training in military action.

Besides this, the man was powerful and impressive both in appearance and in bodily vigor.

And most important of all, he was a brave soldier in war and exceptionally skillful in the use of arms.

Chapter 10 Antiochus Proposes Peace

King Antiochus invaded the territory of Pergamum; but when he learned that King Eumenes was present and saw that not only the naval but also the land forces were coming against him, he began to consider opening negotiations for peace at once with the Romans, Eumenes, and the Rhodians.

So he moved with his whole army to Elaea, occupied a hill opposite the city, stationed his infantry on it, and encamped his cavalry—more than six thousand strong—close by the city itself.

He himself took position between these forces and sent messengers into the city to Lucius about a settlement.

The Roman general then called together the Rhodians and Eumenes and asked each to state plainly what seemed best in the present situation.

Eudamus and Pamphilidas were not opposed to a settlement, but the king said that peace was at present neither honorable nor practicable.

“How,” he said, “could the outcome be honorable if we make peace while shut up behind walls?

And indeed how can it be practicable now? Without the consul being present, how could any agreed terms be valid without his approval?

Besides, even if some sign of agreement were reached with Antiochus, neither the fleet nor the army could properly go home before the people and senate had ratified the terms.

We would then have nothing left but to winter here waiting for their decision, doing nothing while consuming the supplies and resources of our allies.

Then, if the senate should refuse the settlement, we would have to begin the war afresh from the beginning, after letting the present opportunity pass—an opportunity in which, if the gods are willing, we may bring the whole matter to an end.”

Such was Eumenes' view. Lucius approved the advice and answered Antiochus's envoys that no settlement could be made before the proconsul arrived.

When Antiochus's people heard this, they at once began to ravage the territory of Elaea.

After this Seleucus remained in that district, while Antiochus continued his march and entered the plain called Thebe.

There, having moved into a rich and prosperous region full of resources, he filled his army with every kind of plunder.

Chapter 11 Prusias Refuses To Help Antiochus

When King Antiochus returned to Sardis from the expedition just mentioned, he kept sending messages to Prusias, urging him to join his alliance.

In earlier times Prusias had not been unwilling to make common cause with Antiochus, because he was very much afraid that the Romans were crossing into Asia in order to overthrow all monarchs.

But a letter reached him from the brothers Lucius and Publius. When he received it and read it, his thinking changed greatly, and he gained a reasonable foresight of what was coming.

For the men around Publius had written with great clarity, and had added many proofs to make their case convincing.

They did not merely defend their own policy,

but that of the Roman people as a whole, showing that they had not taken kingdoms away from the kings who originally held them; rather, in some cases they had themselves established rulers, and in others had enlarged their power and made their dominions many times greater.

They cited Indibilis and Colichas in Spain, Massanissa in Libya, and Pleuratus in Illyria.

All of these, they said, had been raised by Rome from small and insignificant dynasts into acknowledged kings.

In the same way they mentioned Philip and Nabis in Greece. Though they had defeated Philip in war and reduced him to hostages and tribute, after receiving from him only a slight proof of goodwill they had restored his son and the young men who had been hostages with him, released him from tribute, and returned many cities taken in war.

And although they could have removed Nabis altogether, they had not done so, but had spared him, tyrant though he was, after receiving the customary guarantees.

In view of all this they urged Prusias by letter not to be afraid for his throne, but confidently to choose the Roman side, since he would never regret such a decision.

After hearing these arguments Prusias changed his mind. And when envoys headed by Gaius Livius also arrived and met with him, he gave up all expectation of support from Antiochus.

Antiochus, having failed in this hope, came to Ephesus; and reflecting that only by mastering the sea could he prevent the crossing of the land army and in general keep the war away from Asia, he resolved to fight a naval battle and decide the issue by a contest at sea.

Chapter 12 Pirates

Polybius says that when the pirates caught sight of the Roman ships sailing toward them, they suddenly turned and made their retreat.

Chapter 13 Antiochus Sends an Envoy To Discuss Peace

After his defeat in the sea battle Antiochus stayed at Sardis, wasting time and delaying in the larger conduct of the war.

As soon as he heard that the enemy had crossed over, his spirit was crushed and he lost hope; so he decided to send to Lucius and Publius to negotiate a settlement.

He chose Heracleides of Byzantium and sent him out with instructions to cede the cities of Lampsacus and Smyrna, and also Alexandria, from which the war had originally taken its beginning.

Likewise, if the Romans wished to take away any other cities in Aeolis and Ionia that had chosen their side in the present war, he was prepared for that too.

In addition, he would pay half the expense they had incurred in the war against him.

These were the instructions Heracleides had for the public audience; but for Publius in private he had other proposals, which I shall explain in due course.

When this envoy reached the Hellespont and found the Romans still waiting in the camp where they had first encamped after crossing,

he was at first delighted, thinking that their remaining where they were and not yet moving on would help his negotiations.

But when he learned that Publius was still on the other side, he was troubled, because the greatest weight in the matter rested on Publius's judgment.

The reason why the army remained in its first camp and why Publius was apart from the forces was that he was one of the Salii.

As I said in my work on the constitution, this is one of the three priestly bodies by which Rome performs its most notable sacrifices to the gods.

During the season of that sacrifice, the law requires that these Salii not change their location for thirty days, wherever they may happen to be caught.

This happened to Publius then. Just as the army was about to cross over, that sacred period overtook him, so that he could not change place.

As a result, Scipio was separated from the army and remained in Europe, while the forces that had crossed stayed where they were and could do nothing further, awaiting the arrival of the man just mentioned.

Chapter 14 Antiochus Tries To Negotiate

After some days, when Publius had arrived, Heracleides was summoned before the council and spoke on the instructions he carried.

He said that Antiochus would withdraw from Lampsacus and Smyrna and also from the city of Alexandria, as well as from any cities in Aeolis and Ionia that had chosen the Roman side.

In addition, he would undertake to pay half the expense they had incurred in the present war.

He also said much else on the same subject, urging the Romans not to test fortune too far, since they were men, and not to make the scope of their power boundless, but to set limits to it—if possible, the limits of Europe.

Even that, he said, would be a great and astonishing dominion, since none of their predecessors had attained it.

But if they were determined to lay hold of some part of Asia as well, let them define what parts those were, and the king would go to the utmost of his power to satisfy them.

After this had been said, the council decided that the general should reply that Antiochus ought to pay not half the cost of the war but all of it, since the war had arisen originally not because of Rome but because of him.

As for the cities, he must not free only those in Aeolis and Ionia, but give up all his dominion on this side of Taurus.

When the envoy heard this answer from the council, and saw that the demands went far beyond his instructions, he made no further attempt in the public meeting but instead devoted himself to courting Publius privately.

Chapter 15 Scipio Scorns Antiochus's Secret Proposal

When he found a suitable opportunity, he spoke of the proposals entrusted to him.

First, the king would restore Publius's son without ransom.

For at the beginning of the war Scipio's son had fallen into the hands of Antiochus's people.

Second, the king was ready even now to give whatever sum of money Publius might name, and after that to make the resources of his kingdom common with him, if only he would support the peace terms proposed by the king.

Publius said that he accepted the offer concerning his son and would be deeply grateful if Antiochus fulfilled that promise.

But as for the rest, he said the king entirely failed to understand his own interest, not only in this private approach to him, but in the public negotiations as well.

If Antiochus had made these offers while still master of Lysimacheia and of the entrance into the Chersonese, he would quickly have obtained his aim.

Likewise, even after giving up those places, if he had come to the Hellespont with his army, clearly prepared to prevent our crossing, and had then negotiated on these same points, he might still have achieved what he wanted.

But now, after allowing our forces to set foot in Asia and accepting not only the bridle but even the rider, he comes to propose equal terms of peace. Naturally he must fail and be disappointed in his hopes.

Therefore Publius advised him to take better counsel about the present and to look truly at the situation.

In return for the king's promise about his son, he said he would give advice worth the favor offered: the king should yield on every point, but under no circumstances fight the Romans.

After hearing this, Heracleides returned and reported the details to the king.

Antiochus, believing that no harsher terms could be laid on him if he were defeated in battle than those already being demanded, gave up the business of negotiation and made every kind of preparation for a decisive struggle.

Chapter 16 Zeuxis and Antipater Sent to Negotiate Peace

After the victory the Romans took possession of Sardis and its citadel, and then Musaeus came from Antiochus under flag of truce.

Publius and his associates received him graciously, and he said that Antiochus wished to send envoys to discuss the whole settlement.

Accordingly he asked that safe conduct be given to those who came. When this was granted, he returned.

After some days envoys came from King Antiochus: Zeuxis, formerly satrap of Lydia, and Antipater his nephew.

Their first concern was to meet King Eumenes, because they feared that, owing to the earlier friction, he might be especially eager to harm them.

But contrary to expectation they found him moderate and mild, and so at once moved on to the general audience.

Summoned into the council, they said much else besides, urging the Romans to use their success with gentleness and magnanimity.

They declared that this was not so much to Antiochus's advantage as to that of the Romans themselves, since fortune had now handed them mastery and dominion over the inhabited world.

In the end they simply asked what Antiochus must do to obtain peace and friendship with Rome.

The men in the council had already sat together and deliberated about these matters, and now instructed Publius to set out the decision.

Chapter 17 The Roman Terms To Antiochus

Publius said that the Romans never became harsher after victory.

Therefore the envoys would receive from Rome the same answer that they had already received before the battle, when they came to the Hellespont.

Antiochus must withdraw from Europe and from all Asia on this side of Taurus.

In addition, he must pay the Romans fifteen thousand Euboic talents as compensation for the cost of the war.

Of this, five hundred were to be paid immediately, another twenty-five hundred when the people ratified the settlement, and the rest over twelve years, one thousand talents each year.

He must also pay Eumenes the four hundred talents still owed to him and the grain still lacking under the treaty made with Eumenes' father.

Along with this he must surrender Hannibal the Carthaginian, Thoas the Aetolian, Mnasilochus the Acarnanian, and the Chalcidians Philo and Eubulidas.

As security for all this, Antiochus must at once provide twenty hostages of the sort specified.

Publius announced these terms on behalf of the whole council. Since Antipater and Zeuxis agreed to them, everyone resolved to send envoys to Rome to ask the senate and people to ratify the treaty.

So they separated on those terms, and in the following days the Romans divided their forces.

A few days later, when the hostages had arrived at Ephesus, Eumenes and the envoys from Antiochus immediately began preparations to sail to Rome.

In the same way envoys also went to Rome from the Rhodians, the Smyrnaeans, and almost all the peoples and states dwelling on this side of Taurus.

Chapter 18 Eumenes Persuaded to Speak

Olympiad 147, year 3. Affairs in Italy.

At the opening of summer, after the Roman victory over Antiochus, King Eumenes was in Rome, together with Antiochus's envoys and those from Rhodes and many others.

Nearly everyone in Asia had sent ambassadors to Rome immediately after the battle, because at that time all hopes for the future rested for all alike with the senate.

The senate received everyone graciously, but gave King Eumenes the grandest reception of all, both in its formal meeting of him and in its hospitality; next after him came the Rhodians.

When the time for audience arrived, they first called in the king and asked him to speak openly about what he wanted from the senate.

Eumenes answered that if he had wished to obtain some favor from others, he would have used the Romans as counselors, so as neither to desire anything improper nor to ask for anything beyond what was fitting.

But since he now stood before the Romans themselves as a petitioner, he thought it best to place both his own interests and those of his brothers in their hands.

When one of the elder senators rose and urged him not to be afraid but to say what seemed best to him, since the senate was resolved to do all it could for him, Eumenes remained of the same opinion. After some time had passed, the king withdrew.

The senate then deliberated privately on what ought to be done.

It was resolved to invite Eumenes again and encourage him to speak freely about what had brought him there, since he knew Asian affairs and his own interests more exactly than anyone else.

After this decision he was called back in, and when one of the elder senators explained the resolution, he was compelled to speak on the matter.

Chapter 19 King Eumenes In the Senate

So he was forced to address the question. He said that he would add nothing further on his own concerns, but would continue entirely to leave those matters in Roman hands. One point only troubled him—the question of the Rhodians.

That was why he had now been brought to speak about the present situation.

For they had come no less eagerly to advance the interests of their own city than he had come to advance those of his own kingdom.

Yet, he said, their words would give an impression opposite to their true purpose, and this would be easy to recognize.

Once admitted, they would say that they had come neither to ask anything at all from the Romans nor in any way to injure him, but to plead for the freedom of the Greeks who lived in Asia.

They would further say that this was not so much a favor to themselves as something that befitted the Romans and was consistent with their past deeds.

Such would be the appearance created by their speech; but the real disposition behind it would be the opposite.

For if the cities were freed, as they urged, Rhodian power would greatly increase, while his own would in a way be ruined.

The very name of freedom and autonomy would draw away from him not only those cities now to be freed, but even those already subject to him from earlier times, once the Romans openly showed that this was their chosen policy; all these would be added to the Rhodians.

That is the natural course of events. Men who think they have been liberated through Rhodian action will be their allies in name, but in reality they will readily do whatever the Rhodians order, being bound to them by the greatest obligation.

Therefore, gentlemen, he urged them to watch this point carefully, lest they unknowingly strengthen one ally beyond measure while unreasonably weakening another,
