I am not unaware that some historians, when they wish to show us the causes of the war that arose between the Romans and Perseus, first point to the expulsion of Abrupolis from his own principality, after he had raided the mines around Pangaeum following Philip's death.

Perseus came to the rescue, defeated him, and completely drove him out of his dominion.

After that they cite the invasion of Dolopia and the appearance of Perseus at Delphi,

and further the plot laid against King Eumenes at Delphi and the murder of the envoys from Boeotia, from which some say the war of Perseus against the Romans sprang.

But I maintain that it is of the highest importance both for writers and for serious learners to know the causes from which each event is generated and grows; yet most historians confuse these matters because they fail to keep hold of the distinction between a pretext and a cause, and again between a pretext and the beginning of a war.

And now, since the events themselves remind me of this, I have been compelled to renew the same discussion.

For of the matters just mentioned, the earlier ones are pretexts; but the later ones—the plot against King Eumenes, the murder of the envoys, and other similar things that happened at the same time—are obvious beginnings of the war that arose between the Romans and Perseus and of the overthrow of Macedonian power.

But in the strict sense none of these is its cause. This will be clear from what follows.

For just as we say that Philip son of Amyntas conceived and determined upon carrying out the war against the Persians, while Alexander became the executor of the enterprises his father had resolved on, so too now we say that Philip son of Demetrius first conceived the last war against Rome and had all the preparations ready for this design, while after his death Perseus became the man who carried the plan into action.

If this is true, then this too is clear: the causes cannot have arisen later than the death of the man who resolved upon and planned the war. Yet that is what follows from the account of the other historians, since everything they mention took place after Philip's death.

Chapter 19 Disputes in Crete

Philopoemen had some disagreement in argument with Archon the general. Philopoemen, however, being pleased at the moment by what had been said and changing his mind, praised Archon warmly as a man who had handled the occasion with both skill and cunning.

But for my own part, says Polybius, the remark did not please me then when I was present, since it amounted to praising a man while at the same time doing him moral harm; nor has it pleased me since, as my years have advanced.

For it seems to me that there is a very great difference in moral choice between a practical statesman and a mischievous intriguer, just as there is a similar difference between genuine dexterity and mere clever roguery. The one set of qualities is, so to speak, among the noblest of human things; the other is the very opposite.

But because of the lack of judgment now common among men, the things just mentioned, though they have very little in common, receive the same approval and the same eager admiration.

Chapter 20 Apollonias, Widow of Attalus

Affairs in Asia.

Apollonis, the wife of Attalus, father of King Eumenes, was a woman of Cyzicus and for many reasons worthy of remembrance and distinction.

For the fact that, though she was originally a private citizen, she became a queen and preserved that exalted place to the very end—not by the attractions of a courtesan, but by modesty, dignity in public life, and noble character—makes her deserve an honorable memory.

And further, though she outlived her husband by no short time, after bearing four sons she preserved toward all of them without surpassing measure the same goodwill and motherly affection down to the end of her life.

Her sons won a fine reputation during their visit by rendering their mother the gratitude and honor that were her due.

For taking their mother between them by both hands, they escorted her around the sanctuaries and through the city with all due attendance.

At this sight the spectators were greatly moved.

They welcomed and honored the young men, and recalling the story of Cleobis and Biton, compared their conduct with theirs, giving to the splendor of those old examples a further height through the lofty rank of kings.

This happened at Cyzicus after the settlement with King Prusias.

Chapter 21 Ostiagon Tries to Become King of All the Gauls

Ostiagon the Galatian, king of the Gauls in Asia, set his mind on transferring to himself the sovereignty of all the Gauls.

He possessed many resources for this aim, both by nature and by experience.

For he was generous, high-minded, gracious in personal dealings, and intelligent.

And what counted most among the Gauls, he was manly and capable in matters of war.

Chapter 22 Aristonicus

Affairs in Egypt.

Aristonicus, the eunuch of Ptolemy king of Egypt, had been brought up with the king from childhood.

As he grew older, he showed a courage and cast of mind more manly than one would expect in a eunuch.

For he was by nature a soldierly man and spent most of his time in such pursuits.

He was likewise effective in his dealings with others and possessed sound common sense, which is rare.

Besides all this, he was naturally well disposed toward acts of kindness to other people.

Book XXIII

Chapter 1 Demetrius Before the Senate

Olympiad 149, year 1. Affairs in Italy.

In the 149th Olympiad an exceptionally large number of embassies gathered at Rome from Greece, more than had usually been seen before.

For Philip had been compelled, under the treaty, to submit disputes with his neighbors to legal arbitration; and when it became known that the Romans were ready to hear accusations against him and were taking care for the safety of those who had claims against the king,

all the peoples bordering on Macedonia appeared, some in a private capacity, some representing cities, and some entire ethnic groups, bringing charges against Philip.

Along with them came envoys from Eumenes, accompanied by Athenaeus, the king's brother, to accuse Philip concerning the cities in Thrace and the military aid sent to Prusias.

Demetrius, Philip's son, also arrived to answer all these complainants, bringing with him Apelles and Philocles, who were then considered the foremost of the king's friends.

Envoys came from the Spartans as well, one from each political group in the city.

The senate first summoned Athenaeus. It accepted the crown he brought, worth fifteen thousand gold staters, warmly praised Eumenes and his brothers in its reply, and urged them to remain steadfast in the same policy.

After that the magistrates brought in Demetrius and invited all Philip's accusers to speak, calling them forward one embassy at a time.

But the embassies were so numerous, and their appearances lasted for three days, that the senate found itself at a loss over how each individual case should be handled.

Envoys had come from Thessaly both collectively and separately from each city; so too from the Perrhaebians, the Athamanians, the Epirotes, and the Illyrians.

Some were contesting territory, some persons, some livestock, and others contracts or private wrongs committed against them.

Some said they could not obtain justice under the treaty because Philip blocked the legal process, while others attacked the judgments already given as corrupted, alleging that Philip had bribed the judges.

Altogether the accusations were so varied and tangled that they were difficult to sort out.

Chapter 2 Demetrius in the Senate

So the senate, unable itself to disentangle the issues and judging that Demetrius ought not to be required to answer each charge one by one,

especially since it felt kindly toward him and saw that he was still very young and far from equal to such a knot of complicated business,

and since above all it wanted not to hear Demetrius' advocacy but to learn Philip's real intentions,

released Demetrius from pleading the cases and instead asked the young man and the friends with him whether they had any written memorandum from the king about these matters.

Demetrius said that they did, and when he produced a small document the senate ordered him to state the substance of the written instructions, giving a summary of Philip's answer to each accusation.

In it Philip claimed either that he had done what the Romans ordered, or that, if something had not been done, the blame lay with his accusers.

To most of the responses he had also added phrases such as, "and yet Caecilius and the envoys with him did not treat us fairly in this matter," or again, "and yet we are suffering this unjustly."

Since this attitude of Philip's ran through all the replies, the senate, after hearing the men who had come, adopted a single decision covering the whole business.

Through the presiding magistrate it received Demetrius with great honor and kindness, addressed him in many encouraging words, and replied that it trusted that in all the matters mentioned by him, whether spoken aloud or read from the memorandum, what was right had been done or would be done.

But, it added, so that Philip too might understand that the senate was granting this favor for Demetrius' sake, it would send envoys to inspect whether everything was being carried out in accordance with the senate's wishes, and at the same time to make clear to the king that he was receiving this considerate treatment because of Demetrius.

That was how this affair was settled.

Chapter 3 Philip's Jealousy Roused

After these men, the envoys from Eumenes were admitted. They accused Philip both for the aid he had sent to Prusias and for his conduct in Thrace, saying that even now he had not withdrawn his garrisons from the cities there.

Philocles wished to reply on these points, since he had served as envoy to Prusias and had now been sent by Philip to the senate on this business.

But the senate listened only briefly and answered that, unless the envoys found everything in Thrace arranged according to the senate's decision and all the cities handed back under the control of Eumenes, it could no longer tolerate continued disobedience in that region.

Thus the growing tension between Philip and Rome was for the moment checked by Demetrius' presence.

Yet this embassy of the young prince contributed no little to the eventual ruin of the royal house.

For the senate, by placing its favor so openly in Demetrius, lifted the young man up, but deeply offended both Perseus and Philip, since it seemed that the Romans were showing kindness not for their sakes but for Demetrius'.

Titus too, by drawing the young man aside and advancing him through private conversations, greatly helped the same development.

He flattered Demetrius by suggesting that the Romans would soon establish him on the throne, and he irritated Philip's circle by writing that Demetrius should be sent again to Rome with as many of his friends as possible, and those of the greatest usefulness.

By taking advantage of these openings Perseus soon persuaded his father to consent to Demetrius' death.

I will explain in the following narrative how all this was managed in detail.

Chapter 4 The Spartan Ambassadors

After this the envoys from Sparta were called in. There were four different parties among them.

The group led by Lysis spoke on behalf of the old exiles, arguing that they should recover all the property from which they had originally gone into exile.

Areus and Alcibiades, by contrast, proposed that each exile should receive property worth one talent out of his former holdings, while the rest should be distributed among those worthy of citizenship.

Serippus argued that the existing constitutional arrangement should remain in place, the same one under which Sparta had once shared citizenship with the Achaeans.

Representatives of those who had been executed or banished under decrees of the Achaeans, headed by Chaeron, appeared as well, demanding permission to return and the restoration of the constitution in that form, ***

and they all addressed arguments against the Achaeans suited to their own particular causes.

Since the senate could not reach a clear judgment on the separate disputes, it appointed three men who had already before this been sent to the Peloponnese on these matters: Titus, Quintus Caecilius, and Appius Claudius.

After considerable discussion before them, all agreed that the exiles and the men condemned to death should be restored, and that Sparta should remain associated with the Achaean League.

But they disputed with one another over the property, namely whether each exile ought to select from his former estate goods worth a talent, ***

and so that they might not begin the whole controversy over again from the start, a written record was drawn up of the points agreed on, *** and all affixed their seals to it.

Titus and his colleagues, wishing also to bind the Achaeans into the agreement, summoned Xenarchus and those with him.

These men were then acting as envoys from the Achaeans, partly to renew the alliance and partly to attend to the Spartan dispute.

Unexpectedly asked whether they assented to what had been written, they found themselves in difficulty.

For they were displeased at the restoration of the exiles and the condemned, since this ran contrary to Achaean decrees and to the inscribed tablet; yet they approved the document as a whole because it stated that Sparta must remain united politically with the Achaeans.

So, torn between perplexity on the one side and awe of these Roman commissioners on the other, they too set their seal to it.

The senate then selected Quintus Marcius as envoy and sent him both to Macedonia and to the Peloponnese.

Chapter 5 Deinocrates of Messene

When Deinocrates the Messenian arrived at Rome as an envoy and found that Titus had been appointed by the senate as envoy to Prusias and Seleucus, he was delighted, thinking that Titus, both because of their friendship—

for the two had become close during the war in Laconia—and because of his quarrel with Philopoemen, would come to Greece and manage all Messenian affairs according to Deinocrates' own wishes.

So he put everything else aside, attached himself closely to Titus, and rested all his hopes on him.

This Deinocrates of Messene was by practice, and also by nature, a man fit for camp and court.

He gave the appearance of complete political ability, but the appearance was false and superficial.

In military matters, through readiness and boldness, he surpassed most men and was brilliant in personal danger.

In ordinary society too he was agreeable and easy in conversation, lively and urbane in company, and at the same time much given to love affairs.

But in public or political business—fixing his attention firmly, foreseeing the future with confidence, making preparations, and speaking effectively before a crowd—he was incapable from start to finish.

Even then, though he had set great evils in motion for his homeland, he thought he was doing nothing of real consequence. He went on living in the same way as before, foreseeing nothing, carried away by romance, drinking-parties, and entertainments day after day.

Titus, however, forced him to catch at least some brief glimpse of the seriousness of the crisis.

For once, seeing him at a drinking-party dancing in long robes, Titus said nothing at the time; but the next day, when Deinocrates met him and made some request concerning his country,

he replied, "Deinocrates, I will do everything I can. But I am amazed that you can dance after drinking, when you have set such serious troubles in motion among the Greeks."

At that moment he seems to have drawn himself together a little and to have learned that he was displaying habits and tastes ill suited to the situation.

Even so, he came to Greece with Titus convinced that, in a single stroke, Messenian affairs would be arranged according to his own wishes.

But Philopoemen and his circle clearly understood that Titus had received no instructions from the senate concerning Greek affairs, and so they remained quiet, simply waiting for his arrival.

After Titus landed at Naupactus he wrote to the Achaean general and the demiourgoi, ordering them to summon the Achaeans to an assembly.

They wrote back that they would do so if he first stated in writing what subjects he wished to discuss with the Achaeans, since the laws required magistrates to specify this.

As Titus did not dare to write that down, the hopes of Deinocrates and of the so-called old exiles—who had in fact only recently been driven out of Sparta—and in general the whole expectation raised by Titus' arrival, all collapsed in this way.

Chapter 6 Ambassadors from the Spartan Exiles

Affairs in Greece.

At about the same time envoys were sent to Rome by the Spartan exiles, among them Arcesilaus and Agesipolis, who, though still a boy, had once become king at Sparta.

Some pirates fell upon these men at sea and killed them,

but the others appointed with them made their way safely to Rome.

Chapter 7 Philip and Perseus are Jealous of Demetrius

Affairs in Macedonia.

When Demetrius returned from Rome to Macedonia bringing the Roman replies, in which the Romans placed all their favor and confidence in him and declared that whatever they had done or would do was being done for his sake,

the Macedonians welcomed Demetrius warmly, believing that they had been released from great fears and dangers—

for they expected the war from Rome to break upon them very soon because of Philip's obstructive conduct—

but Philip and Perseus were not pleased by what was happening. They did not like it that the Romans seemed to pay no attention to them, but to ascribe all their goodwill to Demetrius.

Philip concealed his displeasure, but Perseus, who was far inferior to his brother not only in his goodwill toward Rome but in almost every other respect as well, both by nature and by training, took it badly.

What weighed on him most was his fear for the succession, lest, despite being the elder, he should be pushed aside for the reasons already mentioned.

Therefore he began to corrupt the friends of Demetrius ***.

Chapter 8 Death of Demetrius

When Quintus Marcius and his colleagues came on embassy to Macedonia, Philip withdrew entirely from the Greek cities in Thrace and removed his garrisons, though he did so in bitterness and with many groans.

He also set in order all the other matters on which the Romans were giving commands, wanting to show them no sign of estrangement while gaining time to turn back to preparations for war.

In pursuit of this design he led an army out against the barbarians.

Marching through the heart of Thrace, he invaded the lands of the Odrysae, the Bessi, and the Dentheletae.

When he reached the city called Philippopolis, the inhabitants fled up into the high ground, and he seized the city in a sudden attack.

After this he overran the whole plain, plundering some places and taking pledges from others, and then returned, leaving a garrison in Philippopolis.

But after some time that garrison was expelled by the Odrysae, who broke the pledges they had given the king.

Chapter 9 The Senate Refuses to Help Either Messene or Achaia

Olympiad 149, year 2. Affairs in Italy.

In the second year the senate, after embassies had arrived from Eumenes, Pharnaces, Philip, the Achaean nation, the Spartans who had been expelled from their city, and also those who still held Sparta, dealt with their business.

Envoys from Rhodes also came on behalf of the misfortune that had befallen the people of Sinope.

To them, and also to the envoys of Eumenes and Pharnaces, the senate replied that it would send representatives to inspect the situation at Sinope and the matters disputed between the kings.

Since Quintus Marcius had recently returned from Greece and had already made matters clear concerning Macedonia and the Peloponnese, the senate had no need of many more speeches.

So, after calling in the envoys from the Peloponnese and Macedonia, it listened to what they said, but based its replies and settlement of the issues not on the ambassadors' speeches, but on Marcius' report.

For with regard to King Philip, he had reported that Philip had indeed carried out the commands laid upon him, but had done everything resentfully, and that, if he got the chance, he would do anything against Rome.

Therefore the senate gave Philip's envoys a reply of this sort: it praised Philip for what he had done, but thought he must be careful from now on not to seem to act in any way contrary to Roman interests.

About Peloponnesian affairs Marcius had reported that the Achaeans did not want to refer anything to the senate, but carried themselves proudly and undertook to manage everything on their own.

He said that if the Romans would for the moment merely disregard their wishes and show even a slight sign of displeasure,

Sparta would quickly align itself with Messene, and then the Achaeans would come running to Rome with great eagerness.

Accordingly, to the Spartans under Serippus the senate replied—wanting to keep the city in suspense—that it had done everything it could for them, but did not at present think this matter belonged before itself.

And when the Achaeans asked either, if possible, for help under the alliance against the Messenians, or at least for precautions to prevent anyone from Italy from importing arms or grain into Messene, the senate paid attention to neither request.

Instead it answered that, even if the people of Sparta or Corinth or Argos should break away, the Achaeans should not be surprised if they were not conducting their leadership in a way acceptable to Rome.

By publishing this reply, which amounted to a public invitation to anyone wishing, under Roman protection, to revolt from the Achaean constitution, the senate then kept the envoys in Rome, waiting to see how matters at Messene would turn out for the Achaeans.

Such was the situation in Italy.

Chapter 10 Philip's Desperate Measures

Affairs in Macedonia.

At this time some dreadful beginning of troubles fell upon King Philip and upon all Macedonia, something well worth observing and remembering.

It was as though Fortune had resolved at the proper moment to exact from him punishment for all the impieties and crimes he had committed in the course of his life, and therefore had set before him avenging spirits, penalties, and the ghosts of those ruined through him.

Staying with him night and day, these torments punished him until life left him, so that everyone was compelled to admit the truth of the proverb that Justice has an eye, and that human beings should never despise it.

First they planted in him the idea that, if he meant to go to war with Rome, he should uproot the leading men from the most distinguished and coastal cities, together with their wives and children, and transfer them inland to the region then called Emathia, but formerly Paeonia,

and should fill those cities with Thracians and other barbarians, on the assumption that their loyalty would be firmer in a crisis.

As this was carried out and people were torn from their homes, there arose such grief and such an uproar that the whole country seemed like a land taken by the spear.

Curses and appeals to heaven against the king were uttered not only in secret now, but openly.

After this, wanting to leave nothing alien or hostile in the kingdom, he wrote to the officials set over the cities ordering them to search out the sons and daughters of the Macedonians he had put to death and place them under guard,

especially meaning those connected with Admetus, Pyrrhichus, Samus, and the others who had perished with them.

At the same time he included all the rest who had been deprived of life by royal command, quoting, it is said, this verse:

"A fool, who kills the father and leaves the sons behind."

Since most of these were prominent because of their fathers' rank, their misfortune too became conspicuous and pitiful to all.

Fortune introduced a third act into the drama at the same period, namely the matter of Philip's sons.

As the young men plotted against one another, and reports of this were brought before him, he was tortured by having to decide which of his sons he must become the killer of, and which one he had more reason to fear for the rest of his life, lest in old age he should suffer something similar himself.

With his mind in such distress and turmoil, who would not reasonably conclude that some divine wrath had descended upon his old age because of the lawless deeds of his earlier life?

This will become even clearer from what follows.

Philip king of the Macedonians, after killing many Macedonians, also took action against their sons, repeating, they say, the same verse:

"A fool, who kills the father and leaves the sons behind."

***

And because his soul was driven almost mad by these things, the quarrel between his sons was enflamed along with all the troubles already described, Fortune seeming intentionally to bring all these disasters onto the stage at one and the same time.

The Macedonians make offerings to Xanthus and carry out a purification with horses in full armor.

Chapter 11 Philip Addresses his Sons

"One must not merely read tragedies, myths, and histories, but also understand them and apply one's mind to this lesson.

In all of them one may see that brothers who fall into anger and rivalry against each other and let it run too far destroy not only themselves, but utterly ruin their households, their children, and their cities.

But all those who have had the moderation to cherish one another and to bear with each other's failings prove the preservers of all these things and live out their lives with the noblest reputation and glory.

I have often directed your attention to the kings at Sparta, telling you that they preserved for their fatherland the leadership of Greece for so long because, obeying the ephors as though they were parents, they endured sharing the kingship with one another.

But when they quarrelled and turned the government into monarchy, then they made Sparta taste every kind of evil.

And finally, as if showing you a visible example and placing it before your eyes, I continually pointed to Eumenes and Attalus,

who inherited a small and insignificant dominion and enlarged it until it was inferior to none, for no other reason than their harmony with one another, their agreement, and their ability to preserve mutual respect.

Yet, though you heard all this, you did not take it to heart; on the contrary, as it seems to me, you were sharpening your anger against each other."

Chapter 12 The Fall of Philopoemen

Affairs in Greece.

Polybius says that he rose and went on ahead, weighed down partly by sickness and partly by age, for he was in his seventieth year.

But mastering his weakness by force of his old habit, he came from Argos to Megalopolis in a single day. —

Philopoemen, general of the Achaeans, was captured by the Messenians and killed with poison, a man inferior to none of his predecessors in virtue, though weaker than Fortune, even though throughout his earlier life she had seemed to work with him.

It seems to me that the common proverb is right: a human being may meet with success, but to be successful to the very end is impossible.

Therefore we should call the men of old fortunate, not as though any of them enjoyed unbroken good fortune—for why should we vainly flatter Fortune with a false phrase?—

but rather those who have had her favorable for the longest part of life, and who, when she does change her mind, encounter only moderate disasters. —

... Lycortas, who was in no way inferior to him. —

Philopoemen, after seeking distinction continuously for forty years in a democratic and many-sided political system, completely escaped the envy of the masses in every respect,

though for the most part he conducted public affairs not by courting favor, but with frankness. And that is something one would rarely find. —

Chapter 13 Character of Hannibal

It is remarkable, and the strongest possible sign that this man was born to command and was far superior to others in practical ability,

that although he spent seventeen years in the field, passed through numerous barbarian peoples, and employed many foreign and differently-speaking men in enterprises that seemed desperate and astonishing, not one of those who once shared his plans and entrusted themselves to him ever plotted against him or deserted him.

Chapter 14 Character of P. Cornelius Scipio Africanus

Publius, after pursuing distinction in an aristocratic constitution, won such goodwill from the masses and such trust from the senate that,

when someone undertook to prosecute him before the people according to Roman custom and made many harsh and bitter accusations,

he came forward and said only that it was not fitting for the Roman people to listen to anyone accusing Publius Cornelius Scipio, the man through whom the accusers themselves possessed the freedom to speak.

On hearing this, the crowd at once broke up and all left the assembly, leaving the accuser there alone. —

On another occasion, when in the senate there was a need for money for an urgent public purpose, and the quaestor said that because of a certain law he would not open the treasury on that day, Scipio said that he himself would take the keys and open it,

for he himself had been the cause of the treasury's being shut at all.

Again, when someone in the senate asked him to render an account of the money he had received from Antiochus before the treaty for paying the army, he said that he had the ledger, but that he ought not to submit to an audit from anyone.

When the man kept pressing him and told him to produce it, Scipio ordered his brother to bring the document. When it had been brought, he held it out and tore it to pieces before everyone's eyes, telling the man who demanded the account to look for it among those scraps,

and then asked the others how it was that they wanted an accounting of how the three thousand talents had been spent and through whose hands,

but did not ask at all how the fifteen thousand talents they were receiving from Antiochus were entering Rome, through whose agency, or how they had become masters of Asia, Libya, and Iberia.

As a result, not only were all the others struck silent with amazement, but even the man who had demanded the account said no more.

Let this be said by us both for the sake of the glory of these departed men and to stir later generations toward noble actions. —

Chapter 15 Submission of the Messenians

It is not right to destroy the crops of those opposed to you. For Polybius says, "For my part I never agree with those who carry their anger against their own people so far that they not only strip their enemies of the year's produce,

but even destroy the trees and the built works, leaving no room for repentance.

Those who do such things seem to me gravely mistaken. For to the same degree that they think they are terrifying their enemies by ravaging the land and taking away not only present means of life but future hopes as well, to that same degree they make men savage and turn the anger of those who have once gone astray into something unchangeable." —

Chapter 16 Lycortas Defeats Messene

Lycortas, the general of the Achaeans, had broken the spirit of the Messenians by the war. *

The Messenians had long been terrified of their leaders, but now at last some of them dared to speak out, trusting in the enemy reserve force, and said that envoys should be sent to negotiate a settlement.

Deinocrates and his associates, no longer able to face the people because they were hard-pressed *** by the turn of events, gave way and withdrew to their own homes.

The majority, encouraged by the older men and especially by the envoys from Boeotia,

who had already come earlier about a settlement—Epaenetus and Apollodorus—and who happened opportunely to be in Messene at that moment, quickly appointed envoys and sent them out, begging pardon for what had been done.

The Achaean general took his colleagues with him, heard the envoys out, and said that there was only one possible reconciliation between the Messenians and the League:

they must immediately hand over to him those responsible for the revolt and for the murder of Philopoemen, submit all other matters to the judgment of the Achaeans, and admit a garrison at once into the citadel.

When these terms were reported to the crowd, those who had long been bitterly disposed against the men responsible for the war were eager to surrender and arrest them; and those who were persuaded that they would suffer nothing severe from the Achaeans readily agreed to entrust the rest of the matter to their decision.

In short, having no real choice in the present circumstances, they unanimously accepted the proposals.

The general therefore immediately took possession of the citadel and led the peltasts into it.

After that he took selected men from the camp, entered the city, gathered the populace together, and addressed them in language suitable to the crisis, promising that they would never regret the confidence they were placing in him.

The final decision on the whole issue he referred to the nation—for by what was almost a coincidence the Achaeans were again assembling at Megalopolis for the second synod—

but as for those charged with responsibility, all who had taken part in the immediate killing of Philopoemen he ordered to remove themselves from life at once *** —

Chapter 17 Arguments For and Against Admitting Sparta

The Messenians, by their own ignorance, had brought themselves to the very edge of ruin, but through the magnanimity of Lycortas and the Achaeans they were restored to their original position in the federal union.

At this same time Abia, Thuria, and Pharae separated themselves from Messene and, after each set up its own inscribed stele, joined the common federation independently.

When the Romans learned that affairs at Messene had turned out in the proper way for the Achaeans, they ignored their earlier reply and gave a different answer to the same envoys, making it clear that they had taken measures to prevent anyone from Italy from bringing either arms or grain into Messene.

From this it became obvious to everyone that they were very far from neglecting outside affairs unless absolutely necessary; quite the opposite, they were annoyed whenever everything was not referred to them and carried out according to their judgment.

When the envoys from Rome arrived in Sparta bringing this answer, the Achaean general, as soon as he had finished settling affairs at Messene, summoned the people to the city of the Sicyonians.

Once the Achaeans had assembled, he laid before them a proposal to admit Sparta into the federation,

saying that the Romans had declined the arbitration previously entrusted to them concerning that city, for they had now answered that affairs at Sparta were no concern of theirs,

while those who at present controlled Sparta wished to take part in the federation.

Therefore, he urged them to admit the city, for this would be advantageous in two ways. First, they would be receiving men who had preserved their loyalty to the League.

Second, they would not have as partners in the constitution those old exiles who had behaved ungratefully and impiously toward them; rather, by confirming the policy of those who had excluded such men from the city, they would both uphold the decision already taken and pay them the gratitude they deserved, with the favor of the gods.

With these and similar arguments Lycortas urged the Achaeans to receive Sparta.

But Diophanes and certain others tried to support the exiles, urging the Achaeans not to join in crushing men who had been banished, and not, because of a handful of people, to strengthen those who had impiously and unlawfully driven them from their fatherland.

Chapter 18 Sparta Included In the League

Such were the arguments made by both sides. After hearing them both, the Achaeans decided to admit the city; and after an inscribed stele had been drawn up, Sparta was politically united with the Achaeans,

the men then in possession of the city agreeing to receive such of the old exiles as were not thought to have committed any outrageous act against the Achaean nation.

After ratifying these measures, the Achaeans sent envoys to Rome, headed by Bippus of Argos, to explain everything to the senate.

The Spartans likewise appointed envoys led by Chaeron.

And the exiles sent Cletis and Diactorius to appear in the senate in opposition to the envoys from the Achaeans.

Book XXIV

Chapter 1 The Spartan Exiles Refused

Olympiad 149, year 3. Affairs in Italy.

When envoys had arrived at Rome from the Spartans, from the Spartan exiles, and from the Achaeans, and at the same time also from Eumenes, from king Ariarathes, and from Pharnaces, the senate dealt first with these latter embassies.

A short time earlier the envoys with Marcus, whom they had sent regarding the war between Eumenes and Pharnaces, had reported back and had made clear both Eumenes' moderation in every respect and Pharnaces' greed and general arrogance.

So after hearing the envoys now present, the senate did not require many arguments, but answered that it would again send commissioners to investigate more carefully the matters in dispute between the kings.

After this the exiles from Sparta entered, together with the envoys from the city itself; and after listening to them at length, the senate did not censure the men from the city for what had taken place.

To the exiles, however, it promised that it would write to the Achaeans about securing their return home.

A few days later the envoys headed by Bippus of Argos, who had been sent by the Achaean people, entered and explained the settlement of the Messenian question.

The senate, showing displeasure at none of the arrangements, gave the envoys a gracious reception.

Chapter 2 Treaty Between the Achaeans and the Messenians

Affairs in Greece.

When the Spartan exiles arrived in the Peloponnese from Rome and brought letters from the senate to the Achaeans asking them to make provision for the exiles' return and safety in their homeland,

the Achaeans decided to postpone deliberation on the matter until their own envoys should come back.

After giving this reply to the exiles, they set up the inscribed treaty with the Messenians, granting them, besides the other generous terms, exemption from taxes for three years, so that the devastation of the territory might burden the Achaeans no less than the Messenians.

But when Bippus and his companions returned from Rome and explained that the letters about the exiles had been written not because the senate was eager for the measure, but because the exiles had pressed the matter,

the Achaeans resolved to stand by the existing arrangements.

Chapter 3 Mount Haemus in Thrace

In Crete the beginning of serious troubles was being set in motion—if indeed one should speak of a "beginning" of troubles in Crete.

For because civil wars there are unceasing, and because the savagery they show one another is extreme, beginning and end are the same thing in Crete; and what some people might think a paradoxical statement can there be seen happening constantly.

Chapter 4 Troubles in Crete

Affairs in Macedonia.

Mount Haemus lies toward the Pontus, the greatest and highest of the mountains in that region, dividing Thrace more or less in the middle. Polybius says that from it both seas can be seen, but he is not right; for the distance to the Adriatic is great, and many things obstruct the view.

Chapter 5 Attalus Goes to Rome

Olympiad 149, year 4. Affairs in Italy.

After Pharnaces, Attalus, and the rest had made terms with one another, all withdrew with their own forces to their respective countries.

At this time Eumenes had recovered from his illness and was staying at Pergamum. When his brother arrived and explained what had been arranged, he approved what had been done and decided to send all his brothers to Rome,

partly because he hoped to bring the war with Pharnaces to an end through their embassy, and partly because he was eager to introduce his brothers, both to their own private friends and hosts at Rome and to the senate as a body.

Since Attalus and those with him were also eager for the journey, they set out.

When they arrived at Rome, everyone in private life welcomed the young men warmly, since they had become acquainted with them during the campaigns in Asia; and the senate gave their presence an even more splendid reception.

It provided them with generous hospitality and the fullest support, and met them graciously in audience.

When Attalus and his companions entered the senate, they first renewed at greater length the previous expressions of goodwill, and then, after accusing Pharnaces, asked the senate to take some action by which he might receive the punishment he deserved.

After hearing them graciously, the senate replied that it would send commissioners who would use every possible means to end the war.

That was the situation in Italy.

Chapter 6 Murder of Apollonides At Sparta

Affairs in Greece.

About the same time king Ptolemy, wishing to involve himself with the Achaean League, sent an embassy promising to provide a complete squadron of ten fifty-oared ships.

The Achaeans gladly accepted the offer, both because the gift seemed worthy of gratitude and because the expense appeared to amount to not much less than ten talents.

Having resolved this, they appointed Lycortas, Polybius, and with them Aratus son of Aratus of Sicyon as envoys, to thank the king both for the arms and the money he had previously sent, to receive the ships, and to make arrangements for bringing them back.

They chose Lycortas because, when Ptolemy renewed the alliance, he was serving as general and had zealously cooperated with him at that time;

Polybius, though younger than the legal age, because his father had acted as envoy to Ptolemy in renewing the alliance and had brought to the Achaeans the gift of the arms and the money;

and similarly Aratus because of his inherited ties of friendship with the royal house.

This embassy, however, never set out, because Ptolemy died about that time.

Chapter 7 Chaeron the Spartan Demagogue

At the same time there was in Sparta a certain Chaeron, who had happened to serve the previous year as envoy to Rome, a man clever and effective in action, but young, obscure, and brought up in a popular style.

By stirring up the mob and venturing on measures no one else had dared to attempt, he quickly won a reputation with the masses.

First he seized the land which the tyrants had granted to the sisters, wives, mothers, and children left behind by the exiles, and distributed it among the poor at random and unevenly on his own authority.

After that, treating public property as though it were his own, he spent the revenues without regard for law, public decree, or magistrate.

This angered certain men, and they pressed to have auditors of the public accounts appointed according to the laws.

Chaeron saw what was happening, and, conscious that he had badly mishandled the city's affairs, he had Apollonides—the most distinguished of the auditors and the man best able to expose his greed—attacked as he was leaving a bathhouse in broad daylight; he sent men against him and had him stabbed to death.

When news of this reached the Achaeans and the people were outraged at what had happened, the general set out at once and came to Sparta. He brought Chaeron to trial for the murder of Apollonides, condemned him, and placed him in custody.

He also urged the remaining auditors to make a genuine investigation into the public funds, and to see that the relatives of the exiles recovered once more the properties of which Chaeron had deprived them a short time before.

Chapter 8 Pharnaces Invades Cappadocia

At this time, when Hyperbatus the general brought before the assembly the question of what should be done about the letters from Rome concerning the return of the Spartan exiles,

the party of Lycortas urged that they should stand by the existing arrangements, because the Romans, they said, were only doing what suited them by listening within reasonable limits to men who seemed to have been wronged in the matter of their property.

But whenever someone showed them that some of the requests were impossible, and others would bring great disgrace and damage upon their friends, they were not accustomed to persist or to force such demands through.

Therefore, even now, if anyone shows them that by obeying what is written the Achaeans would violate the oaths, the laws, and the inscribed agreements that hold our federal union together,

they will retreat and agree that we are right to stand firm and to ask to be excused from what they have written. Such was what Lycortas and his party said.

But Hyperbatus and Callicrates urged obedience to the Roman letters, and said that neither law nor inscription nor anything else should be considered more binding than this.

As this dispute went on, the Achaeans decided to send envoys to the senate to explain the points made by Lycortas.

They immediately appointed as envoys Callicrates of Leontium, Lydiadas of Megalopolis, and Aratus of Sicyon, and after giving them instructions in accordance with this policy, sent them off.

But when they arrived at Rome, Callicrates entered the senate and was so far from presenting the case in accordance with his instructions that, from the very outset, he undertook not only to denounce his political opponents boldly, but even to lecture the senate.

Chapter 9 Eumenes and Pharnaces

For he said that the Romans themselves were responsible for the Greeks' refusal to obey them, and for their disregard of both written orders and verbal instructions.

For in all democratic states at present there were two tendencies: one held that people ought to follow what the Romans wrote, and should regard neither law nor inscription nor anything else as more important than Rome's decision;

the other appealed to the laws, the oaths, and the inscribed agreements, and urged the masses not to violate these lightly.

This latter position, he said, was by far the more Achaean in character and the more successful with the multitude.

As a result, disrepute and slander among the crowds attended those who chose the Roman side, while the opposite fell to those who resisted.

So if the senate gave some clear sign, the politicians would quickly shift toward the Roman preference, and the masses too would follow them out of fear.

But if this side were neglected, everyone would incline to the other position, because it appeared more honorable and finer in the eyes of the people.

Thus even now certain men, though offering no other claim to justice but ambition, were receiving the highest honors in their own states simply because they seemed to oppose your written instructions, on the pretext of keeping their own laws and decrees in force.

Therefore, if the Romans are indifferent to having the Greeks obey them and comply with what they write, he said they should continue the course they are now following.

But if they want their instructions to be carried out and none of their written orders treated with contempt, they must give this matter the attention it deserves.

Otherwise, they should clearly understand that the opposite of their intentions will happen—which, he said, had in fact already happened.

For quite recently, in the Messenian affair, although Quintus Marcius had taken many steps to ensure that the Achaeans made no decision about the Messenians without Roman approval,

they disregarded him and voted for war; they not only devastated the whole country unjustly, but also drove some of the noblest citizens into exile, and others, after taking them in surrender, tortured in every way and put to death, merely because they appealed to Rome concerning the disputed matters.

And now again, although the Romans had for a long time been writing about the return of the Spartan exiles, the Achaeans were so far from obeying that they had even set up an inscribed stele and sworn agreements with those who held the city, pledging that the exiles should never be restored.

In view of all this, he urged them to take thought for the future.

Chapter 10 Callicrates Sent to Rome

After Callicrates had spoken these and similar words, he withdrew.

Then the exiles came in, briefly explained their own case, added some appeals to common pity, and departed.

The senate judged that Callicrates had said things advantageous to its own interests, and learned from him that it ought to strengthen those who supported its decrees and humble those who opposed them.

Thus, from that time onward, it first set itself to weakening in their own states the men who took the noblest course,

and to gathering around itself those who ran to it, whether justly or unjustly. As time went on, the result for Rome was that it came to have plenty of flatterers but few genuine friends.

At that moment, regarding the return of the exiles, it wrote not only to the Achaeans urging them to lend support, but also to the Aetolians, Epirotes, Athenians, Boeotians, and Acarnanians, summoning them all, as it were, as joint witnesses in order to crush the Achaeans.

And as for Callicrates himself, passing over his fellow envoys in silence, it inserted into its reply a remark that each state ought to have men like Callicrates.

Armed with these replies, the man returned to Greece exultant, not knowing that he had become the originator of great evils for all the Greeks, and especially for the Achaeans.

For even at that time it was still possible for them to maintain something like equal frankness in their dealings with the Romans, because they had kept faith in the most critical times from the moment they chose the Roman side—I mean in the wars against Philip and Antiochus.

And since the Achaean nation had grown and advanced in the best direction from the period covered by my history, this in turn became the beginning of its change for the worse: the audacity of Callicrates.

The Romans, being human beings and possessed of a noble spirit and good intentions, feel pity for those who have suffered misfortune and try to grant favors to all who seek refuge with them.

But whenever someone reminds them of what is just, having kept faith, they draw back and, so far as they can, correct themselves in most matters.

Callicrates, however, when he went to Rome at this time, was supposed to speak for the rights of the Achaeans; instead he acted in the opposite way, and by dragging in the Messenian affair—a matter about which the Romans were not even making accusations—returned to Achaea magnifying the fear inspired by Rome.

And by his embassy he overawed and broke the spirit of the masses, since the common people had no idea what he had truly said in the senate. First of all, he was elected general, and, to add to the other evils, he did so by bribery;

and after taking office he restored the exiles from Sparta and from Messene.

Chapter 11 Callicrates Turns Traitor

Philopoemen and Aristaenus, both Achaeans, were unlike each other both in natural character and in political choice.

Philopoemen was by nature well fitted, in both body and spirit, for military action; the other for civil deliberation.

In political judgment they differed in this way. Once Roman supremacy had become fully entangled with Greek affairs, both in the period of the wars against Philip and that against Antiochus,

Aristaenus conducted the policy of the state so as to do at once everything that suited the Romans, and in some matters even before they gave orders.

Still, he tried to appear to hold to the laws, and he cultivated that impression, giving way whenever any of them clearly conflicted with what the Romans wrote.

Philopoemen, on the other hand, agreed to and supported without excuse everything the Romans asked that was consistent with the laws and the alliance,

but whenever they ordered anything beyond those limits, he could not bring himself to comply willingly. Instead he said they must first make a legal case,

and then press their claim again; and if even then they failed to persuade, one should at last yield under protest and only then do what was required.

Chapter 12 Rome and the Achaean League

Aristaenus used such arguments as these before the Achaeans in defense of his own policy. He said that it was impossible, while holding out both the spear and the herald's staff at once, to preserve friendship with Rome.

"But if we are able to look them in the face and have the power to do so ...

if not, and if not even Philopoemen dares to say this ... one must be of one mind with the Romans in present circumstances,

why, by reaching for impossibilities, should we throw away what is possible?" For, he said, every policy has two aims: what is honorable and what is advantageous. Those for whom the attainment of honor is possible should cling to it if they govern rightly; but those for whom it is impossible must take refuge in advantage.

To miss both, he said, is the clearest mark of poor judgment. And this plainly happens to those who agree without excuse to everything ordered, yet do so unwillingly and with hesitation.

Therefore we must either show that we are capable of refusing obedience, or, if we do not dare even to say that, we must be ready to comply promptly with all commands."

Chapter 13 Comparison Between Philopoemen and Aristaenus

Philopoemen said one should not judge him so ignorant that he was unable to measure either the difference between the Roman and Achaean constitutions or the superiority of Roman power.

But since it is the nature of every superiority always to treat those under it more harshly, he asked whether it was really advantageous to cooperate with the impulses of the stronger power and put no obstacle in its way, so that we might as quickly as possible experience its heaviest commands—or rather, to struggle against it and hold out, so far as we are able, for as long as we can.

And even if they do issue commands, by reminding them of these considerations and checking their impulse we will at least restrain to some extent the bitterness of their power—especially since, as you yourself say, Aristaenus, the Romans up to the present care greatly for keeping oaths, treaties, and faith with allies.

But if we ourselves condemn our own rights from the outset and immediately, like men taken by the spear, present ourselves as ready for everything commanded, what difference will there be between the Achaean nation and the Sicilians or the Capuans, who have long been acknowledged slaves?

Therefore, he said, one must either concede this: that no justice has any force with the Romans; or, if one does not dare say that, one must make use of what is just and not abandon one's own cause, especially when we possess the greatest and noblest advantages in dealing with Rome.

For he said that he knew clearly this time would one day come for the Greeks, when they would be forced to do everything commanded.

"But would one wish to see that time come as quickly as possible, or as slowly as possible? Surely," he said, "as slowly as possible."

"That," he said, "is the difference between Aristaenus' policy and my own. He is eager to see the inevitable arrive as soon as possible and to assist it as far as he can; but I resist it and try to push it back, so far as it is possible for me."

From what has been said, it is clear that the policy of the one was honorable, and that of the other decorous, and that both were in fact safe.

Thus, when the greatest crises then confronted both Romans and Greeks in the wars against Philip and Antiochus, both men nevertheless preserved unimpaired the rights of the Achaeans in relation to Rome.

Yet a report circulated that Aristaenus was more favorably disposed toward the Romans than Philopoemen.

Chapter 14 Aristaenus's Attitude to Rome

Affairs in Asia.

In Asia king Pharnaces, once again disregarding the appeal that had been made to Rome, sent Leocritus during the winter with ten thousand troops to ravage Galatia,

while he himself, as spring was appearing, gathered his forces with the intention of invading Cappadocia.

When Eumenes learned this, he was deeply troubled because Pharnaces was overstepping every limit of good faith, yet he was compelled to act in much the same way.

And when he had already assembled his forces, Attalus and those with him sailed back from Rome.

Once they had come together and exchanged views, they immediately marched out with the army.

When they reached Galatia they no longer found Leocritus there. Cassignatus and Gaizatorix, who had taken Pharnaces' side the year before, sent messages to them asking for safety and promising to do whatever was ordered.

But Eumenes and his party rejected them because of their earlier disloyalty, and then advanced with their entire army against Pharnaces.

Starting from Calpitus, they reached the river Halys on the fifth day, and after six more days' march they moved on to Parnassus.

There Ariarathes, king of the Cappadocians, joined them with his own forces, and together they entered the territory of the Mocissi.

Just as they had encamped, news came that Roman envoys had arrived to negotiate a settlement.

When king Eumenes heard this, he sent Attalus to receive them, while he himself doubled his forces and carefully put them in order, both to meet the actual demands of the campaign and because he wished to show the Romans that he was capable, by his own power, of defending himself against Pharnaces—

Chapter 15 Philopoemen's Policy

—and of defeating him in war. When the envoys arrived and urged that the war be ended, Eumenes and Ariarathes said that they were ready for anything asked of them,

but they requested the Romans, if possible, to bring them together in conference with Pharnaces, so that by hearing the arguments face to face they might see more fully his faithlessness and cruelty.

If that was not possible, they asked the Romans themselves to act as fair and impartial judges of the dispute.

The envoys undertook to do everything possible and honorable, but they demanded that the army be withdrawn from the country,

for it was absurd that, while envoys were present and making proposals for peace, the operations of war should continue and the two sides should keep harming one another.

Eumenes and his party agreed, and immediately broke camp and marched off toward Galatia.

The Romans then met with Pharnaces and first demanded that he enter into discussions with Eumenes' party, since in that way the business would most likely be brought to a conclusion.

But when he resisted this point and finally refused outright, it was at once clear to the Romans that he was plainly condemning himself and had no confidence in his own case.

Nevertheless, since they were determined by every means to end the war, they persisted until he agreed to send plenipotentiaries by sea to Pergamum to conclude the peace on whatever terms the envoys should prescribe.

When the envoys had arrived and the Romans and Eumenes' party came together, the latter proved ready to accept everything for the sake of bringing the peace to completion.

But the representatives from Pharnaces disputed every point, would not stand by what had already been agreed, and kept introducing fresh demands and changing their minds. The Romans quickly saw that they were laboring in vain, for Pharnaces was not the sort of man to come to terms.

So when the conference accomplished nothing, the Romans departed from Pergamum, the envoys of Pharnaces were dismissed to return home, the war was left to continue by itself, and Eumenes' party again turned to preparations for it.

At that time the Rhodians urgently drew Eumenes to their side, and he set out with great eagerness to deal with the matters concerning the Lycians ...

Book XXV

Chapter 1 Destruction of Celtiberian Cities

Olympiad 150, year 1. Affairs in Spain.

When Polybius says that Tiberius Gracchus destroyed three hundred Celtiberian cities, Poseidonius remarks mockingly that the historian meant to do Gracchus a favor by calling towers "cities," the way they do in triumphal processions.

And perhaps the point is not unbelievable; for both generals and historians are easily drawn into this kind of falsehood, dressing up events to make them look finer.

Chapter 2 The Accession of Perseus

Affairs in Asia.

Because the attack upon him had been sudden and severe, Pharnaces was ready to accept whatever terms were proposed; so he sent envoys to Eumenes and Ariarathes.

When Eumenes and Ariarathes accepted these proposals and at once sent envoys of their own to Pharnaces, and when this exchange had taken place several times on both sides, the settlement was ratified on these terms:

There was to be peace forever between Eumenes, Prusias, and Ariarathes on the one side, and Pharnaces and Mithridates on the other.

Pharnaces was not to invade Galatia on any pretext whatever; and any earlier treaties between Pharnaces and the Gauls were to be void.

Likewise he was to withdraw from Paphlagonia, restoring the inhabitants whom he had previously carried off, together with their arms, missiles, and the rest of their equipment.

He was also to restore to Ariarathes the districts he had taken from him, together with the equipment already there, and the hostages.

He was also to give back Tium on the Pontus, which after some time Eumenes later granted to Prusias as a generous favor.

It was further written that Pharnaces should restore all prisoners without ransom, as well as all deserters.

In addition, from the money and treasure that he had carried off from Morzius and Ariarathes, he was to pay the aforesaid kings nine hundred talents,

and to add three hundred talents for Eumenes toward the expenses of the war.

A further clause imposed on Mithridates, the satrap of Armenia, a payment of three hundred talents, because he had broken his treaty with Eumenes and made war on Ariarathes.

Included in the treaty, among the dynasts of Asia, were Artaxias, ruler of the greater part of Armenia, and Acusilochus;

and among those in Europe, Gatalus the Sarmatian; and among the autonomous communities, the people of Heraclea, the Mesembrians, the people of the Chersonese, and along with them the Cyzicenes.

Finally, the treaty specified how many hostages Pharnaces must give and who they were to be; and when these also had arrived, the armies broke up and marched away from the place.

Such was the outcome of the war waged by Eumenes and Ariarathes against Pharnaces.

Chapter 3 First Acts of Perseus as King

Olympiad 150, year 2. Affairs in Macedonia.

After renewing his friendship with the Romans, Perseus at once set about winning influence in Greece, inviting into Macedonia men who had fled because of debt, men driven into exile by convictions, and men who had withdrawn under charges affecting the royal interest.

He posted notices about this at Delos, Delphi, and the sanctuary of Athena Itonia, offering those who came down not only personal safety but also recovery of the property from which each had fled.

Within Macedonia itself he also cancelled debts owed to the crown and released those who had been confined in prisons on charges against the royal authority.

By doing this he raised the hopes of many, seeming to hold out fair expectations of himself to all the Greeks.

In the rest of his way of life too he displayed the dignity proper to kingship.

For in outward appearance he was impressive, and for every bodily demand that belongs to an active public life he was well fitted; even in expression and bearing he had a gravity and composure well suited to his age.

He had also escaped his father's self-indulgence, both in women and in drinking. He himself drank moderately at dinner, and so did the friends in his company.

Such was the tone of the opening of Perseus' reign.—As for king Philip,

when he had grown powerful and gained mastery over the Greeks, he proved more faithless and lawless than any man; but when fortune later turned against him, he became more moderate than any man.

And after he had suffered a complete reverse in his general position, he tried in every possible way to give his kingship a firmer practical foundation.

Chapter 4 Character and First Measures of Perseus

Olympiad 150, year 3. Affairs in Italy.

After the consuls Tiberius and Claudius had been sent against the Istrians and Agrians, the senate, now that summer was already drawing to its close, dealt with the envoys who had come from the Lycians,

men who had reached Rome only after the Lycians had already been defeated, though they had in fact been dispatched a considerable time earlier.

For when the people of Xanthus were just about to enter the war, they had sent Nicostratus and his colleagues as envoys both to Achaea and to Rome.

When these men then arrived at Rome, they stirred many of the senate to pity by setting before their eyes both the harshness of the Rhodians and their own desperate situation.

At last they brought the senate to the point of sending envoys to Rhodes to make clear that, when the records were consulted of what the ten commissioners had arranged in Asia while settling affairs with Antiochus, it was found that the Lycians had been assigned to the Rhodians not as a gift, but rather on the footing of friends and allies.

Yet even when the settlement had been made in these terms, the result did not please many people at all.

For the Romans seemed to be acting as umpires between the Rhodians and the Lycians because they wanted the Rhodians' accumulated resources and treasuries to be drained away,

having heard both of the bridal escort that the Rhodians had recently provided for Perseus and of their review of ships.

For a short time before this the Rhodians had conspicuously displayed, with great magnificence, the full strength of all the vessels they possessed.

A large supply of timber for shipbuilding had in fact been furnished to the Rhodians by Perseus, and he had also presented a gold headband to each of the upper-deck rowers who had recently escorted his bride Laodice.

Chapter 5 Lycians Revolt Again

Affairs of Rhodes.

When the envoys from Rome arrived at Rhodes and explained the senate's decision, there was an uproar in Rhodes and great agitation among the politicians, because they were indignant that the Lycians were said not to have been given to them as a gift, but to stand to them only in an allied relation.

For just when they thought the Lycian question had been satisfactorily settled, they now saw the beginning of a fresh crisis taking shape.

As soon as the Romans arrived and made this declaration to the Rhodians, the Lycians immediately rose again in faction and were ready to endure anything for the sake of autonomy and freedom.

The Rhodians, however, after hearing the envoys and concluding that the Romans had been deceived by the Lycians, at once appointed Lycophron and his colleagues as ambassadors to instruct the senate on the points just mentioned.

That was the state of the matter at the time, when it still did not seem likely that the Lycians would once again revolt.

Chapter 6 The Dardanian Envoys Complain about Perseus

Olympiad 150, year 4. Affairs in Italy.

When the envoys from Rhodes arrived, the senate heard their speech and postponed its reply.

But when the Dardanians came and described both the numbers of the Bastarnae and the great size of the men and their boldness in danger,

and also made clear the collusion of Perseus and the Gauls, saying that they were more anxious about him than about the Bastarnae and therefore begging for Roman aid,

and when Thessalians were also present, supporting the Dardanians' testimony and themselves urging the Romans to help,

the senate decided to send certain men who would be eyewitnesses of what was being reported.

So they immediately appointed Aulus Postumius and sent him out, together with some young men.

Book XXVI

Chapter 1 Antiochus Epiphanes

Antiochus, though called Epiphanes, was nicknamed Epimanes from his conduct. Polybius says of him that he would sometimes slip away from the court, eluding his attendants, and then be seen wandering about aimlessly in some quarter of the city with only two or three companions.

Most often he was found at the silversmiths' and goldsmiths' shops, chatting and showing his enthusiasm for craftsmanship with the metalworkers and other artisans.

At other times he would mix with ordinary townsmen and converse with anyone he happened to meet, and he would even drink with visiting foreigners of the humblest sort.

If he learned that some young men were feasting together, he would appear among them without any warning, bringing horns and musicians with him in reveling fashion, so that most people, startled by the oddity of it, would get up and run away.

He would often lay aside his royal dress, put on a toga-like robe, and walk about the marketplace canvassing for office, shaking hands with some men and even embracing others as he asked for their vote, sometimes as though he were seeking the aedileship and sometimes the tribunate.

And when he had won the office, he would sit down on the ivory curule chair in the Roman manner, hear the business cases conducted in the marketplace, and decide them with great seriousness and eagerness. By this he left sensible people perplexed:

some thought him a simple, guileless man, while others thought him mad. His conduct in giving presents was similar. To some he gave knucklebones made from gazelle horn,

to others dates, and to others gold.

He would even encounter certain men by chance whom he had never seen before and give them unexpected gifts.

In the sacrifices offered by cities and in honors shown to the gods he surpassed all previous kings.

One may judge this from the Olympieion at Athens and from the statues around the altar at Delos.

He even bathed in the public baths when they were crowded with ordinary townsmen, with jars of the costliest perfumes brought in for him.

Once, when someone said, "How fortunate you kings are, to use such things and smell so sweet," he said nothing to the man; but on the next day, when that fellow was bathing, Antiochus came in and had a very large jar of the most expensive perfume, the kind called stacte, poured over his head,

with the result that all the bathers jumped up and rolled themselves in the perfume, then kept slipping and falling because it was so sticky, providing laughter for everyone, including the king himself.

Chapter 1a

Olympiad 151. Affairs of Antiochus.

Polybius, in the twenty-sixth book of the Histories, calls him Epimanes rather than Epiphanes because of his conduct. For he not only came down to associate with common townsmen, but even drank with visiting foreigners and with the very meanest people.

And if, he says, he became aware that some young men were feasting together anywhere, he would appear with horn-music and a band, so that most people, startled by the strangeness of it, would leap up and run away. He often even cast off his royal dress, put on a toga-like cloak, and walked about the marketplace.

Book XXVII

Chapter 1 Affairs In Boeotia: The War with Perseus

Olympiad 152, year 1. The war with Perseus.

At this time envoys arrived: from the Thespians, Lases and Callea with their party, and from Neon, Ismenias.

Lases and his colleagues were placing their own city in Roman hands, while Ismenias was offering all the cities in Boeotia together, as a single body, to the discretion of the commissioners.

This proposal was exactly contrary to the policy of Marcius and his associates; what best suited them was to divide the Boeotians city by city.

So they gladly received and warmly courted Lases and his party, as well as the men from Chaeronea, Lebadea, and all the others who had come from individual cities,

but they made a public example of Ismenias, brushing him off and treating him with contempt.

Indeed some of the exiles joined in attacking him and nearly stoned him to death, if he had not fled for refuge beneath the Roman doorway.

At the same time disturbances and civil conflict were taking place in Thebes.

One side said the city must be entrusted to the Romans, while the men of Coronea and Haliartus, who had gathered in Thebes, still claimed control of affairs and insisted that they must remain in alliance with Perseus.

For a while the two factions were evenly matched. But when Olympichus of Coronea was the first to change sides and declared that they must stand by the Romans, there came a complete swing and reversal in the temper of the crowd,

and first they compelled Dicetas to go as envoy to Marcius and his colleagues to make a defense of the alliance with Perseus.

After that they expelled Neon and Hippias, rushing to their houses and ordering them to defend themselves for the policy they had managed; for these were the men who had arranged the alliance.

Once these men had withdrawn, the Thebans immediately assembled, voted honors and gifts for the Romans, and then ordered the magistrates to put the alliance into effect.

Finally they appointed envoys to hand over the city to the Romans and to bring back their own exiles.

Chapter 2 Romans and Perseus Try to Secure Greece

While these things were being carried through at Thebes, the exiles at Chalcis put forward Pompides and brought charges against Ismenias, Neon, and Dicetas.

Since the mistaken policy of the men already mentioned was plain enough, and since the Romans were strengthening the hand of the exiles,

Hippias and his party were brought into such extreme unpopularity that they even ran the risk of their lives at that very moment from the rush of the crowd, until the Romans provided them with a little security by restraining the mob's attack.

When the Thebans arrived carrying the decrees and honors already mentioned, each matter was answered with rapid effect, since the cities lay very close to one another.

After receiving the Thebans, Marcius and his colleagues praised the city and advised them to restore the exiles to their homes.

They immediately instructed all the cities to send embassies to Rome, each one separately placing itself under Roman protection.

And since everything was turning out according to their intention—for their object was to dissolve the Boeotian nation and to destroy the goodwill of the masses toward the Macedonian royal house—

they sent for Servius from Argos and, leaving him at Chalcis, advanced into the Peloponnese; while Neon, after a few days, withdrew to Macedonia.

Ismenias and Dicetas were then led off to prison, and after some time they took their own lives.

Thus the Boeotian nation, which had preserved its common federal union for a long time and had surprisingly survived many varied crises, was then dissolved and broken up into separate cities, because it had rashly and irrationally chosen the side offered by Perseus, panicking in a childish and thoughtless way.

Aulus and Marcius, when they reached the city of the Argives, conferred with the magistrates of the Achaeans and asked Archon the general to send a thousand soldiers to Chalcis to guard the city until the Roman crossing.

Archon readily complied. So after accomplishing these measures among the Greeks during the winter, and after meeting with Publius, they sailed back to Rome.

Chapter 3 Rhodes Prepares to Assist Rome

At the same period Tiberius, Postumius, and Junius were making a tour of the islands and the cities in Asia and spent the greatest part of their time in Rhodes,

though in those days the Rhodians had no need of supervision.

For Agesilochus, who was then serving as prytanis, a man of high standing who later also went on embassy to Rome, had even earlier, as soon as it became clear that the Romans were about to make war on Perseus, urged the people in other respects as well to share the same hopes as Rome, and had advised the Rhodians to put forty ships in readiness,

so that, if some need should arise from circumstances, they would not still be making preparations at the moment they were called upon, but, already ready, could carry out the decision at once.

By laying these points before the Romans at that time and showing them the preparations before their eyes, he sent the envoys away with the city in high favor. Tiberius and his colleagues, after welcoming the Rhodians' goodwill, carried the report back to Rome.

Chapter 4 Perseus Sends a Statement to the Greeks

After the conference with the Romans and the Greek states, Perseus set down in a letter the whole of his legal case and the arguments spoken on either side,

partly because he supposed he would appear to have the stronger claim in justice, and partly because he wished to test the disposition of each state.

So to the other states he sent the letters by ordinary couriers, but to Rhodes he sent envoys along with them, Antenor and Philip.

When these men arrived, they delivered the written statement to the magistrates; and a few days later, appearing before the council, they urged the Rhodians for the present to remain quiet and watch the course of events.

But if the Romans, contrary to the treaties, should attempt to lay hands on Perseus and the Macedonians, then they were to try to bring about a settlement.

For this, they said, was advantageous to everyone and especially fitting for the Rhodians.

The more they reached after equal speech and frankness, and continually stood forward as champions not only of their own freedom but also of that of the rest of the Greeks, the more they ought to foresee and guard against the opposite policy to the best of their ability.

When the envoys had spoken these and similar words, what they said pleased everyone.

But because the Rhodians were already committed to goodwill toward Rome, and because the sounder judgment prevailed among them, though they received the envoys kindly in all other respects, they insisted in their reply that Perseus must not call on them for anything of such a kind as would make them appear to act against the will of the Romans.

Antenor and his colleagues did not accept that answer; but, satisfied with the rest of the Rhodians' courtesy, they sailed back to Macedonia.

Chapter 5 Perseus Sends Alexander to Boeotia

Perseus learned that some of the cities in Boeotia were still holding fast to their goodwill toward him, and he sent Antigonus, the son of Alexander, as envoy.

When he arrived in Boeotia, he passed over the other cities because he found no opening for closer dealings there,

but he entered Coronea, Thisbae, and also Haliartus, and urged the people to hold fast to their goodwill toward the Macedonians.

They gladly accepted what he said and voted to send envoys to Macedonia, so he sailed away and, on meeting the king, gave him a full report on the situation in Boeotia.

A little later the envoys also arrived and asked him to send help to the cities that had chosen the Macedonian side,

for the Thebans, they said, were pressing them hard and harassing them because they would not agree with them or choose the side of Rome.

When Perseus heard this, he said that because of the truce he could not send military help to anyone at all,
