but he urged them generally to defend themselves against the Thebans as best they could, while not making war on the Romans, but remaining quiet.

Chapter 6 The Boeotians and Rhodians

When the Romans had heard the envoys who had come from Asia speak about Rhodes and the other cities, they summoned the envoys sent by Perseus.

Solon and Hippias and their party tried to say something about the whole situation and to appease the senate, but for the most part they defended themselves against the charge of the plot against Eumenes.

When they had finished their defense, the senate, having long since resolved on war, ordered them to leave Rome at once, and all other Macedonians who happened to be staying in Italy to depart within thirty days.

After this they called in the consuls and urged them to seize the moment and not delay.

Chapter 7 War With Perseus Begun

While Gaius was still lying at anchor off Cephallenia, he sent the Rhodians a letter about dispatching ships, entrusting the letter to a certain athletic trainer named Socrates.

When the letter reached Rhodes, Stratocles was serving as prytanis in the second half-year of his term.

When the matter was brought forward for debate, Agathagetes, Rhodophon, Astymedes, and many others thought the ships should be sent and that they should join the war at once from the beginning, without making any pretext.

But Deinon, Polyaratus, and their party, though already displeased by the friendly attitude that had been shown toward the Romans, now put forward King Eumenes as a pretext and began to corrupt the inclination of the masses.

For the Rhodians had long felt suspicion and hostility toward Eumenes, first dating from the war against Pharnaces, when Eumenes was blockading the mouth of the Hellespont to keep ships from sailing into the Black Sea, and the Rhodians intervened and stopped him,

and then, in more recent times, the quarrel had been stirred up again by the Lycian disputes over certain forts and a tract of land that lay on the border of the Rhodian Peraea and was continually being ravaged by troops under Eumenes.

Because of all this they were ready enough to listen to anything said against the king.

So Deinon's party seized on this opportunity and tried to discredit the letter, saying that it had come not from the Romans but from Eumenes, who wanted by every possible means to drag them into the war and saddle the people with needless expense and suffering.

As proof of what they said, they pointed to the fact that the man who had brought the letter was just such a person as this, whereas the Romans were not accustomed to act in that way, but sent communications of this kind with great seriousness and official protection.

They said this even though they knew perfectly well that the letter had in fact been written by Lucretius, because they wanted to teach the masses not to do anything readily for the Romans, but in every matter to be difficult and to provide occasions for suspicion and resentment.

For their purpose was to estrange the people from their goodwill toward Rome and, so far as they could, entangle them in friendship with Perseus.

These men were devoted to that course because Polyaratus, being more boastful and vain, had burdened his estate with debt, while Deinon, being greedy and reckless, had from the beginning been drawn to the profits that came from powerful lords and kings.

At this point Stratocles the prytanis rose and, after speaking at length against Perseus and much in favor of the Romans, urged the majority to ratify the decree for dispatching the ships.

They immediately made ready six quadriremes, sent five of them to Chalcis with Timagoras appointed to command them, and the remaining one to Tenedos under a commander named Timagoras.

When he reached Tenedos, he came upon Diophanes, who had been sent by Perseus to Antiochus; he did not get possession of Diophanes himself, but he did capture his crew.

Lucretius received all the allies who had come by sea with kindness and then released them from this service, saying that the situation did not require naval assistance.

Chapter 8 Perseus Summons a Council

After the Macedonian victory, when a council had been gathered around Perseus, some of his friends pointed out that the king ought to send an embassy to the Roman commander,

and even now declare himself willing to pay the Romans the tribute that his father, when defeated, had previously promised, and to give up the same places.

For if the Romans accepted the settlement, they said, the war would end honorably for the king after his success in the field, and in general the Romans would in future be more cautious, now that they had had experience of Macedonian valor, not to impose anything unjust or oppressive on the Macedonians.

But if they refused to accept out of angry pride over what had happened, then heaven would justly be offended with them, while he, because of his moderation, would have both gods and men fighting on his side.

This view was approved by most of his friends, and Perseus agreed, so envoys were sent at once: Pantauchus son of Balacrus and Midon of Beroea.

When they arrived before Licinius, the commander immediately called a council. After the envoys had explained the message they had been instructed to deliver, Pantauchus and his colleague were asked to withdraw, and the Romans deliberated on the situation before them.

They unanimously decided to give the harshest answer possible.

For among the Romans this is in every way an established ancestral custom: in times of setback they show themselves most headstrong and severe, but in times of success most moderate.

Everyone would agree that this is a noble trait; but whether it is always practicable in certain circumstances, one might reasonably question.

At any rate, on that occasion they gave this answer: Perseus must place himself and all that concerned him in their hands, and in general give the senate authority to decide, as it thought best, about Macedonian affairs.

When Pantauchus and his colleague heard this, they returned and reported it to Perseus and his friends.

Some of them were shocked by such arrogance, grew angry, and advised Perseus to send no more embassies or messages about anything whatever.

Perseus, however, was not that sort of man. Instead he kept adding to the amount of money offered and sent to Licinius again and again.

But he made no progress, and most of his friends reproached him, saying that though he was the victor he was acting like the defeated party, as if everything had gone wrong for him.

So in the end, abandoning hope in further embassies, he was forced to move his camp back again to Sicyrium.

Chapter 9 Moral Effect of Perseus's Successes

When news of the cavalry engagement and the Macedonian victory spread through Greece, the feelings of the masses for Perseus flared up like fire, though most of them had previously kept those feelings concealed.

Their state of mind, as it seems to me, was something like this: what happened was much the same as in athletic contests.

For there too, whenever a humble and far inferior challenger is matched against a famous athlete thought to be unbeatable, the crowd immediately gives its support to the weaker man, urges him to be bold, and throws itself into his efforts.

And if he even brushes the other's face and leaves some visible mark from the blow, the whole crowd is at once thrown into excitement.

Sometimes they even begin jeering at the other man, not because they hate him or think little of him, but because, in a surprising way, their sympathies are stirred and they naturally give their favor to the weaker side.

But if someone checks them at the right moment, they quickly change and immediately recognize their own mistake. Cleitomachus is said to have done just this.

He seemed irresistible as an athlete, and his fame had spread throughout the inhabited world. So King Ptolemy, eager to put an end to that reputation, is said to have trained the boxer Aristonicus with great care and sent him out, since he seemed to have exceptional natural gifts for that purpose.

When Aristonicus arrived in Greece and was matched against Cleitomachus at Olympia, the crowd, it seems, leaned toward Aristonicus from the very beginning and kept encouraging him, delighted that someone had at least dared to stand up to Cleitomachus.

And when, as the contest went on, he appeared to be holding his own and even landed a telling blow, there was loud applause, and the mass of spectators broke out together, shouting encouragement to Aristonicus.

At that point, they say, Cleitomachus stepped back and paused a little to catch his breath; then he turned to the crowd and asked them what they meant by cheering Aristonicus and supporting him as much as they could,

whether they knew that he was fighting unfairly, or whether they failed to understand that Cleitomachus was now competing for the honor of the Greeks, while Aristonicus was competing for that of King Ptolemy.

Did they really want an Egyptian to carry off the Olympic crown by defeating Greeks, or a Theban and Boeotian to be proclaimed victor in boxing over his rivals?

After Cleitomachus said this, they say that the crowd's feeling changed so completely that Aristonicus was defeated more by the sudden reversal of the spectators than by Cleitomachus himself.

Chapter 10 The Unthinking Multitude

What happened with Perseus and the crowds was very similar to this.

For if someone had stopped them and frankly asked whether they wished so great a supremacy to fall into the hands of one man and wanted to experience monarchical power that was answerable to no one in any respect, I think they would quickly have come to their senses, taken back what they were saying, and swung round to the opposite view.

And if someone had briefly reminded them of the hardships the Greeks had suffered from the Macedonian royal house, and of the advantages they had gained from Roman power, I think they too would immediately have repented and changed their minds.

But at that moment, in their first unthinking impulse, the approval of the masses for the news that was being announced was obvious enough: they were delighted, out of sheer surprise, if someone had appeared at all capable of standing up to the Romans.

I have gone into this matter to this extent so that no one may rashly reproach the Greeks for ingratitude in the attitude they showed at that time, through ignorance of the impulses that naturally belong to human beings.

Chapter 11 Invention of the Cestros

The cestros was a new invention in the war with Perseus.

The missile was made like this: it was two palms in length, with the socket and the projecting point equal in size.

Into this was fitted a wooden shaft, a span long and a finger's breadth in diameter.

Into the middle of this shaft three very small wooden fins were fixed.

Because the sling had two thongs of unequal length, the missile was loosely set between them in the middle.

Then, while the sling was being whirled and the thongs were taut, it stayed in place; but when one of the two thongs was released at the moment of discharge, it slipped free,

and flew from the sling like a lead bullet, striking with violent force and badly mangling anyone it happened to hit.

Chapter 12 Character of Cotys

Cotys was a man impressive in appearance and outstanding in military matters; and in character he was anything but a Thracian.

For he was temperate, and he showed a gentleness and depth of spirit worthy of a freeborn man.

Chapter 13 Indecisive Result of the First Campaign

II. Affairs in Egypt.

Ptolemy, the commander in Cyprus, was not Egyptian in his ways at all, but a sensible and capable man.

For when he took over the island, while the king was still an infant, he applied himself diligently to raising money, but he gave absolutely nothing to anyone, though the royal administrators often asked him for funds and bitterly criticized him for never releasing anything.

But when the king came of age, he gathered together a considerable sum of money and sent it off.

As a result, King Ptolemy himself and the courtiers approved of his former frugality and of his refusal to part with any money.

Chapter 14 Dispute at Rhodes

Olympiad 152, year 2. The war with Perseus.

At the time when Perseus broke off operations in the war against the Romans, Antenor arrived from Perseus to negotiate the ransom of the prisoners who had sailed with Diophanes, and a serious division arose among the Rhodian statesmen over what ought to be done.

The party of Philophron and Theaetetus was completely opposed to entering into such an entanglement, while the party of Deinon and Polyaratus favored it.

In the end they came to an arrangement with Perseus for the redemption of the prisoners.

Chapter 15 Charops of Epirus

Cephalus came from Epirus. He had previously had ties with the Macedonian royal house, but was then compelled by circumstances to choose the side of Perseus. The cause of this was as follows.

There was an Epirote named Charops, a man of fine character and a friend of the Romans, who, when Philip had occupied the passes into Epirus, was responsible for driving Philip out of Epirus and for enabling Titus to gain control of both Epirus and the Macedonians.

This man had a son, Machatas, whose own son was Charops.

When the father died while this boy was still under age, the elder Charops sent him to Rome with the protection appropriate to his station, so that he might learn the Roman language and letters.

After some time, this young man returned home, having become acquainted with many people there.

The elder Charops then died. The young man, unstable by nature and full of every kind of wickedness, became puffed up and attached himself to the prominent men.

At first no one paid him any attention, but the men who held the leading place both in age and in reputation, the party around Antinous, managed public affairs according to their own judgment. But when the war with Perseus broke out,

this young man at once began to slander the men just mentioned before the Romans, using as his pretext their earlier connection with the Macedonian royal house,

while in present circumstances he watched everything closely and interpreted every word and action of theirs in the worst possible way, suppressing some facts and adding others, and so made his accusations against them convincing.

Cephalus, however, was in every other respect a prudent and steady man, and at this crisis too he held to the soundest judgment.

At the outset he prayed to the gods that the war might not break out and that matters might not be decided by force.

But once the war was actually under way, he wished to fulfill Rome's claims under the alliance fairly, while beyond that he did not want to run to them in a servile way or render any service beyond what was proper.

When Charops actively employed his slanders against him and treated everything done contrary to Roman wishes as deliberate malice, the men already mentioned at first ignored him, since they were conscious of no plans hostile to Rome.

But when they saw the Aetolians Hippolochus, Nicander, and Lochagus being carried off to Rome without cause after the cavalry action, and when they saw that the accusations brought against them by the party of Lyciscus had been believed, men who in Aetolia represented the same political tendency that Charops did in Epirus, then, foreseeing what was coming, they began to take counsel for their own safety.

They therefore resolved to try every possible means to prevent themselves from being carried off to Rome without a hearing because of Charops' slanders.

Thus Cephalus and his friends were forced, contrary to their own preference, to choose the side of Perseus.

Chapter 16 Plot to Kidnap a Roman Consul

The party of Theodotus and Philostratus committed an act that was openly impious and a clear breach of faith.

For when they learned that the Roman consul Aulus Hostilius was coming, on his way to the camp in Thessaly, and thought that, if they delivered Aulus to Perseus, they would both give the strongest proof of loyalty and do the Romans the greatest harm at that moment, they kept writing to Perseus and urging him to hurry.

The king wanted to advance at once and join them, but since the Molossians had occupied the bridge over the river Aous, he was prevented from making the attempt and was first forced to fight them.

It happened that when Aulus arrived among the Phanoteis he lodged with Nestor of Cropia, and thus gave his enemies just the opportunity they needed against him; and if some turn of fortune had not decided matters for the better, I do not think he would have escaped.

But as it was, Nestor somehow, with almost divine foresight, perceived what was coming and forced him to move on from there to Gitana during the night.

So, abandoning the overland route through Epirus, he put to sea and sailed to Anticyra, and from there made his way into Thessaly.

Chapter 17 Pharnaces, King of Pontus

Pharnaces proved to be the most lawless of all the kings before him.

Chapter 18 Attalus Wants his Brother's Honours Restored

While Attalus was wintering at Elateia and clearly knew that his brother Eumenes was deeply distressed and offended because the most distinguished honours granted to him had been annulled in the Peloponnese by a common decree, though Eumenes concealed these feelings from everyone,

Attalus decided to send messages to certain men in Achaea, eager by his own efforts to have his brother's honours restored, not only the honorific monuments but the inscribed honours as well.

He did this because he was convinced that he could give his brother no greater favour, and above all that by this action he would show the Greeks the brotherly affection and nobility of his own character.

Chapter 19 Antiochus Protests Ptolemy's War Plans

When Antiochus saw that the authorities in Alexandria were now openly making preparations for the war over Coele-Syria, he sent envoys headed by Meleager to Rome,

instructing them to address the senate and formally protest that Ptolemy was the one making the first attack on him, in defiance of every principle of justice.

Chapter 20 The Need of Promptness and Persistence

Perhaps in every human undertaking one should measure each action by the right moment, for timing has the greatest power; but this is especially true in war.

For in such matters the balance can swing very sharply in either direction, and to miss the critical moment is one of the gravest errors.

Many people seem to desire what is noble, but few dare to attempt it, and of those who do attempt it, very few carry through to the end what duty requires in each case.

Book XXVIII

Chapter 1 Antiochus and Ptolemy Appeal to Rome

Olympiad 152, year 3. Affairs in Italy.

Since the war over Coele-Syria had already begun between Kings Antiochus and Ptolemy, envoys came to Rome: from Antiochus, Meleager, Sosiphanes, and Heracleides; from Ptolemy, Timotheus and Damon.

At that time Antiochus held the advantage in the affairs of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.

For ever since Antiochus, the father of the king now reigning, defeated Ptolemy's generals in the battle near Panium, all the regions just mentioned had been subject to the kings in Syria.

So Antiochus, thinking that possession won in war was the strongest and noblest title, pursued the matter as though he were defending property that was his own.

Ptolemy, on the other hand, believed that the former Antiochus had unjustly taken advantage of his father's orphaned condition and stripped them of the cities of Coele-Syria; so he could not bring himself to yield those places to him. That was why Meleager and his party came,

with instructions to call the Senate to witness that Ptolemy, against every rule of justice, had been the first to lay hands on territory that was not his.

Timotheus and his colleagues came both to renew friendly relations and to speak about ending the war with Perseus, but above all to observe the interviews of Meleager's party.

They did not dare speak about ending the war, however, because Marcus Aemilius advised them against it. So, after renewing the friendship and receiving answers in line with what they had requested, they returned to Alexandria.

To Meleager and his colleagues the Senate replied that it would entrust Quintus Marcius to write to Ptolemy on these matters in whatever way he judged advantageous and consistent with his own good faith. This, then, was how the matter was handled for the present.

Chapter 2 Embassy from Rhodes

About this same time, and now with summer already drawing to a close, envoys also arrived from Rhodes: Agesilochus, Nicagoras, and Nicander.

They came to renew the friendship, to obtain permission to ship out grain, and at the same time to answer the slanders being spoken against their city.

For faction at Rhodes seemed to be quite open: Agathagetus, Philophron, Rhodophon, and Theaetetus rested all their hopes on the Romans, while Deinon and Polyaratus looked to Perseus and the Macedonians.

As a result, when objections were repeatedly raised in the course of their public business and deliberations were pulled in opposite directions, those who wanted to invent stories against the city found plenty of opportunities.

Nevertheless, on that occasion the Senate took no notice of any of this, though it knew clearly what had happened among them; and it granted them permission to export one hundred thousand medimni of grain from Sicily.

That was the business the Senate handled privately with the Rhodian envoys.

After that it gave a similar answer to all the other envoys who had arrived from Greece and were pursuing the same policy.

Such was the state of affairs in Italy.

Chapter 3 Pressure Put On Achaia and Aetolia

II. The war with Perseus.

At this time Aulus, serving as proconsul and wintering in Thessaly with the army, sent envoys to the regions of Greece, Gaius Popilius and Gnaeus Octavius.

They first came to Thebes, where they praised the Thebans and urged them to preserve their goodwill toward the Romans.

Then, as they went on through the cities of the Peloponnese, they tried to show the people the Senate's mildness and humanity by producing the decrees that had been issued a little earlier.

At the same time, through their remarks, they let it be understood that they knew the men in each city who were hanging back beyond what was proper, and likewise those who were pressing forward.

And it was plain to everyone that they were displeased with the laggards no less than with those who openly opposed them.

By this they drove many people into uncertainty and bewilderment about what words or actions would best meet the demands of the present moment.

Gaius and his colleague, when the Achaean assembly had been convened, were said to have intended to accuse Lycortas, Archon, and Polybius,

and to show that these men were out of sympathy with Roman policy and, though quiet for the moment, were not naturally so disposed, but were watching events and waiting for their opportunity.

They did not dare to do this, however, because they had no reasonable pretext against the men just named.

So when the council was assembled for them at Aegium, they addressed the Achaeans in a speech at once cordial and exhortatory, and then sailed away to Aetolia.

Chapter 4 Discussion of the Aetolian Congress

And again, when an assembly had been convened for them at Thermon, they came before the people and delivered speeches full of exhortation and professions of goodwill.

But the real object for which they had the assembly in hand, they said, was that the Aetolians must give them hostages.

After they had stepped down, Proandrus rose and wanted to set forth certain services he had rendered that were useful to the Romans, and to accuse those who were slandering him. Thereupon Gaius rose again,

and although he knew perfectly well that Proandrus was no friend of Rome, he nevertheless praised him and confirmed everything he had said.

After him Lyciscus came forward and, though he brought no accusation against anyone by name, cast suspicion on many.

For he said that the Romans had acted rightly in dealing with the ringleaders by taking them off to Rome—meaning Eupolemus and Nicander—

but that their associates and supporters were still left in Aetolia, and that all of them ought to meet with the same correction, unless they surrendered their children to the Romans as hostages.

His hints were aimed especially at Archedamus and Pantaleon.

When he yielded the floor, Pantaleon rose and briefly denounced Lyciscus, saying that he shamelessly and basely flattered those who held the upper hand.

Then he turned against Thoas, thinking that he was the man who gave the accusations against them their greatest credibility, since no quarrel between the two of them was thought to exist.

Reminding him partly of what had happened in the time of Antiochus, and partly reproaching him for ingratitude because, after he had been surrendered to the Romans, he had unexpectedly been saved through the embassy of Pantaleon and Nicander,

he quickly worked the crowd up so far that they were ready not only to shout Thoas down whenever he tried to speak, but even to stone him with one accord.

After this had happened, Gaius briefly reproached the Aetolians for stoning Thoas, and at once departed with his fellow-envoy for Acarnania, saying no more about the hostages. Meanwhile affairs in Aetolia were full of mutual suspicion and complete disorder.

Chapter 5 Lycortas Advises Neutrality

When an assembly of the Acarnanians was convened at Thyrrheion, Aeschrion, Glaucus, and Chremas, who were on the Roman side, urged Gaius and his colleagues to place a garrison in Acarnania.

For, they said, there were men among them who were steering affairs toward Perseus and the Macedonians.

But Diogenes gave the opposite advice. He said that no garrison ought to be introduced into any city, since that was a measure reserved for peoples who had become enemies and had been defeated by the Romans.

The Acarnanians, having done nothing wrong, did not deserve to admit a garrison in any way at all.

As for the party of Chremas and Glaucus, he said that they wanted to build up a personal domination for themselves, and so they were slandering their political opponents and trying to bring in a garrison that would strengthen their own grasping ambitions.

After this had been said, Gaius and his colleagues saw that the crowd disliked the idea of garrisons and, wishing to keep in step with the Senate's policy, agreed with Diogenes' view, commended it, and departed for Larisa to rejoin the proconsul.

Chapter 6 Council of the Achaeans

The leading Greeks decided that the situation created by this embassy required close attention.

So they brought together those who agreed with them in their general political outlook: Arcesilaus and Ariston of Megalopolis, Stratius of Tritaea, Xenon of Patrae, and Apollonidas of Sicyon; and they took counsel about the crisis before them.

Lycortas remained fixed in the policy he had held from the first, judging that they should give no help either to Perseus or to the Romans, but likewise should oppose neither side.

To cooperate, he thought, would be disadvantageous for all the Greeks, since he foresaw how great the power of the victors would become.

But to oppose the Romans was dangerous, because in earlier times they had already come into conflict over public affairs with many Romans, including some of the most eminent.

Apollonidas and Stratius, on the other hand, thought that they should not deliberately set themselves against the Romans; but they said that men who tumbled headlong in their eagerness, who used public business to store up private favor with the Romans, and who acted in this way against the laws and against the common interest, ought to be checked and boldly resisted.

Archon said that they must follow the times, give their enemies no opening for slander, and not allow themselves to fall into the same condition as Nicander and his associates, who, before they had learned by experience what Roman power was, had brought themselves into the gravest troubles.

Polybius, Arcesilaus, Ariston, and Xenon shared this opinion.

Accordingly, they resolved that Archon should at once go forward for the office of strategus, and Polybius for the command of the cavalry.

Chapter 7 A Speech of Polybius

After these events had just taken place, and after Archon's party had already reached the conclusion that they must cooperate with the Romans and their friends, it so happened, by a fortunate turn, that Attalus made his request while they were ready to receive it.

So they readily gave him their assent and promised to support what he asked.

When Attalus had sent envoys, and these men appeared at the first assembly and addressed the Achaeans about restoring the honors paid to the king, urging them to do this as a favor to Attalus,

the crowd showed no clear opinion, and many rose to contradict the proposal for a variety of reasons.

Some, because they had originally been responsible for removing the honors, wanted to confirm the wisdom of their own policy; others, because of private grievances, thought they had found an opportunity to strike at the king; and some, from jealousy of those supporting the measure, were eager to prevent Attalus from carrying his proposal.

Archon rose to support the envoys,

for the matter called for the opinion of the strategus. But after saying only a few words he withdrew,

because he was wary of seeming to give this advice for profit, since he had spent a considerable sum of money in securing his office.

As great uncertainty prevailed, Polybius rose and made a number of arguments; but above all he won over the majority by pointing to the original decree of the Achaeans about these honors, in which it had been written that the improper and illegal honors should be removed—not, by Zeus, all of them.

He said that Sosigenes and Diopeithes, who were serving as judges at that time and were privately at odds with Eumenes, had seized on this opportunity to overturn all the honors granted to the king.

In doing so, they had acted contrary to the decree of the Achaeans, contrary to the authority given them, and, most of all, contrary to justice and what was fitting.

For the Achaeans had not resolved to abolish the honors of Eumenes because they had suffered some wrong at his hands; rather, because he had asked for rewards greater than his benefactions deserved, they had voted to remove only the excess.

Therefore, just as those judges, by putting their private hostility ahead of what was honorable for the Achaeans, had overthrown all the honors, so now the Achaeans, considering their own duty and dignity the highest authority, ought to correct the judges' error and, in general, the unreasonable treatment shown to Eumenes,

especially since the favor they were about to grant would rest not only on the king himself, but even more on his brother Attalus.

When the people approved what he said, a decree was drafted ordering the magistrates to restore all the honors of King Eumenes, except any that contained something unbecoming to the Achaean League or contrary to law.

So in this way, and at this moment, Attalus corrected the unjust treatment that had been shown in the Peloponnese regarding the honors belonging to his brother Eumenes.

Chapter 8 Perseus Sends Pleuratus to Genthius

Perseus sent envoys to King Genthius: Pleuratus the Illyrian, who was living with him as an exile, and Adaeus of Beroea.

He instructed them to explain what he had accomplished in the war, both against the Romans and against the Dardanians, and also what he had done for the present against the Epirotes and the Illyrians, and to invite Genthius into friendship and alliance with himself and the Macedonians.

So they made their journey beyond Mount Scardus through the region called Desert Illyria, which the Macedonians not long before had laid waste in order to make Dardanian incursions into Illyria and Macedonia more difficult.

Even so, Adaeus and his party came through those districts with great hardship to Scodra, and when they learned that Genthius was staying at Lissus they sent messengers on to him.

He quickly summoned them, and when they met him they spoke on the matters included in their instructions.

Genthius did not seem averse to friendship with Perseus, but as his excuse for not immediately agreeing to what was asked, he pleaded lack of funds and said that he could not undertake a war against Rome without money.

With this answer Adaeus and his companions set out on their return.

Perseus meanwhile arrived at Stuberra, sold the booty, and rested his forces while waiting for Pleuratus and the others.

When they arrived and he heard Genthius' reply, he at once sent Adaeus back again, together with Glaucias, one of his bodyguards, and as a third envoy the Illyrian, because he knew the Illyrian language,

giving them the same instructions as before, as though Genthius had not clearly explained what he needed and what, once provided, would allow him to comply with the request.

After they had set out, Perseus himself broke camp and marched with his army toward Uscana.

Chapter 9 Unwise Parsimony of Perseus

At this time the envoys who had been sent to Genthius returned, having accomplished nothing more than the earlier embassies and bringing no new result,

because Genthius remained of the same mind, ready enough to join Perseus in the same enterprise, but saying that he needed money.

Perseus ignored this and again sent Hippias and his party to confirm the agreement, leaving out the central point and saying that he would somehow make Genthius well disposed.

So one is at a loss whether such conduct should be called mere irrationality or a kind of heaven-sent delusion. For my part, I think it is rather such a delusion, when men set their hearts on bold enterprises and risk their lives, yet neglect the very thing that holds their plans together, though they see it and have the power to do it.

For if Perseus at that time had been willing to spend money, both publicly on states and privately on kings and political leaders—not lavishly, as his resources allowed, but only in moderation—it would have turned out that all the Greeks and all the kings,

or at least most of them, would have been won over. I do not think any sensible person will dispute this.

But as things stood, by good fortune he did not take that path, by which, if he had succeeded, he would have gained an overbearing mastery of everything, or, if he had failed, would have made many others share the same fate as himself.

Instead he took the opposite course, by which only a very few Greeks were driven into utter folly at the crisis of the action.

Chapter 10 Perseus Blames Hippias for the Failure

Perseus, after suffering a general failure when the Romans entered Macedonia, laid the blame on Hippias.

But it seems to me easy enough to criticize other people and to detect the mistakes of one's neighbors; the hardest thing of all is to do what one can oneself and to understand one's own position. That, too, is what happened in the case of Perseus.

Chapter 11 Heracleum Captured by the Testudo

Heracleum was taken in a rather unusual way. On one side of the city the wall was low for a short stretch, and the Romans selected three detachments for the assault.

The first locked their shields together above their heads, so that by the close-set mass of the arms they looked like a sloping tiled roof. After this came two other detachments in succession ... This "tiled-roof" formation was a tactical arrangement,

which the Romans even practiced as part of their mock exercises.

Chapter 12 Achaean Aid To Rome Declined

III. Greek Affairs

Because Perseus intended to come into Thessaly with an army and decide the whole issue by force of arms, Archon and his colleagues thought it best to answer the suspicions and slanders against them once again by their actions themselves.

So they introduced before the Achaeans a decree that they should make a general levy and march into Thessaly, taking their full part in the struggle alongside the Romans.

When this decree had been ratified, the Achaeans decided that Archon should take charge of assembling the army and making preparations for the expedition, and that envoys should be sent to the consul in Thessaly to explain the Achaean decision and ask when and where they should join their army to his.

They immediately appointed Polybius and others as envoys, and gave Polybius special instructions: if the general approved the arrival of the army, his fellow envoys were to send word back at once explaining this, so that they might not miss the right moment,

while he himself was to see to it that the whole force found markets in the cities through which it marched and that the soldiers lacked none of their necessities.

With these instructions the men just mentioned set out.

They also appointed Telocritus and his colleagues as envoys to Attalus, carrying the decree concerning the restoration of the honors of Eumenes.

At the same time King Ptolemy had applied to the Achaeans because the customary rites performed for kings when they come of age had now taken place in his case.

Judging that it was proper for them to mark the occasion, they voted to send envoys to renew the goodwill already existing between the League and the kingdom, and they at once appointed Alcithon and Pasiadas.

Chapter 13 Marcius Declines Assistance from the Achaeans

Polybius and his colleagues found that the Romans had moved on from Thessaly and were encamped in Perrhaebia, between Azorus and Doliche.

So, because of the critical circumstances, they postponed their audience, but shared in the dangers involved in the advance into Macedonia.

But when the army had marched down into the region around Heracleum, it seemed that the time had come for an interview, since the general appeared to have accomplished the greatest part of what lay before him.

Taking this opportunity, they presented the decree to Marcius and made clear the purpose of the Achaeans: they had resolved, as a whole people, to share with him in the same struggles and dangers. Besides this, they pointed out that every request made of the Achaeans by the Romans during the present war, whether written or delivered by message, had been accepted without objection.

Marcius warmly approved the zeal of the Achaeans, but released them from the hardship and expense, since the situation no longer required assistance from allied forces. So the other envoys returned to Achaea,

but Polybius remained there and took part in the business at hand,

until Marcius, on hearing that Appius Cento was asking the Achaeans for five thousand soldiers to serve in Epirus, sent the aforesaid Polybius off, urging him to see that the troops were not granted and that the Achaeans did not incur so great an expense to no purpose; for Appius, he said, had no sound reason for asking for the soldiers.

Whether he did this out of concern for the Achaeans or because he wanted Appius to achieve nothing is hard to say.

At any rate, when Polybius withdrew to the Peloponnese, letters from Epirus had already arrived, and not long afterward the Achaeans had assembled at Sicyon, so he found himself in a very great difficulty.

When the deliberation was opened on the soldiers Cento was requesting, Polybius decided that he could not possibly disclose the private instructions Marcius had given him; yet to oppose the aid openly, when no clear reason appeared for doing so, was altogether dangerous.

Since the situation was awkward and full of complications, he used, for the immediate crisis, the senate's decree ordering that no one should comply with written demands from generals unless they acted in accordance with a decree of the senate.

And no such authority was attached to the letters.

Thus he carried the point, and the question was referred to the consul, and through this means the nation was relieved of an expense amounting to more than a hundred and twenty talents.

Yet he gave those who wished to slander him before Appius an opening, because he had cut short Appius's attempt to obtain the reinforcement.

Chapter 14 Treachery of the Cydonians

At this time the Cydonians committed a deed universally acknowledged to be dreadful and a flagrant violation of sworn faith.

For although many acts of that sort had taken place in Crete, what happened then seemed to surpass the ordinary measure even of such crimes.

They were bound to the Apolloniates not only by friendship, but by political union, and in general by partnership in all the rights that human beings regard as sacred; and concerning these obligations there stood a sworn treaty in the name of Zeus of Ida.

Yet in breach of that sworn agreement they seized the city of the Apolloniates, slaughtered the men, plundered their property, and, after dividing among themselves the women, children, city, and territory, kept possession of it.

Chapter 15 The Cydonians Ask Help from Eumenes

In Crete, the Cydonians were afraid of the Gortynians, because in the previous year they had narrowly escaped losing their city when Nothocrates and his party attempted to seize it. So they sent envoys to Eumenes, asking for help under the terms of their alliance.

The king selected Leon and sent him off in haste with three hundred soldiers.

When they arrived, the Cydonians handed over the keys of the gates to Leon and entrusted the city as a whole to him.

Chapter 16 Dissensions In Crete and Rhodes

At Rhodes the strife between rival parties kept growing more and more intense.

For when the senate's decree reached them, explaining that they should no longer pay attention to the commands of military leaders, but to the senate's own decrees, and when the majority approved the senate's foresight,

Philophron and Theaetetus and their associates seized on this opening and pressed the matter forward, saying that envoys ought to be sent to the senate, to Quintus Marcius the consul, and to Gaius, the commander of the fleet.

By that time it was already known to everyone which Roman magistrates were going to arrive in Greece.

So, though opposition was voiced, the proposal carried, and at the beginning of summer Agesilochus son of Hegesias was sent to Rome,

along with Nicagoras son of Nicander; while to the consul and the admiral they sent Agepolis,

Ariston, and Pasicrates, with instructions to renew their friendly relations with the Romans and to answer the accusations that some people were making against their city,

while Agesilochus and his colleagues were at the same time to speak about the export of grain.

What these men said to the senate, what answers the senate gave them, and how they returned after receiving every mark of goodwill, I have already recounted in the section on Italian affairs.

But on this point it is useful to remind the reader repeatedly, as I also try to do, because we are often compelled to report the audiences and negotiations of embassies before describing the circumstances of their appointment and dispatch.

For since in each year, while writing the events that properly belong to it, I try to bring together in one place a summary of the actions of each people, it is clear that this must necessarily happen in the course of the narrative.

Chapter 17 Antiochus Invades Egypt

Agepolis and his colleagues came to Quintus and found him encamped in Macedonia near Heracleum, where they delivered the instructions they had been given.

After hearing them out, he said that he himself paid no attention to these slanders, and he urged them as well not to listen to anyone who dared to speak against Rome. He added many other expressions of goodwill besides.

He also wrote the same sentiments in a letter to the people of Rhodes.

Agepolis was greatly encouraged by the reception as a whole; and Quintus, taking him aside privately, said that he was amazed the Rhodians were not trying to bring the present war to an end, especially since that course suited their interests so well.

Whether he did this because he suspected Antiochus, fearing that if he gained possession of Alexandria he might become a dangerous additional enemy to the Romans while the war against Perseus was dragging on,

for by this time the war over Coele-Syria had already become entangled,

or whether, seeing that the issue with Perseus would soon be decided now that the Roman armies had entered Macedonia,

and holding high hopes about the outcome, he wanted to prod the Rhodians into presenting themselves as mediators and, once they had done so, to give the Romans plausible grounds for deciding to deal with them however they saw fit,

it is not easy to say with certainty. But I think the latter explanation is more likely, judging from what happened to the Rhodians shortly afterward.

In any case, Agepolis and his colleagues then went on from there to Gaius, and after receiving from him even more exceptional marks of goodwill than from Marcius, they quickly returned to Rhodes.

When the embassy reported back, and both generals seemed to have rivaled one another in friendliness, both in their conversation and in their formal replies, all the Rhodians were lifted up in spirit and full of confidence, though not all in the same way.

Those of sound judgment were delighted by the goodwill of the Romans, but the restless and unhealthy elements reasoned among themselves that such excessive kindness was a sign that the Romans were afraid of the crisis and that events were not turning out as they had expected.

And when Agepolis happened to let slip to some of his friends that he had received private instructions from Marcius to mention before the council the question of ending the war,

then Deinon and his circle became completely convinced that the Romans were in grave difficulties.

So they sent envoys to Alexandria as well, to put an end to the war then being fought between Antiochus and Ptolemy.

Chapter 18 Antiochus IV. Epiphanes

King Antiochus was energetic in action, bold in his designs, and worthy of the royal office, except in his operations around Pelusium.

Chapter 19 Envoys Sent to Antiochus

After Antiochus took control of affairs in Egypt, Comanus and Cineas, having met in council with the king, decided to convene an advisory assembly made up of the most distinguished leaders to deliberate about the crisis at hand.

The first decision of the council was to send to Antiochus, to negotiate a settlement, the envoys from Greece who happened to be staying there.

At that time there were two embassies from the Achaean League: one to renew friendly relations, represented by Alcithus of Aegium, son of Xenophon, and Pasiadas; and another concerning the festival of the Antigoneia.

There was also an embassy from the Athenians concerning a gift, headed by Demaratus, and two sacred delegations: one for the Panathenaea, led by Callias the pancratiast, and the other concerning the Mysteries, in which Cleostratus conducted the business and delivered the speeches.

There were also present Eudemus and Hicesius from Miletus, and Apollonides and Apollonius from Clazomenae.

King Ptolemy also sent Tlepolemus and Ptolemy the rhetorician as envoys.

These men accordingly sailed up the river to meet him.

Chapter 20 Antiochus Epiphanes In Egypt

At the time when Antiochus occupied Egypt, the envoys sent to arrange a settlement joined the envoys from Greece. He received the men graciously and made their first reception notably splendid.

On the following day he granted them an audience and told them to speak on the matters for which they had been instructed.

The Achaean envoys spoke first, then Demaratus on behalf of the Athenians, and after him Eudemus of Miletus.

Since they were all speaking at the same moment of the same issue, the substance of their individual speeches was naturally much alike.

All of them laid the blame for what had happened on Eulaeus, and by appealing to Ptolemy's kinship with Antiochus and to the king's youth, they begged Antiochus to put aside his anger.

Antiochus agreed with all this and even strengthened their case further, but then began to speak in defense of his original rights, by which he tried to establish that the regions of Coele-Syria properly belonged to the kings of Syria,

supporting his position by referring to the dominion of Antigonus, the first ruler who held the kingdom in Syria, and citing the concessions granted to Seleucus by the kings of Macedonia after Antigonus's death.

Next, building on these points, he appealed to the final acquisition made by his father Antiochus in war,

and, above all, he denied the agreement which the men in Alexandria said had been made between the recently deceased Ptolemy and Antiochus's father: namely, that Coele-Syria was to be given to him as a dowry when he married Cleopatra, the mother of the present king.

After speaking on this case, and convincing not only himself but also those who had come to meet him that his claims were just, he then sailed to Naucratis.

There too he treated the people kindly, gave a gold coin to each of the Greeks living there, and then advanced against Alexandria.

To the envoys he promised that he would give his answer when Aristides and Theris returned to him.

For, he said, he had sent them to Ptolemy, and he wanted the envoys from Greece all to be fully informed and to serve as witnesses.

Chapter 21 Eulaeus Convinces Ptolemy to Give Up the Kingdom

Eulaeus the eunuch persuaded Ptolemy to gather up the money, surrender the kingdom to his enemies, and withdraw to Samothrace.

Who, if he paused to consider this, would not admit that bad companionships do the greatest harm to people?

For when a man, far removed from danger and at so great a distance from his enemies, with such great resources at hand, in control of such strong positions and such multitudes of subjects, did not even make one move toward what duty required, but immediately and without a struggle gave up a kingdom so famous and so fortunate—who would not say that this was the sign of a spirit made soft and wholly corrupted? If this had really been Ptolemy's natural disposition,

then we should have blamed nature and laid the responsibility on nothing external.

But since his later actions cleared nature of the charge, showing that Ptolemy was in fact steadfast enough and brave in danger, it is plain that one may reasonably trace the cause of the cowardice he showed at that time, and of his impulse to flee to Samothrace, to the eunuch and to the companionship in which he had been raised.

Chapter 22 Antiochus Leaves Alexandria

After leaving off the siege of Alexandria, Antiochus sent envoys to Rome.

These were Meleager, Sosiphanes, and Heracleides.

He set aside a hundred and fifty talents: fifty as a ceremonial gift to the Romans, and the rest to be distributed as presents to certain of the Greek cities.

Chapter 23 Envoys from Rhodes to Antiochus

During those same days envoys sailed from Rhodes to Alexandria to negotiate a settlement, the delegation led by Praxon; and not long afterward they also arrived at Antiochus's camp.

When the audience took place, they spoke at length, putting forward both the goodwill of their own city toward both kingdoms, the close connection of the kings with one another, and the advantage that peace would bring to each side.

But while the envoy was still speaking, the king cut him short and said there was no need for many words.

The kingdom, he said, belonged to the elder Ptolemy; with him he had long ago made terms and stood on friendly terms. If those in the city now wished to bring him back, Antiochus would not prevent it.

And he did indeed act accordingly.

Book XXIX

Chapter 1 Speech of L. Aemilius Paullus

Olympiad 152, year 4. Affairs in Italy.

For he said that they had only one occupation, both at dinner parties and in their conversations while walking about: seated in Rome, they managed the war in Macedonia, now criticizing what the generals were doing, now going through what they had left undone.

From this, he said, no benefit ever came to public affairs, but much harm had often resulted in many cases; and at times the commanders themselves were seriously damaged by these ill-timed displays of clever talk.

For slander always has something sharp and stirring about it, and when the mass of people has been prejudiced by constant chatter, the generals become easy for their enemies to despise.

Chapter 2 Gaius Popilius Laenas Sent to Alexandria

Because the senate learned that Antiochus had become master of Egypt and had come close to taking Alexandria as well,

and because it judged that the growth of this king's power touched its own interests, it appointed as envoys Gaius Popilius and his colleagues,

to put an end to the war and, more generally, to inspect the state of affairs.

Such, then, was the situation in Italy.

Chapter 3 Genthius Forms an Alliance with Perseus

II. War against Perseus.

When Hippias and his companions, whom Perseus had sent as envoys to Gentius about the alliance, arrived before winter,

and explained that the king was ready to undertake war against the Romans if he were given three hundred talents and the proper guarantees for the whole agreement,

Perseus, when he heard this and judged Gentius' cooperation necessary, chose Pantauchus, one of his chief friends,

and sent him off with instructions first to settle the matter of the money and to exchange sworn pledges for the alliance, then to take whatever hostages from Gentius Pantauchus thought fit and send them on, and to receive from Perseus whatever hostages Gentius should specify in the written terms, and besides this to arrange the transport of the three hundred talents.

Pantauchus at once set out and, arriving at Meteon in the land of the Labeatae, met Gentius there and quickly brought the young king round to sharing Perseus' hopes.

When the oaths for the alliance had been sworn and put into writing, Gentius immediately sent the hostages whom Pantauchus had specified, and with them Olympion to receive from Perseus the oaths and the hostages, while others were to take charge of the money.

Along with this, Pantauchus persuaded Gentius also to send envoys of his own, who, together with those being sent by Perseus, would go to Rhodes to negotiate a common alliance.

For if that were accomplished, and the Rhodians too entered the war, he declared that the Romans would be altogether easy to defeat.

Gentius, persuaded by these appeals, appointed Parmenion and Marcus and sent them out with instructions that, once they had received the oaths and hostages from Perseus and agreement had been reached about the money, they were to go on embassy to Rhodes.

Chapter 4 Genthius Joins Perseus

So all these men proceeded to Macedonia. But Pantauchus stayed at Gentius' side and kept reminding and pressing the young king not to delay his preparations, but, while ready, to seize positions, cities, and allies in advance; above all he urged him to prepare for a struggle at sea.

For since the Romans were completely unprepared in this sphere, both on the coasts of Epirus and in Illyria, everything proposed would be accomplished without a fight by Gentius himself and the forces he sent out.

So Gentius, persuaded by these arguments, busied himself with preparations both by land and by sea.

Perseus, meanwhile, when the envoys and hostages from Gentius arrived in Macedonia, set out from the camp by the river Elpeius with all his cavalry and went to meet them at Dion,

and when he met them he first gave the oaths for the alliance in the presence of all the cavalry. For he greatly wished the Macedonians to know clearly of Gentius' cooperation, hoping that with this additional advantage they would be more confident.

Next he received the hostages and handed over his own to Olympion and his companions. The most distinguished among them were Limnaeus son of Polemocrates and Balacrus son of Pantauchus.

After this he sent those who had come for the money on to Pella to receive it there, while he dispatched the envoys bound for Rhodes to Thessalonica, to Metrodorus, instructing them to hold themselves ready for the voyage. That embassy also succeeded in persuading the Rhodians to join the war.

After arranging these matters, he sent Herophon as envoy to Eumenes, a man whom he had employed on such missions before, and Telemnastus the Cretan to Antiochus,

telling him not to overlook the opportunity and not to suppose that Roman arrogance and harshness concerned Perseus alone,

but to understand clearly that unless he too now took a hand, preferably by ending the war, but if not by helping Perseus, he would soon experience the same fortune himself.

Chapter 5 Difficulty of Explaining the Intrigues of Perseus and Eumenes

In dealing with this matter I was at a loss what I ought to do. For to write in detail and with exact precision about such negotiations as the kings carried on secretly with one another seemed open to criticism and altogether unsafe,

while on the other hand to pass over completely what appeared to have been the most decisive element in this war, and the thing by which many of the later difficulties found their causes made clear, seemed to me a sign of sheer idleness and total lack of courage.

And so I was led to write briefly what seemed likely to be true, and the probabilities and indications by which I came to this judgment, since I was present at the time and was more struck than most people by each of the events that took place.

Chapter 6 Reasons to Suspect Intrigue between Eumenes and Perseus

I have already stated that Cydas the Cretan, while serving in Eumenes' army and being highly honored by him, first met with Cheimarus, one of the Cretans serving with Perseus, near Amphipolis, and then, when he came close to the wall at Demetrias, spoke first with Menecrates and then with Antimachus.

And the fact that Herophon twice went as an envoy from Perseus to Eumenes, and that on that account most of the Romans came to hold a not unreasonable suspicion about King Eumenes, is clear from what happened in the case of Attalus:

for they allowed him to come to Rome from Brundisium and to conduct whatever business he wished, and in the end they gave him a friendly reply and sent him away,

although he had done them nothing noteworthy, either before or during the war with Perseus;

whereas Eumenes, who had provided them with the greatest services and cooperated with them most of all in the wars against Antiochus and Perseus, they not only prevented from going to Rome, but also ordered him to leave Italy within a fixed number of days, though it was midwinter.

From this it is plain that some sort of intrigue had taken place between Perseus and Eumenes, and that because of it the Romans had become so alienated from Eumenes.

What this intrigue was, and how far it went, is what we must now examine.

Chapter 7 Eumenes Intrigues With Perseus

It is easy to see that Eumenes would not have wished Perseus to prevail in the war and become master of everything.

Quite apart from the inherited enmity and ill will they had toward each other, the similarity of their positions was enough in itself to create distrust, jealousy, and, in general, the deepest hostility between them.

What remained was for them to deceive and outscheme each other through secret dealings; and that is what both of them did.

For when Eumenes saw Perseus in difficulty, hemmed in on every side and willing to accept any terms at all in order to end the war, and when he saw him sending embassies year after year to the Roman generals about this business,

and when he saw the Romans themselves dissatisfied with the whole course of events—partly because the war had made no progress until Paulus took command, and partly because affairs in Aetolia were in an unsettled state—

he thought it quite possible that the Romans might consent to some settlement and bring the war to an end.

And he believed that he himself was especially well suited to act as mediator and bring this about.

With these ideas in mind, he began the year before to test Perseus through Cydas the Cretan, asking how much he would be willing to pay for such a chance.

Chapter 8 Struggle between Eumenes and Perseus

This, I think, was the beginning of their connection.

And when one compares the two men, one the most unscrupulous and the other the most money-loving, their contest naturally became ridiculous.

For Eumenes kept holding out every hope and every kind of bait, convinced that he would catch Perseus with promises;

while Perseus rushed eagerly toward what was held out to him, yet could never bring himself to swallow it far enough to part with any money of his own.

The bargain they haggled over was this: Eumenes asked for five hundred talents as the price of standing idle in the fourth year and not cooperating with the Romans, either on land or at sea; and for ending the war altogether he demanded fifteen hundred, promising at once to give hostages and guarantees.

Perseus accepted the proposal about hostages, naming how many were to be sent, when they were to be sent, and how they were to be kept safe at Cnosus.

But as for the money, he said it would be shameful both for the giver and even more for the receiver to appear to remain neutral for pay; however, he said he would send the fifteen hundred talents by Polemocrates and his companions to Samothrace, where they could be deposited.

Since he himself was master of Samothrace, while Eumenes, like a bad doctor, preferred a retainer to payment after the treatment, he at last gave up the attempt when he found that his own cleverness was no match for Perseus' meanness.

So they parted on even terms, like good wrestlers leaving the contest of greed a draw.

Some of these details became known immediately, others later reached Perseus' close friends; and from them we were enabled to learn that avarice is, so to speak, the fastening-pin of every vice.

Chapter 9 The Avarice of Perseus

I will add one further point of my own: avarice not only does harm, it also makes men foolish.

For who would not remark the ignorance of both kings? How on earth did Eumenes imagine that, in spite of the deep hostility between them, he would be trusted and would receive such a large sum of money, when he could give Perseus no sufficient guarantee that it would be returned if he failed to carry out his promises?

And how could he suppose that, after taking so large a sum, he would escape the notice of the Romans?

Even if he had managed to hide it at the time, he would certainly not have escaped discovery later.

At the very least, he would necessarily have had to exchange his quarrel with Rome for the money he received; and because of that he was about to lose both the money itself and his kingdom, and very likely his life as well, once he appeared as an enemy of the Romans.

For even as things stood—when he had done nothing, but had merely entertained the scheme—he was brought into the gravest danger; what, then, ought one suppose would have happened to him if the plan had been carried through to completion?

And again, who would not marvel at Perseus for thinking anything more profitable or more urgent than to give the money and let Eumenes swallow the bait?

For if Eumenes had carried out even part of his promises and ended the war, the payment would have been well spent.

But if that hope had failed, Perseus would at least have thrown him into open hostility with Rome; for Perseus himself had complete control over making the whole transaction public.

And how valuable that would have been to Perseus, whether he succeeded in the war or failed, is easy to see:

he would have regarded Eumenes as the guilty cause of all his misfortunes, and there was no more effective way he could have avenged himself on him than by making him an enemy of Rome.

So what was the cause of such obvious folly? Avarice. What else could one say?

One man, in order to get what did not belong to him, overlooked everything else and was ready to do anything;

while the other, in order not to give anything away, was willing to endure anything and to ignore everything else.

Accordingly, Perseus' dealings with the Gauls and with Genthius were of a piece with this—

Chapter 10 Rhodes Decides to Seek Peace

When the vote was put before the Rhodians, the proposal to send envoys to negotiate a settlement won the day.

This was how the council settled the Rhodian opposition, as I have explained in my discussion of public speaking.

In that division, the men who sided with Perseus proved stronger than those who were trying to save their country and its laws.

The prytaneis immediately appointed envoys to bring the war to an end: Agepolis, Diocles, and Cleombrotus were sent to Rome; Damon, Nicostratus, Agesilochus, and Telephus to the general and to Perseus.

But they did not stop there. They went on in the same course and added to it, making their offence beyond excuse:

for they at once sent envoys to Crete, to renew their former friendly relations with all the Cretans and to urge them to look at the times and the danger, to stand with the people of Rhodes, and to choose the same enemies and friends as they did;

and they planned to speak in the same way in private to the individual cities.

Chapter 11 Turbulent Assembly at Rhodes

When the envoys from Genthius, together with those led by Parmenio and Morcus and accompanied by Metrodorus, arrived at Rhodes, and the council had been summoned,

the assembly was in a complete uproar. The men around Deinus and Polyaratus were now openly daring to speak on Perseus' behalf, while the party around Theaedetus was stunned by what was happening.

For the arrival of the galleys, the number of cavalry that had been lost, and Genthius' defection crushed them.

So the outcome of the assembly followed naturally from what has just been said:

the Rhodians voted to give both kings a friendly answer, to tell them that they had decided to put an end to the war, and to urge each of them not to make difficulties over peace terms.

They also received Genthius' envoys at the common hearth with great friendliness.

Chapter 12 On Proportion in History

Again, other writers have gone on at length about the Syrian war. The reason for this is what I have already explained more than once.

For when men take a simple and straightforward subject and yet want not the facts but the bulk of their books to make them seem like historians, and want that sort of display to create the impression of importance, it becomes necessary for them to make small things big,

and to dress up matters that were briefly stated, and in some cases to turn incidental happenings into full-scale actions and affairs—staging contests and announcing battle lines in which sometimes ten infantrymen fell, sometimes only a little more, and cavalry even fewer than that.

As for sieges, geography, and similar topics, no one could say their treatment is adequate, so far as they develop them at all, because they have no material to work with.

But the opposite is true for those who write universal history:

and so one should not blame us as if we were dragging out events when we sometimes pass over things that others have given great attention and embellishment, and sometimes mention them only briefly; rather, one should trust that we give each subject the treatment it deserves.

For when those writers describe, somewhere in the course of their whole work, the siege of Phanoteia or Coroneia or Haliartus, they are forced to set out every contrivance, every bold move, and every detail of the siege,

and beyond that to dwell on the capture of Tarentum, Corinth, Sardis, Gaza, Bactra, and, above all, Carthage, adding details of their own; yet they are not at all satisfied if we give a plain and truthful account of such matters.

The same judgment should apply to our treatment of battles and speeches, and likewise to the other parts of history:

in all these matters we would fairly deserve much forgiveness, and the same is true of what I am about to narrate, even if I should seem inconsistent in my subject matter, in my handling of events, or in my style of expression;

and also if I should sometimes slip in the names of mountains, rivers, or local places. The size of the undertaking itself is excuse enough in all these matters,

unless I am caught deliberately making false statements for gain; for that I ask no pardon, as I have repeatedly and expressly said in this work.

Chapter 13 Character of Genthius

In the twenty-ninth book, the same writer says that Genthius, king of the Illyrians, committed many shameful acts in his life because of his heavy drinking, being drunk night and day alike:

and after killing his brother Plator, who was about to marry the daughter of Monunius, he himself married the girl and treated his subjects with savage cruelty.

Chapter 14 Scipio Nasica and Fabius Maximus Volunteer to Outflank the Macedonians

The first man to volunteer to lead the outflanking movement was Nasica, also called Scipio, the son-in-law of Scipio Africanus; later he became a man of great influence in the Senate.

The second was Fabius Maximus, the oldest of Aemilius' sons, still only a youth, who stood up eagerly.

Aemilius was pleased and gave them not as many men as Polybius says, but as many as Nasica himself says he received, in a letter he wrote to one of the kings, about these events.

The Romans were holding their own stoutly against the force of the parma shields and the Ligurian shields.

Chapter 15 A Cretan Deserter Brings Intelligence to Perseus

Meanwhile Perseus, seeing that Aemilius was staying still and not reckoning with what was happening, when a Cretan deserter slipped away from the road and came to him with news of the Roman outflanking move,

was thrown into confusion. He did not move his camp, but handed over ten thousand mercenary foreigners and two thousand Macedonians to Milo and sent them off, urging them to hurry and seize the mountain passes.

Polybius says that the Romans fell on them while they were still asleep, but Nasica says there was a sharp fight and real danger on the heights.

Chapter 16 Battle of Pydna

Polybius says that when the moon was eclipsed, the rumor spread among many of Perseus' Macedonians that it meant the king himself was being eclipsed.

This made the Romans bolder and brought the Macedonians low in spirit.

So true is the saying that war is full of empty alarms.

Chapter 17 Perseus Loses His Resolve

Lucius, though he had never seen a phalanx at all until he saw one in Perseus' army, used to tell people in Rome afterward that he had never seen anything more frightening and formidable than a Macedonian phalanx, even though he had seen and taken part in many battles, like anyone else.

Many schemes seem plausible and possible in theory, but when they come to practical use, like counterfeit coins thrown into the fire, they no longer live up to their first design.

Perseus, with only one thought in mind — either to win or to die — did not hold steady in his spirit at that moment, but lost heart, like cavalry scouts who break and run.

As time went on and the strain grew heavier, Perseus' spirit gave way, like athletes in poor condition; for when danger drew near and everything had to be decided, he could not keep his courage firm.

Chapter 18 Ambitious Youth

The Macedonian king, as Polybius says, lost his nerve just as the battle was getting under way and rode off to the city, pretending that he was sacrificing to Heracles — fitting cowardly rites for a cowardly man, and prayers that the god would not accept.

Chapter 19 The Senate Makes an Example of the Rhodian Ambassadors

At the time when Perseus, after his defeat, was making his escape, the senate decided to summon the Rhodian ambassadors, who had come to ask for an end to the war.

Fortune seemed, as if by design, to put the Rhodians’ ignorance on display before the stage — if one should call it ignorance of the Rhodians, and not rather of the men who were then dominant at Rhodes.

When the party led by Hegesipolis entered, they said that they had come to end the war. For the Rhodian people, seeing that the war had dragged on for a long time, and seeing that it was harmful to all the Greeks and also to the Romans themselves because of the enormous expense, had come to that view.

But now that the war had ended according to the Rhodians’ wishes, they had come simply to congratulate the Romans. Such, briefly, was what the men around Hegesipolis said.

The senate, taking advantage of the moment and wanting to make an example of the Rhodians, delivered a reply whose main point was this:

They did not think that this embassy had been sent by the Rhodians for the sake either of the Greeks or of themselves, but for Perseus.

For if they had been sent on behalf of the Greeks, the more fitting time would have been when Perseus was ravaging Greek territory and cities, while encamped in Thessaly for almost two years.

But to let that time pass by, and now to come eagerly seeking an end to the war, when our armies had entered Macedonia and Perseus was shut in with only the faintest hope of survival, made it plain to anyone who judged matters rightly that they had sent their embassy not to end the war, but to rescue Perseus and save him as far as they could.

For that reason, they said, the Romans were under no obligation at present either to show them favor or to answer them kindly.

That was the senate’s decision for the Rhodian ambassadors.

Chapter 20 Perseus an Example of the Impermanence of Fortune

Then the man who took up the Roman language addressed those in the senate, telling them to look at what was before their eyes and, with Perseus standing there in view, not to boast excessively about successes, not to plot anything arrogant or ruinous against anyone, and in general never to trust present good fortune.

Rather, he said, it was precisely when a man was enjoying the greatest success, whether in private life or in public affairs, that he should be most mindful of the possibility of a reversal.

For only in that way could a person show moderation even amid prosperity.

He said that this was what distinguished foolish men from sensible ones: the one class learn only from their own misfortunes, the other from the misfortunes of others.

Chapter 21 Uncertainties of Fortune

That is why one is often reminded of the words of Demetrius of Phalerum.

In his treatise on Fortune, wishing to show people clearly how changeable Fortune is, he began with the age of Alexander, when Alexander brought down the Persian empire, and said this:

"If you were to keep in mind not an endless time or many generations, but only the fifty years immediately before our own day, you would recognize the harshness of Fortune here.

For would you have believed, fifty years earlier, if any god had foretold it, that by this time not even the name of the Persians would remain at all — those who had been masters of almost the whole inhabited world — while the Macedonians, whose name was scarcely known before, would become masters of it all?

And yet Fortune, whose action in our lives is unpredictable, who is always making new things out of what lies beyond our reckoning and showing her power through the unexpected, is even now, in my view, making this plain to all men:

she has brought the Macedonians into the prosperity once enjoyed by the Persians, because she has used these blessings with them too, until she decides something else about them.

"And that is what has now happened in the case of Perseus. So Demetrius, as though inspired by some divine mouth, has spoken prophetically about the future.

As for myself, when I came in my narrative to the time at which the kingdom of Macedon was destroyed, I did not think it right to pass the moment by without comment, since I had myself witnessed the event; rather, I wanted both to speak fittingly on the matter and to recall Demetrius’s words.

For it seems to me that he made a statement more divine than merely human, since he had foretold what would happen almost a hundred and fifty years beforehand."

Chapter 22 Further Problems for Eumenes

After the battle between Perseus and the Romans had been brought to an end, King Eumenes fell into what seemed, to most people, a strange and unexpected situation; though in truth, if one looks at the course human affairs usually take, it was nothing out of the ordinary.

For Fortune is quite able to upset reasoned plans, and even when she has helped a man and added her own weight to his side, she can turn around again, as if repenting, and immediately spoil what has been achieved.

That is exactly what happened then in Eumenes' case.

For just when he believed that his own rule was now secure and that the coming years would be easy, since Perseus and the whole Macedonian kingdom had been utterly overthrown, he suddenly ran into the gravest danger, because the Galatians in Asia unexpectedly took advantage of the moment and rose up.

Chapter 23 The Ptolemies Ask Help From Achaia

In the Peloponnese, during the winter, ambassadors arrived from both kings — Ptolemy and Ptolemy — asking for help, and this led to repeated and highly spirited debates.

The party around Callicrates, Diophanes, and Hyperbatus did not like the idea of granting aid.

But Archon, Lycortas, and Polybius thought it right to give the kings help in accordance with the existing alliance.

For by then it had happened that the younger Ptolemy had been proclaimed king by the crowd because of the crisis, while the elder had come back from Memphis and was ruling jointly with his brother.

Since they were asking for every kind of support, they sent Eumenes and Dionysodorus to the Achaeans, requesting one thousand foot soldiers and two hundred cavalry, with Lycortas to command the infantry and Polybius the cavalry.

They also sent word to Theodoridas of Sicyon, asking him to raise a body of one thousand mercenaries.

This happened because the kings had previously formed a close acquaintance with the men we have mentioned, as a result of the events already described.

When the envoys arrived, the Achaean congress was meeting at Corinth. They accordingly came forward and, after recalling the many proofs of goodwill the Achaeans had shown toward the Egyptian kingdom and setting out the danger the kings were then in, they asked them for help.

The majority of the Achaeans were ready to go to the kings' assistance — both because the kings at that time wore the diadem and exercised royal authority — and not merely with a detachment, but with their full levy; for the party around Callicrates objected,

saying that in general they should not meddle in such matters, and certainly not at that time, but should keep themselves entirely available for Roman needs.

For at that very moment there was especially expected to be a crisis over the whole situation, since Quintus Philippus was wintering in Macedonia.

Chapter 24 The Achaeans Agree to Help the Ptolemies

When many of the people became uncertain and feared that they might seem to fall short of Roman expectations, Lycortas and Polybius took up the argument again and taught them,
