among other things, that in the previous year the Achaeans had voted to march with their full levy alongside the Romans and had sent Polybius as envoy, but Quintus, after accepting their goodwill, had declined the help, saying that he had no need of it because he had already secured the invasion route into Macedonia.

From this it was clear that their supposed concern for Roman needs was only a pretext for preventing aid from being sent.

So they urged the Achaeans not to overlook the present moment, seeing how great the danger then surrounding the kingdom was, but to keep faith with the agreements and benefactions, and above all with the oaths, by carrying out the treaty.

But when the majority again became inclined toward sending help, the party around Callicrates blocked the motion, intimidating the magistrates by claiming that under the laws it was not lawful to debate aid in the public assembly.

After some time, however, when the congress had been summoned to the city of the Sicyonians, where not only the council but all men over thirty were present, and after several speeches had been made,

Polybius in particular argued first that the Romans did not need help — and he seemed to be speaking not without good reason, since he had spent the previous summer in Macedonia in the camp of Philippus —

and second, that even if the Romans did need the alliance, the Achaeans would still not be unable to provide help because of the two hundred cavalry and one thousand infantry who were to be sent to Alexandria; for if they were acting wisely, they could field thirty or forty thousand fighting men.

The majority were won over by what they heard and leaned toward sending the allied force.

So on the second of the two days, on which by law those who wished to do so were required to present motions, Lycortas proposed that the aid should be sent, while Callicrates proposed that ambassadors should be dispatched to reconcile the two kings with Antiochus.

When these motions were put forward again, a lively contest followed, but the men around Lycortas clearly had the advantage.

For the comparison between the two kingdoms was very striking.

It was hard to find any act of friendship at all between Syria and the Greeks in earlier times, although the present king's generosity was well known among them;

whereas from Egypt there had been so many and such great acts of kindness toward the Achaeans in earlier times that no one could ask for more.

By presenting this contrast, Lycortas made a strong impression, since the difference between the two kingdoms on this point was so great.

For just as it was not easy to count the benefactions of the Alexandrian kings, so it was impossible to find any act of goodwill done by the dynasty of Antiochus for the Achaeans in the course of affairs.

Chapter 25 Antiochus Forced To Leave Egypt

For a time Andronidas and Callicrates kept using arguments in favor of making peace, but since no one was listening to them, they resorted to a trick.

A letter-carrier happened to come from the road into the theater, bringing a letter from Quintus Marcius, in which he urged the Achaeans, in line with Roman policy, to try to reconcile the kings.

This was also in fact what the Senate had done, sending envoys with Numisius to bring about a settlement between the kings.

But this actually told against their case: for the men with Titus had failed to achieve reconciliation and had returned to Rome completely unsuccessful.

Still, Polybius and his faction did not want to argue against the letter, out of consideration for Marcius, and withdrew from the debate. Thus the proposal to help the kings came to nothing.

The Achaeans then decided to send ambassadors to make the reconciliation, and Archon of Aegira, Arcesilaus, and Ariston of Megalopolis were appointed.

The envoys from Ptolemy, having failed to secure the alliance, then handed over to the magistrates the letter from the kings, which asked the Achaeans to send Lycortas and Polybius to take part in the present war.

Chapter 26 Antiochus Renews the War

Forgetting what he himself had written and said, Antiochus resumed the war against Ptolemy.

So true are Simonides' words: "It is hard to be good."

For it is easy enough to have impulses toward what is noble, and even to hold to them for a while; but to remain steady through every trial, and never to put anything above honor and justice, is difficult indeed.

Chapter 27 Popilius Makes Antiochus Stop the War

When Antiochus had come up with the intention of seizing Pelusium from Ptolemy,

the Roman commander Popilius met him. The king greeted him from a distance by voice and extended his right hand; but Popilius, having the tablet ready at hand on which the Senate's decree was written, held it out to him and ordered Antiochus to read it first,

as I think, because he did not consider it right to exchange the sign of friendship before he knew the attitude of the man receiving him — whether he was to be a friend or an enemy.

When the king had read it and said that he wished to consult his friends about the matter, Popilius did something that seemed harsh and entirely overbearing:

with the vine-rod he happened to have in his hand, he drew a circle around Antiochus and ordered him to give his answer about the contents of the letter before stepping outside that ring.

The king, startled by what had happened and by the display of authority, hesitated briefly and then said that he would do everything the Romans asked. Then Popilius and his companions took his hand and all greeted him warmly.

The order contained in the letter was that the war with Ptolemy should be ended at once.

So a fixed number of days was granted him, and within that time he withdrew his forces into Syria, in pain and anger, though at present submitting to the situation.

Popilius and his companions then set matters in order at Alexandria and urged the kings to live in peace with one another; at the same time they ordered them to send Polyaratus back to Rome.

Then they sailed off to Cyprus, intending also to drive the forces stationed there out of the island without delay.

When they arrived and found that Ptolemy's generals had been defeated in battle and that the situation in Cyprus in general was in confusion, they quickly had the army withdraw from the country and remained there until the forces had sailed off to Syria.

In this way the Romans preserved Ptolemy's kingdom, which was all but ruined.

Thus Fortune so shaped the affairs of Perseus and the Macedonians that the outcome in Alexandria and in the whole of Egypt was decided by it: that is, by the earlier decision of what should be done with Perseus.

For if that had not taken place and been settled, I do not think Antiochus would have obeyed the orders given him.

Book XXX

Chapter 1 Attalus Comes to Rome

Olympiad 153, year 1. Affairs in Italy.

At this time Attalus, the brother of King Eumenes, came from him to Rome.

His stated reason was that, even if the Galatian disturbance in the kingdom had not occurred, he would still have come to Rome to congratulate the Senate and receive some public mark of distinction for having fought on their side and shared all their dangers in a friendly spirit.

But as things stood, the Galatian crisis also forced him to come to Rome at that moment.

Since everyone received him graciously, both because of the familiarity formed during the campaign and because he seemed to be well disposed toward them, and since the welcome he met with was greater than he expected, his hopes rose high, because he did not know the true reason for his reception.

So he came close to ruining his own position and the whole kingdom.

For most Romans had become estranged from King Eumenes and his goodwill, and were convinced that during the war he had played a crooked game, talking with Perseus and watching for opportunities against them.

Therefore some of the prominent men took Attalus in hand and urged him to put aside the embassy on his brother's behalf and speak instead about his own interests.

For, they said, the Senate wished to establish for him a separate power and kingship because of its estrangement from his brother.

As a result Attalus was greatly elated and in private conversations gave assent to those who were pushing him in that direction.

At last he even came to an understanding with certain men of standing that he would enter the Senate and speak on these matters.

Chapter 2 Stratius Sent to Attalus

With opinion at Rome standing this way about Attalus, the king, foreseeing what was coming, sent Stratius the physician to Rome, a man in whom he had the greatest confidence,

showing him some things and instructing him in others to use every device to keep Attalus from following those who wanted to destroy their kingdom.

When Stratius arrived in Rome and got Attalus into his hands, he used many different arguments, for he was a man of good sense and persuasive power.

But only with difficulty did he accomplish his purpose and call Attalus back from his irrational impulse, setting before his eyes the fact that for the present he shared the kingship with his brother, differing from him only in not wearing a diadem and not being styled king, while in every other respect he possessed equal and identical authority.

And for the future he was universally acknowledged as heir to the throne, with that hope not far off, since the king, because of bodily weakness, was always expecting death, and because he had no children could not leave the realm to anyone else even if he wished.

For no natural son had yet been recognized by him, the one who later succeeded to the throne.

Above all, he said, he was astonished that Attalus was doing such harm to the needs of the present moment.

They ought to give great thanks to all the gods if, by standing together and acting with one mind, they could drive off the Galatian danger and the threat now hanging over them.

But if he should now fall into faction and quarrel with his brother, it was obvious that he would bring down the kingdom and deprive himself both of his present authority and of his future hope, while also depriving his brothers of their rule and influence within it.

By pressing these points and others like them, Stratius persuaded Attalus to remain with the existing arrangement.

Chapter 3 Attalus At Rome

Accordingly, when the man already mentioned entered the Senate, he congratulated it on what had happened and defended the goodwill and zeal he had personally shown in the war against Perseus.

In the same way he also urged at length that envoys should be sent to check the Galatians' recklessness and restore them to their former disposition.

He also spoke about Aenus and the city of Maronea, asking that these should be granted to him as a gift.

But he kept silent to the end about any attack on the king and about dividing the kingdom.

The Senate, however, supposing that he would later approach them privately on these questions, promised to send the envoys, honored him lavishly with the customary gifts, and also promised that it would give him the cities just mentioned.

But when, after immediately receiving these courtesies, he set out from Rome without doing any of the things they expected, the Senate, disappointed in its hopes, had nothing else it could do.

So, while he was still in Italy, it declared Aenus and Maronea free cities, thereby withdrawing its promise, and sent Publius Licinius and his colleagues as envoys to the Gauls.

What instructions it gave them is not easy to say, but it is not hard to infer them from what happened afterward.

This will become clear from their actions.

Chapter 4 Rhodian Ambassadors Argue Against War

Envoys also came from Rhodes, first the party led by Philocrates, and after them those led by Philophron and Astymedes.

For when the Rhodians received the answer that Agesipolis and his colleagues had obtained immediately after the battle, and saw from it the Senate's anger and threatening posture toward them, they at once sent the embassies just mentioned.

But Astymedes and Philophron, perceiving from their interviews, both public and private, the suspicion and estrangement people felt toward them, fell into complete discouragement and helpless distress.

And when one of the praetors mounted the Rostra and called on the crowd to make war on Rhodes,

then indeed, utterly losing their composure because of the danger threatening their country, they went so far as to put on dark clothing and in their appeals no longer tried to persuade or make demands of their friends, but begged them with tears not to decide on any irreparable measure against them.

Some days later Antony the tribune introduced them, the same man who had dragged down from the Rostra the praetor who was urging war; and Philophron spoke first, followed by Astymedes.

Then, after uttering what the proverb calls a swan-song, they received such an answer that they seemed released from their total fear of war,

but regarding the specific charges against them the Senate rebuked them harshly and bitterly.

The sense of the reply was this: if it were not for a few men who were their own friends, and especially for these envoys themselves, the Senate well knew how it ought, justly, to deal with them.

Astymedes thought that he had spoken well on behalf of his country, but he pleased neither the Greeks then staying at Rome nor those living at home.

For afterward he published in writing the speech he had composed in defense of Rhodes, and to most people who took it in hand it seemed bizarre and altogether unconvincing.

For he framed his defense not only from the just claims of his own country, but still more from accusations against others.

By setting benefits and services side by side and comparing them, he tried to make those of others seem false and small, while he magnified those of the Rhodians as much as he could.

And conversely, the faults of others he reproached bitterly and maliciously, while those of the Rhodians he tried to cover over, so that by the comparison their own might appear slight and deserving of pardon, whereas those of their neighbors might appear grave and wholly beyond excuse, though, as he said, all who had gone wrong had already obtained pardon.

This kind of defense, however, would never seem fitting for a statesman.

Even in cases where men have acted together in certain secret matters, we do not praise those who, out of fear or for profit, turn informer against their accomplices; rather,

we approve those who accept every torture and punishment and do not make any of their fellow-plotters share the same disaster. These are the men we accept; these are the men we consider noble. But the man who, because of some vague fear, lays all other people's errors before those in power and revives matters that time was carrying off into forgetfulness among the rulers—how could he fail to offend all who hear of it?

Chapter 5 The Rhodians Try To Excuse Themselves

After receiving the reply already mentioned, the party with Philocrates set out home at once, while Philophron, Astymedes, and their associates stayed where they were, keeping close watch so that nothing said or done against their country would escape their notice.

When this answer reached Rhodes, the people thought they had been freed from their greatest fear, the fear of war, and so they found it easier to bear everything else, harsh as the situation still was.

So it always happens: when men expect greater disasters, lesser troubles are forgotten.

Accordingly they immediately voted a crown for Rome worth ten thousand gold pieces, and appointed Theaetetus to serve both as envoy and admiral. At the beginning of summer they sent him with the crown, together with Rhodophon and the rest of the embassy, to try by every possible means to conclude an alliance with the Romans.

They acted this way because they did not want a formal decree and embassy to suffer a public rebuff if the Romans decided otherwise. Instead, they preferred to make the attempt under the admiral's own authority, since the laws gave an admiral that power.

For the Rhodian constitution was so practical in its workings that, although the people had for almost a hundred and forty years shared with Rome in some of the most distinguished and admirable enterprises, they had never entered into a formal alliance with them.

It is worth explaining why the Rhodians managed their affairs in this way.

They did not want any ruler or dominant power to despair of receiving help and alliance from them, and so they refused to bind or commit themselves in advance by oaths and treaties. Instead, by remaining uncommitted, they aimed to profit from the hopes each party placed in them.

On this occasion, however, they were especially eager to obtain this mark of honor from the Romans. It was not that they were desperate for an alliance, nor that they were afraid of anyone at that moment except the Romans themselves,

but that by giving special weight and dignity to the move they hoped to strip away the suspicions of those who were entertaining hostile thoughts about their city. But just after Theaetetus and his party had sailed,

the Caunians revolted, and the people of Mylasa occupied the cities in the district of Euromus.

At the same time the Senate issued a decree that all the Carians and Lycians who had been assigned to the Rhodians after the war with Antiochus were to be free.

The Rhodians quickly set matters right in the case of the Caunians and the people of Euromus.

They sent Lycon with troops and forced the Caunians to submit to them again,

although the people of Cibyra came to their aid; and when they campaigned against the cities in the district of Euromus, they defeated the men of Mylasa and Alabanda in battle, both peoples having marched with their armies against Orthosia.

But when the decree about the Lycians and Carians reached them, they again became deeply alarmed, fearing that their gift of the crown had been wasted, and that their hopes of an alliance had been vain as well.

Chapter 6 Greek States and the War With Perseus

Polybius says: I have already called my readers' attention to the conduct of Deinon and Polyaratus.

For the crisis and the reversal were serious not only at Rhodes, but in almost every Greek state.

So it would be useful to examine the intentions of the politicians in each place and determine which of them acted rationally and which failed in their duty,

so that those who come after us, with these cases set before them like models, may in similar emergencies truly pursue what is worth choosing and avoid what is to be shunned, and may not, by failing to see what is fitting at the final moment of life, suffer the same fate in their last hour as in the actions of their earlier career.

Now it turned out that there were three distinct classes among those who came under accusation because of the war with Perseus.

One class consisted of men who were not pleased to see the whole issue decided and the rule of the inhabited world falling under a single power, but who nevertheless neither helped nor opposed the Romans in any definite way, instead leaving the outcome to Fortune.

Another class consisted of those who were glad to see the struggle coming to a decision and wanted Perseus to win, but were unable to draw either their own fellow citizens or men of their own people over to their view.

A third class consisted of those who did draw their states with them and turned their constitutions over to the alliance of Perseus. How each of these groups managed its own affairs is worth examining.

Chapter 7 Examples of Three Classes of Statesmen

Antinous, Theodotus, and Cephalus, together with their associates, brought the Molossian people over to Perseus.

When events turned wholly against their designs, and danger closed in on them and disaster came near, they all advanced together to meet the crisis and died bravely.

For that reason these men deserve praise, because they did not surrender themselves or let themselves fall into a condition unworthy of the life they had previously lived.

In Achaea, Thessaly, and Perrhaebia, on the other hand, a number of men came under accusation because they had remained quiet, as though they were waiting on events and favoring Perseus.

But they had never uttered any such proposal in public, nor were they caught either writing or sending messages to Perseus about anything; they kept themselves above reproach.

Therefore such men were right to stand their defense and submit to judgment, and in the end they disappointed all expectations.

For when a man knows himself guilty of nothing shameful, it is no less a mark of cowardice to remove himself from life out of fear—whether frightened by the attacks of political rivals or by the power of the victors—than it is to cling to life in a way that violates what honor requires.

Again, in Rhodes and Cos, and in several other cities, there were men who favored the cause of Perseus. They even dared to speak for the Macedonians in their own states, denounce the Romans, and urge joint action with Perseus, but they were unable to swing their governments over to alliance with the king.

The most prominent of these were Hippocrates and his brother Diomedon among the Coans, and Deinon and Polyaratus among the Rhodians.

Chapter 8 Shameless Conduct of the Supporters of Perseus

Who could fail to condemn the policy of such men? Their fellow citizens knew everything they had done and said; the letters sent from Perseus to them and from them to Perseus had been intercepted and brought to light;

even the couriers going back and forth on both sides had fallen into their enemies' hands. Yet they still could not bring themselves to yield or remove themselves from the scene, but kept on contesting the case.

By persisting in this way and clinging to life when all hope was gone, they destroyed whatever appearance of courage and daring had attached to them, and left later generations no room even for pity or indulgence.

For when they were convicted face to face by their own handwritten letters and by the testimony of their agents, they seemed not merely unfortunate, but even more shameless than unfortunate.

There was a man named Thoas among those who made these voyages, and he had often sailed to Macedonia on missions from the men just mentioned.

When the turn of events came, conscious of what he had done, he was afraid and withdrew to Cnidus. But the Cnidians put him in custody, and when the Rhodians demanded him, he was brought to Rhodes.

There, under torture, he was convicted and confessed, and his testimony matched all the signs contained in the letters captured from the prisoners, as well as the letters sent by Perseus to Deinon and Polyaratus and by those men to him.

From all this one could only wonder what reasoning Deinon was using when he still chose to cling to life and endure such a public disgrace.

Chapter 9 Polyaratus of Rhodes

In sheer folly and cowardice, Polyaratus far surpassed Deinon.

For when Popilius ordered King Ptolemy to send Polyaratus to Rome, the king, out of consideration both for his country and for Polyaratus himself, decided not to send him to Rome, but chose instead to send him to Rhodes, since that was also what Polyaratus was asking.

So he provided a small boat, handed Polyaratus over to a certain Demetrius, one of his friends, and sent him off. He also wrote to the Rhodians about the transfer.

But when Polyaratus put in at Phaselis during the voyage and conceived whatever notion it was, he took suppliant boughs in his hands and fled to the public hearth.

If anyone had asked him what he actually wanted, I am persuaded that he could not even have said. For if he wanted to reach his own country, what need was there for suppliant boughs? That was already the destination intended by the men escorting him.

And if he wanted to go to Rome, then whether he wished it or not, that was bound to happen. What other possibility was left? There was no other place that could receive him safely.

Even so, when the people of Phaselis sent to Rhodes and asked them to come fetch Polyaratus and take charge of him, the Rhodians wisely decided to send an unarmed escort vessel,

but they forbade its commander to take Polyaratus aboard, because the men from Alexandria had been ordered to convey him on to Rome.

When the ship arrived at Phaselis, Epichares, who was in command of it, refused to receive the man on board.

But Demetrius, who had been appointed by the king to conduct his transfer, ordered him to get up and sail on, and the people of Phaselis backed him, because they were afraid that otherwise some blame from the Romans would fall on them.

So Polyaratus, overwhelmed by the situation, went back aboard the boat with Demetrius. But during the departure, seizing a favorable moment,

he ran off and took refuge again, this time in Caunus, and there likewise begged the Caunians to help him.

When they too pushed him away because they were aligned with Rhodes, he sent messages to the people of Cibyra, begging them to receive him into their city and send him an escort.

For he had some claim on that city because the sons of Pancrates the tyrant had been brought up under his care.

They were persuaded and did what he asked, but when he arrived in Cibyra he threw both himself and the Cibyratae into even greater difficulty than before, when he had been at Phaselis.

For they neither dared to keep him with them, because they feared danger from Rome, nor were they able to send him on to Rome, because they had no experience in maritime matters, being entirely an inland people.

In the end they were forced to send envoys to Rhodes and to the Roman commander in Macedonia, asking them to take charge of the man.

And when Lucius wrote to the Cibyratae to keep Polyaratus under careful guard and send him to Rhodes, and to the Rhodians to arrange transport by sea so that he might be conveyed safely into Roman hands, and both parties obeyed these written instructions,

in this way Polyaratus finally came to Rome, after making as public a spectacle as he could of his own folly and cowardice, and after being handed over, through his own stupidity, not only by King Ptolemy but also by the people of Phaselis, the Cibyratae, and the Rhodians.

Why, then, have I gone on at such length about Polyaratus and Deinon?

Not in order to seem to trample on their misfortunes. That would be altogether shameful. Rather, by making their folly plain, I hope to better prepare those who fall into similar crises to think and decide well.

Chapter 10 Statue-bases for Perseus Used by Aemilius

Nothing shows more clearly at once the swiftness and instability of Fortune than when a man finds that the very things he thought he was laboring hardest to prepare for his own honor have in fact been made ready for his enemies.

For Perseus was having columns made, and Lucius Aemilius, finding them unfinished, completed them and set up his own statues on them.

He admired the position of the city and the advantageous site of the acropolis for commanding both the regions inside the Isthmus and those beyond it.

After noting the strength of Sicyon and the importance of the city of Argos, he came to Epidaurus.

Having long been eager to see Olympia, he set out there.

Polybius:

Lucius Aemilius entered the sacred precinct at Olympia, and when he saw the statue he was astonished. He said that Pheidias alone seemed to him to have reproduced the Zeus of Homer, because although he had formed great expectations of Olympia, he had found the reality greater than what he had expected.

Chapter 11 The Greek Prisoners In Italy

The Aetolians had long been accustomed to make their living from plunder and other such lawless practices.

And as long as they were free to prey upon and loot the Greeks, they drew their livelihood from that, regarding every land as enemy territory.

But afterward, when the Romans took control of affairs and they were cut off from support from outside, they turned upon one another.

Even before this, in their civil war, there was no sort of outrage they did not commit.

And not long before, after having tasted one another's blood in the massacres at Arsinoe, they were ready for anything, their minds so brutalized that they would not even allow their leaders to offer advice.

That is why conditions in Aetolia were full of disorder, lawlessness, and murder, and nothing they did was carried out with calculation or settled purpose. Everything was done blindly and in confusion, as if some violent storm had burst upon them.

Chapter 12 Epirus Also In Turmoil

The people of Epirus were acting in much the same way.

For to the extent that most of them were more moderate than the people of Aetolia, to that same extent their leader was more impious and lawless than anyone else.

For I do not think there ever has been, or ever will be, a man more savage or more reckless than Charops.

Chapter 13 The Romanising Party Takes Command Throughout Greece

After the fall of Perseus, as soon as the whole issue had everywhere been decided, embassies were sent from all sides to congratulate the Roman commanders on what had happened.

Since affairs had swung completely over to the Romans, those in every state who were thought to be friends of Rome came to the surface because of the times, and these men were appointed both to embassies and to other public business.

So there came to Macedonia from Achaea Callicrates, Aristodamus, Agesias, and Philip;

from Boeotia the party of Mnasippus, from Acarnania the party of Chremas, from the Epirotes the party of Charops and Nicias, and from the Aetolians the party of Lyciscus and Tisippus.

When all these men had gathered together and were eagerly competing for the same purpose, and when no one opposed them because all their political adversaries had given way to circumstances and withdrawn completely, the men already mentioned carried their scheme through without a struggle.

As for the other cities and the federal leagues, the ten commissioners issued their instructions through the generals themselves, specifying which men were to go to Rome.

For the most part, these were the very men whom the persons already mentioned had drawn up against their own political rivals, except for a very few who had plainly done something compromising.

But to the Achaean League they sent as envoys two of the most distinguished men among the ten, Gaius Claudius and Gnaeus Domitius,

for two reasons. First, they were afraid that the Achaeans might refuse to obey the written order, and that Callicrates and his associates might even be put in danger, since they were thought to have engineered the accusations against all the Greeks,

which was in fact true; and second, because nothing definite had been found in the captured documents against any of the Achaeans.

So after some time the commander sent the letters and the envoys concerning these men, although in his own judgment he did not approve of the slanders made by Lyciscus and Callicrates, as later events themselves made clear.

Chapter 14 Noisy Scene In A Roman Theatre

It takes the same kind of spirit to stage contests well, to manage lavish preparations and a magnificent drinking party properly, and to draw up a battle line against the enemy with a general's skill.

Chapter 15 How to Hold Good Games

Polybius says that Paulus destroyed seventy cities of the Epirotes after the overthrow of the Macedonians and of Perseus. Most of them belonged to the Molossians, and he enslaved a hundred and fifty thousand people.

Chapter 16 Aemilius in Epirus

After the kings in Egypt had been freed from the war against Antiochus, they first sent Numenius, one of their Friends, as an envoy to Rome to give thanks for the benefits that had been done for them.

They also released Menalcidas the Spartan, who had made energetic use of the crisis that had come upon the kingdom for his own restoration, because Gaius Popilius had requested this favor from the kings on his behalf.

Chapter 17 Reaction of the Egyptian Kings

At this time Cotys, king of the Odrysians, sent envoys to Rome, asking that his son be restored to him and offering a defense of his cooperation with Perseus.

The Romans, thinking that they had already achieved their purpose, since the war against Perseus had ended as they wished, and that their dispute with Cotys no longer mattered,

allowed him to recover his son, who had been given as a hostage to Macedonia and had been captured along with the children of Perseus,

wishing to display their own clemency and greatness of spirit, and at the same time to bind Cotys to them by such a favor.

Chapter 18 Cotys, King of the Odrysae

At the same time King Prusias also came to Rome to congratulate the senate and the generals on what had happened.

This Prusias was in no way worthy of the title of king. One may judge this from the following.

When Roman envoys first came to him, he met them with his head shaved, wearing a white felt cap, a toga, and shoes—in short, dressed exactly like those who have only recently been freed among the Romans, whom they call liberti.

And after greeting the envoys he said, "You see before you your freedman, eager in every way to gratify you and imitate your customs." It would not be easy to find a baser remark.

Then, when he made his entrance into the senate, he stood facing the assembly at the doorway and, lowering both hands, bowed in reverence to the threshold and to the men seated there, crying out, "Hail, saving gods!" He left no possible excess of cowardice, effeminacy, and flattery for those who might come after him.

And in the audience itself he carried on in a manner consistent with this, about which even to write would have been indecent.

Having made himself utterly contemptible, he received on that very account a kindly answer.

Chapter 19 Prusias and Eumenes

Now just when he had received his answers, it happened that Eumenes arrived.

This put the senate in considerable difficulty; for they were prejudiced against him and firmly fixed in their opinions about him, yet did not wish in any way to make their feelings obvious.

For since they had previously proclaimed this king to all the world as their foremost and greatest friend, if they now admitted him to an audience and allowed him to make his defense, then, if they answered in accordance with their real opinions,

they would expose themselves for having valued such a man so highly in earlier times; but if, out of deference to appearances, they gave him a gracious reply, they would be overlooking the truth and the interests of their country.

So, since something unwelcome was likely to follow from either course, they found this solution to the dilemma.

Because they were generally displeased by visits from kings, they issued a decree that no king should come to them.

Afterwards, learning that Eumenes had landed in Italy at Brundisium, they sent the quaestor with the decree and instructed him to ask whether he had any business with the senate;

and if he needed nothing, to tell him to leave Italy as quickly as possible.

When the quaestor met him, the king, recognizing the senate's intention, in the end said nothing more than that he had no need of anything.

And so Eumenes was prevented from going up to Rome.

This policy also had another practical consequence.

For as a great danger from the Gauls hung over his kingdom, it was obvious that because of this humiliation all the king's allies would be disheartened, while the Gauls would be doubly encouraged for the war.

And so, being absolutely determined to humble him by every means, they adopted this course.

While these events were still taking place at the beginning of winter, the senate dealt with all who had arrived on embassies—

for there was neither city nor dynast nor king that had not sent an embassy at that time to offer congratulations on what had happened—

and answered them all in a fitting and gracious manner, except the Rhodians.

These it dismissed while giving various hints about what was to come. It was still postponing a decision about the Athenians.

Chapter 20 Eumenes Prevented from Visiting Rome

The Athenians came as envoys, at first on behalf of the safety of the people of Haliartus.

But when they were refused a hearing on that point, they changed their approach and spoke about Delos, Lemnos, and the territory of the Haliartians, asking that possession of them be granted to themselves; for they had been given a double set of instructions.

As for Delos and Lemnos, no one could blame them, since they had long laid claim to these islands; but regarding the territory of the Haliartians, one might justly censure them.

For not to do everything possible to restore a city that was among the most ancient in Boeotia after its fall, but instead to blot it out altogether by taking away even the future hopes of its former inhabitants,

would plainly seem fitting to no Greek people, and least of all to the Athenians.

For to make their own city open to all, while destroying the cities of others, would seem in no way consistent with the character of their state.

Nevertheless, the senate gave them Delos and Lemnos and the territory of the Haliartians. This, then, was how matters concerning the Athenians were settled.

As for Lemnos and Delos, according to the proverb they had taken a wolf by the ears;

for they endured many hardships in their disputes with the Delians, while from the territory of the Haliartians they gained not so much profit as reproach.

Chapter 21 The Athenians and Rhodians

At this time Theaetetus appeared before the senate and spoke about the alliance.

But the senate postponed consideration of the matter, and meanwhile he died a natural death, for he was more than eighty years old.

Then exiles from both Caunus and Stratoniceia came to Rome and were admitted before the senate, and a decree was passed ordering the Rhodians to withdraw their garrisons from both Caunus and Stratoniceia.

Philophron, Astymedes, and their colleagues, after receiving this reply, sailed home in haste,

fearing that if the Rhodians failed to comply with the order to remove the garrisons, they would create fresh grounds for accusation.

Chapter 22 Death of Theaetetus of Rhodes

Lucius Anicius, who had also served as a Roman general, after defeating the Illyrians and bringing Gentius, the king of the Illyrians, captive along with his children, celebrated victory games at Rome and did things that were utterly ridiculous, as Polybius relates in Book 30.

For he sent for the most distinguished performers from Greece and built an enormous stage in the circus, and first he brought on all the flute-players together.

These were Theodore the Boeotian, Theopompus, Hermippus, and Lysimachus, all men of the highest reputation.

He stationed them on the front of the stage with the chorus and ordered them all to play at once.

But when they were going through their rhythms with the proper movements, he sent instructions that they were not playing well and told them they ought rather to compete with one another.

When they were at a loss, one of the lictors showed them that they should turn, advance against each other, and stage something like a battle.

The flute-players quickly understood, and, taking up behavior well suited to their own theatrical excesses, created a tremendous uproar.

Turning the middle choruses to face the outer ones, the flute-players blew with absurd force and drove them against one another in turns, waving their pipes about.

At the same time the choruses beat time, charged across the stage against their opponents, and then wheeled about and retreated again.

And when one of the dancers, tightening his belt and turning at the right moment, raised his fists like a boxer against the oncoming flute-player, then the spectators at last broke into extraordinary applause and shouting.

While these groups were still contending in battle order, two dancers were brought into the orchestra with musical accompaniment, and four boxers mounted the stage along with trumpeters and horn-blowers.

With all these performers going at once, what resulted was beyond description. And as for the tragic actors, Polybius says, whatever I might choose to say would seem to some people like mockery.

Chapter 23 Public Hatred of Callicrates and His Faction

At this time the Cnossians, together with the Gortynians, made war on the Raucians and swore agreements with one another that they would not end the war until they had taken Raucus by force.

Meanwhile the Rhodians, when they received the news about the Caunians and saw that Roman anger was still not subsiding, even though they had obeyed every instruction in accordance with the replies they had been given, immediately appointed Aristotle and his colleagues as ambassadors and sent them to Rome, instructing them to make another attempt concerning the alliance.

When they arrived in Rome, at the height of summer, they entered the senate and at once explained how the people had obeyed the commands laid upon them, and they pleaded for the alliance, speaking at length in many different ways. The senate gave them a reply

in which it passed over friendship in silence, and regarding the alliance said that it was not proper for it to grant that request to the Rhodians at present.

Chapter 24 Delight at Peraea

For the inhabitants of the Peraea were like slaves unexpectedly released from their chains,

who, unable to believe the good fortune before them, go beyond normal behavior, because they think that those they meet do not recognize or clearly see that they have truly been set free, unless they do something strange and out of the ordinary.

Chapter 25

This same king, when he heard about the games that Aemilius Paulus, the Roman general, had held in Macedonia, wanted to surpass Paulus in magnificence. So he sent envoys and sacred messengers to the cities to announce the games he would hold at Daphne, and this stirred great eagerness among the Greeks to come to him.

He began the festival with a procession arranged in the following way.

At the head marched five thousand men in Roman equipment, wearing chain-mail cuirasses, all in the prime of life. After them came five thousand Mysians.

Close behind them were three thousand Cilicians armed in the style of light infantry, wearing golden crowns.

After these came three thousand Thracians and five thousand Gauls. Next marched twenty thousand Macedonians, five thousand men with bronze shields, and another corps with silver shields; after them came two hundred and forty pairs of gladiators.

Behind these were the cavalry: one thousand Nisaean horsemen and three thousand of the regular cavalry. Most of them had harness plated with gold and wore golden crowns, while the rest had silver-plated harness.

After them came the cavalry known as the Companions, about one thousand strong, all with gold-plated harness. Next to them was the regiment of the Friends,

equal to them both in numbers and in splendor. After these came one thousand picked horsemen, followed by the corps called the Agema, thought to be the finest body of cavalry,

about one thousand strong. Last came the cataphract cavalry, aptly named because both horses and riders were covered with armor. They too numbered one thousand five hundred.

All those mentioned above had purple caparisons, and many had trappings embroidered with gold and figured designs.

After these came one hundred six-horse chariots and forty four-horse chariots, then a chariot drawn by elephants and one drawn by a pair of horses. Behind them came thirty-six elephants, fully caparisoned, one after another.

The rest of the procession is hard to describe, so it must be given only in summary. About eight hundred young men marched in it wearing golden crowns, there were about one thousand well-fed oxen, the sacred delegations numbered just under three hundred, and there were eight hundred elephant tusks.

The number of statues cannot be fully described. Images were carried of all the gods and divine beings spoken of or worshiped among mankind, and in addition of heroes as well, some gilded and others dressed in robes embroidered with gold.

Alongside all these were displayed the stories proper to each of them, presented according to the traditional accounts in lavish tableaux.

There also followed images of Night and Day, of Earth and Sky, and of Dawn and Midday.

One may judge the quantity of gold and silver plate from this: for one of the king's friends, Dionysius the secretary, had one thousand boys in the procession carrying silver vessels, and none of them weighed less than one thousand drachmas.

Six hundred royal pages also passed by carrying gold vessels. Then two hundred women sprinkled perfumes from golden jars.

After them came eighty women carried in litters with golden feet, and five hundred seated in litters with silver feet, all magnificently adorned. These were the most striking features of the procession.

Chapter 26

When the games, gladiatorial combats, and hunts had been completed over a period of thirty days, during which he presented the spectacles, for the first five days everyone in the gymnasium was anointed from golden vessels with saffron ointment.

There were fifteen of these vessels, and an equal number for cinnamon and nard perfume. In much the same way, on the following days fenugreek, marjoram, and iris perfumes were brought in, all remarkable for their fragrance.

For the banquets, sometimes one thousand dining couches were laid out and sometimes one thousand five hundred, furnished with the utmost luxury.

Chapter 27

After the games had been brought to an end, just when they were over, the envoys headed by Tiberius arrived, acting in effect as spies.

Antiochus received them with such tact and friendliness that not only did Tiberius and his colleagues suspect nothing serious or obstructive in his conduct regarding the affairs of Alexandria, but they even condemned those who said anything of the kind, because his welcome was so extraordinarily gracious.

Indeed, besides all his other courtesies, he even yielded the palace itself to the envoys, and in outward appearance almost his diadem as well, though this was not his real disposition,

but rather the exact opposite, since he was very unfriendly toward the Romans.

Chapter 28

They granted autonomy to the envoys from the Galatians of Asia, on condition that they remained in their own settlements and did not serve on campaigns outside their own borders.

Chapter 29

Throughout the Peloponnese, when the envoys arrived and explained the replies they had received, there was no longer mere uproar, but open anger and hatred against Callicrates and his circle.

One may judge the hatred felt for Callicrates, Andronidas, and the rest of their party from the following.

At the festival of the Antigoneia in Sicyon, all the baths had their common tubs, with separate basins set beside them into which the more refined bathers were accustomed to step privately.

Whenever one of the party of Andronidas and Callicrates got into one of these, none of the bystanders dared get in afterward until the bath attendant had let out all the water that was there and poured in fresh clean water.

They did this because they thought they would be polluted if they stepped into the same water as those men.

As for the hissing at the common festivals of the Greeks, and the jeering whenever any one of the men already mentioned tried to make a public proclamation, no one could easily describe it fully.

Even schoolboys, as they came back from their classes through the streets, were bold enough to call them traitors to their faces. Such was the resentment and hatred that had spread against the men in question.

Chapter 30

When many embassies from different places had arrived in Rome, the most notable being those from Rhodes under Astymedes, from the Achaeans under Euryas, Anaxidamus, and Satyrus, and from Prusias under Python, the senate took their business in hand.

The envoys from Prusias accused King Eumenes, saying that he was taking away some of their territory and not withdrawing from Galatia at all, nor obeying the decrees of the senate.

Instead, they said, he was drawing into his own camp those who favored his interests, while in every possible way diminishing those who preferred the Roman side and wished to conduct their public life in accordance with the senate's decisions.

There were also envoys from the cities of Asia who accused the king, hinting at collusion with Antiochus.

After hearing the accusers, the senate neither dismissed the charges nor revealed its own opinion, but kept its judgment to itself, being generally suspicious of both Eumenes and Antiochus.

At the same time it was always adding something to the Galatians' cause and strengthening them in the matter of their freedom.

The commissioners with Tiberius, when they returned from their embassy, were unable either to learn anything more precise themselves or to make anything clearer to the senate about the affairs of Eumenes and Antiochus than what they had already thought while still in Rome.

So thoroughly had the kings forestalled them by the graciousness of their reception.

Chapter 31

After this the senate summoned the Rhodians and gave them a hearing.

Astymedes came in and spoke with restraint, and much better than on the previous embassy.

For he gave up accusing others and instead turned to pleading for pardon, like men under the lash begging to be spared the blows, saying that his country had already suffered penalties enough, greater than its offense deserved.

He then went on to explain its losses,

summarizing them point by point. First, he said, they had lost Lycia and Caria, regions on which they had spent a great deal of money from the beginning, having been compelled to wage three wars over them, and from which they had once received considerable revenues.

"But perhaps," he said, "that can still be justified. You yourselves gave those districts to our people as a favor because of our goodwill, and when suspicion and estrangement arose between us, you could plausibly think it reasonable to take them away again.

But Caunus, surely, we bought for two hundred talents from the generals of Ptolemy, and Stratoniceia we received as a great favor from Antiochus, the son of Seleucus.

From these two cities together a yearly revenue of one hundred and twenty talents came to our people. Of all this income we have been deprived,

because we wished to obey your commands.

By doing this you have laid a heavier burden on the Rhodians for a single mistake than on the Macedonians, who were your enemies at all times.

And the greatest blow of all to our city is this: your making Delos a free port has ruined our harbor revenues, and you have taken away the people's political voice, by which both the business of the harbor and every other concern of the city had previously enjoyed the protection suited to them.

That this is true is not hard to learn.

In earlier times the harbor dues produced a million drachmas, but now you have taken away a hundred and fifty thousand. So, Romans, your anger has indeed struck at the principal resources of the city.

If the offense and estrangement had really been shared by the whole people, then perhaps even you might reasonably seem justified in maintaining an unrelenting anger that was hard to appease.

But if you know clearly that only a few men were responsible for this folly, and that all of them have perished at the hands of the people itself, why do you remain irreconcilable toward those who bear no blame,

when to everyone else you seem the gentlest and most magnanimous of all men?

Therefore, gentlemen, the people, having lost its revenues, its political voice, and its equal standing, the very things for which in earlier times it had been ready to endure every risk,

asks and entreats all of you, now that it has suffered blows enough, to let your anger cease and to restore the alliance, so that this may become plain to everyone: that you have laid aside your anger toward the Rhodians and returned to your original policy and friendship.

For that is what the people needs now,

not an alliance of arms and soldiers."

After speaking in this way, and to much the same effect besides, Astymedes was thought to have adapted his speech well to the circumstances.

Still, what helped the Rhodians most in obtaining the alliance was the recent arrival of the commissioners with Tiberius.

For they testified, first, that the Rhodians had obeyed every decree of the senate, and second, that all those responsible for the estrangement had been condemned to death among them. In this way they overcame those who spoke against the Rhodians and secured the alliance with Rome.

Chapter 32

After some time the envoys from the Achaeans entered, carrying instructions consistent with the replies they had previously received.

These instructions were to say that they were astonished that, in a matter on which the senate had itself already decided, it was now calling on them to give judgment.

So Euryas and his colleagues appeared and once again made it clear that the nation had neither heard the defense of the accused nor delivered any judgment upon them.

They asked the senate to take thought for these men, so that they might obtain a trial and not be destroyed without judgment,

and above all that the senate itself should investigate the case and identify those truly liable to the charges. But if, because of its many distractions, it could not do this, then it should entrust the matter to the Achaeans, who would deal with the guilty in a spirit that hated wrongdoing.

The senate heard the envoys, who spoke in accordance with their instructions, but it was embarrassed because it was exposed on every side.

For it did not think that it belonged to it to conduct the trial, and yet to release the men without a trial seemed plainly likely to bring ruin upon those in Greece who were Rome's friends.

So, being compelled by the situation and wishing altogether to take away the hope that many still had for the safety of the detained men, in order that the masses, shutting their eyes, might submit in Achaea to Callicrates and in the other states to those thought to be the Romans' men, it sent back this reply:

"We do not think it advantageous either for the Romans or for your own states that these men should return home."

When this answer was issued, it produced not only complete dejection and paralysis of spirit among the detained men, but among the Greeks as well something like a common mourning, since the reply seemed altogether to take away hope of safety from those under accusation.

And when the answer given to the Achaeans concerning the accused men was published throughout Greece, the masses were crushed in spirit, and a kind of despair spread among men,

whereas Charops, Callicrates, and all the leaders of the same policy once more lifted their heads high.

Book XXXI

Chapter 1 War in Crete

A. Olympiad 154, year 1. Affairs in Italy.

Tiberius made the Cammani subjects of Rome, partly by force and partly by outwitting them.

When several other embassies had also arrived in Rome, the Senate gave audience to Attalus and Athenaeus and their party.

For Prusias had not only been actively engaged in spreading slanders against Eumenes and Antiochus himself, but had also stirred up the Galatians, the people of Selge, and many others in Asia to support the same cause.

For this reason King Eumenes had sent his brothers, to answer the accusations brought against him.

When they appeared before the Senate, they were judged to have made a satisfactory defense against all their accusers; and in the end they not only cleared away the charges brought against them, but were even honored before returning to Asia.

Even so, the Senate did not let go of its suspicion against Eumenes and Antiochus, but appointed Gaius Sulpicius and Manius Sergius as envoys and sent them out,

to inspect conditions among the Greeks, and also to settle for the Megalopolitans and the Lacedaemonians the dispute about the contested territory,

but above all to investigate the affairs of Antiochus and Eumenes, lest any preparations and any common enterprise against Rome should be developing between them.

Chapter 2 Gauls in Asia Granted Autonomy

Demetrius son of Seleucus, who had already long been kept in Rome as a hostage, had for some time been thought to be detained contrary to justice.

For Seleucus his father had given him on his own account as a pledge of good faith; but after Antiochus had succeeded to the throne, Demetrius ought not to remain a hostage on behalf of Antiochus' children.

Yet in the earlier period he kept quiet, chiefly because he was powerless, for he was still only a boy.

But now, being in the full prime of life, he came into the Senate and spoke, demanding and entreating them to restore him to his kingdom; for the sovereignty, he said, belonged more properly to him than to the sons of Antiochus.

After speaking at length on this claim, he pressed his case most strongly by saying that Rome was at once his fatherland and the city that had reared him, that he regarded all the sons of the senators as brothers and the senators themselves as fathers, since he had come there while still an infant and was now twenty-three years old.

All who heard him felt the appeal inwardly; yet the Senate as a body resolved to keep Demetrius in detention and to help secure the throne for the boy who had been left behind. It did this,

as it seems to me, because it took note of Demetrius in his full vigor, or rather because it judged that the youth and weakness of the boy who had inherited the kingdom better served Roman interests.

This was made clear by what happened afterward.

They at once appointed as envoys Gnaeus Octavius, Spurius Lucretius, and Lucius Aurelius and sent them out to regulate the affairs of the kingdom,

in the way the Senate itself had decided, because no one would stand in the way of what they ordered, since the king was a child and those who managed affairs were glad that the government had not been handed over to Demetrius; for this was what they most wanted.

So Gnaeus and his colleagues set out with instructions first to burn the decked warships, then to hamstring the elephants, and in general to cripple the royal power.

They were also instructed to examine the situation in Macedonia, for the Macedonians, being unaccustomed to a democratic and deliberative constitution, were in civil conflict with one another.

Gnaeus and his party were also to inspect the affairs of the Galatians and the condition of the kingdom of Ariarathes.

And after some time a letter was sent on to them from the Senate instructing them, if possible, to reconcile the kings at Alexandria as well.

Chapter 3 Grand Festival At Daphne

At the same time envoys arrived from Ariarathes, who had only recently succeeded to the throne of Cappadocia, to renew the friendship and alliance already existing,

and in general to urge the Senate to welcome the king's goodwill and eagerness, which he showed both publicly and privately toward all Romans.

After hearing their speech, the Senate renewed both the friendship and the alliance, and, approving the king's general policy, treated him with kindness.

This happened chiefly because Tiberius and his colleagues, when they had been sent out to inspect the affairs of the kings, came back and spoke favorably both of the king's father and of the kingdom as a whole.

Trusting their report, the senators gave the envoys a gracious reception and likewise approved the king's overall course.

II. Affairs in Greece.

The Rhodians, having recovered from the distress that had overtaken them, sent envoys to Rome headed by Cleagoras,

to ask that Calynda should be granted to them,

and also, concerning those who possessed property in Lycia and Caria, to request from the Senate that they might be allowed to hold it, as they had before.

They also voted to set up in the sanctuary of Athena a colossal statue of the Roman people, thirty cubits high.

Chapter 5 Roman Envoys Come to Antioch

When the people of Calynda revolted from the Caunians, and the Caunians afterward undertook to besiege them, the Calyndians at first appealed to the Cnidians.

When the Cnidians came to their aid, they held out against their enemies for a time,

but, anxious about what would happen next, they sent an embassy asking the Rhodians to take them and their city into their protection.

The Rhodians sent support both by land and by sea, raised the siege, and took over the city.

It so happened that the Senate also confirmed their possession of Calynda.

Chapter 6 Complaints Against Eumenes

III. Affairs in Asia.

Gaius Gallus, apart from the irrational conduct just mentioned, when he arrived in Asia posted notices in the most prominent cities,

ordering anyone who wished to accuse King Eumenes to appear at Sardis at an appointed time.

Then he himself came to Sardis, took his seat in the gymnasium, and for about ten days listened to the accusers,

accepting every kind of foul and abusive language against the king, and in general dragging in every possible affair and accusation,

like a man unbalanced in mind and eager to win distinction in his quarrel with Eumenes.

And the more harshly the Romans seemed to deal with Eumenes, the more the Greeks were drawn toward him, since human nature always gives its sympathy to the man under pressure.

Chapter 7 The Achaean Prisoners Detained

King Ariarathes of Cappadocia received the envoys who had been sent to Rome, and, judging from the answers they brought back that his throne now stood on firm ground because he had gained the goodwill of the Romans, he offered thank-offerings to the gods for what had happened and entertained the leading men.

After this he sent envoys to Lysias and his party at Antioch, eager to recover the bones of his sister and mother.

He decided not to bring any charge of impiety over what had happened, because he did not want to provoke Lysias and his party and so fail in his purpose, though he took the matter deeply to heart; instead, he gave the envoys instructions suited to their rank and sent them off.

When Lysias and his party consented, and the bones were brought back to him, he received them with great honor on their arrival and buried them beside his father's tomb with proper care.

Chapter 8 Envoys from Achaia in the Senate

At this time envoys arrived from Rome, first those with Marcus Junius, to clarify the king's disputes with the Galatians.

For when the Trocmi had been unable by their own efforts to cut off any part of Cappadocia for themselves, they brazenly manufactured a case and, by appealing to the Romans, tried to slander Ariarathes.

That is why the envoys with Junius were sent. The king addressed them as was fitting and otherwise treated them with kindness, so that he sent them away speaking well of him.

After this, when envoys arrived with Gnaeus Octavius and Spurius Lucretius and again discussed with the king his disputes with the Galatians,

he spoke only briefly and in general terms about those matters, saying that he was ready to accept whatever judgment was made, and then devoted the greater part of his speech to affairs in Syria, since he knew that Octavius and his party were proceeding there,

pointing out to them the instability of the kingdom there and the rashness of the men in charge of it, and also promising that he would follow with a force and support the situation until they returned safely from Syria.

The envoys with Gnaeus, approving in every respect the king's goodwill and eagerness,

said that for the present they had no need of an escort, but that in the future, if any need arose, they would let him know without hesitation; for they judged him to be one of Rome's true friends.

Chapter 9 The Senate Suspicious of Eumenes and Antiochus

In Syria King Antiochus, wanting to raise money, resolved to march against the temple of Artemis in Elymais.

But when he reached the place, his hopes were disappointed, because the barbarians living around the sanctuary would not permit this act of sacrilege.

So he withdrew, and on his retreat he died at Tabae in Persia.

Some say that he went mad, because certain signs of divine anger appeared in response to the lawless outrage he had attempted against that sanctuary.

Chapter 10 Sulpicius Gallus Investigates Eumenes

B. Olympiad 154, year 2. Affairs in Italy.

After the kingdom had been divided between the Ptolemies, the younger Ptolemy came to Rome, wishing to set aside the partition that had been made between himself and his brother.

He said that he had not agreed to it willingly, but had done what was demanded only because circumstances had forced him.

He begged the Senate to assign Cyprus to him, arguing that even if this were done his share would still be far inferior to his brother's.

But the supporters of Canuleius and Quintus testified against Menyllus and the envoys who had come from the elder brother, saying that the younger brother owed not only Cyrene but even his life to them, since the hostility and estrangement of the crowds toward him had become so severe.

That was why, when the settlement concerning Cyrene had been granted to him unexpectedly and beyond hope, he had gladly accepted it, had offered sacrifices, and had both received and sworn the oaths with his brother.

Ptolemy, however, disputed all this. The Senate, seeing on the one hand that the division had been completely settled, but on the other wishing in practical terms to break up the kingdom, now that the brothers themselves had supplied the pretext for division, agreed to the younger brother's requests for its own advantage.

For this has long been a Roman practice in policy: by taking advantage of the ignorance of neighboring peoples, they strengthen and extend their own power in practical ways, while at the same time gratifying those who make mistakes and seeming to bestow favors on them.

So, seeing the scale of Egyptian power and fearing that if it should ever obtain a capable protector it might grow more ambitious than was proper,

they appointed Titus Torquatus and Gnaeus Merula as envoys to escort Ptolemy to Cyprus and at the same time carry out both his design and their own.

They sent them off at once, with instructions to reconcile the brothers and secure Cyprus for the younger without war.

Chapter 11 Death of Antiochus Epiphanes

At this same time, when the disaster involving Gnaeus had taken place,

that is, when he had been killed, and when envoys sent by King Antiochus, men dispatched by Lysias, had arrived and spoken at length to show that the king's friends had had no part in the deed,

the Senate dismissed the envoys, not wishing to give any decision on the matter or to reveal its opinion at all.

Demetrius, alarmed by what had been reported, summoned Polybius and asked him in perplexity whether he ought to approach the Senate again about his own affairs.

Polybius urged him not to stumble twice against the same stone, but to place his hopes in himself and dare something worthy of a kingdom, since the present moment, he said, offered many openings.

Demetrius took the meaning of this, and for the moment said nothing; but a little later he shared the matter with one of his close companions, Apollonius.

Apollonius, who was innocent by nature and very young, advised him to make one more attempt with the Senate. He was convinced that, although they had unreasonably deprived him of the kingdom, they would at least release him from his hostage status.

For it was completely absurd, he said, that now that Antiochus' son had succeeded to the kingdom in Syria, Demetrius should remain a hostage on his behalf.

Persuaded by these arguments, Demetrius once more entered the Senate and begged them at least to free him from the obligation of being a hostage, since they had decided to secure the kingdom for Antiochus.

But although he spoke at still greater length on this point, the Senate remained with the same decision, as was only natural.

For even before, it had not resolved to preserve the rule for the boy because Demetrius had failed to make a just claim, but because that course served its own interests.

And since the whole situation remained in the same condition, it was natural that the Senate's judgment should also remain fixed on the same policy.

Chapter 12 Demetrius son of Seleucus

Yet Demetrius, after having wasted his breath in that final appeal and recognizing that Polybius had advised him well not to stumble twice against the same stone,

repented of what had happened; and being high-minded by nature and possessing courage equal to the decision he had to make, he immediately called for Diodorus, who had recently arrived from Syria, and confided his situation to him.

Diodorus had once been Demetrius' tutor, and, being a shrewd man who had closely observed conditions in Syria, he pointed out to him

that since affairs there were in confusion because of the murder of Gnaeus, and since the masses distrusted Lysias' circle while Lysias' circle distrusted the masses, and since the Senate was convinced that the outrage committed against its envoys had been the work of the king's friends, this was the best possible time for him to appear on the scene.

For the people there would quickly transfer the kingship to him, even if he arrived with only a single attendant, and the Senate would no longer dare to support or reinforce Lysias and his party after what they had done.

The only thing left, he said, was for them to get away from Rome unnoticed, so that no one would suspect his plan.

When this seemed good, Demetrius sent for Polybius, told him what had been decided, and asked him to help take charge of the attempt and think through how his escape should be managed.

Now at this time Menyllus of Alabanda happened to be in Rome as an envoy from the elder King Ptolemy, sent to support his cause and justify him against the younger Ptolemy. Polybius already had a strong friendship and bond of trust with Menyllus.

Thinking therefore that Menyllus would be useful in the present need, Polybius introduced him to Demetrius with great eagerness and zeal.

Menyllus, after joining the enterprise, undertook to prepare a ship and complete the other arrangements for the voyage.

He found at the mouth of the Tiber a Carthaginian sacred ship lying at anchor, and hired it.

These ships are specially selected from Carthage, and the Carthaginians send on them their ancestral firstfruits to the gods at Tyre; but he openly hired this one for his own return passage.

So he made the monthly provisioning without arousing suspicion, and openly gave orders and spoke with the sailors.

Chapter 13 Ariarathes of Cappadocia

Once everything was ready on the shipmaster's side, and Demetrius only had to complete his own arrangements, he sent his foster-father ahead to Syria to gather intelligence and observe what was happening there among the populace.

His companion Apollonius had shared in the plan from the beginning; and, since there were two brothers, Meleager and Menestheus, he disclosed the undertaking to them, but to no one else among his followers, though they were more numerous.

These men were Apollonius' own sons. Their father had enjoyed great influence with Seleucus, but when Antiochus took over the kingdom he had withdrawn to Miletus.

As the day agreed upon with the sailors drew near, there had to be a farewell entertainment at the house of one of his friends before the departure.

For it was impossible to hold the dinner at his own quarters, since he was accustomed to invite everyone in his circle with great care.

Those who knew of the plan were to dine at home and then come to the ship, each bringing one servant-boy with him; the rest they had sent on to Anagnia, intending to follow themselves on the next day.

At this time Polybius happened to be ill and confined to bed, but he knew everything that was being done, because Menyllus kept continually informing him of each new development.

So Polybius, anxious that habit might get the better of Demetrius — since he was naturally fond of drinking parties and still altogether young — and that drunkenness might create some difficulty at the moment of departure,

wrote a short note, sealed it, and at dusk sent one of his own servants with instructions to call out Demetrius' cupbearer, hand him the note without saying who he was or who had sent it, and tell him to give it to Demetrius at once for immediate reading.

Everything was done as arranged, and Demetrius took the note and read it.

The note contained these thoughts:

The man who acts with the future in mind goes forward prepared.

Night gives equal cover to all, but to the daring it gives more.

Dare something,

risk it, act, fail, or succeed — anything rather than betray yourself.

Stay sober, and remember to mistrust: these are the sinews of good sense.

Chapter 14 Ambassadors from Ariarathes to Rome

After reading this and understanding the situation, and who the men were and who had sent them, Demetrius at once pretended that he was going aboard for the voyage and slipped away, his friends escorting him part of the way.

When he reached his lodging, he sent off the unnecessary servants to Anagnia, ordering them to take the nets and the dogs and meet him at Circeii.

For that was where he regularly liked to hunt wild boar with special zeal; indeed, this had been the original beginning of his friendship with Polybius.

After this he explained the plan to Nicanor and his companions and urged them to share the same hopes.

Since they all accepted the proposal eagerly, he ordered them to go back at once to their lodgings and instruct their servants to go on ahead before dawn to Anagnia and, together with the hunters, meet them at Circeii,

while they themselves were to take traveling clothes and return to him, telling their servants that on the next day they would join Demetrius at the place already mentioned.

When everything had been done as described, they set out by night for Ostia, to the mouth of the Tiber.

Menyllus went on ahead and spoke with the sailors, saying that a message had come to him from the king, and that for this reason he himself had to remain in Rome for the present, but should send to the king the most trustworthy of the young men, from whom he would learn everything concerning his brother.

So he said that he himself would not embark, but that the young men who were to sail would arrive about midnight.

The shipmasters were indifferent, because the freight agreed on had been paid to them from the beginning and they had long had everything ready for the voyage.

The party with Demetrius arrived as the third watch was ending: there were eight of them, with five servant-boys and three younger attendants.

Menyllus then talked matters over with them, showed them the monthly provisions, and further introduced them fully to the shipmaster and the passengers; after that they went aboard.

At first light the captain weighed anchor and put to sea, having absolutely no suspicion of what was really going on, but thinking that he was simply carrying some soldiers from Menyllus to Ptolemy.

Chapter 15 Rhodes Asks Rome for Calynda

On the next day in Rome no one was likely to go looking for Demetrius or for the companions who had left with him.

Those who stayed behind with him thought that he had gone off to Circeii, while those at Anagnia were coming to meet him at the same place, expecting that he would be there.

So the escape remained completely unnoticed until one of the servant-boys, after being flogged at Anagnia, ran off to Circeii, intending to join Demetrius there.

Not finding him there either, he ran back to Rome, expecting to meet him on the road.

When he failed to encounter him anywhere, he revealed the matter to Demetrius' friends in Rome and to those who had been left behind at the house.

So when Demetrius was looked for on the fourth day after his departure, what had happened was suspected.

On the fifth day the Senate at once met to consider the matter; by then Demetrius was already beyond the strait near Sicily.

They therefore gave up the idea of pursuit, both because they thought he had already gained too great a lead on the voyage — for he had a strong following wind — and because they foresaw that even if they wished to stop him, they would be unable to do so.

After some days they appointed as envoys Tiberius Gracchus, Lucius Lentulus, and Servilius Glaucia,

who were first to inspect affairs among the Greeks, then to cross over into Asia and keep watch on the situation concerning Demetrius, examine the intentions of the other kings, and clear up the disputed issues involving the Galatians that were mentioned earlier.

This was why they appointed Tiberius, because he had been an eyewitness of the whole situation.

And this was the state of affairs in Italy.

Demetrius, meanwhile, was intent on the arrival of the man who was to be sent to him.

and so great too are the judgments and counsels of good men, that they often save not only friends but even enemies and change their characters for the better.
